Rosh Hashanah 2026: The Jewish people must answer the shofar’s call to unity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:52:58 UTC
14:52:58 KST

As we approach the upcoming Days of Awe, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur 5787, 2026, I find myself reflecting on the prayer of Unetaneh Tokef, the stirring and poetic liturgy we collectively recite during the Mussaf service:
On Rosh Hashanah it is written, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed: Who shall live, and who shall die. Who by water and who by fire. Who by famine and who by thirst. Who shall have rest, and who shall wander. Who shall be humbled, and who shall be exalted.
There are few passages in our prayer services that confront us so starkly with the uncertainty and unpredictability of human life. Unetaneh Tokef refuses to allow us to hide behind familiarity and comfort. In those short, searing lines, the illusions of certainty fall away. We stand before God vulnerable, humbled, and at God’s mercy. We confront our fragile state as human beings. We acknowledge how much is beyond our control, and we submit ourselves to God’s will.
While the prayer might leave us with a sense of trepidation, it also provides us with resolve and opportunity: U’teshuvah, u’tefillah, u’tzedakah – repentance, prayer, and charity – are the powers we possess to earn another year of life.
These are not abstractions from another time and place. They are guideposts that illuminate for us how to live our lives today. And their message is reinforced by the sound of the shofar.
The blast of the shofar is not a single note. Instead, we hear three distinct sounds: Tekiah, a whole sound. Shevarim, a broken sound. Teruah, a whimpering cry. These sounds, heard in succession, are gathered together into one unmistakable call.
We do not hear the voice of the shofar in solitude. An entire community stands together, on the same day, in the same room, awakened from the same slumber, summoned by the same ancient sound.
For me, this is a fundamental meaning of the Days of Awe. They begin with private reflection, examining our own actions, our own relationships, and our own responsibilities. But they cannot end there. Ultimately, we choose to stand together before God as one people, bound by one history, one destiny, and one eternal covenant.
This year has been particularly trying for the Jewish community, here in Detroit and around the world.
We have witnessed antisemitism creep from the margins of society toward its center – on our campuses, in our halls of government and on our very own streets. We have watched ancient hatred find new language and new audiences. We have felt, at times, that some of the allies we had counted upon chose to keep their distance and remain silent.
But what has touched me most deeply is something I will carry with me long after this year’s end.
Throughout this difficult year, I have witnessed the Jewish people step forward for one another with kindness and love. I have seen Jews reaching across communities and across continents to help their Jewish brethren.
I have seen individuals and organizations forge relationships that strengthen our community and uplift those around us. I have seen Jewish schools and day care centers, synagogues and Federations, community centers and campus Hillels, social service agencies and senior centers refuse to wait for someone else to come to their rescue, instead joining together to protect themselves and one another.
I saw this spirit of shared responsibility in Montreal, where 440 trained volunteers and a federation command center helped secure the Jewish institutions of their community. I saw it in Washington, where more than 400 community leaders from 41 states came together to advocate on Capitol Hill for the safety and security of Jewish life across America.
I have seen it in the extraordinary generosity of the North American Federation system, helping bring comfort, aid, and security to families and communities rebuilding their lives in Israel since October 7. And I have seen it in the foresight of the Israeli government, committing to help strengthen Jewish education throughout the Diaspora.
And in West Bloomfield, Michigan, we felt that same spirit deeply when the courageous Detroit community came together to support our brothers and sisters at Temple Israel during one of the darkest moments we have faced. The kindness, courage, and love shown by every facet of the Jewish community shone a powerful light that reminded us that when one part of our community is threatened, we all feel the pain, and we all share the responsibility to respond.
I have seen the Jewish people uplift Torah, uplift one another, and build strength and resolve together. That word – together – is not sentimental. It is vital. And it is sacred.
When our ancestors listened for the first time to the sound of the shofar at Mount Sinai, preparing to receive the Torah and enter into our eternal covenant with God, they stood as our sages described, k’ish echad b’lev echad – as one person with one heart.
Not because every Jew thought the same way. Not because every Jew saw the world the same way. And certainly not because disagreement had completely faded away.
Unity is not the absence of disagreement
We must remember that unity is not the absence of disagreement. Unity is the recognition that what binds us together is greater than what divides us. It is the understanding that despite our differences, despite the forces that attempt to pull us apart, we remain k’ish echad b’lev echad – one people, with one heart.
Rosh Hashanah is the birthday of the world. Throughout the prayer service, we are asked to imagine the world as the Almighty intended it to be: whole, just, unified, loving, and at peace, and we accept upon ourselves to proclaim God as King of the universe.
From Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur, we measure the distance between that vision and the world as it actually is. And we acknowledge that distance with complete honesty and humility – recognizing where we have fallen short, while trusting that our sincere prayers will be heard and accepted.
Repentance is always possible. For one person. For one community. And for an entire people.
This year, I pray that we meet this moment with clarity, faith, and resolve: that we remain clear-eyed about the threats confronting us, without allowing that reality to turn into fracture; that we remain vigilant without becoming fearful; and that we defend ourselves without forgetting who we are, what we stand for, and how deeply connected we are to one another.
In the end, we are one people. We serve the same God, who stands with us, who wants the best for us, and who asks us to become better – more compassionate, more kind, more loving, more unified and less afraid.
May every member of the Jewish people be written and sealed for a year of life, health, blessing and peace. May the prayers we offer during these sacred days not remain only words upon our lips, but deeply embedded in our hearts, resulting in commitments we will live by each and every day.
Shana Tova u’metukah. May you and your loved ones be inscribed and sealed for a good and sweet new year.
The writer is the chair of the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA).

====================================================================================================

Giving surplus a second life, Jerusalem’s food rescuers are turning leftovers into a lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:52:55 UTC
14:52:55 KST

Cast your minds back to those “halcyon” days of the COVID-19 mandatory vaccines, masks, lockdowns, and all manner of logistical nightmares. Chiefly among the latter was the ordinarily simple matter of ensuring you had all the necessities of keeping body and soul together, naturally including vittles.
“Food security” was a term bandied about with high regularity as supplies of staples such as plain old bread were often not guaranteed.
On my own moshav in the Jerusalem Hills, the arrival of the truck from Tnuva with its consignment of dairy products, or the appearance of the delivery man from the Angel bakery firm, were greeted with much glee and palpable relief.
Even if we are not visited by another pandemic anytime soon, in more normal circumstances we would do well to abide by the sagacious words of Britain’s favorite centenarian, iconic nature show frontman, and writer, Sir David Attenborough. When asked about the one thing he would like us all to remember with regard to Mother Earth, he simply replied: “Don’t waste.”
That sounds like a simple enough matter which can be applied in all sorts of quotidian areas. How about, for example, getting into the habit of arming ourselves with reusable bags the next time we pop along to our local makolet or supermarket, instead of merrily accruing plastic bags on offer at such enterprises.
Getting food to those who need it most
It is also a sentiment that sits particularly well with Daniella Seltzer. In fact, you could say it is her credo.
Seltzer is one of the movers and shakers behind the Jerusalem Food Rescuers initiative, which set up house at the Wholesale Market in Givat Shaul in 2019. The idea was to garner items from the crate loads of veggies and fruit coming into the vast market compound, pieces that were a little under- or overripe, bruised, or just might not look tempting to utopian TV commercial image-brainwashed shoppers.
As one can easily imagine, it wasn’t exactly smooth-going to begin with. The truck drivers hauling products from all over, site managers and supervisors, et al were used to getting the stuff through the gates, and duly apportioning it in accordance with their tried-and-tested, well-oiled procedure.
They weren’t about to let “an intruder” run their eyes and hands over the merchandise before it got to them. Or were they? Gradually, with due deference and persistence, Seltzer and her comrades in redemptive arms gained the trust and, eventually, respect and cooperation of the hard-nosed wholesale market folks.
Seltzer and the Rescuers team – almost all volunteers – are now the initial stop in the processing continuum and get to sift their way through the fruit and veggies first. The perceived inferior-quality products are subsequently sorted and find their way to various collection points, such as community centers, dotted around all areas of Jerusalem.
There, Jerusalemites of all walks of life, ages, and ethnic origins can then access healthy foodstuffs, gratis or at very affordable prices, that otherwise would probably not feature in their and their family’s daily diet.
Now Seltzer is taking the Jerusalem Food Rescuers’ work to another level by initiating the Jerusalem Urban Food Forum and a concomitant formula for leveraging efforts to make better use of food resources around the city.
The plan identifies approximately 2,200 food-based enterprise businesses in Jerusalem with potential relevance to food rescue. That includes restaurants and cafés, supermarkets, grocery stores, fruit and vegetable shops, bakeries, food producers, caterers, and institutional kitchens.
Coordinating all of that, and succeeding in gathering, pooling, and distributing the edible offloads from all those businesses, presumably, involves layered management dynamics.
“This points to the need for a citywide mechanism that can connect surplus food sources with community demand in real time,” the plan explanatory material notes. Seltzer reckons that, once up and running smoothly, that could yield around 7,000 tons of food a year.
She also cautions that municipal collaboration is the linchpin here. She says City Hall would need to invest in “coordination, business participation, logistics, digital tools, and community distribution capacity.”
Jerusalem commits to global urban food policy efforts
There appears to be goodwill coming from that direction, with Mayor Moshe Lion signing the Milan Urban Food Policy Pact in June, thereby adding Jerusalem to the ranks of over 300 cities worldwide committed to building and cultivating more efficient food systems that help to get healthier nutrition to folks who couldn’t ordinarily manage that. The local signatories of the Pact roster include Tel Aviv, Bethlehem, and Jericho.
That, of course, has all sorts of implications. As the World Health Organization (WHO) states – in case it wasn’t patently clear – in its healthy diet guidelines: “Diet plays a critical role in shaping the health and wellbeing of both individuals and populations, and unhealthy diets are a major risk factor for disease and disability.”
Interestingly, there wasn’t a lot of talk about that in the context of COVID when, besides all the emergency measures and constraints imposed on us, that might have been an opportune time to advise us to nurture our immune systems by, for example, steering clear of processed foods and sugar-rich products. In so doing, we would have improved our health and made our bodies more resilient to future pandemics or any potentially harmful bacteria that may come our way at some stage.
Doing our best to make fruit and vegetables – good natural sources of vitamins, iron, fibers, and potassium – available to all and sundry makes complete sense. Seltzer and the other members of the Food Rescuers gang are all for that, and spreading the word as far and wide as possible.
“The idea is to establish a network of cities, working individually and in tandem, to generate a system whereby there is greater accessibility to healthy food, with greater efficiency and enhanced connectivity between various municipal departments and personnel,” Selzer explains.
Cohesion is the name of the game
The plan aims to involve as many components of the human and economic urban fabric in the venture: “We need to take all the players in the city and get them to operate with greater synchronicity. That is a feature of the Milan Urban Food Policy.”
The global urban concept also calls for mutually beneficial cross-border dynamics. “The idea is for cities to work together, and to learn from each other through Best Practices, to see what works best.”
The initiative’s nonprofit core philosophy adds an endearing quality to the venture. “I believe it is all carried out voluntarily,” Seltzer notes. “It is wonderful. In Milan they created a [municipal] department that feeds off the [Milan Urban Food Policy Pact] website. That is amazing.”
There are various takes on how to make better use of available comestible resources. While the Italian unit’s purview includes overseeing the work of physical food rescue hubs, Greece’s Boroume model opts for a more streamlined, decentralized approach based on matching food donors directly with recipient organizations. That obviates the need for a central holding facility for collection and distribution.
Then there is the Canadian Second Harvest food recovery system, which facilitates the collection of surplus, healthy food from businesses and redirects it to charities to fight both hunger and environmental waste.
Addressing Jerusalem’s poverty woes
Back here, in sunny, socioeconomically disadvantaged Jerusalem, Seltzer says the plan offers a slew of benefits and sorely needed solutions in all sorts of practical areas. That includes a resounding financial bottom line.
“Jerusalem’s annual food loss may reach more than 200,000 tons, with an economic value approaching NIS 1.8 billion,” she says.
Those are simply stunning statistics made all the more egregious by another startling figure – around 40% of the capital’s residents live below the poverty line. That’s approximately twice the national average. However, that sorry state of affairs is somewhat offset by the Rescuers’ work.
To date, the nonprofit has salvaged 1,300 tons of food and has provided a similar number of local families with a regular supply of food. They are also doing their best to maintain food security efforts in the long run and have educated close to 10,000 school students about the ins and outs of food sustainability.
Lion’s signature on the Pact paper may have paved the way for Jerusalem to join hands with a global network of cities that understand food as a strategic urban issue, but there are plenty of facts on the ground to be addressed before the theory can become a health-inducing, nutrition-supportive local reality.
Seltzer would love to see our local purse string holders follow Milan’s lead.
“If we are going to make this plan work, we need to have a dedicated department set up in the municipality. The department should engage in food as an urban infrastructure, just like any other area [of municipal activity] which is critical [for life in Jerusalem].
“We have an education administration, and people who engage in transport, housing, etc., and we have food, the most basic need in life, which is ignored. It is so obvious that it is missed.”
Taking a food breather
The evidence of that is in full view on downtown and neighborhood streets, with hundreds of food outlets packed most hours of the day as many of us guzzle down portions that are way too generously proportioned for our health and are often simply not nutritious.
Contemporary lifestyles also come into the remedial equation, as technology makes deeper inroads into the natural order of things, encroaches on a gentler, healthier daily tempo, and screams out for eating on the fly.
How many of us, for example, other than, perhaps, on Shabbat, sit down together with family and friends to enjoy a relaxing, joyful, and possibly bonding repast?
I remember visiting a friend in Chicago many years ago, long before the advent of the Internet and smartphones, looking on in amazement as her siblings and parents, in turn, descended on the kitchen, secured their helping of dinner, and promptly disappeared into their bedrooms to chow down in front of their individual TV sets. Nowadays, there are, of course, even more entertainment and online information distractions that get in the way of harmonious mealtime intervals.
The Jerusalem Food Rescuers’ plan addresses that largely unnoted feature of daily 21st-century life.
A systematic umbrella review on family mealtimes, conducted by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the United States in 2023, found that more frequent family meals are associated with protection against poorer diet, obesity, risk behaviors, poorer mental health and wellbeing, and weaker educational outcomes among children and adolescents.
That report followed a 2015 NIH document which found that frequent family meals were associated with better dietary and psychosocial outcomes for children and adolescents.
It stands to reason if we view the nuclear family group as an emotional and physical staple of individual and societal health. The Jerusalem paper soberly notes that “not every family has the time, space, money, kitchen, stability, or emotional bandwidth to eat together regularly.”
That’s where outside help can come in handy. “The policy question is how schools, communities, and cities can create more opportunities for shared, dignified eating,” it continues.
Hadar Lavi, director of the Social Sustainability Department of the Municipality of Jerusalem, says City Hall is right behind Seltzer and her co-workers’ efforts.
“Jerusalem is promoting urban food policy by joining the international Milan Urban Food Policy Pact, and establishing the Jerusalem Urban Food Forum, in conjunction with the Jerusalem Food Rescuers, and elements from academia and civil society,” her statement read.
The benefits offered by the citywide initiative resonate with Lavi. “The Forum addresses the development of urban food policy vision with a view to furthering a sustainable food system, reducing food waste, bolstering food security and promoting healthy nutrition in the city.”
Lavi also singles out the Rescuers’ sterling work in the field. “The Jerusalem Food Rescuers are playing a significant role in bringing the issue to the urban agenda, connecting different parties and leading professional dialogue. This is a joint process which is evolving, and which is designed to formulate practical measures for Jerusalem’s unique needs.”
That makes for a well-articulated official statement, and one can only hope that, with Seltzer and her team spearheading solutions for this ongoing pressing need, the financial wherewithal and political backing will be there to put it all into universal, personal, ecological, and financial practice.
“Food rescue should be understood as part of urban policy, not only charity,” Seltzer stresses in her Plan notes.
“It connects waste reduction, food security, climate action, business participation, community resilience, public health, and education. The Jerusalem Urban Food Forum can be the place where these pieces are finally coordinated into one practical citywide plan.”■

Ethiopia and Israel share a new year - and an opportunity to deepen their historic ties - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:52:54 UTC
14:52:54 KST

Ethiopia and Israel share a relationship that is both ancient and extraordinary. Our ties trace back more than three millennia to the legendary encounter between the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon; a narrative that continues to symbolize the deep cultural, spiritual, and historical affinity between our peoples.
The outgoing year was significant for Ethiopia-Israel relations. Among the most notable developments was President Isaac Herzog’s visit to Ethiopia. During the visit, he held bilateral discussions with Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The discussions focused on further strengthening the longstanding relationship and expanding cooperation between the two countries.
Another important milestone was the convening of the Fourth Ethiopia-Israel Joint Political Consultation on January 6, 2026, in Jerusalem. The consultation provided an important opportunity to review the progress achieved in bilateral engagement and to identify avenues for further strengthening cooperation.
The relationship between Ethiopia and Israel rests on a long history of people-to-people ties and growing opportunities for practical cooperation. Looking ahead, both countries have considerable scope to deepen collaboration in areas such as agriculture, water management, innovation, technology, health, education, investment, and other fields of mutual interest.
The shared New Year on September 11 offers a symbolic reminder that, despite our different histories and traditions, Ethiopia and Israel have important interests in peace, development, innovation, and human prosperity.
Ethiopia’s development momentum: From GERD to energy leadership
Last year, Ethiopia marked its New Year with the inauguration of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), in the presence of leaders and dignitaries from Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, Barbados, and across the region and continent.
The GERD has now become much more than a project under construction. It has become a major instrument of Ethiopia’s development and energy transformation, generating more than 52% of domestic electricity supply and enabling Ethiopia to supply electricity to Djibouti, Kenya, and Sudan. A power purchase agreement has also been concluded with South Sudan and Tanzania.
Building on this achievement, Ethiopia is pursuing additional investments in energy infrastructure, including plans for three further dams on the Abbay (Blue Nile) River. At the same time, the Koysha Hydropower Project on the Omo River, with a planned generating capacity of 2,200 megawatts, is progressing toward completion, with completion expected by 2027.
These investments are designed to substantially expand Ethiopia’s energy capacity and strengthen its potential to become a net energy exporter.
It is exercising its sovereign right to develop and utilize its natural resources while remaining committed to international law, international norms, and responsible regional cooperation.
Ethiopia has no intention of causing significant harm to downstream countries. Its objective is fair and equitable utilization of shared resources and the creation of mutually beneficial, win-win outcomes.
It believes that development and regional cooperation should reinforce – not undermine – one another. Its commitment to development is therefore firm, and it will continue to pursue projects that improve livelihoods, expand opportunity, and strengthen the foundations of national prosperity.
A new wave of strategic mega-projects
The inauguration of the GERD was accompanied by the announcement of a new wave of mega-projects with a combined value of approximately $30 billion, reflecting an ambitious drive toward industrialization, self-reliance, and long-term economic transformation.
Among the most ambitious initiatives is a proposed nuclear power plant, which Ahmed described as a project comparable to the GERD in scale and significance.
Ethiopia is also investing heavily in aviation and logistics. Ethiopian Airlines has commenced construction of a major new airport project, announced as a future continental aviation hub with an initial capacity of approximately 60 million passengers annually.
The project is intended to strengthen Ethiopia’s position as a leading gateway for African air transport, trade, and logistics.
In the energy sector, Ethiopia has also moved into commercial natural-gas production in the Somali Region. The development includes a facility with an annual output capacity of 111 million liters of liquefied natural gas, while a second project is expected to increase capacity substantially.
The broader investment includes a natural-gas power plant with a planned generation capacity of 1,000 megawatts and a fertilizer complex designed to produce approximately 3 million metric tons of urea annually.
Taken together, these initiatives point to a broader national strategy: expanding productive capacity, strengthening energy security, reducing dependence on imports, and creating the infrastructure necessary for sustained economic growth.
Democratic institutions and national dialogue
Another important milestone during the outgoing year was the successful conduct of Ethiopia’s seventh general election on June 1, 2026. According to the National Electoral Board of Ethiopia, voter turnout across regions and city administrations was exceptionally high, ranging from 94% to 99%.
The Prosperity Party secured a comprehensive parliamentary majority, winning in the majority of constituencies.
Extensive preparations were undertaken well in advance, with significant attention devoted to enabling citizens to exercise their constitutional right to vote and to conducting the electoral process peacefully and inclusively.
Equally significant was the National Dialogue Conference organized by the Ethiopian National Dialogue Commission. Around 4,000 Ethiopians participated in this historic national gathering and deliberated on eight fundamental national agenda items.
The National Dialogue provides an important platform for Ethiopians with different perspectives to engage constructively, identify areas of common ground, and develop recommendations to address long-standing challenges.
Its ultimate value lies not simply in the discussions themselves, but in its potential to strengthen national consensus, social cohesion, and a shared vision for Ethiopia’s future.
Green Legacy and Ethiopia’s climate diplomacy
The Green Legacy Initiative is another area in which Ethiopia has registered significant progress. At a time when the country and the wider region are increasingly exposed to severe climate shocks, Ethiopia is placing growing emphasis on environmental restoration, climate resilience, and sustainable development.
Launched in 2019, the Green Legacy Initiative is a home-grown tree-planting campaign designed to address climate change, environmental degradation, and food-security challenges. Ethiopia has also taken steps to institutionalize the initiative.
In December 2024, Parliament unanimously ratified legislation establishing the Green Legacy Initiative and Degraded Land Rehabilitation Special Fund, with 0.5% to 1% of the federal annual budget earmarked for landscape restoration through forestry and agroforestry.
The initiative also seeks to strengthen livelihoods and food security through planting fruit trees and other productive species that can contribute to household income, nutrition, and community resilience. The United Nations has recognized the initiative’s contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals, including SDG 2 on zero hunger.
Ethiopia’s growing climate and environmental diplomacy is reflected in several international milestones, including its selection to host the second Africa Climate Summit, recognition during the 80th session of the Food and Agriculture Organization, and its bid to host the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32).
These achievements demonstrate an important principle: environmental action can be simultaneously a development strategy, a climate-resilience strategy, and an instrument of international diplomacy.
Economic performance and export growth
The outgoing year also saw strong economic performance. Ethiopia registered GDP growth of 10.2%, placing the country among the faster-growing economies in Africa and globally by 14%. Coffee remained a flagship export, generating more than $3.5 billion, while gold exports generated approximately $5.5 billion.
Oilseeds, horticultural products, livestock, and textiles also continued to contribute to Ethiopia’s export performance.
These results are important not only as economic indicators, but also as evidence of Ethiopia’s broader effort to diversify production, strengthen exports, attract investment, and build a more productive and resilient economy.
Looking ahead: A new year of opportunity
Ethiopia enters the New Year with a new government following the June 2026 general election. The incoming government is expected to set out policies and strategies to consolidate the country’s growth trajectory, strengthen national institutions, and advance Ethiopia’s development ambitions.
At the same time, Ethiopia will continue to play an important role in the diplomacy and geopolitics of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. The country’s geographic position, economic weight, energy potential, and diplomatic engagement give it an important stake in regional stability, connectivity, and cooperation.
The task ahead is therefore both ambitious and clear: to translate economic growth and major infrastructure achievements into broader prosperity; to strengthen peace, national cohesion, and democratic institutions; to expand productive partnerships; and to ensure that Ethiopia’s development contributes to a more stable, connected, and prosperous region.
As Ethiopia and Israel welcome the new year together, this shared date can serve as a symbol of friendship, renewal, and opportunity. May the coming year bring greater peace, prosperity, and cooperation to both our nations and to the region we share.
New Year’s message
On this special occasion, I once again extend my warmest wishes to the Ethiopian people and government, and to the people and government of the State of Israel.
May the new year be one of peace, prosperity, stability, and renewed partnership.
To Ethiopia: Melkam Addis Amet!
To Israel: Shana Tova!
Happy New Year to all!
The writer is the Ethiopian ambassador to Israel.

Vietnam celebrates 81st National Day in Tehran, eyes a new chapter with Iran
Ambassador Nguyen Luong Ngoc highlights Vietnam-Iran friendship at Tehran reception
TEHRAN — The Vietnamese Embassy in Tehran hosted a warm and lively diplomatic reception on the evening of Saturday, September 12, to mark the 81st anniversary of the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
The event brought together a large number of guests, including Iranian officials, foreign diplomats from various embassies, and Vietnamese, Iranian and international friends. From the moment they arrived, guests received an exceptionally warm welcome from His Excellency Mr. Nguyen Luong Ngoc, Vietnam’s Ambassador to Iran, and the embassy team.
81 years of independence and progress
His Excellency Mr. Nguyen Luong Ngoc, Vietnamese Ambassador to Iran, delivered a speech on this occasion, the full text of which is presented below:
Excellency Dr. Hamid Ghanbari, Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran,
Dear Ambassadors, Chargés d’Affaires,
Distinguished guests, Vietnamese Iranian and international friends.
Today, I am very pleased and honored to join you in commemorating the 81st anniversary of the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam.
On 2 September 1945, President Ho Chi Minh, the beloved leader of the Vietnamese people, proclaimed to the world the birth of an independent and free Viet Nam. This momentous historical milestone became the National Day of Viet Nam. Since then, independence and self-reliance have remained fundamental principles throughout the cause of national defense and development.
Over the past 81 years, Viet Nam has transformed from a newly independent country emerging from war and hardship into a dynamic economy worth US$514 billion. Within 2025, GDP grew by 8.02%, with GDP per capita exceeding US$5,000; total import and export turnover reached US$930 billion; foreign investment amounted to US$38.5 billion; and the country welcomed over 21 million foreign visitors.
At present, Viet Nam now maintains trade relations with 230 countries and territories and diplomatic relations with 195 countries, including 30 countries with which Viet Nam has established Strategic Partnerships and Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships.
After four decades of the Renovation process, Viet Nam has undergone profound transformation and become deeply integrated into the global economy. It has remained steadfast in pursuing the goals of national independence and socialism, placing the people at the center of development, promoting economic development alongside social progress and equity, and ensuring that no one is left behind.
Having experienced many wars, Viet Nam deeply cherishes peace and has always made every effort to preserve it through dialogue and diplomatic means. Viet Nam pursues a policy of being a friend to all countries, proactively promoting international integration, while remaining steadfast in safeguarding its independence, sovereignty and national identity.
In a rapidly changing and increasingly complex world, Viet Nam is moving towards a growth model driven by science and technology, innovation, high-quality human resources and strategic self-reliance.
The 14th National Congress of the Communist Party of Viet Nam set the goal of making Viet Nam a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income status by 2030, with annual GDP growth of 10% or higher. To achieve this goal, Viet Nam is focusing on three strategic breakthroughs: firstly, institutional reform; secondly, promoting science and technology, innovation, digital transformation and the green economy; and finally, improving the quality of human resources while developing strategic infrastructure.
Viet Nam also continues to deepen international integration and diversify its partnerships. The Middle East is a region of important geopolitical significance and abundant energy potential. Viet Nam hopes that the region will soon achieve lasting peace and stability through negotiations and dialogue, based on respect for national sovereignty, the Charter of the United Nations and international law.
Distinguished guests,
Viet Nam and Iran established diplomatic relations on 4 August 1973. From the outset, bilateral relations have been built on enduring principles: respect for independence and sovereignty, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs, and respect for each other’s legitimate interests.
Although geographically distant, Viet Nam and Iran share long histories, attach great importance to independence, sovereignty and national identity, and occupy important geopolitical positions.
Over the past 53 years, Viet Nam has consistently valued friendly and mutually beneficial cooperation with Iran, regarding it as an important partner in the Middle East.
The two countries have maintained strong political trust and expanded cooperation in economic and cultural fields, exchanges of delegations and people-to-people contacts. In 2023, we proudly celebrated the 50th anniversary of our diplomatic relations through a range of meaningful and practical activities.
In April 2026, President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian affirmed that Viet Nam–Iran relations have great potential and should continue to be deepened and expanded.
In July 2026, General Secretary and President of Viet Nam To Lam proposed four directions for promoting bilateral relations: strengthening political trust; giving priority to economic cooperation; creating breakthroughs in science and technology; and expanding cooperation in culture, education and training, and tourism.
Trade continues to be a priority area. Our two economies have many complementary strengths. Viet Nam has strong advantages in rice, coffee, pepper, cashew nuts, textiles and garments, seafood, processed foods, electronics and consumer goods. Iran has strengths in industry, construction, pharmaceuticals, materials, minerals, fruits and meat products. Bilateral trade increased from US$133 million in 2023 to US$170 million in 2025.
These results demonstrate that there is considerable room for further cooperation between Viet Nam and Iran, not only in trade but also in science and technology, education, culture and people-to-people exchanges, etc.
Dear friends,
In this new era of development, Viet Nam–Iran relations should be built not only on the tradition of more than half a century of friendship, but also on new, practical and effective cooperation. We are confident that bilateral relations will continue to develop in a manner commensurate with the potential and interests of both sides.
On this occasion, we would also like to express our sincere thanks for the valuable support and effective cooperation extended by the State, Government of Iran, its ministries, provinces and friends over the past years. We particularly thank the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Iran, H.E Dr. Hamid Ghanbari, and to all of you for joining us on this special occasion.
As part of today’s program, we are delighted to have a special musical performance featuring Vietnamese and Iranian songs. We would like to express my deeply thanks to Mr. Mahdi Norouzi, CEO of the Isttgah Institute, and all the artists for their dedication and hard work in preparing for today’s event. I would also like to extend our special thanks to Mahan Air and RostTrip for their generous sponsorship and support for this program.
We hope that the videos of the Vietnamese songs recorded during this event will reach a wider Iranian audience, fostering greater mutual understanding and bringing our two peoples even closer together. I also believe that this evening is not only a formal diplomatic occasion, but also a warm gathering of close friends, brought together by firm handshakes, genuine affection and warm-hearted energy.
Once again, please accept our sincere thanks and very best wishes to all of you.
May the friendship between Viet Nam and Iran continue to flourish, for the cooperation and prosperity of our two peoples, and contribute to peace, stability and development in the region and throughout the world.
Thank you.
A new, more dynamic chapter in Iran–Vietnam relations
Also speaking at the event, Dr. Hamid Ghanbari, Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Iran, said: “Vietnam is an important member of ASEAN, and plays a significant part in the economic architecture of Southeast Asia, and Iran enjoys a strategic geopolitical position, and this gives our cooperation a wider perspective. Iran and Vietnam can serve not only as economic partners, but also as gateways to the respective regions.”
He emphasized: “We have political will, complementary economic capacities, and many opportunities that remain to explore; with the practical approach and focus on implementation, we have confidence that we can open a new and more dynamic chapter in relations between Iran and Vietnam.”
Music, video and culture bring the two peoples closer
The reception included a diverse cultural program featuring live music and Vietnamese and Iranian songs, as well as a beautiful music video about Vietnam. The ambassador expressed hope that the videos of Vietnamese songs recorded during the event would reach a wider Iranian audience, fostering greater mutual understanding and bringing the two peoples even closer together.
A taste of Vietnam: Pho and a shared table
Guests then enjoyed a dinner featuring a variety of Vietnamese and Iranian dishes. The culinary highlight was undoubtedly a steaming bowl of pho, Vietnam’s iconic rice-noodle soup. Its fragrant, slow-simmered broth, silky noodles, fresh herbs and tender beef came together in a bowl that was both comforting and refined. Each spoonful carried the savory depth of Vietnamese street food and the warmth of a shared table — a delicious, aromatic taste of Vietnam that lingered long after the last noodle.
A journey to remember: Vietnam through the eyes of an Iranian guest
For me, this evening was more than a diplomatic occasion — it was a return to cherished memories. In November 2024, I travelled on a long journey to Vietnam and visited many of its cities. During that remarkable trip, I was deeply impressed by the country’s natural beauty, the culture and warmth of its people, their hospitality, their historic spirit of resistance, and their tireless hard work. I was equally struck by the country’s tourism policies.
Being present at the National Day celebration and watching the music video that was screened brought those sweet memories vividly back to life. Now that direct flights has been established between our two countries, I hope that many people from both nations will visit each other’s country, become acquainted with one another’s cultures, and that the ties between Iran and Vietnam will grow ever stronger.

The Energy Ministry said the increases were temporary and reflected an exceptional rise in the cost of procuring petroleum products from international markets, alongside the major overhaul of the Banias refinery, a key supplier of fuel to the domestic market.
The latest increases came just over a week after another adjustment took effect on Sept. 4, when gasoline and diesel prices were each raised by five pounds per liter, while household and industrial gas prices remained unchanged. ■

Preservation and development of Old Sofia – focus of KvARTal Festival

News
Preservation and development of Old Sofia – focus of KvARTal Festival
Sunday 13 September 2026 08:11
Sunday, 13 September 2026, 08:11
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
Font size
In 2016, a new festival was born in the center of Sofia in the small streets surrounding the mosque, the Central Market Hall, and the Central Mineral Baths, an area that surprises visitors with its remarkable buildings and an atmosphere preserved from the last century. "KvARTal Fest" was one of the first attempts to answer the question, "Why haven't we noticed them until now?" while aiming to showcase the district's cultural and historical potential.
Today, in 2026, KvARTal Festival is a beloved and eagerly awaited event held around the Day of Sofia on September 17th.
This year’s program - running from September 18 to 20, features over 60 locations: galleries, studios, cultural spaces, spots for dining and tasting the flavours of Old Sofia, pedestrian festival zones, music stages, installations, exhibitions, tours, a children’s architecture zone, workshops, and other initiatives dedicated to history, architecture, and cultural heritage. We spoke with the festival’s initiator, Martina Stefanova, about the eleventh edition.
Martina Stefanova
PHOTO Yoan Kolev
“The festival aims to invite visitors to the capital and Sofia residents to the old historic city, in order to experience it through flavours, history, and various educational programs. It is a festival where we get to feel the city and come to love our history, because without history, there is no future.”
This year, the festival’s main theme focuses on the future of Sofia’s historic center and the preservation of its cultural heritage. Prior to the festival's opening, the "Future of the Old City" forum will take place on September 16. Architects, experts, and professionals in the sphere of cultural heritage will participate in the event. Representatives from all relevant institutions have been invited to discuss topics such as 20th-century architecture, archaeology, the city's mineral water heritage, including its baths, as well as the future of museums.
PHOTO Martina Stefanova
"It is important that we are announcing two new initiatives this year," Martina Stefanova says. "The first is 'Adopt a Building,' which we will present to companies and citizens wishing to donate for the restoration of a historic building. The other key initiative is the 'Neighborhood Charter.' This charter will be available at various locations throughout Old Sofia. Anyone will be able to sign it. Our goal is to call upon the authorities to preserve the area and to restore it to its original state."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
One of the festival events takes us back to the early 20th century, when the first chocolate factory in the Balkans was established in Sofia. It was the work of industrialist Velizar Peev, and during the three days of the festival, its building at 12 George Washington Street will serve as one of the venues offering visitors engaging experiences:
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"In the hall, across various floors and in the courtyard, we will showcase vintage furniture, as some pieces have already been restored, while others await restoration and a new owner. We are creating an exhibition that bridges the past and the future, featuring old furniture alongside works by contemporary artists, including modern art, sculpture, and installations. The event will also feature a vinyl music program and a lecture on vintage furniture, as well as the styles of furniture and architecture spanning the Art Nouveau, Secession, and later Modernist periods. It promises to be a fascinating three-day program, which you can also follow on our social media channels."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"The past in the future tense" – perhaps that is how we should define the essence of KvARTal Festival, believing that its mission to preserve and develop this part of the capital will unfold right before our eyes.

Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:43:00 UTC
14:43:00 KST

Author
Hristina Taseva
News
Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Bulgarians in Chile aim to establish their own association and maintain closer contact with the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad
Sunday 13 September 2026 08:00
Sunday, 13 September 2026, 08:00
PHOTO personal archive
Font size
Moving to Chile is like stepping into a new reality, where the distances, nature, and geographical features are completely different. This distant and little-known country is home to around one hundred compatriots, among them Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, who has been living there for 30 years. She moved to Chile in 1997 with her Chilean husband and their two children, after they had lived in Bulgaria for 10 years. Today, she describes this step as a good decision, although there were also many uncertainties.
PHOTO Hristina Taseva
''I have a big, as they call it, corn family, like an ear of corn with many kernels on the cob. Families in Chile are always close-knit, like the kernels on a cob, and there is always someone who can help you. I became part of this family and felt like one of them. I spoke Spanish and very quickly found a job. This is extremely important because this is how social connections are established'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
According to Miroslava, Chileans are not inclined to emigrate and prefer to build their lives at home. She attributes this characteristic to their islander mentality, as they live with a sense of being cut off from the world around them. Their country is vast in size. On one side, it borders the Pacific Ocean, while on the other are the Andes — a vast mountain range resembling a wall. To the north, the Atacama Desert stretches for 2,000 kilometers, while to the south lies Antarctica, which is also like a desert, but a cold one.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
It is therefore no surprise that over the past five years, Chile has increasingly attracted the interest of the most avid Bulgarian tourists. Miroslava works as a tour guide and says that her fellow Bulgarians are amazed by this distant country. “To go to Chile, you have to have a special taste for adventure, and anyone who goes there is amazed”, she says. From the desert, you find yourself in Polynesia and on Easter Island, which is Chilean territory.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
“They are very surprised because when they leave for Chile, they do not know what they are going to see. They set off for a country they do not know, but they are amazed by what they see. They usually spend more than 15 days in the country. This is because of the great distances: Chile has 4,000 kilometers of coastline along the Pacific Ocean. These distances cannot be covered by land; you have to fly. That is why you cannot get so quickly from the desert to Patagonia, or from Patagonia to Easter Island — it takes time. They are very surprised by the diversity of nature, by landscapes that look like those on the Moon or Mars. In the Atacama Desert, there is an area called the Mars Valley because the landscape is the same, and lunar rovers and Mars rovers have been tested there. It is a very dry place, with high levels of ultraviolet radiation, stunning landscapes and volcanoes.”
Miroslava is one of the active members of the Bulgarian community in Chile and takes part in organizing events to mark March 3, Baba Marta, and religious holidays. How will the community continue to develop?
Rayna Mandzhukova in Chile (April 2026)
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
''There are only a few of us Bulgarians in Chile, around 100, unlike in Argentina, where there are around 20,000. In Chile, Bulgarians have come either for work, like the musicians, or they are employees of shipping companies who were sent from Europe because Chile has large ports with links to North America, Japan and China. There are also people who came here with a Chilean husband or wife. There are not many of us, and so far we have not had a real organization, but I hope that we will have one now, thanks to the visit four months ago by Rayna Mandzhukova, Director of the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad. Following this meeting, the Bulgarians became enthusiastic about setting up an organization, and most likely, when I return, we will try to establish such a foundation. This would give us the opportunity to organize exhibitions and allow children to take part in the agency’s competitions — for songs, children’s drawings, camps, and so on. I hope that the next time I come, I will be able to tell you that we already have a foundation'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
We say goodbye to Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, agreeing to keep following the developments surrounding the future Bulgarian association and to share the most important aspects of its work.
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

Brics embraces AI but leaves job displacement largely unaddressed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:42:41 UTC
14:42:41 KST

Brics New Delhi Declaration backs AI-driven growth and worker re-skilling but leaves unanswered what happens to jobs lost to automation.
NEW DELHI: Brics has set out an ambitious plan to prepare people for an AI-driven economy, but its New Delhi Declaration leaves a key question largely unanswered — what happens to workers whose jobs are lost or sharply changed because of automation and AI?The declaration calls AI an “immense opportunity to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all” and backs wider access to AI, while stressing safety, security, inclusion and reliability. But on employment, its response is largely to prepare workers for changing skill needs rather than spell out what happens when technology replaces existing work.The declaration commits Brics countries to strengthen cooperation in “forecasting skills needs by analysing labour market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors”. It also welcomes Brics Connect, the “BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies”, focused on skills for changing labour markets.The declaration addresses some changes already taking place. It calls for nationally tailored approaches to expand social protection for gig and platform workers and recognises the need to protect workers moving across borders, including through portability of benefits. It also notes an initiative to establish an “International Digital Platform for Remote Employment” for Brics countries.But there is no equivalent, specific commitment on workers whose existing jobs may disappear because of AI.
The declaration does not propose a Brics system to identify occupations exposed to automation, provide transition support to affected workers or measure AI-related job losses.That gap stands out because Brics is simultaneously encouraging wider use of AI across its economies. Its Centre for Industrial Competencies supports manufacturing companies, including SMEs, in adopting Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI.
Brics does recognise some AI-related risks beyond employment. In the intellectual property section, it notes “risks relating to misappropriation and misrepresentation of knowledge, heritage, and cultural values” that are insufficiently represented in datasets and AI models.For workers the declaration promises labour markets that are “future-ready”, “ensuring that no worker is left behind”.

Drones struck one of Russia’s largest oil refineries in the Krasnodar Krai
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 13, drones attacked the Slavyansk Oil Refinery in the Krasnodar Krai. The plant supplies fuel to Russian military forces.
During the night of September 12–13, drones struck the Slavyansk Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. This was reported by the "Exilenova+" Telegram channel, according to UNN.
Details
Photos and videos showing the aftermath of the attack have appeared online.
Additionally
The Slavyansk Oil Refinery is one of Russia’s largest independent oil refineries, located in the city of Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Krasnodar Krai. It processes 5.2 million tonnes of feedstock (oil and gas condensate) per year.
The refinery’s main products are gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, aviation kerosene, and vacuum gas oil. The refinery is involved in supplying fuel to Russian military forces.
The facility has been attacked by drones repeatedly. This occurred in April and May 2024, December 2025, and January and June 2026.
Recall
Russian forces increased the number of their attacks on Ukraine using jet-powered drones. They are faster than comparable UAVs with piston engines, making them more difficult for Ukrainian air-defense units to intercept and destroy.

New details on Iran-Oman Hormuz agreement released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:06:45 UTC
14:06:45 KST

Iran and Oman will soon announce a final agreement on new entry and exit routes for the Strait of Hormuz at a meeting with Persian Gulf foreign ministers, but the deal does not mean the strait will reopen, an informed source said.
The source said that intensive technical and diplomatic talks between Iran and Oman culminated in a final agreement in late August. The understanding is strictly between Iran and Oman, with other countries attending only to be informed of the details of the route and transit arrangements, so that their tacit non-objection is made clear to the international community.
Under the agreement, the entry route into the Persian Gulf will lie entirely in Iranian territorial waters, and part of the exit route from the Persian Gulf will also be in Iranian territorial waters. Transit along this route will be under Iranian arrangements. Once implemented, the southern route, which the United States insisted on opening and which was the main cause of the recent tension, will be closed.
In addition to Iran, Oman and other Persian Gulf coastal states, Iraq will also attend the meeting. These countries will only be informed of the outcome of the Iran-Oman talks, while decisions on the details were made in technical meetings between Iran and Oman.
Crucially, the source stressed that the understanding does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will open. Iran has conveyed seven conditions to the U.S. side through intermediaries for the strait to be reopened. Until those seven conditions, approved by Iran's highest military authorities, are implemented, the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed.
The understanding therefore means that if the strait is to open, it will open on the basis of this agreement, which represents a major step for Iran's exercise of sovereignty over the waterway. The opening of the strait depends entirely on American behaviour in implementing Iran's conditions.

From tiny houses to skis: This Swedish company is finding creative uses for retired wind turbines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:05:19 UTC
14:05:19 KST

What happens to decommissioned wind turbines and blades? Some are finding new life as buildings.
Europe is on track for a record wind year, with 8.8 GW of new capacity installed in the first half of 2026 – a 30 per cent jump year on year.
That’s enough electricity to power around seven million European households and replace fossil fuel imports equivalent to 25 LNG tankers a year, according to industry nonprofit WindEurope.
But every turbine that goes up eventually means one coming down – and manufacturers are still working out how to make sure none of the materials go to waste.
Up to 90 per cent of a wind turbine’s mass is made of easily recyclable materials like steel, copper, aluminium and concrete. Composite materials, which make up the majority of blades, are more problematic.
“Separating the composite materials from the resin requires specialised processes, often involving high temperatures or other energy-intensive treatment methods,” Eva Julius-Philipp, Director of Environment and Sustainability of Business Area Wind at Vattenfall, tells Euronews Earth. “In some cases, these processes can affect the quality and value of the recovered materials, making large-scale recycling more challenging.”
Since introducing a landfill ban on blades, nacelle covers and nose cones in 2021, the Swedish company has come up with some creative alternatives.
From blades to buildings: Turbine components get a second wind
From the ground, it’s hard to appreciate just how large wind turbines are. Putting it into perspective, Vattenfall teamed up with design studio Superuse to turn a retired wind turbine nacelle cover – which houses the mechanical and electrical equipment – into a compact living space.
Four metres wide, 10 metres long and three metres high, the box once sat atop an Austrian wind tower. It’s now a tiny house fitted with a kitchen, bathroom and living space equipped with a heat pump, solar panels and a solar water heater.
It was showcased at Dutch Design Week in 2024 as part of an initiative exploring how materials could be reused with as little energy and emissions-intensive processing as possible.
Blades, too, have been re-envisioned as building materials. After being decommissioned in 2023, the 57 blades from Danish onshore wind farm Nørre Økse Sø found new life as a facade for a multistorey carpark in the city of Lund.
It’s opened the door to a multitude of inventive uses for retired blades, from frames for solar panels to alpine skis.
“Projects such as the Tiny House, blade-based building projects and recycled skis are not yet a large-scale solution, however they are intended to help us gain experience, develop new applications and stimulate the market for circular solutions,” says Julius-Philipp.
Provided it’s safe to do so, extending the operational lifetime of existing components through reuse and refurbishment is the preferred option, she adds.
Recycling wind turbine blades: A multilayered challenge
Wind turbine blades can be between 50 and 100 metres long and are designed to spin in harsh weather for up to 25 years. What makes them so durable is also what makes them difficult to recycle: materials such as glass fibre, carbon fibre, epoxy resin, balsa wood, metals and various fillers pressed tightly together in layers.
Aiming to achieve 100 per cent circularity for these composite materials by 2030, Vattenfall is working on new ways of reusing, repurposing, refurbishing and recycling blades.
“When composite materials cannot be recycled at a high value, they can be processed through energy recovery and/or cement co-processing,” says Julius-Philipp.
Currently, Vattenfall uses mechanical recycling processes to turn blade material into composite flakes or fillers for new products, while pyrolysis – a thermal recycling process – recovers fibres and other secondary materials.
But technology isn’t the only challenge: “Decommissioned blades do not become available in a steady and predictable flow, which makes it harder for recycling solutions to scale economically,” adds Julius-Philipp.
As the first generation of major European wind farms reaches the end of its operational lifespan in the coming years, more blades will enter retirement, increasing the need for solutions that are “scalable, cost-efficient and low in energy use,” she adds.
The EU has not yet enforced a ban on landfilling decommissioned blades. Only Austria, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands have their own binding national bans, and WindEurope is now pushing Brussels to make the commitment legally binding across all member states.
“What is needed now is a regulatory framework that enables circular value chains and secondary raw materials to scale,” says Julius-Philipp, who hopes the European Commission’s Circular Economy Act, expected to be proposed later this year, will help provide it.
Designed to recycle: The future of turbine blades?
Increasingly, manufacturers are taking end-of-life into consideration when designing turbine blades.
Siemens Gamesa’s RecyclableBlades, which are used at Vattenfall’s offshore windfarm Hollandse Kust Zuid (HKZ) in the Netherlands, are one example.
These blades use a resin type that dissolves in a low-temperature, mildly acidic solution. This separates the resin from the other materials in the blade: fiberglass, carbon fiber, plastic, wood and metal, without significantly impacting their properties – allowing for a broader use of the recycled materials in new high-quality products.
“While recyclable blades are not yet widely adopted, we see growing emphasis on developing technologies that enable more efficient blade recycling and help retain the value and quality of the recovered materials,” says Julius-Philipp.

US cannot claim Moon under its international obligations — Lunar Embassy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:04:24 UTC
14:04:24 KST

NEW YORK, September 13. /TASS/. The United States, like other countries, has no right to claim ownership of the Moon under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the press service of Lunar Embassy, an organization specializing in selling property rights to plots on extraterrestrial bodies, told TASS.
"The UN Outer Space Treaty of 1967 was ratified by nearly all the worlds' countries, including the United States, and which agreement states that no Governmental or Sovereign entity may own, have authority or any jurisdiction over any of the celestial bodies within our solar system," the organization said, adding, "So no, the United States or any other country by their own commitment and obligation, cannot take possession of, or own, the moon. They have all taken themselves out of that conversation by their own accord."
At the same time, the organization said the treaty does not prohibit private individuals from asserting claims, a loophole that Lunar Embassy founder Dennis Hope took advantage of. "This same treaty, makes no such statement or restriction to individuals, a glaring and likely intentional loophole within the document, and as such, the Lunar Embassy founder Dennis Hope, as individual, laid claim to the moon of earth, all other planets in our solar system, and their moons in entirety," the company said.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump called the Moon the property of the United States, posting a photograph of Earth's satellite on Truth Social with the caption "The Moon is ours" followed by a US flag.

UK government to offer clearer guidance on student loans after repayment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:01:00 UTC
14:01:00 KST

University students taking out student loans are to be warned that the terms and conditions could change so they are better informed about what they are signing up to, the government has said.
In July, a report by MPs said slideshows that compared student loan repayments to the cost of a mobile phone contract, and YouTube videos that did not mention the fact that conditions could be altered amounted to mis-selling by the government.
The Treasury committee’s investigation followed a furore last November when the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, announced that the repayment threshold on plan 2 loans in England would be frozen at £29,385 for three years from April 2027. The threshold is currently £28,470 for this plan.
Some students had been led to believe that the thresholds would rise in line with inflation each year.
The committee’s report said the government had a “moral obligation” to reverse the freeze to maintain students’ trust and honour the terms under which the loans were sold to them.
In its response, published on Sunday, the government acknowledged the difficulties faced by graduates repaying loans, and said it kept “all aspects of the student finance system under review”, but did not commit to any change in policy.
It said it would redesign the guidance for new students to make it clear and unambiguous.
However it rejected the committee’s recommendation to issue new loans on a contractual basis so that terms could not be changed at a later date, saying it needed to be able to adapt the system to changing economic circumstances in order to keep taxpayers’ contributions stable.
In August, 121 MPs and peers from across party lines signed a letter to the new chancellor, John Healey, calling on him to urgently review the repayment system.
The letter said the frozen thresholds combined with inflation-linked interest rates meant young teachers, nurses, engineers, and entrepreneurs were facing “historically high” effective marginal tax rates.
“For many middle-income graduates, the combination of income tax, national insurance, and student loan repayments means they see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise,” it said.
Responding to the government’s commitment to offer clearer guidance, the chair of the Treasury committee, Meg Hillier, said: “The commitment to right a historical wrong by updating the information so that prospective students are properly informed before taking out a massive loan is an important step forward.
“Unfortunately, though, it doesn’t help graduates who are angry that they didn’t receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing.”
Hillier welcomed the fact that a reversal of the threshold freeze had not been ruled out.
“I recognise that finances are tight but I continue to urge the chancellor to look at this again. I sincerely hope he will use his upcoming budget to give graduates some much-needed breathing space.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university, starting with improved and clearer guidance for those taking out loans.
“That includes increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants to expand opportunities for people from all backgrounds, and [we have] raised the repayment threshold for plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021.
“We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way.”

Europe dominates ranking of the world’s most beautiful cycling routes – these are rides to try
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

From the vineyards of Tuscany and lavender fields of Provence to the rugged Scottish coast and the peaks of the French Alps, Europe is home to some of the world’s most spectacular cycling routes, according to new research.
Tourism on two wheels is on the rise with a surge of 292% in Google searches for “cycling holiday”. There’s so much more to a cycling trip than just the bike, though, and new research has revealed the most beautiful routes worldwide.
It’s good news for European cycling fans, as a majority of the top 15 in the ranking are based on the continent.
A study by adventure booking platform Explore used eye-tracking software to assess the reactions of 200 participants to 52 renowned and attractive cycling routes from around the world.
The technology measured how quickly each route caught their attention and how long it held it for, and the metrics were combined into a weighted "eye-catching" score out of 100 to provide a definitive ranking.
“There's something about seeing a country from the saddle that no other kind of travel can match; you're moving fast enough to cover real ground, but slow enough to take it all in,” said Luke Judd, travel expert at Explore.
“What's interesting about this research is that it puts science behind what cyclists have always debated: which views genuinely stop us in our tracks.”
Canada’s Bow Valley Parkway, a scenic winding route between Banff and Lake Louise, was far and away the most popular option, with a score of 97 out of 100.
It was followed closely by Australia's Great Ocean Road, on the southwest coast of Victoria, which was awarded a score of 94.
Despite the top two being some distance from Europe, and the list spanning four continents, eight out of the 15 are actually in Europe itself.
Here’s where to head for a beautiful cycling experience closer to home.
European destinations dominate the rankings
In third place, with a score of 91, are the stunning Tuscany Gravel Routes in Italy. Most famous for the professional one-day race held there in the spring, the stunning route features cypress tree-lined climbs, working vineyards and centuries-old hilltop towns.
With a score of 90, the Elbe Cycle Route in Germany is in fourth place.
It follows the Elbe River for around 1,220 kilometres from Czechia towards the North Sea, and the route passes through Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, skirts several German states and travels right through Hamburg, offering a journey through historic cities, countryside and some of eastern and northern Germany’s most interesting landscapes.
In sixth place, Amsterdam Cycle Route 10 has a score of 86. The Netherlands goes hand in hand with cycling, and there’s arguably no better way to explore Amsterdam than by bike.
This circular route offers a brilliant introduction to the city and its surroundings, taking you past canals, parks and historic neighbourhoods before heading into quieter countryside.
In seventh and eighth places, with scores of 82 and 81 respectively, are Italy’s Stelvio Pass and the Provence Lavender Route in France.
While the Stelvio Pass is notorious as one of the most difficult cycling routes in the world – and the second-highest in the Alps – the Provence Lavender Route is, mercifully, significantly easier.
The scenic trip is best taken in the summertime when lavender plants are in full bloom. It winds through rolling countryside, hilltop villages and the Luberon and Valensole Plateau’s vast fields of purple blooms.
It’s back to challenging routes with Scotland’s North Coast 500, which is in 11th place with a score of 78.
Starting and finishing in Inverness, this route is more than 800km long and can take even the most competent cyclists up to five days to complete. Despite its trickiness, it’s well worth it for those who want to experience the rugged beauty of the Scottish coast.
The Route des Grandes Alpes is one of Europe’s great mountain road trips, stretching from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean through some of the French Alps’ most spectacular scenery.
It’s in 13th place, with a score of 78 – the same as the North Coast 500 in Scotland – and isn’t easy either. Expect towering peaks, deep valleys, mountain passes and picturesque villages along the way. It’s fairly challenging, with long, winding and sometimes steep sections, so it’s best suited to experienced cyclists.
The last European entry in the top 15 is the Lake Ohrid Circuit in 14th place, with a score of 76. The trip covers roughly 90 to 96 kilometres and crosses an international border between North Macedonia and Albania.
Those tackling it will take in the historic towns of Ohrid and Struga and the Monastery of Saint Naum near the southern border, as well as Pogradec on the Albanian lakeside. Just remember to bring your passport in order to experience the whole route.
The world’s top 15 most beautiful cycling routes
How each route is ranked according to an “eye-catching” score out of 100:

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling

Unknown Publisher

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
India spent decades casting Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker. A tribunal ruling handed Islamabad the chance to return the favour
Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.
On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir.
The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement.
It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland.
