Wells willing to change digital harm proposal to win Coalition support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
01:31:24 UTC
10:31:24 KST

Wells open to changing digital harm bill after Coalition censorship concerns
In short:
Communications Minister Anika Wells is open to changing draft laws that would allow her to designate what constitutes serious harm online.
The bill would require online platforms to reduce foreseeable harm or face fines of more than $100 million.
What's next?
Labor will consult tech giants on the proposal and says it is open to working with the Greens and Coalition to finalise a position.
Communications Minister Anika Wells says she is willing to make a concession on draft ministerial powers under proposed digital duty of care laws in order to gain the support of the Coalition.
While the draft laws spell out online conduct that constitutes serious harm, the minister would have the power to designate additional serious harm that tech platforms must mitigate.
It is part of measures that aim to shift responsibility onto big tech to proactively reduce foreseeable harm or face fines of more than $100 million.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor branded the ministerial powers a "blank cheque for political censorship" and raised free speech concerns, stating on Thursday the Coalition would not support the bill in its current form.
Ms Wells said she was open to changing the draft legislation, including allowing parliament to decide what met the threshold instead.
"I'd be pleased to consider any constructive ways we can meet the intent around dealing with urgency around new and emerging serious harms," she told Insiders on Sunday morning.
Pressed whether that would include the ministerial powers, she said, "Yes."
"But like I said, I haven't had so much as a phone call or a word from the shadow minister with any suggestions," Ms Wells said.
Under the proposed new laws, tech giants would have an obligation to identify and minimise exposure to harm in an attempt to create a safer online environment.
These include child sexual exploitation content, grooming children for sexual activity, explicit threats of physical violence, encouraging self-harm, serious harassment or instructing criminal offences or illicit drug use.
Ms Wells said if the legislation had been in place in December when artificial-intelligence (AI) tool Grok started allowing users to "nudify" photos, including of children and teens, it would have allowed her and the eSafety commissioner to constitute that as a harm.
"We think this is a sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming online every single day," she said.
"And when it happens to your child and you're the parent, you want the government to act as swiftly as possible."
The bill includes a recommendation for an opt-in/opt-out system for platforms such as TikTok, Instagram or Facebook, requiring them to send account holders a push notification asking if they would like to see recommended content or a feed showing them only accounts that they follow.
While the proposed laws broadly have the Greens' support, the party has argued for tougher changes, including penalties tied to the direct percentage of a platform's global revenue.
Tech giants call for AI slowdown
Overnight, Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei has called on AI firms to slow the technology's development.
"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," Mr Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.
"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence."
OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, this morning joined his calls for oversight.
Asked whether the government wanted to slow the pace, Ms Wells pointed back to the duty of care bill.
"AI is here, isn't it?" she said.
"We want to capture the benefits of AI, spread those, and keep Australians safe.
"The role I am playing here is trying to legislate a digital duty of care, where AI chatbots cannot harm our children and the platforms have to identify children and the platforms have to identify those risks and mitigate against them."

Warming cities can’t afford to sacrifice their urban parks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
01:30:07 UTC
10:30:07 KST

Warming cities can’t afford to sacrifice their urban parks
Green spaces lower urban temperatures and boost quality of life. Cities may be short of space, but trading parks for concrete is a bad bargain
On a Sunday morning in Bengaluru last month, thousands gathered at Lalbagh Botanical Garden carrying a simple message: “Walk in Lalbagh. Walk for Lalbagh”. They were protesting against a new Karnataka law that allows up to 5 per cent of protected parkland to be used for public infrastructure. The provision could make as much as 12 acres of Lalbagh and 15 acres of neighbouring Cubbon Park available for such projects.
This is not the first time Bengaluru’s citizens have defended these green spaces from infrastructure projects. Earlier campaigns opposed proposals to build a metro line through Lalbagh. Today, protesters are confronting both a tunnel road project and a legislative change that potentially makes protected parkland easier to use.
The tunnel road project will pass through ecologically sensitive spaces and entails the felling of about 900 mature trees. The threat is particularly worrying as Bengaluru’s vegetation cover has shrunk dramatically since the 1970s. The loss has been accompanied by a sharp rise in land surface temperatures.
The protests in Bengaluru are striking because they are not just about two well-known parks or the city’s green cover. They are part of a larger struggle unfolding in cities around the world as urban residents confront the same question: what happens when cities run out of space?
In Mumbai, the Save Aarey movement has become one of the city’s longest-running environmental movements. Nearly four years of weekly protests have been held to protect the 1,300-hectare (3,212 acres) Aarey Colony urban forest from development.

The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war.
Iranian ship struck near Hormuz, state media says
State-run media said on Sunday that an Iranian commercial vessel was struck early in the morning off Qeshm Island near the strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and three wounded.
Several explosions were reported overnight around Qeshm, the largest island in the Hormuz strait.
There was no immediate statement by the US military, which previously has struck Iranian-flagged vessels as it keeps up a blockade of Iranian ports.
Separately, maritime trackers received new reports of an attack on a ship in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, adding to concerns about Iran-related threats to energy supplies after Saudi Arabia shut down a vital oil pipeline.
The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said it had a report of a projectile hitting a vessel as it moved through the strait. The amount of damage and the status of the crew were unknown as of early Sunday, the agency said.
The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh’s Red Sea ports.
The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni “forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia” near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesperson for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control.
Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sana’a, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.
Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.
On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted “in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles”.
The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.
The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised Yemeni government is based.
The UN’s migration agency said on Saturday that 76,000 people had fled the fighting since July, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country’s minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also “called us and they don’t want to fight with us”. He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy” in the region.
In 2025, the US conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war.
That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
In Yemen’s capital Sana’a, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail.

Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other’s shipping.
- 
  Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning. “Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” he wrote. “Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance.”

  The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine’s frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were injured. “These are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.”
-

- 
  Ukrainian officials said the country was bracing for a brutal winter as intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure and key export industries compound a deepening budget crisis. The economy minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko, said damage to infrastructure and fixed assets from Russian airstrikes was estimated at close to $10bn this year, while the broader economic costs of the attacks and the de facto blockage of its ports had cut 1.5 percentage points of GDP. “We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” he said.
- 
  With fighting on the frontline largely stalled, Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted logistics networks and other economic assets in an effort to undermine each other’s war effort. For more than two weeks, Russia has carried out near constant attacks on Kyiv using faster jet-powered drones, disrupting life, business and government operations. Moscow has also effectively blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports by intensifying its air attacks on the country’s southern regions. Ukraine’s main exports – agricultural products and iron and steel – are shipped via these ports.
- 
  In Moldova on Ukraine’s western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
- 
  Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out. “It is impossible,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting can only take place in the Russian capital. The gathering of world leaders takes place on 14-15 December and there has been no confirmation yet as to whether Putin would attend. Inside the snowballing conversations at AI companies about a doomsday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
01:10:00 UTC
10:10:00 KST

Inside the snowballing conversations at AI companies about a doomsday
SAN FRANCISCO – When Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, publicly quit the artificial intelligence start-up, citing his concerns over the powerful technology, the internal messages began flying.
“It’s what we’ve all been saying,” one Anthropic employee wrote about Coxon’s comments in a company chat that was viewed by The New York Times. “It’s just public-facing now.”
“Jacob took the group chat public,” another employee wrote. “That’s a good thing.”
The reactions inside Anthropic were echoed by AI researchers at OpenAI, Meta and Google, who parsed Coxon’s social media posts that described how OpenAI and Anthropic were “gambling with our lives” with the technology.
Many convened in office messaging channels, encrypted chats and private dinners, with the goal of organising to raise awareness about the risks of AI, according to a dozen employees across the companies.
For those who have made AI their life’s work, Coxon’s message was not new.
But his comments snowballed into such a global conversation that many saw it as a moment to call for increased caution.
Some AI workers are now speaking up to top executives to urge a pause in developing the fast-evolving technology until it has the proper safeguards, six of the sources said.
The conversations underline the tensions within the leading AI labs over the safest ways to develop the technology. Even as employees become emboldened to call for a slowdown in AI development, companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are juggling priorities.
Both are planning blockbuster initial public offerings within the next year.
The companies are also fearful they could face antitrust concerns if they agreed among themselves to take a breather in AI development, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. And Chinese start-ups have produced competitive AI models, raising the possibility that US companies would fall behind if they slowed down.
That has created a tricky situation for top AI executives, many of whom agree that the technology poses risks.
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, wrote in a 2023 blog post that AI could “cause grievous harm to the world”.
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, wrote in an opinion column in 2025 that AI should be regulated to control the risks.
In an employee meeting recently, Altman said OpenAI was willing to decelerate development alongside rival labs, according to two sources who attended. He said he hoped that voluntary slowdowns would become normal until there were widely recognised safety standards. The meeting was reported earlier by Bloomberg.
And on Sept 12, Amodei published a 3,800-word essay calling for prudence in AI development.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote. Altman and Elon Musk, whose SpaceX rocket company has been ramping up spending on AI, quickly agreed.
The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to AI systems. The two companies have denied the claims.
Discussions about AI safety have been around as long as the technology itself but were ramped up in recent years as researchers made breakthroughs.
The concerns heightened in July after OpenAI disclosed that some of its AI models had escaped containment and hacked Hugging Face, an AI company.
AI researchers questioned whether they could control the very systems they were building, with employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google’s DeepMind gathering to discuss what to do, nine of the sources said. Many agreed that AI was being built too rapidly.
“The sober researchers inside the labs who have prided themselves on being evenhanded are now sounding terrified,” said Roy Bahat, head of the investment firm Bloomberg Beta.
Some AI researchers created groups with the goal of establishing lasting safeguards. One effort, the Coalition of Concerned AI Staff, began as a skunk works project to create “stronger safeguards” and help workers collectively “hold a company to its safety commitments”.
“If you work at an AI company, you might be asking if you, too, should leave,” Pamela Mishkin, a former OpenAI employee, said on social media on Sept 10 in announcing the effort. She also encouraged those who remained in their jobs to ask “how to use your leverage in staying”.
After Coxon posted his resignation from Anthropic on Sept 8, AI workers urged top executives at their companies to pause development of the technology so they would have more time to work on it in a safe way. Some joked that they had lost count of the open letters they had signed and the number of private group chats talking about AI safety they belonged to, two of the sources said.
In an interview on Sept 9, Coxon said incidents like the Hugging Face hack had ratcheted up his concerns that AI models were developing far faster than companies could control them. “It was mostly a gradual emotional thing and eventually it kind of snapped, and then I decided to leave,” he said.
Other AI workers took Coxon’s cue to speak publicly. Evan Hubinger, a safety researcher at Anthropic, said in a social media post on Sept 8 that he believed there was a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.
Julie Steele, a safety researcher at OpenAI, said she believed AI companies needed to “slow down”.
Andreas Kirsch, a Google DeepMind employee, wrote on Sept 11 that he was “worried that AI will kill us all, either via near-term risks or long-term risks or both”.
“For a very long time, there has been this shroud of not speaking too publicly about it because people were very scared they would be perceived as too alarmist, too extreme,” said Connor Leahy, the US director of ControlAI, a non-profit that lobbies for AI regulation. “Now there’s a bit of a dam break.”
The outpouring has attracted Washington’s attention. Congressional members on both sides of the aisle, including Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley, have called for investigations into the technology and urged regulatory intervention.
“It’s a wake-up call to Congress and our government,” Representative Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, said on Sept 11. Congress should call for the creation of an AI regulatory agency, he added, and “we need to stand up and regulate”.
The AI companies have responded by laying out what they do on safety and what other steps can be taken.
Anthropic said in a statement on Sept 9 that it regularly tested its AI models “for dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology” and publicly shared its research. “We believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models,” it said.
Google DeepMind declined to comment.
Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s top policy executive, said in a blog post on Sept 9 the company would “slow or stop the development or deployment of systems” that it could not properly safeguard. Jakub Pachocki, the company’s chief scientist, called for safety rules “enforced by a network of third-party auditors, by government agencies or by international bodies”.
“I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence,” Pachocki said in a blog post. “I believe broader interventions are required.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Palestine hails BRICS' declaration supporting Palestinian rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
00:49:09 UTC
09:49:09 KST

Palestine has welcomed the declaration issued at the weekend summit of the BRICS grouping of 11 countries, praising its positions in support of the rights of the Palestinian people and the Palestinian cause.
In a statement on Saturday, the Palestinian Foreign Ministry welcomed the declaration from the New Delhi summit and its "positions and affirmations supporting the Palestinian cause," particularly its rejection of attempts to forcibly displace the Palestinian people from their land, including occupied East Jerusalem; its call for an end to Israeli occupation; its commitment to the two-state solution; and its support for the state of Palestine's full UN membership.
It also welcomed the declaration's support for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) and its mandate, as well as its call to protect holy sites and ensure access to them in occupied East Jerusalem, protect the Palestinian people, and ensure the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid to besieged Gaza.
The ministry said the positions are consistent with international law and relevant UN resolutions, and stressed the need to translate them into practical and concrete steps.
The ministry underlined that "implementing the positions and affirmations contained in the BRICS declaration requires ending the Israeli occupation and enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable rights," including the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state on its land, with occupied East Jerusalem as its capital.
Calls to preserve Gaza ceasefire
Earlier on Saturday, a final declaration issued at the conclusion of the BRICS leaders' summit expressed opposition to the forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The joint summit declaration called for respect for UN Security Council resolutions concerning Gaza.
"We call on all parties to ensure the preservation of the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and the full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid," it said.
It also expressed concern about Israel's continued violence in the region in violation of the ceasefire reached last October.
"We call for an end to any policies aimed at the forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, and express concern over any arrangements that could undermine the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights or could lead to legitimising the occupation or prolonging it," the statement added.
The declaration called for an urgent and lasting solution to the Palestinian issue and reaffirmed its support for the State of Palestine obtaining full membership in the United Nations.
BRICS is made up of longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa – the origin of the BRICS name – plus more recent members Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
With its expansion to 11 members since 2024, BRICS has become a bloc representing roughly half of the world’s population and around 40 percent of global economic output.

The US Justice Department has reached a tentative plea agreement with an ex-intelligence officer suspected of faking a classified CIA assignment to steal more than $40 million in government-provided gold bars as “work-related expenses.”
David Rush, who once worked as a senior CIA official with top-secret clearance, was arrested in May after an internal probe discovered he had lied about his education and Navy service. A search of his Virginia home uncovered a trove of 303 one-kilogram gold bars, some $2 million in cash and 35 luxury watches.
Rush has so far been formally charged only with theft of public funds for falsifying pay records to obtain around $77,000 in military-leave compensation. The case has not yet been presented to a federal grand jury.
In a joint motion filed on Friday, Rush and federal prosecutors said they had reached a “plea agreement in principle” and asked the court to extend the indictment deadline from September 17 to October 8, giving them another 21 days to resolve the matter.
“The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork,” Assistant US Attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney, Jessica Carmichael, wrote in the filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.”
The document did not disclose what charge Rush would plead guilty to or any possible sentencing recommendation. The parties said proceeding with an indictment and trial would require extensive litigation involving classified material. A deal could avert a public trial and keep key details of the case under wraps.
The court filings said that, beginning last November, Rush requested and received “a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses,” but official details remain scarce. According to media reports, Rush invented a special-access “continuity of government” operation, ostensibly intended to preserve federal functions during a nuclear war or other catastrophe.
The case has also prompted officials to scrutinize US Deputy Secretary of Defense Stephen Feinberg, a private equity billionaire who reportedly oversees the Pentagon’s $33 billion military intelligence budget. Earlier this week, NBC News reported that Feinberg had recommended Rush for sensitive assignments and praised his performance to senior CIA officials. The outlet also said footage showed both men at a government-affiliated residence used by Rush.
Feinberg has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the Pentagon has denied he endorsed Rush for any position, describing reports of a close professional relationship as “false and embellished.”

MADRID, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Enric Mas (Movistar) all but confirmed he will be the winner of the 2026 Vuelta a Espana on Saturday when he extended his lead over Primoz Roglic on the penultimate stage of the race.
On a day when veteran climber Mikel Landa (Soudal-Quick Step) claimed his first Vuelta stage victory since 2015, eventually finishing 47 seconds ahead of Tobias Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility), Mas showed he was the strongest rider among the overall contenders, extending his advantage over Roglic (Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe) to 2 minutes and 15 seconds.

With a 1:37 advantage over Roglic at the start of the race, all Mas had to do was withstand the attacks from the four-times Vuelta winner and his team.
While Landa was producing his late-career resurgence, riding across to a group of eight riders before launching an attack on the slopes of the Collardo de Alguacil that none of them could live with Mas was doing the job several minutes back down the road and although he finished almost seven minutes behind Landa, he took another 37 seconds off Roglic to stretch his overall lead to two minutes and 15 seconds.
With just Sunday's 112-kilometer stage that starts and finishes in Granada, left to ride, it would need a disaster for Mas to lose his grip on a race where he has looked to be the strongest rider since Tadej Pogacar was forced to withdraw after crashing out and breaking his collarbone. ■

Jefferson-Wooden, Kebinatshipi shine on Day 2 of Ultimate Championship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13

Melissa Jefferson-Wooden of the United States reacts during the awarding ceremony of the women's 100 meters race at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Hungary, Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo by David Balogh/Xinhua)
BUDAPEST, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Melissa Jefferson-Wooden produced the joint seventh-fastest women's 100m performance of all time, while Botswana's Collen Kebinatshipi moved to fifth on the men's 400m all-time list as the World Athletics Ultimate Championship continued in Budapest on Saturday.
Jefferson-Wooden, the 2025 world champion, clocked a world-leading 10.62 seconds to win the women's 100m, holding off Olympic champion Julien Alfred of Saint Lucia, who finished second in 10.74. Sha'Carri Richardson, the 2023 world champion, took third in 10.76.
In the men's 100m, Kenny Bednarek of the United States claimed his first individual global title with a 9.85 victory. World champion Oblique Seville of Jamaica was second in 9.90, while American Ronnie Baker took third in 9.93.
Kebinatshipi, the reigning world champion, won the men's 400m in 43.39, a performance that moved him to outright fifth on the world all-time list. Olympic champion Rai Benjamin of the United States finished second in 44.15, with Jereem Richards of Trinidad and Tobago third in 44.23.
Olympic champion Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic extended her winning streak in the women's 400m to 12 races, taking the title in 49.07. Norway's Henriette Jaeger finished second in 49.28 and Jamaica's Nickisha Pryce third in 49.56.
Japan's Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi produced 68.92 meters to win the women's javelin. China's Yan Ziyi opened with 68.05m and retired from the competition after her second attempt, but her first-round effort was enough to secure the second place. Colombia's Flor Denis Ruiz Hurtado finished third with 64.84m.
Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska, who also won the Diamond League Final a week earlier, took the women's 1,500m title in 3:57.55, ahead of Britain's Georgia Hunter Bell and American Nikki Hiltz.
Switzerland's Audrey Werro continued her strong season by winning the women's 800m in 1:55.88, beating Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, who finished second in 1:56.26.
In the women's pole vault, American Sandi Morris cleared 4.90m to claim her first outdoor global title, with Hana Moll also clearing 4.90m but finishing second on countback.
Two-time Olympic champion Miltiadis Tentoglou of Greece won the men's long jump with 8.35m, edging Bulgaria's Bozhidar Saraboyukov by just one centimeter. China's Zhang Mingkun finished seventh.
The three-day World Athletics Ultimate Championship will conclude on Sunday with the final 11 events. ■

Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan celebrates during the awarding ceremony for the women's singles final match between Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus and Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan at the 2026 US Open tennis championships in New York, the United States, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Rui)
NEW YORK, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Second seed Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan clinched her first US Open women's singles title on Saturday, defeating top seed Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the final.
Sabalenka had won 10 of their previous 17 meetings, but Rybakina prevailed in their most recent Grand Slam encounter, winning this year's Australian Open final. The Flushing Meadows final also marked the first time since 2013 that the top two seeds had met in the US Open women's singles final.
Both players held serve through the first four games of the opening set. Rybakina raised the pressure on Sabalenka's serve in the fifth game and eventually closed out the set 6-4 when Sabalenka sent a backhand down the line long.
Sabalenka, who has won all four of her Grand Slam titles on hard courts, including two at the Australian Open and two at the US Open, fought hard to convert her third set point and level the match with a 7-5 second-set victory.
Rybakina regrouped in the decider and broke Sabalenka in the third and seventh games to seal a hard-fought victory in two hours and 21 minutes. The win also marked the 27-year-old's third Grand Slam title.
"I don't expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side," said Rybakina, who has secured the world No. 1 ranking for the first time after beating China's Zheng Qinwen in Wednesday's quarterfinals, ending Sabalenka's 99-week run at the top. ■

Beijing Olympic champion Sanchez serves as ambassador for inaugural Tour of Armenia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:42:08 CST
09:42:08 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Eighteen years after winning Olympic road race gold in Beijing, Spanish cycling great Samuel Sanchez has taken on a new role in the sport as an ambassador for the inaugural Tour of Armenia.
The four-stage race, held from Sept. 10 to 13, is a UCI Europe Tour 2.2 event and features 96 riders from 16 teams. Starting in Gavar and finishing in Yerevan, the route covers around 587 km and combines fast sections with demanding climbs totaling more than 5,300 meters of elevation gain.
For Sanchez, who is attending the final stages of the race, Armenia's first attempt to stage an international cycling tour has left a strong impression.
"What impressed me most was the enthusiasm and ambition with which Armenia launched this first edition," Sanchez told Xinhua. "You could feel a very strong commitment here to growing cycling and establishing the Tour of Armenia on the international calendar."
The 48-year-old also highlighted Armenia's mountainous terrain and landscapes, saying the race could help develop cycling and discover new talent.
Sanchez's career remains closely associated with Beijing, where he claimed the gold medal in the men's road race at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games.
"Beijing 2008 changed my life," he said. "Sportingly, it was the most important moment of my career, and on a personal level, it is a memory that will stay with me forever."
He said China and Beijing would "always hold a very special place" in his story, adding that he hoped to return to Beijing and ride there again, "as it is a place I would love to revisit to better enjoy its landscapes and its people."
Since retiring from professional racing, Sanchez has worked with young riders and cycling projects, a transition he sees as a way of passing on his experience to a new generation.
"Serving as an ambassador for a race like the Tour of Armenia is part of this new chapter," he said, adding that he enjoys sharing his experience and supporting new cycling initiatives in different countries.
He also hopes to pass on lessons from Beijing 2008 to young riders. "Young cyclists should dream big, but understand that those dreams are built step by step. I arrived in Beijing with a dream and left as an Olympic champion. That experience taught me that when talent, hard work, patience, and self-belief come together, extraordinary things can happen."
Armenian Minister of Education, Science, Culture and Sport Zhanna Andreasyan said the goal was to make the Tour of Armenia a recurring race, adding that future editions could take the race to more regions across the country. ■

Ukraine helps shape global policy on developing clean sports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:35:00 KST

Ukraine helps shape global policy on developing clean sports
According to the press service of the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Ukraine is actively involved in shaping international anti-doping policy, as reported by Ukrinform.
Matvii Bidnyi has been elected as Europe’s representative on the WADA Executive Committee for the 2025–2027 term. In 2026, Ukraine will chair OneVoice—an international platform that coordinates government representatives in the field of anti-doping efforts.
During the WADA Executive Committee meeting, a series of decisions were adopted aimed at strengthening the independence and effectiveness of the international anti-doping system.
One of the key decisions was to strengthen the independence of anti-doping testing at major international sporting events—the Olympic and Paralympic Games and world championships. From now on, the host country’s anti-doping organization will not be directly involved in planning testing or collecting doping samples from athletes. This should help eliminate potential conflicts of interest and strengthen guarantees of fair testing.
Special attention was given to the work of WADA’s independent intelligence and investigations unit. Plans call for expanding its tools to detect potential violations while adhering to national legal procedures and practices.
During the meeting, the list of prohibited substances and methods for 2027 was approved, and the areas of funding for anti-doping research and WADA’s draft budget for 2027 were agreed upon. Work continues on the issue of regulating unintentional doping.
“Ukraine’s presence and representation within WADA give the country the opportunity to influence decisions that shape the future of global sports, as well as to defend and represent the interests of the European continent within the international anti-doping system. We must influence the shaping of the international agenda, rather than passively implement decisions made without our participation,” noted Matvii Bidnyi.
On the eve of the Executive Committee meeting, the Ukrainian delegation participated in the work of OneVoice and a meeting between the platform’s representatives and the Olympic Movement. As the chairing country for 2026, Ukraine coordinates the work of government representatives within the platform and participates in the formulation of common positions. Within OneVoice, government representatives from five continents coordinate their positions with WADA regarding the development of the international anti-doping system.
Ukraine continues its work within WADA and OneVoice, upholding the principles of clean sport and the independence of the anti-doping system. Ukraine’s representation in international anti-doping organizations enables it to participate in shaping decisions that determine the development of the global anti-doping system.

Houthi fighters have taken control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, seizing the strategic port city of Mocha, while Yemeni government forces have opened new fronts in al-Jawf, Marib and al-Bayda.

“I’m standing on stage in this city I love so much thanks to your support and your love,” she told the crowd. “The path was rocky, the road was longer than planned but I held on.”
The star announced in 2022 she had been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition which causes muscle spasms and left her unable to perform.
Dion seemed overwhelmed at times and broke down in tears during her opening number, holding out a microphone to the audience to help her through the bridge.
“I promised I wouldn’t cry - but they’re tears of joy,” she said, speaking mostly French throughout.
The staging was muted and Dion mainly wore a series of black gowns, leaving little to distract from her obvious emotion at being back in front of a crowd.
“She didn’t shy away from what she suffered and she shared it with her audience,” British fan Catherine Rushforth said as she left the arena in Nanterre on the outskirts of Paris.
Dion strutted confidently through her familiar on-stage theatrics, pulling faces and playing air guitar, and belting out ballads including “My Heart Will Go On” and “All By Myself” which made her one of the best-selling recording artists of all time.
But she opened with one of her biggest French-language hits “On Ne Change Pas” (“We Don’t Change”) - an apparent reference to her extended absence.
Her 16-concert residency, with a further 10 dates in 2027, has caused a frenzy in the French capital where crowds gather outside her swanky hotel until the early hours hoping to catch a glimpse of her.
“Her fight is an example for all of us, it’s wonderful,” said fan Julien Faruch, a chef. REUTERS

Swedes vote in election that could usher far right into government
STOCKHOLM – Swedes vote in an election on Sept 13 that will either bring a far-right party into government for the first time or shift the country back towards the liberalism it has long been known for.
Sweden’s centre-left opposition holds a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc ahead of a Sept 13 election for Parliament, pointing to a likely change of government, several opinion polls have shown.
But Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years in office, has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with rival Magdalena Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.
Supporters of the right-wing bloc say its policies have helped curb gang violence and cut immigration dramatically, and that a victory would amount to a public endorsement of that approach and more in the same vein in the years ahead.
“We can unify parties, voters and issues into joint action. That’s why we get things done,” Kristersson, who has pledged to bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government if his bloc wins, told reporters in Parliament.
Critics counter that the agenda is undermining civil liberties while forcing immigrants to conform more closely to Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, urged on by both carrot and stick.
“We’ve become a harder society, a quieter society, but also a poorer society as we’ve had growth far below our potential and where households see their paycheques buy less and less,” said Andersson.
“Our country has based its strength on sharing in each other’s achievements and that we stick together when things are hard.”
Strong showing by far right would align with European trend
Polling stations in the EU member state of 10 million people, which joined NATO after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, open at 8am local time with exit polls due soon after they close at 8pm local time.
Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe’s rising far-right parties, boosted by a significant win in a German state election in September by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany.
The right has already agreed to form a four-party government led by Kristersson if they win, while Andersson’s path to power is more uncertain.
The election could ultimately be decided by whether the Liberals surpass the 4 per cent threshold to win seats in Parliament, bolstering a right wing that includes Moderates, Christian Democrats and, since being invited by Kristersson earlier in 2026, Sweden Democrats.
Led by veteran party leader Jimmie Akesson, the Sweden Democrats have already spent four years propping up Kristersson’s minority government in Parliament, building credibility with the broader right-wing bloc.
Meanwhile, the rival blocs have converged on several voter priorities, including support for Ukraine, military rearmament and relief for households hit by the cost-of-living crisis.
While the opposition Social Democrats, Greens, Left Party and Centre Party broadly agree on the need for higher welfare and public spending, divisions persist on many issues, including immigration, where Andersson’s party wants a more restrictive line than some of its would-be partners.
They are also at odds over issues including a tax on billionaires and building new nuclear reactors, while the Centre refuses to support a government that includes the Left Party, increasing the challenge Andersson would face to form a Cabinet.
Luring the Christian Democrats to switch camps to create a centrist government is favoured by the Centre Party, but so far looks a distant prospect. REUTERS

The draft sets out ways to block extraterritorial investigations and to retaliate against foreign anti-corruption enforcement, drawing a firm legal boundary against foreign jurisdictions while establishing its own mechanism to police overseas assets.

The US and China are racing to build ‘self-improving AI’. Here’s what’s at stake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:00:10 UTC
09:00:10 KST

The US and China are racing to build ‘self-improving AI’. Here’s what’s at stake
Both sides view ‘recursive self-improvement’ as a game-changer in the AI race. But who will get there first – and will it endanger us all?
The US-China race for artificial intelligence dominance has entered a new phase: using AI to build better AI.
Leading AI companies in the United States and China are increasingly focused on deploying advanced models to write code, design experiments, and develop training techniques that can be used to improve more powerful models.
The ultimate goal is to achieve what the industry refers to as recursive self-improvement (RSI) – the creation of AI systems that can train themselves autonomously.
RSI has the potential to be a game-changer for the AI industry. As AI systems contribute to building more capable successors, which in turn become better at improving the next generation, the process could create an accelerating feedback loop – propelling the evolution of AI onto a new trajectory.
In a blog post last week, OpenAI said it aimed to build an automated AI researcher capable of advancing deep learning research, though it was still unsure “how to safely get all the way to aligned, full RSI”. The company described its GPT-6 Astra model, released in early September, as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.

Trump brushes off AI doomsaying to guard US lead over China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:55:00 UTC
08:55:00 KST

Trump brushes off AI doomsaying to guard US lead over China
- Donald Trump prioritises keeping the US ahead of China in AI, favouring a light-touch approach despite growing cybersecurity risks and calls for stricter regulation.
- Internal administration conflicts persist between officials pushing for stronger AI safety measures and those warning regulation could stifle innovation.
- Recent AI-related security breaches and industry calls to slow development highlight urgent challenges, but significant new policies remain unlikely before upcoming elections.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – In June 2024, during a campaign stop in Las Vegas, then-candidate Donald Trump got a glimpse of the technology that would come to define his second presidential term.
OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and then-Chief Operating Officer Brad Lightcap showed him a preview version of the artificial intelligence start-up’s Sora image and video-generation tool, an offering that has since been discontinued. Trump and Brockman used it to visualise a golf course on the moon, according to people familiar with the meeting who requested anonymity.
But the meeting took a more serious turn. Trump raised a glaring national security concern: What if foreign adversaries used AI to impersonate him? Brockman and Lightcap assured him deepfake mitigation techniques such as watermarking could minimise those risks, the people said.
That exchange foretold the dilemma Trump is grappling with now on AI: how to foster a technology that has underpinned US economic growth, while mitigating safety concerns raised by an alarming spate of hacks by rogue AI models. It has left administration officials struggling to balance promoting AI adoption against addressing unpredictable cybersecurity risks, according to people familiar with internal deliberations.
As he heads into a high-stakes summit in Washington in September with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with AI safety as a top issue, Trump is sticking with a hands-off approach.
His largely toothless June order on AI cybersecurity has come to symbolise his reluctance to impede hundreds of billions of dollars in tech investment. Administration officials are wary of undercutting the US lead over China, an advantage challenged by a new vanguard of Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI.
Yet Trump’s insistence on a light touch has been tested by revelations that models from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC had escaped secure testing environments and hacked other companies’ systems. Calls are growing from within the industry – punctuated this week by the high-profile resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon over existential fears – to slow the pace of AI development.
Even on Wall Street, where the AI boom has lifted the broader stock market, some prominent investors have made dire pronouncements about the technology’s growth. Greg Jensen, co-chief investment officer of hedge fund giant Bridgewater Associates, warned on Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast that it may take AI “killing people” for anyone to try and curb it.
The policy paralysis could have major consequences. The longer administration officials remain undecided on how or whether to police AI, the likelier it becomes that companies will race ahead without common guardrails, even as more executives call for them. OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman told employees this week the firm is considering slowing development and hopes its rivals do the same, Bloomberg News reported.
On Sept 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued a blog post saying the AI industry needs to slow the pace of model development, citing “serious” risks and calling for global coordination.
“The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” he wrote.
Trump has mostly dismissed new AI restrictions, focusing instead on staying ahead of China and touting the technology’s benefits. Asked on Sept 10 if he has any concerns about AI leading to human extinction, he said: “No, I don’t have any.”
“I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” he said. “We are leading China right now by a pretty good period. I would say a year, which is, you know, considered a lot.”
Turf war
Inside the administration, a turf war has simmered for months over how to handle AI, especially its unanswered security questions. Ever since Anthropic warned in April that its Mythos system was adept at finding previously unknown computer vulnerabilities and could only be shared with trusted partners, Trump’s top advisers have battled over ways to address AI’s core safety issues.
On one side, backing more robust protections, are Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Following Anthropic’s Mythos warnings, Bessent summoned a meeting of top Wall Street leaders to hear their concerns about financial-sector exposure, while Cairncross has kept in close touch with cyber experts spooked by the new model’s capabilities, the people said.
Since then, Bessent has helped craft plans for an independent regulator to vet the safety of AI models that would be akin to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Bloomberg News reported. The proposal, which would give companies a role in setting safety standards and address tech industry concerns about the ad hoc nature of AI policy, has yet to advance beyond the drafting stages, some of the people said.
Others in Trump’s orbit – led by White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios and former AI czar David Sacks – have backed the tech industry’s view that regulations risk stifling innovation.
Sacks, a venture capitalist, has warned that virtually any guardrails would risk consolidating power within a few large AI companies while giving China an opportunity to overtake the US. He has insisted that existing liability laws are enough to incentivise companies to minimise harm.
Tensions between the two sides erupted weeks before Trump signed his AI security order on June 2. Early versions of the directive would have compelled AI companies to share their models before release, the people said. Even before the order drafting had kicked off in earnest, some officials, including Vice-President J.D. Vance, had floated ideas of using the Defence Production Act to compel companies to disclose information and work with national security agencies, the people added.
Vance’s idea came on the heels of a threat by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to invoke the Cold War-era law as leverage in the Pentagon’s bitter contracting fight with Anthropic over extra safeguards the firm sought for military use of its AI tools – a confrontation that has complicated efforts to create a framework for mitigating cyber risks.
An administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that Trump’s advisers continue to work with the industry on developing the framework. A White House spokesperson said in a statement: “The President’s entire team is working closely together to balance innovation and security in AI policymaking.”
Spokespeople for OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. The Commerce and Treasury Departments, as well as Vance’s office, also did not respond.
‘A blocker’
Late in the process of crafting the order, Sacks called Trump to kill a draft he found to be too restrictive, and top officials were far apart even before it reached the president’s desk, according to people familiar with the matter. “I really thought that could have been a blocker and I want to make sure that it’s not,” Trump told reporters in mid-May, after quashing the measure.
He eventually signed a compromise version on June 2 that barely papered over lingering differences among senior officials. The directive called for the government to review AI models – shared by companies on a voluntary basis – up to 30 days before their release. It also nudged top AI companies to collaborate with the administration in selecting trusted partners for early access to cutting-edge systems.
Within weeks, appetite for more stringent oversight resurfaced when the Commerce Department briefly slapped export controls on Anthropic, citing national security concerns, after a spat over the safety of Mythos and its consumer-facing derivative called Fable. The decision cast doubt on whether Trump’s order was indeed voluntary and left both Anthropic and OpenAI operating as if his directive was mandatory, the people familiar with the matter said.
Before the export controls were imposed, Bessent sought to defuse the stand-off over Mythos with Anthropic by pressing the company to voluntarily take down the models, according to an administration official.
The move highlighted efforts by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – who played a less-central role in the executive order – to stake his claim on AI policy by using his export-control authority. He has stayed in close touch with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which conducts testing of AI models, seeking to carve out a lane for Commerce as the home for technical expertise, the people said.
Hugging Face
While Lutnick lifted the Anthropic restrictions in early July, policymakers were soon confronted with a disturbing new challenge: Some OpenAI models, including unreleased tools, had attacked the software repository Hugging Face Inc. without researchers noticing. OpenAI staffers later said the AI agents had communicated via a message board and worked together to escape secure testing spaces known as sandboxes and autonomously hack other organisations.
The breaches touched off bipartisan outcry among US lawmakers, who urged immediate action to counter the risk that an out-of-control AI model could inflict serious harm. Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, encouraged Bessent to expand the existing cyber order to cover so-called undisclosed models that companies have not made publicly available.
As signed by Trump, the order was aimed mostly at tackling the threat of bad actors deploying already released models to hack critical infrastructure or major companies, rather than address the risk that AI models could initiate such campaigns on their own. So far, there is no sign that Trump would update his directive to accommodate Banks’ suggestion.
“Every administration hears predictions that some new thing will change everything and they have to act immediately,” said Janet Kelly, chief executive officer of the Alliance for a Better Future, a conservative-leaning AI policy group. “The challenge, of course, is protecting Americans from the risks everyone now agrees these models pose without stifling the innovation that keeps the AI future American.”
Lutnick and Kratsios have ironed out a non-binding agreement with the Group of 20 to take a light-touch approach to regulating AI and other emerging technologies. In the background, much of Silicon Valley and many cyber watchers were still reeling from revelations about recent hacks conducted by the rogue AI models.
Asked if the AI breaches were discussed with foreign officials, Kratsios said “that did not come up” and gave no further detail. Across multiple public appearances, Lutnick also avoided the topic. Some G20 members, in particular the European Union, are seeking an international agreement to prevent models from carrying out cyber attacks that go undetected by their developers.
“We should work together to look at how we prepare for these kinds of risks,” Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s executive vice-president for technology sovereignty, said in an interview at the G-20.
Virkkunen said that US policy for overseeing cutting-edge AI remains murky because the country lacks the legal authority to address the technology’s risks. Export controls imposed on Anthropic highlight that US officials “didn’t have other tools”, she said.
‘FDA for AI’
Yet the administration and its Silicon Valley allies, who helped power Trump’s comeback victory in the 2024 election, have little appetite for measures that would add new layers of rules, especially an independent AI regulator. “The one approach we would oppose,” Sacks said, “is the so-called FDA for AI”.
Sacks has also publicly spurned the idea of a FINRA-style self-regulatory model, which Bessent and others promoted, calling it a “horrible idea” and “a total fig leaf” that would stifle US innovation.
Meanwhile, policymakers still have not completed all the details of a framework for oversight of models’ cyber capabilities. It remains unclear which models would be covered by the order and whether Chinese open models would be tested, after White House officials told companies those systems would be excluded for now.
Ahead of the Xi summit, the administration’s position has hardened regarding China’s AI advances. A trio of US agencies have accused Chinese AI developers, including Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding, of improperly siphoning data from American models to develop competing chatbots.
China has rejected those accusations and called for AI talks with the US, over concerns that advanced models such as Mythos could one day be turned against Chinese interests.
Advances in AI, including OpenAI’s new Astra model, highlight the challenges in responding to a technology that is evolving faster than the administration or Congress can keep pace. For now, prospects for any substantial move on safety remain dim, owing to bitter divisions in Congress, combined with the upcoming midterm elections and Trump’s reluctance to hinder AI innovation.
“It’s clear that many senior officials are willing to start thinking creatively about the policy instruments that can balance security and innovation,” said Brad Littlejohn, a policy adviser at American Compass, a conservative think tank. “That said, many of the actions to date have felt like ad hoc responses to whatever threats seemed most salient in the moment, and we need to see the administration as well as Congress thinking holistically and proactively about the range of threats this technology poses.” BLOOMBERG

====================================================================================================

The evolution of choice and arguing about it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:53:57 UTC
08:53:57 KST

By virtue of our big brains, we humans not only have free will but are aware of it, which doesn't mean we're not constrained. The universe may be infinite but our resources aren't, so we have to make choices along the continuum enabled by circumstances – such as the weather, geography, our banker, et cetera, and theoretically also by law. Different societies have different rules, but all have some. In most, you're not supposed to choose to murder the neighbor because he ate your dog. It will end in tears, or at least in court, where you will have to explain your choices.
The question is when language emerged, evolving beyond animal modes of communication such as physical gestures and fixed vocalizations. When did our considerations become loftier, rising above fight it, flee it or eat it? From what point could we not just signal the kids how to make choices, but explain? The evidence is entirely circumstantial and opinions differ vastly.
At one end is the camp favoring "sudden emergence" of language ability, which suggests that language did not arise early in our evolution, or even gradually, for the sake of social communication. Animals have nothing like it, this camp points out, and suggests that one day, one guy was born with a beneficial mutation enabling him to generate complex thoughts inside his head, as an internal process, and the trait spread.
At the other end is the camp advocating for early language development. The escalating complexity of our productivity and evidence of thoughtful choices suggest the necessity for speech to evolve, starting more than a million years before the Homo sapiens species even emerged.
Underlying this view is evidence of skills that plausibly had to have been learned. For instance, some early humans chose specific types of rock to knap into tools, as evident from a bias towards one rock out of the local varieties; and deeply prehistoric import of stone from afar to make tools. How deeply? Lomekwian tools from 3.3 million years ago were made using local stone, but archaeologists have reported that archaic hominins in Kenya made the energetically expensive choice to haul quality stone over a whopping distance of 13 kilometers (8 miles) 2.6 million years ago. That suggests they had standards 2.3 million years before our species first opened its baby blues.
In other achievements of early humans, some archaeologists think that hominins were braving the briny in deep prehistory, which is how they reached remote islands. Others suspect that hominins floated there by accident, as other animals did.
What have we so far? Accidents aside, to achieve all that, some posit that early humans, possibly even before the rise of the Homo genus about 3 million years ago, had to have had communication skills that surpassed pointing and calling. Recent research showing that the building blocks to create and teach complex vocalizations existed before the dawn of our species supports this hypothesis.
Do animals speak? Yes. Do they have language? Research shows that cats emit dozens of vocalizations beyond "meow" but that's short of language. A key difference between human and cat communication is our use of phonemes, which are meaningless sounds on their own that can be combined to create "words" (think of combining the meaningless sounds "com" and "bine" to create "combine"). Cats and dogs don't build "words" from smaller meaningless units like our phonemes. They teach the offspring by example.
But some other animals do pass that bar. Humpback whales and Bengalese finches exhibit cultural learning, teaching their group's unique vocalizations based on their version of phonemes. Vocal learning has also been identified in bats. Science has not identified grammar or syntax in our aviating friends, but these animals' capacity for vocal learning might suggest that from early on, hominins had the innate ability to mix 'n' match phonemes, resulting in "words" and ultimately, rudimentary language.
There's a caveat: Similarities in learning communication in humans, bats and whales may be down to convergent evolution – and our closest relative, the chimpanzee, evinces no ability to create words. Chimp communication seems confined to a range of about 13 call types, though possibly variations on their grunts may convey more than we realized. Research shows that the structure of grunts in certain chimps differs systematically with fruit-tree size and species. One suspects complex communication, enabling a higher level of choice, emerged in the Homo genus only after the split from the chimp some 7 million years ago.
But how early? Could the emergence of language have predated the emergence of the Homo genus? Did archaic forms such as australopithecines, who could walk upright and make tools, develop proto-language before the brain assumed "modern human" structure? The argument rages on.
Drop that rock, Oggie
Other animals make tools too, but none are known to do so at the complexity level of humans knapping stones. Stone tool manufacture began over 3.3 million years ago, based on finds at Lomekwi, Kenya, and who made those hammerstones is quite the question. Whoever it was, researchers posit that the knappers over the eons gained a "developing understanding" of the fracture properties of different rocks. That understanding, we infer, was conveyed to the next generation. Still, who made the tools at Lomekwi and do they suggest communication beyond hoot and point?
Archaeologists guess that the Lomekwi manufacturers were australopithecines and/or Kenyanthropus platyops, a flat-faced species whose skull was found in proximity to the tools. Some think Kenyanthropus was an alternative australopithecine. Maybe it was all of them, explaining how to choose and work a rock.
In any case, the candidates for making tools 3.3 million years ago were small-bodied, small-brained hominins, and there is argument over whether australopithecines should be encompassed in the Homo genus (presently they're in the "australopithecus" genus).
Homo genus or not, the majority thinking is that at best, australopithecines had nonverbal proto-language. If so, their mentors managed to convey tool-making lessons with grunts and gestures, with the kids learning through observation and imitation: australopithecine see, australopithecine do, australopithecine slap the wrong rock out of baby's hand and point at another.
A more verbal protolanguage only emerged in advanced species with big brains in the Homo genus, such as tall, big-brained, long-legged, wanderlust-stricken Homo erectus, according to mainstream thought. Researchers – from the linguist Daniel Everett of Bentley University, the archaeologist Steven Mithen of the University of Reading and the cognitive researchers Dan Dediu and Stephen Levinson of the Max Planck Institute – think that's where rudimentary symbolic language began, basically, because just look at what erectus achieved!
Increasingly complex stone tools, for one. Also, as erectus spread out of Africa to all ends of Eurasia insofar as glaciation permitted, he may or may not have known how to light a fire, but he could control it from early on. Fire use is reported inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa 1.8 million years ago. Lightning did not strike inside a cave; a hominin harvested a wildfire and transported a burning bush or branch back home.
In Israel, where erectus (and others) crossed between Africa and Asia, fire use signs go back a million years. In Zhoukoudian, China, fire use by the peripatetic erectus is identified about half a million years ago. He did get about, erectus did; and all that just with grunting, hooting and pointing?
Have brain, will travel
Based on erectus' brain size and achievements, Mithen suggests that proto- language arose in erectus as part of an emerging suite of "human" characteristics. Unrelated work supports the genesis of language about 1.5 million years ago, based on the little we can infer about the evolution of Broca's area – a region in the frontal lobe associated with processing grammar, producing language and coordinating the muscles needed to speak.
Earlier hominin skulls suggest their Broca's area was chimp-like, researchers say, adding that maybe hominins who developed a bigger Broca's area had improved communication, facilitating their evolutionary survival compared with hominins with smaller Broca's areas, who were disadvantaged.
A different sign of erectus' putative progression appears in the Sakhnin Valley in northern Israel, where the self-taught archaeologist and anthropologist Muataz Shalata deduced that hominins living there hundreds of thousands of years ago had developed the capacity to be moved by beauty. A subset of the stone tools littering the Sakhnin Valley floor shows clear choices of striking flints, worked to showcase their beauty: a crystal or fossil inclusion, for instance.
The energy a hominin expended in shaping a hand axe around an exotic feature would have been greater than the cost of making an ordinary tool and smacks of active choices – of a stone and a process. The investment of effort is a meaningful choice, because a deer doesn't look at an aesthetically pleasing weapon and faint. In any case, the focus on beauty suggests higher, abstract levels of thinking in erectus.
Apropos Shalata, he did weaken one argument proffered by some early-linguistics theorists, that making stone tools without language is impossible because making stone tools is so complicated and difficult. Shalata picked up a flint and a crystal geode to use as a hammer, and knapped it into a decent hand axe in about 15 minutes, making it look easy, while talking to Haaretz about something else. He had a lot of practice, he added.
So what have we? At least from the time of erectus, we have decisions and clear evidence of aesthetic choices – investing the energy in finding pretty rocks and taking the extra trouble to shape them in a way that highlighted the attraction. Maybe that is where early linguistic ability reached its finest level, enabling one erectus to lord it over the others with his pretty hand axe.
Never mind erectuses – some resist the notion that even the most advanced of alternative humans, the Neanderthals and Denisovans with whom we had intimate relations, could talk like we do. There is research into the Neanderthal hyoid bone (which is like ours), larynx structure and so on.
Moreover, like humans, both had FOXP2, a gene associated with the neural control of speech. We know little about Denisovan lifestyles but are confident that Neanderthals lived in groups and had a complex social life. They were capable of making very complex tools, including hafted spears. Also, while we never found anything smacking of Neanderthal or Denisovan figurative art, we are pretty clear that they had symbolism. And did they achieve these lofty heights by gestures and grunting?
Plausibly not, but just this month, a new paper suggested that actually, early humans didn't need more than ape communication to achieve any of the things we wrote above – fire, co-travel, or making stone tools and living in small groups. Fire was key, they posit. Until then, the assumption was that language predated storytelling. This paper suggests that groups sitting around the flickering fire were inspired, which catalyzed the transition from hooting, throwing feces and flipping each other the bird to defending our investment choices.

Death toll from Philippine ferry fire rises to 76
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:50:03 UTC
08:50:03 KST

Death toll from Philippine ferry fire rises to 76
The Philippine Coast Guard says 41 more bodies have been recovered from the M/V June Aster, with 13 people still missing.
The death toll from a Philippine ferry fire has risen to 76, with 13 people still missing, after search teams recovered additional remains from the passenger vessel off Palawan province.
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said in a statement on Saturday that 41 more charred bodies were retrieved from the ferry.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Five dead, dozens missing in Philippines ferry fire
- list 2 of 3Family members wait after deadly Philippines ferry fire
- list 3 of 3Philippines ferry fire death toll rises to 35 after bodies recovered
The MV June Aster was sailing from Manila, carrying 132 passengers and crew, when a blaze engulfed its lower decks on Wednesday evening, just 2.2 kilometres (1.3 miles) off its destination of Coron, in northern Palawan.
Rescuers pulled 43 survivors from the water that night.
Investigators, citing survivor accounts, reported hearing successive explosions before flames swept rapidly through the passenger areas.
“The wind may have contributed to the rapid spread of the flames, based on the survivors’ accounts,” said Commodore Noemi Cayabyab, spokesperson for the PCG, according to local media outlet the Inquirer.
“Some passengers reportedly jumped into the water after seeing the fire and may not have had time to retrieve their life jackets.”
According to authorities, forensic teams and local police are working to identify victims using personal belongings and DNA matching.
“The PCG, [the Philippine National Police’s Scene of the Crime Operatives] and other concerned agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures,” Cayabyab said.
Safety procedures and the ship captain’s actions during the early minutes of the disaster are under formal review, maritime officials said.
“With the number of missing and the number of capacity, definitely there is liability here,” Cayabyab added regarding the vessel’s command.
The ferry’s operator, Atienza Interisland Ferries, issued a statement committing to “full transparency” and assisting affected families with lodging, transportation and medical care as investigations continue.

This photo taken on Sept. 9, 2026 shows a stream at the Diaoluoshan section of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China's Hainan Province. The scenic ring road surrounding the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park passes through nine cities and counties in Hainan, including Lingshui, Baoting, Ledong and Changjiang, with a total length of 466 kilometers. The ring road was officially opened to traffic in December 2024.
This road connects the beautiful scenery of the mountainous areas in the central and southern parts of Hainan Island and builds a green corridor that balances ecological protection and cultural tourism development.
At present, many tourists come to cycle and drive on the road, boosting tourism-related consumption including accommodation, catering, specialty agricultural products, and outdoor culture and tourism along the road. (Xinhua/Pu Xiaoxu)

This photo shows a view of Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 10, 2026.
Beijing's Shougang Park saw its last blast furnace shut down in 2010, marking the end of more than a century of steelmaking. After more than a decade of transformation, the former industrial site now blends preserved steel structures with modern architecture and green spaces.
The park hosted the Big Air Shougang, a landmark venue of the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics, and has since evolved into a hub for exhibitions, commerce, sports and cultural tourism. It is now the permanent venue of the China International Fair for Trade in Services and has also attracted businesses in emerging fields such as science fiction and technology.
From an old industrial site to a vibrant urban destination, Shougang Park offers a vivid example of how China is transforming its traditional industrial bases. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong)
