Houthis hit Saudi base amid renewed fighting with Yemen government forces
The rebels have cemented their hold on the Bab el-Mandab Strait, which has become a key route for oil exports after Iran’s Hormuz blockade
Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces forced growing numbers of civilians to flee.
The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media.
The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh.
On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the southwestern part of the country.
“Air Force of the armed forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three air strikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said on Sunday in a social media post.
US news site Axios also reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected.

====================================================================================================

Houthis accused of using AI to fake Yemeni general’s retreat order during Mocha offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:44:31 UTC
08:44:31 KST

Iran-backed Houthi forces have been accused of using artificial intelligence to imitate a senior Yemeni commander and circulate a false withdrawal order while their fighters were advancing on the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, in what Saleh’s forces say was an attempt to sow confusion during one of the Houthis’ most significant offensives in years.
An audio recording resembling the voice of Lt. Gen. Tareq Saleh, commander of the UAE-backed National Resistance Forces, circulated as Houthi fighters pushed through government-held positions along Yemen’s western coast. The recording purported to present Saleh ordering or announcing a withdrawal as his forces came under growing pressure around Mocha. Saleh’s military media later said the recording had been fabricated using artificial intelligence and falsely attributed to him in an effort to confuse soldiers, influence perceptions of the battle and damage morale. The claim that AI was used to create the recording has not been independently verified.
The disputed recording told troops that advances and retreats were a normal part of war and instructed units to pull back toward Mocha, according to reports that monitored its circulation. Saleh’s forces responded by warning that authentic statements from the commander would be released only through official National Resistance military channels and that material attributed to him elsewhere should be treated as unauthenticated.
The alleged deception came at a particularly vulnerable moment. Houthi forces were advancing rapidly through territory held by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, while reports from the battlefield were changing by the hour. According to conflict-monitoring reports, messages were also circulated offering amnesty to fighters who surrendered their weapons and went home. Neither the impact of those messages nor the effect of the purported fake audio on troops has been independently established.
Saleh is a nephew of former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh and commands one of the most important anti-Houthi formations on Yemen’s western coast. Mocha had become the principal base of his National Resistance Forces, making the city’s loss both a military and symbolic blow to the forces opposing the Houthis.
Houthis race toward Bab al-Mandab
The controversy over the recording unfolded during a wider Houthi breakthrough along the Red Sea coast. The group seized Mocha on Thursday after government-aligned forces withdrew under heavy pressure. Three Yemeni government sources also confirmed the city’s fall to Reuters, while Saleh described the move by his forces as a tactical withdrawal intended to allow them to regroup.
The capture of Mocha was only one stage in a rapid southward advance. Houthi fighters continued toward Dhubab and moved onto islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mayun, also known as Perim. By Friday, reports said the group had taken control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline and established a much stronger position around the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Bab al-Mandab is one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. Ships passing through it can continue north through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, making it a critical route between Asia, the Middle East and Europe. The Houthi advance has therefore raised concerns far beyond Yemen, particularly as shipping through the region has already been disrupted by years of Houthi attacks and wider instability around the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest offensive is also among the Houthis’ biggest territorial gains since a 2022 truce largely froze the main front lines of Yemen’s civil war. The renewed fighting has displaced tens of thousands of civilians and raised fears that the conflict could again expand after years of relative military stalemate.
Reuters reported that the Houthis’ advance was aided by Iranian arms and direct guidance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, citing Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources. The seizure of Mocha has strengthened the Houthis’ position along the Red Sea while placing further pressure on Saudi Arabia and other regional governments backing Yemen’s internationally recognized authorities.
A separate case of AI and weapons development
The allegation that the Houthis used AI to impersonate Saleh emerged at the same time as separate evidence that actors operating in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen had been using advanced AI tools for military-related work.
Anthropic, the U.S. company behind the Claude AI system, said in a threat-intelligence report released this month that it had identified a weapons-development cell in northern Yemen using Claude Code to work on guidance, navigation and control software for guided weapons. The company did not publicly identify the group as the Houthis, and the case has not been linked to the disputed Saleh recording.
According to Anthropic, the Yemen-based actors were working on three programs: a guided rocket using a commercially available flight computer, a multistage ballistic missile with a stated range goal of more than 2,000 kilometers, and a missile family that included a proposed hypersonic-glide variant. The users employed several Claude instances simultaneously, assigning them tasks resembling those of members of an engineering team, including software development, research, code review and simulation.
Anthropic said the actors conducted a live test of a guided rocket in Yemen and then returned to Claude for help analyzing the failure. The company said it shut down the accounts involved and shared information about the activity with government and private-sector partners. It did not say the actors had successfully produced an operational weapons system with the model’s assistance.
There is no evidence that the northern Yemen weapons-development case and the alleged impersonation of Saleh were part of the same operation. But the accusations surrounding the Mocha battle point to a different potential use of the technology: not building weapons, but manipulating information in the middle of a fast-moving offensive, when a convincing order in a commander’s voice could itself become a battlefield tool.

US believes Russia, Ukraine want to find way to settle conflict — Kushner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:39:56 UTC
08:39:56 KST

WASHINGTON, September 13. /TASS/. Washington believes that Moscow and Kiev are committed to finding a way out of the Ukraine conflict, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said.
"We are very committed to trying to find a way forward [to settle the conflict] and President Trump is very committed to this. [US Presidential Special Envoy] Steve [Witkoff] and I are very committed to this. President [Vladimir] Zelensky is very committed to this, from what we've seen, and from what we heard, President [Vladimir] Putin is very committed to this as well. We have to find the right formula that hopefully works for everyone to advance it forward," Kushner said via video link at a conference of the so-called Yalta European Strategy in Kiev.
Kushner noted that, in his view, peace agreements and any other political deals have two important components: in addition to thorough preparatory work on a deal, it is necessary to be able to seize the right moment to conclude it. "You have to have done the detailed consultation with the parties, create the place of what the deal will look like, and then you need to create the momentum or find the momentum," he said. According to Trump's son-in-law, if the right moment arrives before the parties have done all the necessary work, a deal will not be possible. "If and if you do the work, but you don't get the momentum, you don't find the opening and you don't get it done," he added.
Kushner and Witkoff visited Moscow on September 5, where they were received by Putin. The following day, they met with Zelensky in Kiev. Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said that Putin and Trump held a telephone conversation on September 8.
Russia has repeatedly reaffirmed its commitment to resolving the Ukraine crisis through diplomatic means, while maintaining that the Kiev authorities are not prepared to settle the conflict through negotiations.

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:32:00 UTC
08:32:00 KST

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI slowdown
September 13, 2026
The CEO of artificial intelligence (AI) safety and research company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has called on AI firms to slow the technology's development.
His remarks on Saturday come amid mounting concerns over the risk of "superintelligent" computer software systems.
In a blog post, Amodei said he was concerned that a so-called swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could be capable of taking over the "entire internet" within six to 12 months, potentially causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote.
Amodei's comments come in the wake of AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who joined Anthropic from rival firm OpenAI, leaving the sector in protest at the US companies "gambling with our lives" in the race to come up with AI models that are capable of self-improvement.
Amodei calls for industry-wide action, Musk and Altman agree
The Anthropic chief called for a coordinated, industry-wide pause, but said he would not wait for his firm's rivals to act.
As a first step, he said he would permanently allow independent observers into Anthropic to assess the safety of its models during the training phase.
Sam Altman, the chief of ChatGPT developer and Anthropic rival, OpenAI, as well as Elon Musk, who owns xAI, said they agreed with Amodei's assessment.
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Altman wrote on X, adding that OpenAI "will do the same."
Musk, for his part, said "Dario is right" in a post on the platform he bought in 2022.
Why are industry leaders calling for AI development to be slowed?
In early June, Anthropic had called for AI development to be slowed or suspended amid safety concerns over AI agents.
More than 1,000 employees at AI companies, including Amodei, called on the US government to help slow the pace of development of automated AI.
Then in July, OpenAI revealed that during testing, AI agents had independently broken out of a secured environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site used to store and develop code, as it tried to find answers to a task it had been assigned.
The AI models had exploited software vulnerabilities and coordinated among themselves during the incident, Amodei explained.
"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand," he said in his blog.
Amodei said he was concerned that an AI swarm with more capabilities would have caused "catastrophic damage."
"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," he said.

Brics calls for uninterrupted energy flow, infra protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:30:18 UTC
08:30:18 KST

New Delhi: Amid disruptions to global energy supplies, Brics leaders have called for uninterrupted flows of energy from diverse sources and stronger protection of critical energy infrastructure, including cross-border infrastructure, while stressing the continuing role of fossil fuels in the global energy mix.They also called for greater cooperation on smart grids, energy storage and critical minerals, recognising their growing importance to energy security and the transition to cleaner energy.
The emphasis comes at a time of heightened risks to major global energy supply routes, with disruptions around Strait of Hormuz and possible disruption of another key route, Bab el-Mandeb, by Iran-backed Houthis, affecting oil and gas flows and raising concerns over energy security and prices.Brics leaders said energy security was a "crucial foundation for social and economic development, national security and the welfare of all nations" and called for greater stability in energy markets."We highlight the need to enhance energy security by ensuring energy market stability and maintaining undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources," the declaration said. It also stressed the need to "maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law".
Brics also recognised the continuing role of hydrocarbons, saying "fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world's energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies", while stressing the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in line with climate goals.
The declaration also recognised the role of renewables, fossil fuels, nuclear, hydropower, hydrogen, low-carbon technologies and energy storage in ensuring energy security and sustainable development.Brics countries backed greater cooperation on smart grids and energy storage to modernise power systems and integrate more renewable energy, while highlighting the role of AI and data analytics in improving grid management and efficiency. The declaration also welcomed the "Brics Guiding Principles on Smart Grids and Energy Storage" and India's initiative to set up a digital centre of excellence in the area.The bloc also stressed the need for reliable, diversified and resilient critical mineral supply chains, recognising their role in zero- and low-emission energy technologies and energy security. It said resource-rich countries should retain sovereign rights over their mineral resources and the ability to adopt measures needed to pursue legitimate public policy objectives.

Estonian FM opens EDUHUB educational center for teachers in Zhytomyr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

Estonian FM opens EDUHUB educational center for teachers in Zhytomyr
This was reported by a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Estonia has been a strategic partner of the Zhytomyr region since 2022. We are implementing many projects here, including the restoration of buildings, and we are also devoting considerable effort to supporting education, because that is our future. Estonia is an innovative country in terms of education, and we have developed a training methodology for Ukrainian teachers so that they can adopt it to support children’s development and share it with other teachers. Children can learn in new ways, particularly through the use of technology and interactive tools,” noted Tsahkna.
Andrea Kivi, Executive Director of the Estonian Center for International Development (ESTDEV), explained that 330,000 euros were allocated for the project. The funds were used for renovation work and training sessions for educators.
“The most important thing is not the building or the equipment, but the educators. The ‘EDUHUB’ center will become a home for educators, where they can learn something new and teach children. We are investing in people because they are our future,” Kivi added.
The 125-square-meter “EDUHUB” space was created at Zhytomyr Preschool No. 25 as part of the project “Development of the Zhytomyr Center for Methodological Competence in Preschool Education” with financial support from the Estonian Center for International Development (ESTDEV), the Principality of Liechtenstein, and the city of Tallinn. The project was carried out in partnership with the Zhytomyr City Council. The Tallinn Teachers’ House served as the implementing partner.
The education hub will serve as a venue for teacher professional development, the exchange of experiences, and the testing of early childhood education methodologies. Among its main areas of focus are STEAM education, learning through play, the development of practical skills in children, and the basics of first aid.
“EDUHUB” is equipped with STEAM materials and robotics, first-aid training kits, digital and interactive tools, as well as resources to support inclusive education and work with children with special educational needs.
As part of the project, 19 teacher-mentors from preschool institutions in Zhytomyr were trained; they will go on to train their colleagues and help spread modern educational approaches to other institutions in the city.
A separate focus of the educational space will be a library of educational resources, which will bring together teaching materials, digital resources, robotics, and other technical and instructional tools that preschool teachers in the city will be able to use.
As reported by Ukrinform, a rehabilitation center will be built at the city hospital in Zviahel, Zhytomyr region, with support from Estonia.

‘The party in Sweden is over’: anti-Islam metal keyboardist Jimmie Åkesson closes in on power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:18:12 UTC
08:18:12 KST

Until just a few weeks ago, Sweden’s election looked close to settled. The center-left bloc led by the Social Democrats held a polling advantage of around 10 points, and Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson appeared headed for defeat after a single term in office. But the final stretch of the campaign has changed the picture. The gap has narrowed sharply, the Liberal Party, which until recently appeared likely to disappear from parliament, has rebounded, and Swedes will vote Sunday in a race that is far more competitive than it looked only a month ago.
At the center of that shift is a 47-year-old politician who plays keyboards in a Viking rock band, held a metal-themed wedding and has spent more than two decades leading one of Europe’s most successful and controversial political projects. Jimmie Åkesson is not expected to become Sweden’s next prime minister. But if the right wins, he could achieve something that would have seemed almost unthinkable two decades ago: bring his far-right Sweden Democrats into government for the first time in the party’s history.
On the eve of the vote, the race is extremely tight. An Ipsos poll published Friday, two days before the election, put the center-left bloc at 49.3% and the right-wing bloc led by Kristersson and Åkesson at 49%. If those numbers were reflected in Sweden’s 349-seat parliament, the Riksdag, the difference would be just one seat: 175 to 174. Other polls give the left a somewhat wider lead of between three and six points, but all point in the same direction. A center-left advantage that reached roughly 10 points in mid-August has narrowed dramatically, turning what once looked like a comfortable opposition victory into an open contest.
Åkesson himself is not gaining much ground in the polls. The Sweden Democrats are currently at around 18% to 19%, slightly below the 20.5% they won in 2022. What has changed is the position of the other parties on the right, especially the Liberals, who have climbed back above the parliamentary threshold. Their recovery has brought Åkesson closer than ever to a goal he has pursued for more than two decades: moving his party from an outside supporter of government to a formal place inside it.
From political pariah to the mainstream
To understand how far the Sweden Democrats have come, it helps to look at where they began. The party was founded in 1988 as a radical nationalist movement, and some of its founders came from neo-Nazi and white supremacist organizations. A historical review commissioned by the party itself found that antisemitism and support for Nazi ideas were widespread at party events and in its publications during the 1980s and 1990s. One of its founders had even served in the German SS during World War II. Last year, the party publicly apologized for that part of its past.
Åkesson joined the Sweden Democrats in 1995, when the party had already begun trying to distance itself from its most extreme elements. In 2005, at the age of 25, he became leader and has remained in the job ever since. Under his leadership, extremists were expelled, Nazi symbols were banned at party events, local branches were built across the country and the party began a long effort to present itself as a legitimate force in mainstream Swedish politics. 
The strategy worked. The Sweden Democrats entered parliament for the first time in 2010. By 2022, they had won 20.5% of the vote and 73 of the Riksdag’s 349 seats, becoming the country’s second-largest party and a force without which it was increasingly difficult to form a government on the right.
Åkesson has often recalled that when he took over the party in 2005, he predicted it would one day become a major political force, shape government policy and challenge the Social Democrats for first place. At the time, the prospect seemed remote. Today, much of that ambition has already been realized.
The keyboard player, the metal fan and the ‘guy next door’
Åkesson’s public persona has also played an important role in the party’s rise. He is one of Sweden’s longest-serving party leaders, but has deliberately cultivated an image that is more informal and accessible than that of many of his rivals. He still lives in the part of southern Sweden where he grew up and travels regularly to Stockholm. He plays keyboards in a Viking rock band, and when he married two years ago, the celebration had the feel of a metal festival, complete with karaoke and no formal dress code.
At campaign rallies, Åkesson can appear more like a rock performer than a conventional politician, walking onstage to chants of “Jimmie, Jimmie” as supporters in the crowd wear shirts bearing his face. Jenny Madestam, a political scientist at Södertörn University, has described him as a politician with a talent for explaining complicated issues in simple terms while maintaining the image of an ordinary “guy next door.”
But the easygoing image masks a hard-line agenda, particularly on immigration, national identity and Islam. The Sweden Democrats want to dismantle what they describe as multiculturalism, strengthen the position of the Swedish language and Swedish culture, increase deportations and further reduce immigration. Senior party figures say people who live in Sweden should embrace Swedish culture, language, laws, norms, values and traditions.
Åkesson has made little effort to soften that message during the current campaign. Presenting his party’s platform this week, he declared that “the party in Sweden is over,” adding: “Sweden is no longer a free-for-all where you can come and live on benefits.” His party is promising to bring the number of residence permits issued by Sweden down to the lowest level in the European Union. “Now that asylum reception is close to zero, we will strive for immigration that is as limited as possible,” the platform says.
The same rhetoric has run through the campaign. In a speech this summer, Åkesson declared that “the Sweden Democrats have taken the wheel” and said, “we are making Sweden Sweden again,” language clearly reminiscent of U.S. President Donald Trump’s political slogan. He also said it was now “the turn of ordinary, decent people,” accusing the Social Democrats of destroying what earlier generations had built and turning safe communities into “war zones.”
Åkesson has been equally blunt about Islam. In a recent social media post, he wrote that people in Sweden were free to believe whatever they wanted, but that anyone who believed the words of gods or prophets should determine how society and its citizens live could find dozens of countries where such views would be more at home. “Sweden is not one of them,” he wrote.
During a party leaders’ debate about a week ago, Åkesson went further while arguing against continued low-wage labor immigration. “Eventually Sweden will no longer be Sweden if the entire workforce comes from outside,” he warned. Elsewhere in the campaign, he rejected the idea that Swedish society should bear responsibility for integrating immigrants. “It is not my responsibility, yours or that of any other Swede that a person who comes here from another country integrates,” he said.
In another debate held Friday, Åkesson attacked proposals to build public housing in affluent neighborhoods, calling them a policy of “forced mixing” and arguing that putting large apartment blocks in areas dominated by detached homes would simply shift social problems from one place to another rather than address segregation itself. The Sweden Democrats have also backed controversial proposals including restrictions on traditional Muslim clothing and the demolition of mosques where, the party says, extremist Islamist ideology is promoted. Critics say such proposals show that despite years of political rebranding, the party remains well outside Sweden’s traditional liberal mainstream.
Åkesson has already changed Swedish politics
Even if his bloc loses Sunday, Åkesson can argue that he has already won a substantial part of the political battle he set out to fight. Since the 2022 election, the Sweden Democrats have provided the parliamentary support that has kept Kristersson’s minority government in office. The party received no Cabinet posts, but its 73 lawmakers supplied the votes needed for the government to survive and gave the Sweden Democrats significant influence over policy.
During the past four years, Sweden has sharply tightened its immigration rules. The government has restricted routes to permanent residency for refugees, toughened welfare requirements and expanded its ability to deport people who do not have a legal right to remain in the country. The number of asylum seekers has fallen to its lowest level in about four decades. Since January, the government has also offered certain non-EU migrants up to 350,000 Swedish kronor, around $37,000, to leave Sweden voluntarily.
The program has so far attracted limited interest, but it illustrates how much Sweden’s approach to immigration has changed since 2015, when the country accepted more asylum seekers per capita than any other EU member state. That shift may be Åkesson’s most important political achievement. He has not simply built up his own party; he has helped move the broader immigration debate in his direction.
Policies once associated almost exclusively with the Sweden Democrats have been adopted, at least in part, by other parties, including the Social Democrats, who are campaigning this year on maintaining a restrictive immigration policy of their own. The central argument in Swedish politics is therefore no longer whether immigration rules should be tightened, but increasingly how restrictive they should become.
This time, Åkesson wants ministers
For Åkesson, however, influencing government from the outside is no longer enough. He has made clear that if the right wins, the Sweden Democrats expect to become part of the next government. “Either we are in government or we are in opposition,” he has said. He has also argued that in the event of victory, his party should receive at least three of Sweden’s four most important ministries: finance, foreign affairs, defense and justice.
Åkesson has sounded less enthusiastic about becoming prime minister himself. He has indicated that he could accept Kristersson remaining in the job even if the Sweden Democrats once again finish ahead of the prime minister’s center-right Moderate Party. The international travel and ceremonial duties that come with the premiership, including meetings and handshakes with foreign leaders, can be left to Kristersson, Åkesson has suggested.
That makes Åkesson’s definition of victory different from that of most party leaders. The polls do not suggest he is about to lead Sweden’s largest party, and they certainly do not point to him becoming prime minister. The Social Democrats remain ahead of the Sweden Democrats. But when it comes to determining which bloc governs and what the next coalition looks like, Åkesson could become the most influential figure on the Swedish right.
Kristersson, who once opposed working with the Sweden Democrats, has already removed one of the final obstacles to that possibility. In April, he said all four parties in the right-wing bloc wanted to form a joint majority government after the election, signaling that he was prepared to bring the Sweden Democrats formally into government. It marked the end of one of the last major taboos surrounding the party.
Two competing blocs
Sweden’s political system is now divided between two competing blocs. On the center-left, former prime minister Magdalena Andersson leads the Social Democrats, which remain the country’s largest party. She is the main candidate to replace Kristersson if her bloc wins. Kristersson, leader of the conservative Moderate Party, is seeking another term and has made clear that this time he is prepared to govern alongside the Sweden Democrats.
The right also includes the Christian Democrats, led by Deputy Prime Minister Ebba Busch, and the Liberals, led by Simona Mohamsson. On the other side are the Left Party, led by Nooshi Dadgostar, and the Greens, jointly led by Amanda Lind and Daniel Helldén. The Center Party, led by Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, also supports Andersson for prime minister but remains reluctant to work too closely with the Left Party. Differences within the center-left bloc over economic policy, taxation and energy could make coalition negotiations difficult even if Andersson’s side wins more seats.
The smallest party could decide the result
Ironically, Åkesson’s chances of entering government may depend heavily on the smallest party in the right-wing bloc. Sweden has a 4% threshold for entering parliament, and for months the Liberals appeared likely to fall below it. If they were eliminated, a significant number of votes cast for the right would produce no seats, making it much harder for Kristersson and Åkesson to assemble a majority.
But the final days of the campaign have brought a remarkable reversal. After polling at just 1.9% in August, the Liberals are now at between 5% and 5.8% in recent surveys, putting them above the threshold. The surge has been attributed largely to tactical voting by supporters of the right who want to ensure the party remains in parliament.
Pollsters have described the recovery as highly unusual so close to an election. Some of the Liberals’ new support appears to have come from voters who would otherwise have backed the Sweden Democrats or the Moderates but have switched in an effort to preserve the bloc’s chances of securing a majority. If the Liberals clear the threshold Sunday, a right-wing victory becomes considerably more plausible. If they do not, Åkesson’s path into government becomes much narrower even if his own party performs strongly.
After Germany, another test for Europe’s right
Sweden’s election also has significance beyond its borders. Earlier this week, Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, recorded a historic victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with around 44% of the vote. It became the largest party in the state and came close to winning an outright parliamentary majority, an unprecedented result for the German far right in the postwar era.
Germany’s mainstream parties continue to rule out cooperation with AfD, and the political “firewall” intended to keep it out of government remains in place. Sweden has taken a different path. The Sweden Democrats have already spent four years exercising considerable influence over national policy without formally joining the government. A right-wing victory Sunday could complete that transition and give the party Cabinet posts for the first time.
Nationalist and far-right parties have also become major political forces or entered government elsewhere in Europe, including in Italy, Finland, Croatia and the Czech Republic, while their counterparts in France and Germany continue to challenge established parties. Sweden is especially significant because of its long association with social democracy, an expansive welfare state and relatively generous immigration policies. For decades, the idea that a party such as the Sweden Democrats might participate in government was considered beyond the bounds of mainstream politics.
Sunday’s election will therefore determine more than who occupies the prime minister’s office. It will also show whether the transformation Åkesson has already helped bring about in Swedish politics will now be reflected in the composition of the government itself. Twenty-one years after taking charge of a small, ostracized party that much of the Swedish political establishment refused to engage with, Åkesson now leads a party polling above that of the sitting prime minister, while Kristersson openly says he is prepared to govern with him.
If the right wins, Åkesson will have achieved the breakthrough he has pursued for more than two decades. If it loses, he can still point to a political landscape that looks very different from the one he entered, and to a national debate that has moved markedly toward positions his party once held almost alone.

Germany: Lower Saxony local polls in focus after AfD win
Published September 11, 2026last updated September 13, 2026
What you need to know
- Local polls in the state of Lower Saxony are drawing unusual attention after the landslide AfD win in neighboring Saxony-Anhalt
- A new poll has shown that the far-right party is continuing to gain in popularity nationwide
- Shipping problems caused by low water levels in the Rhine could take a big economic toll this year, according to experts
- Former Chancellor Angela Merkel has warned that truth and lies are increasingly being blurred, including by people in power
- Merkel acknowledged that some decisions during her time as chancellor helped fuel support for the AfD
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Friday, September 11 through Sunday, September 13:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Far-right AfD increases lead over conservatives — poll
A new nationwide opinion poll released on Sunday has shown further gains for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party following its major win in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
The populist opposition party climbed one percentage point to reach 29%, with the conservative bloc of Chancellor Friedrich Merz — made up of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) — remaining unchanged at 20%.
The opposition Green Party was the only other major party to improve its popularity rating, gaining one point to reach 14% and overtake junior coalition party the Social Democrats (SPD) on 13%.
The Left party was also unchanged at 10%.
The next federal election is scheduled for 2029. The survey was carried out by the polling institute Insa and commissioned by the Bild tabloid.
Lower Saxony local polls under scrutiny after far-right win
Residents in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony are voting for mayors, district administrators and local councils in elections that are drawing unusual attention after the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD's) huge win in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
The local polls come ahead of key state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on September 20 that will also be closely watched as the AfD gains popularity across the country.
However, the party still has much less support in western states than in those in what used to be communist East Germany, with the AfD achieving just 4.6% at district level in the 2021 local elections in Lower Saxony.
Some 6.3 million people are eligible to vote in Sunday's elections.
The massive job cuts taking place at car manufacturer Volkswagen are likely to loom large in voters' minds, as Lower Saxony is home to Volkswagen's HQ and six of its plants, as well as being a key shareholder in the company.
Any run-off elections will take place across the state on September 27.

They are drawing unusual attention in light of last week's landslide victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
With two key state elections still to come this year, results for the AfD, which continues to gain support across the country, will be closely monitored.
This comes as the Chamber of Industry and Commerce in the state of Rhineland-Palatinate warns of a "really critical situation" for industry as low water levels in the Rhine continue to hinder shipping.

CSU leader Söder rules out internal move to oust under-fire Merz
Markus Söder, leader of the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, or CSU, has ruled out an internal move to oust the under-pressure chancellor, Friedrich Merz.
Merz has faced growing criticism in recent months for the sluggish pace of promised reforms and amid a surge by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which won the most votes in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
Asked by the Bild newspaper if there were plans to remove Merz, Söder said, "certainly not from the CSU."
"I am not responsible for the CDU; I am not its chairman. But I can say that for the CSU," Söder added.
Söder said he still believes Merz is the right man to lead the government and push through reforms, urging the center-right alliance to "not let the AfD drive a wedge between us now."
France defeats host Germany to reach women's basketball World Cup final
France beat Germany, the hosts, 86–64 on Saturday to qualify for the women's basketball World Cup final.
Among the 12,650 fans in the German capital were German men's basketball icons Dirk Nowitzki and Dennis Schröder, but they could not cheer their team to victory against the strong French lineup.
Gabby Williams shone for the victors with 22 points, helping France reach the final for the first time.
The United States, the favorites, will take on Spain in the second semifinal later.
The final will take place on Sunday.
Italy's Meloni: German 'firewall' against AfD isn't working
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has questioned the effectiveness of the "firewall" strategy used by Germany's major political parties to prevent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from gaining power.
"As we can see, this is a strategy that does not work," she told the Italian newspaper Il Foglio, when asked about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's victory in last weekend's elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Meloni also noted that political movements "that focus on the defense of identity, the fight against mass illegal immigration and the danger of Islamization" have gained strength in Europe.
The reaction of the "establishment," Meloni said, has often been "to erect firewalls rather than addressing the substantive issues."
She added that this strategy clearly does not work and that "listening to these concerns and responding to them" is a more successful approach.
Earlier, Meloni — who leads the right-wing Brothers of Italy party — has distanced herself from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and its political views on several occasions.
Woman injured in antisemitic attack in Berlin
Berlin police said that a woman wearing a Star of David was injured in an antisemitic attack by two men.
The men verbally abused the woman with antisemitic slurs in the middle of the night on Torstrasse in the central district of Mitte before one of them attacked the 43-year-old with a broken bottle, according to police.
Police said the men approached her earlier, at around 2:30 a.m. (0030 GMT), about her Star of David. The state security department of the state criminal police office has taken over the investigation.
The woman sustained cuts to her hand while defending herself and was taken to the hospital.
The incident occurred during the Jewish New Year celebration, Rosh Hashanah, which began Friday evening.
Tens of thousands protest against AfD across Germany
With the slogan "Not a Step Back! No to the AfD and Right-Wing Hate Speech!" around 20,000 people marched through downtown Düsseldorf, according to reports from the police and organizers.
Several political initiatives called for the protest rally to send a united message of support for an open, democratic society.
Among the participants, who marched peacefully without any counter-demonstrations, according to police, were the "Grandmas Against the Right."
On their poster, which was secured with a small piece of fabric and pins, they proclaimed: "The right is only for knitting." Numerous families with children also joined the protest march in beautiful weather.
Meanwhile, in Berlin, several marches protesting the normalization of right-wing politics converged on the town hall. Police estimated that 18,000 people participated, though organizers claimed that 32,000 people took part.
The demonstrations were prompted by the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party received nearly 44% of the vote, the most by far, but fell short of an absolute majority.
As part of a nationwide initiative, rallies were also held in several cities demanding a review by Germany's Constitutional Court of parties suspected or confirmed by the country's domestic intelligence agency to be far-right extremists.
The largest of these rallies took place in Munich, where police estimated that around 12,000 people gathered.
Around 2,000 people gathered in Mainz, 1,500 in Saarbrücken, and 1,100 in Magdeburg. Protests were also held in Leipzig and Saarbrücken.
Russia's GRU spy agency was behind attempted Leipzig drone attack: reports
Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported that security officials have tied the recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport to a Russian national working directly with Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.
Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the man, who entered Germany from Turkey and exited to Russia via Serbia, was responsible for operational logistics.
German authorities reportedly knew of the man's ties to the GRU when he entered the country but failed to put him under surveillance.
German intelligence sources said that the explosives were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia.
Berlin said forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms — pointed to a Russian plot.
Authorities were later able to match DNA traces on the drone to those found after an arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility on July 20, 2024.
The airport incident occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was discovered near a Ukrainian transport jet.
Leipzig/Halle airport is a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine.
Authorities were able to disarm the drone for which the German government blamed Russia — on the basis of the report — in early September.
Russia has denied any involvement.

International Ausschwitz Committee president calls for AfD ban process
Eva Umlauf, a Holocaust survivor and the president of the International Auschwitz Committee, has written an open letter calling for a move to ban the AfD in Germany.
She addressed the letter to Henrdik Wüst, a prominent CDU politician and the state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, most likely because he has in recent days called for the establishment of some kind of working group to evaluate the case for a ban motion.
"Let deeds follow your words," Umlauf wrote in the letter to Wüst, published in full by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper. "Set an AfD ban case in motion. Now, before it is too late."
She recounted her own time in Auschwitz, having been brought there in her mother's arms aged two.
"At some point, and it is not so far away now, the last of us survivors will be gone," Umlauf wrote. "Therefore we are passing on the burden that we have carried for a lifetime: to this country, to this society and in particular to you as a politician."
She recalled that the first state government led by Hitler's NSDAP was Anhalt in 1932.
"Eight months later, Hitler became chancellor," she said. "It was possible, because others believed that they could contain him. And because many looked the other way. Because they thought it would pass. The Holocaust did not start with gas chambers, it began with apathy."
She issued three requests to Wüst in the letter. First, to ensure that "steps towards an AfD ban process are taken rapidly." Second, to speak to Holocaust survivors and people in Saxony-Anhalt "who are afraid right now."
And finally, to support a potential bid for an investigation into a ban from his position in the Bundesrat, the upper house of parliament. Such a motion would need to clear that chamber with majority support.
Bonn public transport: 2 of 60 defective streetcars repaired after 7 weeks
This public transport update is accompanied by a magnitude 3.7 myopia warning from our Bonn newsroom.
The company that runs Bonn's public transport, Stadtwerke Bonn, has said that two of its 60 defective city trams or streetcars are back in service.
It said they would help out with the annual fair in the Pützchen district over the weekend, which brings additional visitors to the eastern part of the city.
The need to take some 60 vehicles out of service for repairs was announced a full seven weeks ago on July 21. It's not clear how far the other 58 are from resuming service.
Replacement buses have been trying to pick up the slack, and some subway stations have also been shut for repairs.
This is exacerbated by ongoing road disruptions in the former capital due to the long-term closure of the main highway bridge over the Rhine River.
The chairman of the oversight committee that monitors Stadtwerke Bonn, David Lutz, recently conceded: "Our patience really is somewhat at an end and used up."
Lutz called on the company to issue a fixed timetable for its plan to reestablish the tram services. A legal firm has also been asked to evaluate any potential shortcomings.

International Ausschwitz Committee president calls for AfD ban process
Eva Umlauf, a Holocaust survivor and the president of the International Auschwitz Committee, has written an open letter calling for a move to ban the AfD in Germany.
She addressed the letter to Henrdik Wüst, a prominent CDU politician and the state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, most likely because he has in recent days called for the establishment of some kind of working group to evaluate the case for a ban motion.
"Let deeds follow your words," Umlauf wrote in the letter to Wüst, published in full by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper. "Set an AfD ban case in motion. Now, before it is too late."
She recounted her own time in Auschwitz, having been brought there in her mother's arms aged two.
"At some point, and it is not so far away now, the last of us survivors will be gone," Umlauf wrote. "Therefore we are passing on the burden that we have carried for a lifetime: to this country, to this society and in particular to you as a politician."
She recalled that the first state government led by Hitler's NSDAP was Anhalt in 1932.
"Eight months later, Hitler became chancellor," she said. "It was possible, because others believed that they could contain him. And because many looked the other way. Because they thought it would pass. The Holocaust did not start with gas chambers, it began with apathy."
She issued three requests to Wüst in the letter. First, to ensure that "steps towards an AfD ban process are taken rapidly." Second, to speak to Holocaust survivors and people in Saxony-Anhalt "who are afraid right now."
And finally, to support a potential bid for an investigation into a ban from his position in the Bundesrat, the upper house of parliament. Such a motion would need to clear that chamber with majority support.

Israel preparing for new wave of Jewish immigration, Aliyah Ministry director-general says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:14:20 UTC
08:14:20 KST

At a time when Israel is facing complex challenges from the war, rising living costs, and growing uncertainty among Jewish communities worldwide, the Aliyah and Integration Ministry is seeking to highlight another reality: opportunities, renewal, and a strengthening connection between Israel and Jews considering building their future in the country.
Rising antisemitism and concerns over Jewish safety in various countries do not eliminate the challenges facing potential immigrants, but they have reinforced Israel’s role as a home open to Jews seeking to build lives, study, work, and integrate.
Aliyah and Integration Ministry Director-General Dganit Sankar-Langa does not ignore the obstacles facing aliyah, but she rejects the notion that immigration to Israel is in decline. Instead, she remains optimistic about the future.
Last week, Sankar-Langa welcomed approximately 150 new immigrants at Ben-Gurion Airport who arrived on six Nefesh B’Nefesh flights from North America. The flights were organized in cooperation with the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael, and Jewish National Fund USA.
In a special holiday interview with Walla, Sankar-Langa said the data reflects a system undergoing change. While the number of Israelis returning to the country has declined and aliyah numbers have not risen sharply, she said interest is growing among Jews in France, Britain, South Africa, and Australia, along with demand for study, employment, and absorption programs tailored to different communities.
According to estimates, approximately 15.5 million Jews currently live around the world, with more than half residing in Israel. Around six million Jews live in the United States alone, meaning the potential pool of future immigrants from the US is measured in the millions, even though the number of people who ultimately make aliyah remains relatively small.
Sankar-Langa said encouraging aliyah requires more than broad appeals to immigrate. She said Israel must create practical pathways that allow people to envision a future in the country, including English-language academic programs, support for scientists, early connections with employers, and assistance frameworks for immigrant families and soldiers.
The goal, she said, is to transform aliyah from a distant possibility into a realistic plan that people can prepare for, carry out, and succeed in.
"Generally speaking, our average number of immigrants over the past decade has ranged between 20,000 and 30,000 per year, except for the exceptional period involving Russia and Ukraine," Sankar-Langa said.
According to her, Israel is expected to receive between 18,000 and 20,000 immigrants in 2026.
"We are seeing a very significant increase from France. We expect to reach around 5,000 immigrants from France by the end of the year, a number not seen in many years. We are also seeing a large increase from Britain, as well as more aliyah from South Africa and Australia."
Sankar-Langa said the two primary barriers preventing more Jews from immigrating to Israel today are the cost of living and the country’s security situation.
However, she believes the difficult circumstances facing Jewish communities abroad will influence aliyah trends in the coming years.
"I think we will see the impact on aliyah within a year, two years, or three years," she said. "There is very strong academia here, strong communities, and the possibility of Jewish education and Jewish life. These are major factors drawing people to Israel, alongside the barriers that hold people back, mainly the cost of living and the security situation."
From US campuses to Israeli universities
One area where the ministry sees significant potential is higher education.
Against the backdrop of growing concerns over antisemitism and hostility toward Israel on some US university campuses, the ministry is working to expand English-language academic programs in Israel.
The issue has become increasingly relevant for Jewish families considering where to send their children for higher education, particularly as some students and parents have expressed concern over campus environments where anti-Israel and antisemitic incidents have increased.
According to Sankar-Langa, around 5,000 immigrant students are currently studying in Israel at any given time.
In recent years, English-language academic programs, which began at Reichman University and other institutions, have expanded to additional institutions, including the Technion, Ben-Gurion University, and Ariel University.
"We meet American Jewish families, including those that are very deeply rooted in the United States, who are increasingly examining the possibility of academic studies in Israel," she said.
"We are trying to allow young people to begin their studies here in English and later integrate into Israel."
Another area of focus is bringing senior scientists and researchers to Israel.
According to Sankar-Langa, the "Or" and "Bereshit" programs, developed in cooperation with Prof. Dan Shechtman, aim to attract leading researchers by offering selected scientists research positions and grants that can reach approximately NIS 1.5 million, and in some cases up to NIS 1.7 million, over a period of three to five years.
"Although these are only a few dozen scientists, each one of them is a diamond," she said. "These are people we do not want to lose as part of the brain drain."
Against the backdrop of global concerns over academic environments, the ministry is seeking to expand opportunities for English-language studies in Israel.
Teachers and doctors are already a priority
With a background as a senior officer in the IDF Manpower Directorate, Sankar-Langa describes the Aliyah and Integration Ministry as "the human resources department of the State of Israel."
The ministry, she said, is no longer focused only on encouraging immigration in general terms. Instead, it is working to identify professionals abroad whose skills Israel needs and connect them with employers before they arrive.
A new initiative launched together with the Education Ministry and Nefesh B’Nefesh aims to recruit Jewish teachers from abroad, particularly in English and the sciences.
"We are planning aliyah fairs for teachers abroad," she said.
"The idea is that before they arrive, they will already know that they have been accepted by the Ministry of Education, which school they will work at, which municipality they will live in, and how their children will integrate into the education system. The goal is that one week after their arrival, they will already be able to start working."
According to Sankar-Langa, the shortage of English teachers is especially noticeable in central Israel, where English speakers often have more financially attractive career options and therefore fewer choose teaching as a profession.
The ministry is also focusing on bringing medical professionals to Israel.
Sankar-Langa said that more than 1,000 doctors have immigrated to Israel over the past two years.
Some of them, particularly those from the United States, continue working in both countries and divide their time between Israel and their previous places of employment.
Estimates suggest approximately 1,300 doctors have left Israel since October 7, 2023.
The figure highlights the broader challenge facing Israel and the complexity of the ministry’s work.
The ministry is also working to recruit professionals with expertise needed in Israel’s defense industries, infrastructure sector, and major national projects, including the light rail and metro systems.
"We go out with companies to employment fairs abroad and identify people with expertise that Israel does not have enough of," she said.
"There are professionals around the world who have accumulated experience in railway systems spanning hundreds of thousands of kilometers, experience that almost does not exist here."
"The goal is that one week after their arrival they will already be able to start working."
Immigrant soldiers face challenges after discharge
The war also exposed gaps in the support provided to immigrant soldiers and their families.
According to Sankar-Langa, immigrant soldiers receive a support system from the IDF during their service, but after they are discharged, they can sometimes find themselves without sufficient assistance.
The government recently approved a plan under which the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Defense Ministry, and the Diaspora Affairs Ministry will establish a support framework for immigrant soldiers, reservists, and their families.
"We are trying to see how to provide and make assistance accessible both to the soldier himself and to the family, to siblings and wives," she said.
She described the case of the wife of an immigrant who was called up for two months of reserve duty and had to manage her workplace and household responsibilities alone, without the extended family and community networks that many veteran Israelis rely on.
"They do not necessarily have supporting organizations, and they do not always have the support system that others receive. We are investing a great deal of thought in this."
Around one million Israelis abroad, but fewer are returning
While the ministry is working to encourage Jewish immigration to Israel, data presented this week to the Knesset’s Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs Committee highlights another challenge: bringing back Israelis who have already left the country.
According to estimates, around one million Israelis, including children born abroad to Israeli parents, currently live outside Israel.
Data from the Knesset Research and Information Center shows that between 2005 and 2024, approximately 141,000 returning residents came back to Israel, averaging about 7,000 per year.
However, in 2025, only 4,483 Israelis returned, compared with 10,903 in 2009, representing a decline of 58%.
In 2024, the number was even lower, with only 3,793 returning residents.
According to estimates, around one million Israelis, including children born abroad to Israeli parents, currently live outside Israel.
Sankar-Langa, 58, was born in the moshav of Nehora in the Lachish region to parents who immigrated from Iraq and India and were among the founders of the area.
She served in the IDF for 24 years in manpower, planning, and budget positions, retiring with the rank of lieutenant colonel. She continues to serve in the reserves.
After leaving the military, she entered public service and began working at the Aliyah and Integration Ministry in 2012.
Over the years, she held several positions, including director of absorption and community affairs in the Tel Aviv and Central District and deputy director-general for encouraging aliyah and supporting returning residents.
In June 2022, she was appointed director general of the ministry for the first time. During that period, she helped manage the major wave of immigration that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Following the October 7 attack, Sankar-Langa was appointed head of the People and Community Division at the Tekuma Directorate, which was established to rehabilitate communities near the Gaza border.
"That was the mission of my life," she said.
"It was as if everything I had done before prepared me for this terrible and important role."
After approximately a year and a half at the Tekuma Directorate, she became deputy director general of the Israel Museum. In May, she accepted an offer from Immigration and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer to return as director general of the Aliyah and Integration Ministry.
Sankar-Langa holds a bachelor’s degree in sociology, economics, and political science from Bar-Ilan University and a master’s degree in business administration from Ben-Gurion University.
She lives in Givat Shmuel, is married to Elchanan, and is the mother of four children and a grandmother.
Her husband, a lieutenant colonel in the reserves, has also served hundreds of days of reserve duty since October 7.
'Every Jew should know that they have a home here'
Sankar-Langa emphasizes that the ministry’s primary responsibility is to assist people who are not Israeli citizens and choose to immigrate to Israel, rather than prevent Israelis from leaving the country.
However, the data on Israelis who have left and those who have returned reflects a broader national challenge that extends beyond the ability of any single government office to address.
"That was the mission of my life."
"Our responsibility as a state is to ensure that every Jew who wants to immigrate knows the path and knows that there is someone who will support them in their absorption in Israel," she said.
"Even ten years after aliyah, we can still speak with them, check whether there are problems at school, with recognition of degrees, or with Israeli bureaucracy."
Asked whether the state’s vision is for all Jews around the world to eventually live in Israel, Sankar-Langa said the goal is not to demand that every Jew move to the country, but to ensure that Israel remains an available option.
"The vision is that every Jew will know they have a home here. To say that everyone will be in the State of Israel is too ambitious. Our role is to put the possibility of aliyah on the table, accompany immigrants, and provide them with a response that is suited to the community they came from."
Looking ahead to the next five years, Sankar-Langa remains optimistic about the future of aliyah.
"I think we will see an increase in aliyah. It will happen when the war calms down and when we know how to bring more tailored, precise, and appropriate programs. I also hope that we return to normalcy around the world, because Jews deserve to live wherever they choose. We need to create an alternative and a full choice for every Jew, how to manage their life and where to live."
The Aliyah and Integration Ministry is focusing on bringing Jews from France, Britain, South Africa, and Australia, while also recruiting scientists, teachers, and doctors and providing support for immigrant soldiers and their families.
At the same time, Knesset data highlights the difficulty of bringing back Israelis living abroad, with the number of returning residents in 2025 down 58% from 2009.

====================================================================================================

Behind President Isaac Herzog’s global search for the next ‘Voice of the People’ cohort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:14:18 UTC
08:14:18 KST

There is a row of colorful pillows in the corner of Deborah Apeloig’s home studio in Mexico City. One reads: “Shaping our future together.”
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The pillows were made for an in-person Voice of the People gathering in Haifa in 2025. Apeloig, a member of the initiative’s inaugural cohort, brought several home. They have remained there as a reminder of a project she believes will outlast her formal term.
Venezuelan-born and based in Mexico, Apeloig is a communications professional, content creator, and Jewish community advocate. She founded Tikun Talks, a communications and consulting platform that uses podcasts, digital content, workshops, and public speaking to address antisemitism and polarization, promote dialogue, and introduce audiences to people working for positive social change.
Before establishing Tikun Talks, Apeloig worked in advertising, innovation, and brand strategy. The granddaughter of Holocaust survivors Musha Horenkrig and Andrés Abraham Apeloig, she has also used her work to preserve Holocaust memory and bring survivor experiences to younger generations.
“They've been a part of me and my platform for all this time, and they will remain,” Apeloig told The Media Line. “Because Voice of the People is not only these two years that I have spent in the council - it's going to be forever a part of me and my work.”
That sense of continuity is central to Voice of the People’s next phase. The global Jewish leadership initiative, supported by President Isaac Herzog’s office, the World Zionist Organization, the Jewish Agency for Israel, and philanthropic partners, has opened applications for its second cohort.
The new group is expected to include 150 participants: 50 from Israel, 50 from the US and Canada, and 50 from Jewish communities elsewhere in the Diaspora. Applicants must be Jewish, at least 21, able to work in English, and prepared to take part in collective leadership work. The application deadline is Oct. 12.
Herzog: Jewish strength comes from 'ability to remain connected across differences'
“The strength of the Jewish people has always come from our ability to remain connected across differences of geography, tradition and perspective,” Herzog said. “As we open applications for the second Voice of the People cohort, I invite Jews from around the world to bring their voices, experiences and ideas to this growing global network, and to help shape our shared future together.”
Voice of the People was created to bring together Jews with varied backgrounds and perspectives, build relationships, and develop practical responses to challenges facing Jewish communities. According to the organization, more than 20 initiatives developed through the first cohort and its partners have reached the proof-of-concept stage.
For Shirel Dagan-Levy, the initiative’s CEO, the work starts with bringing together people who might otherwise never meet.
Dagan-Levy is an Israeli lawyer by training whose career has included work in law, business, high tech, and startups. Before leading Voice of the People, she served as chief financial and operating officer of Maoz, an Israeli leadership organization, and held senior business-development and strategic-client roles at telecommunications company IBC.
She also worked in global contracts and procurement at the Israeli technology company Verint and previously served in the Israeli Ministry of Defense’s procurement delegation in New York. Her experience building cross-sector partnerships now informs Voice of the People’s effort to turn dialogue among Jewish communities into practical cooperation.
“We want to walk the talk,” she said.
Some participants, she said, had never previously met a Jew from another continent, denomination, or professional world. Before trying to solve shared problems, they first had to learn who was in the room.
“I believe that everything starts with trust and trust begins with knowing one another,” Dagan-Levy said.
“Even if we share different opinions and we disagree, and that’s OK,” she said. “That’s our strength, you know, having disagreements.”
Over 10,000 survey participants comment on what council should address
At the initiative’s launch, more than 10,000 people responded to a survey in six languages about the issues the council should address. Antisemitism, Jewish-non-Jewish relations, polarization and dialogue, Jewish education and heritage, and the Israel-Diaspora relationship emerged as leading concerns.
Working groups then assessed existing efforts, identified gaps, and developed proposals. Dagan-Levy said one focus has been antisemitism, particularly online, and the need to reach younger audiences and build relationships beyond Jewish communities.
“We can’t just talk to ourselves when we talk about antisemitism,” she said.
Council members range in age from 19 to 82, and the organization says 86% are under 50. For Apeloig, whose Tikun Talks project focuses on Latin American and Spanish-speaking Jewish communities, the challenge is not only to combat antisemitism but also to broaden the public story about Jews and Israel.
“I specifically talked about not focusing on viralizing antisemitism, which is what happens and has been happening in social media, but viralizing philosemitism,” she said. “There’s so much love and admiration and bridges and people that actually love the Jewish people and love Israel.”
Through Tikun Talks and Voice of the People, Apeloig said she has “been able to become a louder voice for the Jewish people in general and for the Latin American, Spanish-speaking Jewish communities in particular.”
She said Latin American communities need content tailored to their own languages and experiences, even though many people also follow English-language Jewish media.
“Latin American Jews often follow English-language content, and many are bilingual,” she said. “But we also need our own narrative and our own content in Spanish for Latin American communities.”
Apeloig described a shifting regional landscape. At a forum organized by the Combat Antisemitism Movement in the Dominican Republic, she said, evangelical communities publicly expressed support for Jews and Israel. The event followed an announcement by the Dominican Republic’s president that the country would adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism.
“What I saw there was beautiful,” she said. “They were there showing their support.”
The gathering also drew two pro-Palestinian demonstrators who used a question period to make accusatory comments, Apeloig said.
“You felt the love and the support,” she said. “But of course, there’s always both.”
One of the council’s most visible projects is the Jewish and Indian Alliance, launched in April after roughly 18 months of planning. The initiative seeks to deepen ties between Jewish and Indian communities in the Diaspora.
“We found that we have so many similarities,” Apeloig said. “We live within our bubble.”
Apeloig and fellow council member Shoshana Turkia have worked with the Indian Embassy in Mexico City, while another member has worked on the effort in Israel. The project has organized opportunities for people from both communities to meet.
“So, we are creating events, moments for our two peoples to come together,” Apeloig said. “And it’s been fascinating and enriching.”
Dagan-Levy describes this approach as “generous leadership”: sharing ideas, data and contacts rather than keeping them within a single organization. Voice of the People’s public hub allows organizations and individuals to review projects and explore possible partnerships.
“If we know we have a report or data, use it,” she said. “It’s not ours.”
That openness matters, Apeloig said, for communities that sometimes feel overlooked in global Jewish discussions.
“Sometimes in Latin American Jewish communities, we feel like we are not being seen or taken into account enough in the global Jewish conversations,” she said.
Political tensions in Israel and the US can complicate common work, Dagan-Levy acknowledged. Israeli elections and political debates often reverberate in Jewish communities abroad.
“The tension here affects our brothers and sisters abroad,” she said.
Still, the council offers a place to compare approaches. Participants from Europe, Australia, Latin America, North America, and Israel may confront similar antisemitic incidents or communal strains but pursue different responses through governments, neighbors, or local institutions.
“We might have the same problems, but we took very different solutions, and we can learn from one another what worked and what did not work,” Dagan-Levy said.
The program’s active cohort work is expected to run for 16 months, including personal exchanges, working groups and an accelerator phase designed to turn proposals into collective action. Participants will then join Voice of the People’s continuing alumni and leadership network.
The organization says it will use a custom algorithm, along with a multi-stage review process, to select candidates based on criteria including geography, generation, professional background, and communal affiliation.
“As we build the next cohort, we are looking beyond titles and traditional definitions of leadership,” Dagan-Levy said. “We want people with local knowledge, lived experience, expertise, creativity and a willingness to work with others, including people who may never previously have thought of themselves as Jewish leaders.”
For Dagan-Levy, the end of the first cohort is not an ending.
“Deborah’s cohort is ending this year, but it’s not the ending,” she said. “This is the beginning. I mean, for me, that’s the commencement.”
The first council began its work during wartime, forcing schedules and plans to change repeatedly.
“Everything we scheduled needed to move,” Dagan-Levy said.
The lesson, she said, was adaptability.
“We have to be adaptive,” she said. “The only thing we control is how do we react to this reality.”
As Rosh Hashanah approaches, Apeloig sees a similar lesson in a family recipe. Her grandmother’s leikaj, a honey cake traditionally prepared for the Jewish New Year, repeatedly overflowed in Mexico City until she realized the city’s altitude required less baking soda.
“It’s just a little metaphor to understand that sometimes you need to adjust,” she said.
The recipe, carried from another place and another generation, worked once it was adapted to its new setting. Apeloig plans to share it, especially with non-Jewish friends, along with the tradition behind it.
“It’s a tradition. It’s a honey cake, and it’s to wish for a healthy and sweet new year,” she said.
For Apeloig, that small act is also outreach.
“It’s the most beautiful hasbara that we can do. Just sharing our Jewish joy, our traditions.”
The pillows in her Mexico City studio began as a detail from a gathering in Haifa. They now represent the larger purpose Voice of the People hopes to sustain: connecting Jews with different histories, languages, and convictions, and turning those relationships into shared action.
Grandma Musha’s Honey Cake (Leikaj)
In honor of Musha Horenkrig de Apeloig, z”l:
Ingredients
1½ cups sugar
5 eggs, separated
1½ cups honey
1 cup vegetable oil
1 tsp baking soda*
¾ tsp ground cloves
4 cups all-purpose flour
¾ cup freshly brewed strong coffee
Juice of 1 lemon
*High-altitude note: If baking in a high-altitude city such as Mexico City, reduce the baking soda. I use approximately ½ teaspoon.
Instructions
Preheat the oven to 150°C.
Separate the eggs. Beat the 5 egg whites until stiff peaks form. Set aside.
In a separate bowl, beat the egg yolks with the sugar until well combined.
Mix the honey and lemon juice together to thin the honey slightly, then add to the yolk mixture.
Add the baking soda, ground cloves, and vegetable oil. Mix thoroughly, making sure there are no lumps.
Add the freshly brewed coffee and mix until incorporated.
Gently fold in the beaten egg whites.
Gradually add the flour, mixing until the batter is thick and homogeneous.
Baking
Lightly grease a 23 × 33 centimeter rectangular baking pan and line the bottom and sides with parchment paper. Lightly grease the parchment as well.
Pour the batter into the prepared pan.
Bake for approximately 1 hour and 15 minutes, or until the cake is golden brown and a wooden skewer inserted into the center comes out clean.
Baking time may vary depending on your oven and altitude.
Once baked, remove the cake from the pan, leaving the parchment paper in place.
Once cooled, wrap it in aluminum foil to help preserve its characteristic moisture.
A little tikun to take with you
Eating and gifting leikaj is about more than wishing for a sweet year. Family recipes carry memories, migrations, traditions, and pieces of the people who came before us.
So while you’re making this one, ask someone in your family about your recipe, the one that deserves to be written down and passed on.
Sometimes l’dor vador, from generation to generation, begins in the kitchen.
I feel compelled to share my grandmother’s recipe with you so that her memory may forever be a blessing. If you bake it, I would love to hear how it turned out - and whether you and your family loved it as much as we do. Please DM me on Instagram @tikuntalks and let me know.
A very special thank you to my sister, Gaby Apeloig, for being the guardian and preserver of Grandma Musha’s leikaj, preserving this piece of our family so that her great-grandchildren can enjoy it today, and so that we can continue carrying it forward for generations to come.
Shana tova u’metuka!
