====================================================================================================

When politics invades art, an Israeli artist seeks common ground at the Venice Biennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:13:56 UTC
08:13:56 KST

Art should, by definition, occupy lofty spheres way above petty politics and other forms of consciousness manipulation for ultimately Machiavellian ends. But – just in case we hadn’t noticed – it ain’t a perfect world.
Indeed, in a utopian society there wouldn’t be any politics or politicians in the first place. Nor would there be any need for rabbis, priests, imams, doctors, lawyers, police, or any other form of authority with the legal, religious or societal power to tell us what to do and what not to do. We would simply take responsibility for our own lives. Now, wouldn’t that be a fine thing?
Art can – should – grant us some respite from all of the negative existential detritus, and from the anxieties that come with everyday life, especially in this relentlessly troubled part of the world. We should be able to glean a sliver or two of hope that there is something unsullied out there after all, something that offers us a life raft that can raise us up above the daily grind and morass of self-interest shenanigans.
Sadly, that isn’t entirely the case, as Belu-Simion Fainaru knows full well. The Romanian-born Haifa resident is one of the best-known Israeli artists on the global scene today. He is an Israel Prize laureate who principally plies his creative pursuit through sculpture and various installation formats. His name constantly pops up in group exhibitions all over the country and abroad, and he is currently representing Israel at the Venice Biennale, the world’s most prestigious international art show.
Politics has reared its ugly head there, big time, and Fainaru has had to deal with his fair share of adverse reactions, boycotts, and protests, and all with complete disregard of the nature and quality of his offerings in the Israeli pavilion. In words of one syllable, the post-Oct. 7 political agenda-driven flack has left its mark on both the artist and the event.
Belu-Simion Fainaru’s art
Before we dug into the unpleasant underbelly, I wanted to get something of a handle on what Fainaru brought to the Biennale plate, with his installation-based spread on show at the Arsenale facility. It opened there on May 9 and runs through November 22.
The centerpiece, Rose of Nothingness, feeds off the writing of 20th-century Jewish-Romanian German-language poet Paul Celan.
The immediate impression, on viewing the grand assembly, is of an association with black milk, a symbolic liquid that fuses life and death, and matter and spirit.
In Fainaru’s work, black water drips into a rectangular pool, forming a quiet space of delineated emptiness that invites contemplation and lingering presence.
The pool prompts thoughts of ink, which naturally leads one to consider writing and memory, thus binding the artistic experience to collective and individual consciousness.
Celan, a Holocaust survivor, fed off the trauma of his World War II experiences, including his constant torment and feelings of guilt at not being able to save his parents from the Nazis’ killing machine.
The most striking example is his “Todesfugue” (Death Fugue), which opens with: “Black milk of morning we drink you evenings; we drink you at noon and mornings we drink you at night; we drink and we drink.” Hence the Fainaru arrangement.
The explanatory text that goes with the installation notes that the first printed edition of the Talmud was produced – by a Christian printer in the early 16th century – in the canal-strewn city that hosts the biennale. That seminal event, it says, turned the Talmud into “a living, open and continuously evolving visual text.”
With that very much in Fainaru’s mind, “the installation unfolds in the tension between presence and absence, calling for engagement with the experience of time, memory, and sustainability.”
The artist’s choice of creative point of reference, he says, goes beyond pure imagery. “This is not the first time that there has been a connection between my artwork and Paul Celan. He is considered a great poet, but I also identify with him in terms of what he represents. He represents Jewish identity, among his several identities. He was a Holocaust survivor, and so were my parents. So we have a common denominator.”
Fainaru also says there was no disciplinary divide to be navigated. “His writing is very visual. There are all sorts of sentences in his poems which I perceive visually, three-dimensionally.”
That includes the Venice installation core. “Milk is white, so when he talks about black milk, that conjures up thoughts of death, the Holocaust, the purity of milk which has been defiled.”
That, for Fainaru, leads straight into one of the burning existential issues of the day. “There is the ecological aspect. They are polluting the world, poisoning it, destroying it. We are poisoning ourselves, too, so there is something current and visceral about the poem as well.”
Fainaru’s immersive approach to Celan’s writing takes him into less obvious domains. “He expressed evil in a very poetic and limited way, very abstractly. That impacts me. In my own way, even though we are talking about a different discipline, I also try to convey the meaning of evil, abstractly. I talk about loss and the Holocaust, but not through corporeal means but by means of associative connections.”
His approach to documenting current affairs is antithetical to the mainstream media’s strident, angled presentational line. “The media outlets are vitriolic and violent. They are always trying to scare us, and show us very shallow material which is not always connected to reality. They create a reality within reality.”
Israel’s representative – in everything
Since taking up temporary residence at the biennale, Fainaru has had more than his fair share of media encounters.
“I think I have given over 100 interviews,” he says. “There were journalists who were friendlier than others. There were tough, provocative questions.”
Fainaru clearly had to keep his wits about him, to avoid providing hostile journalists with cannon fodder for anti-Israel diatribes.
The general approach was, it seems, to treat Fainaru as Israel’s representative in areas that have absolutely nothing to do with his line of work and with the seasoned collateral that made him an appropriate choice for the Israeli slot in Venice.
The time-honored adage in American entertainment circles holds that there is no such thing as bad publicity, as long as they don’t misspell your name. The saying “I don’t care what the newspapers say about me, as long as they spell my name right” is generally attributed to 19th-century showman-philanthropist-politician P.T. Barnum. “I got so much media attention, while other artists had to beg to get people and journalists to come to see their work,” Fainaru smiles wryly.
He also managed to see the upside of the politically motivated media cacophony.
“I contacted [KAN 11 Israel TV show] Sochen Tarbut [Culture Agent, presented by Kobi Meidan]. They said they had no interest and were busy with Book Week. I was amazed,” Fainaru exclaims. “The whole world was interested in the Israeli exhibition at the Biennale, but they weren’t.”
Then again, having to field journalistic attacks and protesters at the art world’s most prestigious event can wear you down.
“I didn’t know what to do,” says Fainaru. “The Foreign Ministry didn’t interfere with my artistic decisions, but I didn’t get any support for my dealings with the media either.”
Enter the oasis of peace
Betwixt the media cacophony, there were some carefully crafted creations to consider inside the Arsenale, which, by the way, is serving as the temporary Israeli exhibition premises at the Biennale while renovation work on the permanent pavilion drags on and on. No doubt, once again, when it comes to supporting our cultural ventures, the national budget is found wanting.
If members of the public actually want to see Fainaru’s work, and manage to negotiate their way into the Arsenale, they will leave the hubbub behind and find themselves in an oasis of peace and tranquility, where they may, if they so wish, be able to get a breather and reflect on the installation and consider their own inner world.
Rose of Nothingness, curated by Avital Bar-Shay, serves as a remedial furlough through the installation’s dynamics and the calming vibe it exudes. Fainaru feels it goes against much of the current artistic-promotional grain, and is something of a throwback into quieter, less financial bottom-line-oriented, more gentle climes.
I suggested that dropping by the Venetian pavilion might be a good idea for all us post-Oct. 7 traumatized Israelis.
“Israelis do visit, but, like Israelis, they want to cram in as much as they can,” he chuckles. “I don’t know how much time they devote to the works in the exhibition.”
Any artist would like his viewers to tarry a while, to consider the aesthetics and philosophical and emotional underpinning of their exhibits, rather than racing past them in an attempt to tick as many sightseeing boxes as they possibly can.
“Time has significance,” Fainaru posits, “time from the past, memory time, time to be with yourself. You need a place to calm down in, calm others, with everything that is going on around us.”
Ain’t that the truth. And he has provided us with everything we might need to soothe our savage, war-torn breast. Rose of Nothingness, for example, comprises an overhead linear system of pipes, fitted with agricultural drippers, that releases water in measured droplets into a rectangular basin below. The water circulates in a continuous loop, establishing a constant rhythm of drip and pause.
As the biennale notes have it: “This subtle cadence evokes breathing – suspension and renewal – drawing the body into an acute awareness of duration. A reservoir of memory, a bodily experience of presence and duration, pulsates, breathes, and renews in a fragile equilibrium of time and consciousness.”
That sounds thoroughly enticing, and curative, and just what the doctor ordered to drop our pulse down a gear or two and introduce an eye-of-the-storm hiatus amid the relentless fight-or-flee continuum that is the general existential state of affairs in this country.
There are other references to temporal awareness, in various directions, in the Fainaru collection in Venice. The aptly named In Search of Lost Time suggests a seemingly futile quest to claw our way back to a juncture where – at least from our present standpoint – the world seemed a better place.
The work features a wall-mounted clock with backward-moving hands. That suggests intervention in reality, and the possibility of imposing our will on the natural order.
That is something of a leitmotif of Fainaru’s oeuvre.
“The work emphasizes the elusive quality of time and the stratified meanings it carries as a subjective state of consciousness shaped by countless personal and environmental factors,” the curatorial text illuminates.
Nostalgia may not be what it once was and, indeed, may involve a modicum of fantasy, of longing for a past that in fact never existed. Renowned 20th-century British writer W. Somerset Maugham put it neatly when he noted that some people are cast into certain life circumstances by providence: “They have always a nostalgia for a home they know not,” he observed.
“The installation relates to the passage of time, offering a journey in search of lost time,” Fainaru explains. “What appears as forward motion becomes backward movement. Tangible matter becomes memory. The work alludes to the impossibility of summing up or containing time, in the hope that the end point is also a point that preceded the beginning.”
Wishful thinking three years after that fateful day in our southern communities and its violent aftermath. But art can do that. Art can offer a crack in the flow of testing reality, an unexpected change of direction that can generate a fleeting emotional and cerebral watershed which may help us to adopt a more subjective view of some formidable baggage. That might just enable us to take a deep breath, a concomitant step back, and reflect on our experiences in a different, more manageable light.
Solidarity from unexpected quarters
Meanwhile, on the support front, Fainaru was delighted to welcome some political A-listers to his exhibition, including German Minister of State for Culture and the Media Wolfram Weimer.
He had some words of comfort after visiting the Arsenale.
“It is important for Germany to show solidarity with Israel and Israeli artists at the biennale,” he stated. “I was deeply impressed by the installation created by artist Belu-Simion Fainaru for the Israeli pavilion.”
Weimer’s Italian counterpart, Alessandro Giuli, also took the time to view the installation, as did some surprising – and very welcome – guests.
“I got a lot of support from Cuba. Their curator came over wearing a nice hat,” Fainaru chirps with a smile. “He told me he’d been asked to sign a letter calling for a boycott of [the exhibition of] Israel. He told them he only boycotts wars, not artists. He said he’d also praised me to other people, that I supported peace and Palestinians. He said I wasn’t the right person to attack. He also said they [boycotters] were very organized and had lots of financial backing.”
There were additional expressions of endorsement from unexpected quarters. “There were Lebanese who came to the Israeli pavilion and were very complimentary. They also said they hope there will soon be peace and that I can come to Lebanon to exhibit.”
There’s more. “The first visitors we had, as the pavilion opened, were Iranians,” Fainaru adds. “They got to us first thing in the morning. We had a wonderful exchange, like we were longtime pals. The warmest reception we got was from Lebanese and Iranians.”
Perhaps there is hope after all. All we need to do, so it seems, is get together on common ground – say, a shared love of art – thereby circumnavigating the shark-infested political waters, and all will be well. To quote late Beatle John Lennon’s anthemic “Imagine” number: “It isn’t hard to do.” ■
For more information: www.labiennale.org/en/art/2026/national-participations

Arab Hadash-Ta’al, Ra’am parties sign agreement to reduce risk of lost votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:13:51 UTC
08:13:51 KST

Hadash-Ta’al and Ra’am signed a surplus vote-sharing agreement on Friday ahead of Israel’s 26th Knesset elections, saying the deal is intended to strengthen their position in the allocation of surplus mandates and reduce the risk of votes being lost.
The agreement brings together two of the main Arab political factions ahead of the election, with the parties saying it is designed to maximize the impact of Arab voters in the distribution of seats.
“The cooperation between the two central political forces among the Arab public will ensure that no vote is wasted in the campaign to bring down the far-right government of [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and [National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir,” the parties said in a statement. “According to the latest polls, the Arab public holds electoral power that could reach approximately 15 mandates.”
The parties added in their joint statement that “the meaning is clear: The vote of the Arab public has the power to decide the entire campaign and prevent the establishment of another bloodshed government led by Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich.”
Under the agreement, the two lists committed to running a “fair and clean election campaign, without slander, defamation, incitement, or falsification.” They also called on activists and supporters to maintain respectful discourse despite their political disagreements. The agreement is expected to be submitted to the Central Elections Committee after the lists receive approval.
Hadash-Ta’al, Balad reunite under the Joint List, Ra'am runs independently
The move follows Ra’am, Hadash-Ta’al, and Balad running separately in the previous election and not signing a surplus vote-sharing agreement. In the current election, Hadash-Ta’al and Balad have reunited under the Joint List, while Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, is running independently.
A Maariv poll published Friday found that the Joint List would receive seven seats and Ra’am five, giving the two Arab parties a combined total of 12 seats.
Surplus vote-sharing agreements explained
A surplus vote-sharing agreement allows the two parties to pool their surplus votes after the initial allocation of Knesset seats following the elections. If the combined surplus is enough to secure an additional seat, one party can receive it, potentially strengthening the bloc to which the parties belong. The deal is only relevant if both parties pass the electoral threshold.
The agreement does not guarantee that every vote will be “preserved,” but it can increase the chances that one of the two parties will receive an additional seat under the Bader-Ofer method.

Israeli documentary NAZA wins Venice Jury Prize, challenges IDF Gaza civilian death claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
23:13:40 UTC
08:13:40 KST

Israeli directors and journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday.
The film, which takes its title from the Israeli military acronym for “collateral damage,” is based on interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and officers who the filmmakers say were involved in planning and operating systems used during the war in Gaza. The documentary alleges that Israel’s military operations have resulted in systematic mass civilian casualties. Israel has rejected the allegations.
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit on Friday categorically rejected the claims raised in the documentary, saying the film relied on anonymous testimonies from individuals whose identities and military roles could not be verified.
“According to the publications, the film relies on anonymous testimonies from individuals whose identities cannot be verified, including whether they served in the IDF, in what capacity, or whether they were involved in the matters about which the allegations are being made,” the statement said.
The military said the documentary included claims regarding national and military strategy that were “clearly beyond the knowledge of junior-level soldiers,” and said it contained references to situations in which IDF Intelligence Directorate soldiers allegedly interviewed for the film “by definition would not have been involved.”
IDF disputes allegations of deliberate civilian harm
The IDF also criticized what it called the “incorrect use of legal terminology by individuals who are not legal professionals,” as well as “internal and absurd contradictions,” including claims that unintended harm resulting from lawful attacks was carried out deliberately or constituted part of “genocide.”
The IDF said it operates in Gaza to protect Israeli civilians while targeting terrorist organizations, primarily Hamas, “in accordance with international law and the laws of armed conflict.” The military said it strikes military targets and makes “unprecedented efforts to minimize harm to civilians,” while accusing Hamas of embedding its operatives and military infrastructure within civilian areas.
“When specific suspicions of violations of the law by an IDF soldier arise, the IDF is fully committed to investigating them and bringing those responsible to justice through independent enforcement mechanisms,” the statement said.
The military added that soldiers who witness potential violations must report them so investigations can be considered, including individuals interviewed for the documentary. Regarding allegations over the use of artificial intelligence in targeting decisions, the IDF said that “decisions regarding the selection and approval of strikes in the IDF are made by human personnel only, in accordance with IDF guidelines, and not by artificial intelligence.”
The documentary received a lengthy standing ovation following its premiere screening on Thursday, with reports saying applause lasted 24 and a half minutes. It is the second consecutive year that a film focused on the Gaza war has drawn major attention at Venice, following The Voice of Hind Rajab, which tells the story of the killing of a Palestinian child during the conflict.
Abraham responds to criticism of documentary
Speaking after the award announcement, Abraham thanked the jury and addressed criticism of the film in Israel.
“I’m thinking of all the people, the Israeli politicians and journalists back home, who are now attacking this film, and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said. “And so much is being done to ask us to not look at reality.”
Abraham said the Israeli intelligence officers interviewed for the documentary described the killing of Palestinians in Gaza as systematic rather than accidental.
“And the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with told us that this mass killing is systemic. Not by accident. But by design,” he said. “Actions of murder and policies that are based on total dehumanization of Palestinians.”
He added that Palestinian journalists had documented events in Gaza from the beginning of the war and accused Israel of silencing their voices.
“This truth has been documented and known from the very first day, thanks to Palestinian journalists,” Abraham said. “More than 200 of them were killed by Israel in Gaza. Their voices were silenced and denied.”
“We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist,” he added.
Abraham calls for international audiences to watch documentary
Abraham called on audiences in Israel, Europe, and the United States to watch the film, saying it was particularly important for Israelis because “it’s our country that is doing these crimes.”
“It’s really important that Europeans watch it, especially here in Italy, because your government and the German government are blocking pressure on Israel that can end this,” Abraham said, adding that it is also important “that Americans watch it, because that country is funding much of the killing.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

Houthis asked US not to intervene in Yemen conflict – Trump (VIDEOS)
Yemen’s Houthis have asked the United States not to intervene in their escalating conflict with Saudi Arabia, US President Donald Trump has said, as Washington seeks to avoid opening another front in the Middle East.
Houthi forces made major gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week, pushing back Saudi-backed government troops and seizing the strategic ports of Mocha and Dhubab, as well as Perim (Mayun) Island at the entrance to the narrow Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The advance has tightened the group’s grip on one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints while threatening another crucial route for Saudi oil exports.
“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump told reporters on Saturday during a visit to Ireland. “They don’t want us to go after them” and “would much prefer not having us involved,” he added.
Trump said the group was allowing most shipping to pass through the Red Sea, adding that “it’s just one country that they’re not too happy with, and we’ll get that straightened out.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly called Trump twice on Thursday and urged him to order US strikes against the Houthis to stop their advance. Trump declined the request, according to Axios, which cited US officials as saying Washington has no plans for direct military intervention for now.
The US is nevertheless providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting data, and roughly 200 American military personnel are providing non-combat support. CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper also traveled to the kingdom for urgent consultations.
Trump confirmed speaking with the Saudi crown prince but did not disclose details of their conversation. “He’s a good friend of mine,” Trump said. “I can just say everything’s going to work out fine and dandy.”
The Houthis have framed their campaign as a fight to drive Saudi-backed government forces out of Yemen and restore the country’s sovereignty.
“We do not target any country except the Saudi enemy,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a spokesman for the group, told RT on Thursday. “In fact, we are committed to protecting the freedom of maritime navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea.”
Al-Bukhaiti also warned that Houthi forces are prepared for a broader confrontation if outside powers join Riyadh, saying Yemen was capable of fighting “up to three fronts” – against Saudi Arabia, Yemeni government troops and any foreign country that becomes involved.
The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi energy facilities in recent weeks, while Riyadh has blamed drones launched from Iraq for a separate attack that forced it to shut down its key East-West oil pipeline.

Higher gas prices in Europe are price of globalist ideology — Dmitriev

Yemen’s Houthi group said early Sunday that it had carried out an attack with ballistic missiles and drones on a military base in southern Saudi Arabia.
In a statement posted on US social media platform X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack targeted weapons depots and command-and-control rooms at the Sharurah base.
A large barrage of ballistic missiles and drones was used, he said, claiming the strikes hit their targets.
Saree said the attack was in response to continued Saudi attacks on Yemen. He warned of larger strikes deeper inside Saudi territory if they continue.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the Houthi claim.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said earlier Saturday that a projectile landed in the Al-Tuwal governorate in the southwestern Jazan region, injuring two people.
It said the projectile also damaged a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles.
Yemen’s map of territorial control has changed in recent days amid escalating confrontations between government forces and the Houthis since July, following years of relative calm.
The Houthis now control the entire western Al-Hudaydah province, according to the group, after advancing in the western Taiz province and capturing the coastal city of Mokha and its Red Sea port.
Their advance also brought them close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime passageways.
Government forces, meanwhile, have made gains in the northern Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border and approached its provincial capital, Al-Hazm.
Clashes are also continuing on fronts in the Marib, Al-Bayda, and Al-Dhale provinces.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis captured the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014.
A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Palestine welcomes declaration of BRICS summit, praises positions supporting Palestinian rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:58:18 UTC
07:58:18 KST

Esra Tekin
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Palestine on Saturday welcomed the declaration issued at the weekend summit of the BRICS grouping of 11 countries, praising its positions in support of the rights of the Palestinian people and the Palestinian cause.
In a statement, the Palestinian Foreign Ministry welcomed the declaration from the New Delhi summit and its “positions and affirmations supporting the Palestinian cause,” particularly its rejection of attempts to forcibly displace the Palestinian people from their land, including Jerusalem; its call for an end to Israeli occupation; its commitment to the two-state solution; and its support for the state of Palestine’s full UN membership.
It also welcomed the declaration’s support for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) and its mandate, as well as its call to protect holy sites and ensure access to them in Jerusalem, protect the Palestinian people, and ensure the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip.
The ministry said the positions are consistent with international law and relevant UN resolutions, and stressed the need to translate them into practical and concrete steps.
It urged the international community to “assume its legal and political responsibilities, and work to implement and enforce international legitimacy resolutions” to ensure an end to crimes and violations committed by the Israeli occupation, as well as all forms of displacement, settlement expansion, and annexation, while protecting the Palestinian people and enabling them to exercise their legitimate national rights, foremost among them their inherent right to self-determination.
The ministry underlined that “implementing the positions and affirmations contained in the BRICS declaration requires ending the Israeli occupation and enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable rights,” including the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state on its land, with Jerusalem as its capital.
Declaration urges preservation of Gaza ceasefire, full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid
Earlier Saturday, a final declaration issued at the conclusion of the BRICS leaders’ summit expressed opposition to the forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The joint summit declaration called for respect for UN Security Council resolutions concerning Gaza.
“We call on all parties to ensure the preservation of the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and the full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid,” it said.
It also expressed concern about the continued violence in the region despite the ceasefire reached last October.
“We call for an end to any policies aimed at the forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, and express concern over any arrangements that could undermine the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights or could lead to legitimizing the occupation or prolonging it,” the statement added.
The declaration called for an urgent and lasting solution to the Palestinian issue and reaffirmed its support for the State of Palestine obtaining full membership in the United Nations.
BRICS is made up of longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa – the origin of the BRICS name – plus more recent members Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
With its expansion to 11 members since 2024, BRICS has become a bloc representing roughly half of the world’s population and around 40% of global economic output.
The 18th BRICS Leaders Summit is due to end Sunday.

Source: Kushner at the annual YES forum in Kyiv on 12 September

Quote: "President Putin's laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]

Celine Dion overcomes rare neurological disorder to perform first concert in 6 years

2026-09-12

Celine Dion overcomes rare neurological disorder to perform first concert in 6 years
Celine Dion wept tears of joy on Saturday as she fulfilled her dream of returning to the stage after years battling a rare neurological disorder, with a sold-out concert in Paris.
The 58-year-old French Canadian singer appeared visibly moved as she opened her first full concert in six years with her 1990s French-language ballad "On ne change pas" ("One Doesn't Change"), singing to a crowd of 30,000 enthralled fans.
"These are, of course, tears of joy. I'm so delighted to see you," Dion said, blowing kisses to the audience at the packed Plenitude Arena on the western edge of Paris.
Her return to the stage underscored a remarkable comeback after stiff-person syndrome, an incurable condition that causes stiffness and cramps, forced her to cancel shows and cast years of uncertainty over whether she would ever perform again.
"The path was rockier than expected," she said, speaking in French and English.
"But I held on to a faint ray of light in the distance, deep in the mountains."
"Tonight, I want to sing for you, sing for myself, sing for life," she added.
The largely female crowd sported sequined dresses and tops, glittered cheeks and T-shirts emblazoned with the star's image or nods to her biggest hits.
"It's unreal to be here!" said Elisabeth Landry, a 38-year-old Quebecer who lives near the star's hometown of Charlemagne.
"I was convinced we'd never see her again, especially not embarking on a run of concerts like this."
French daily Le Parisien said former first lady Michelle Obama was "discreetly attending this first concert."
Just hours before, one of the best-selling singers of all time greeted admirers outside her luxury hotel a short walk from the Arc de Triomphe.
Albertina Cabral, a fan from the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo, said she could barely put her feelings into words.
"It's unbelievable to stay here and to go to the concert and to see Celine so close," she said. "And she's feeling good, she's happy."
Paris spared no effort in welcoming Dion, drawing thousands of fans from across the world, including some who flew in from as far away as the French Polynesian island of Tahiti.
For days, Paris played host to costume contests, giant karaoke parties and tribute cruises on the Seine.
On Friday, the iconic cauldron rose above the Tuileries Garden, echoing the diva's surprise appearance up the Eiffel Tower to perform "Hymn to Love" by Edith Piaf during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics in 2024.
A lyric from the song, "I'd go and fetch the moon if you asked me to," along with the singer's first name, was projected in big letters onto the balloon.
The suburban train station serving the arena has been temporarily renamed "Celine."
Chloe and Katy Rydquist, who traveled from London, had spent around $2,000 on their tickets, saying Dion's return to the stage justified the cost.
"She's a legend," Chloe said.
The star's residency is projected to generate hundreds of millions of euros in economic benefits.
She kicks off her 26-date run with 16 sold-out shows in September and October, before returning for another 10 in May.
Fans who missed out on tickets have found other ways to catch a glimpse of their idol.
Dion has regularly stepped outside the Royal Monceau hotel to greet waiting fans, at times breaking into song and dance with them well into the early hours.
Over her four-decade career, Dion has sold around 260 million albums in English and French, with hits including "It's All Coming Back to Me Now" and "Because You Loved Me."
Dion revealed in late 2022 that she had been diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome. According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, the rare disorder is believed to be an autoimmune condition in which your immune system attacks the healthy cells of your body by mistake.
It can cause "stiff muscles in the torso, arms, and legs," as well as "greater sensitivity to noise, touch, and emotional distress, which can set off muscle spasms," according to the NIH.
It impacts twice as many women as men, the NIH said, and is also believed to be a progressive disorder that worsens over time. While symptoms can be treated with medication, there is no cure.
According to the Johns Hopkins Stiff-Person Syndrome Center, the disorder is estimated to impact only one to two people per one million in population.
Dion has described it as making her feel as though she is being strangled, with cramps so intense they have left her with broken ribs.
She has returned to the stage after what she has described as years of training "like an athlete," doing ballet and Pilates several times a week, as well as voice therapy.

Tens of thousands march across Germany to protest far-right party AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:37:03 UTC
07:37:03 KST

Tens of thousands march across Germany to protest against far-right AfD
Protesters in about 20 cities, including Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, demand the banning of the Alternative for Germany.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across Germany to protest against the Alternative for Germany (AfD) after the far-right party won a state election by a landslide.
About 150,000 demonstrators turned out in roughly 20 cities on Saturday, including Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, in rallies organised by Pruef, a campaign group pushing for a ban on the AfD.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3AfD is rising, but it can still be stopped
- list 2 of 3What are the implications of AfD’s electoral rise for Germany and Europe?
- list 3 of 39/11 at 25: How the ‘War on Terror’ helped mainstream Europe’s far right
Protesters carried signs reading “Ban the AfD now” and “Democracy needs no alternatives.”
“A broad cross-section of civil society is taking to the streets to prevent the enemies of the constitution … from gaining government power,” said Christoph Bautz, head of Campact, another campaign group involved in the protests, which put turnouts at about 25,000 in Hamburg and 12,000 in Munich.
According to police, several thousand more joined separate demonstrations in Berlin.
The AfD held its own counter-rally in the German capital, attended by Kristin Brinker, the party’s lead candidate for Berlin’s upcoming regional election.
The protests follow a stunning result for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, a state in eastern Germany, where the party took nearly 44 percent of the vote on September 6 — far ahead of the roughly 17 percent won by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has long dominated German politics.
The AfD, known for its anti-immigration stance and friendly posture towards Russia, fell just short of an outright majority and is now in talks with other parties to try to form a government, which would make it the first far-right party to lead a German state since the Nazi era ended in 1945.
AfD state leader Ulrich Siegmund called the result historic, telling supporters: “The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with us.” He has since signalled openness to working with other parties, after previously saying he wanted to govern alone.
The AfD’s growing strength has deeply unsettled many Germans, given the country’s history and its commitment to never repeating it.
The party is projected to win 39 of 83 seats in the state parliament, three short of a majority. It now needs a coalition partner, though all mainstream parties have so far refused to govern with the AfD under a longstanding policy known as the “firewall.” The far-right party has never joined a governing coalition anywhere in Germany, at either state or national level.
The unease has fuelled growing calls to ban the AfD altogether, though that would be legally difficult in Germany, and Chancellor Merz has been reluctant to pursue it.

Psychologist on new social contract: Same people will do same thing, only call it something else
He expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform, responding to a question about whether Ukraine truly needs a new social contract.
“A social contract, like any contract, if possible, presupposes the equality of the parties,” Pokalchuk noted.
According to him, historical experience shows that theoretical concepts of a social contract have not been implemented in the form described by philosophers and political scientists.
“And the social ideas that have emerged since—I don’t know—the time of John Locke, for example—are purely speculative. Even by their own authors, these socio-philosophical assumptions have never been effectively implemented, because that’s not how it works. They’re just nice words,” said the social psychologist.
At the same time, in his opinion, a certain social contract is possible in local communities, particularly at the level of local self-government. Although even there are certain caveats, because “all electoral tactics are linked to the corruption of local authorities.”
“That’s why I don’t believe in a social contract. Because if it’s concluded by the same people as yesterday, they’ll simply do the same things, only call it by a different name,” Pokalchuk believes.

However, the then TMC govt had not given land for it. During an event Friday, CM Suvendu Adhikari revealed that DRDO had sent a letter for the project but the then TMC govt at the helm did not respond. "I have okayed it. This will be a big project for West Bengal's development," he said. A source in DRDO also confirmed to TOI that the missile testing project is coming up in Bengal.
The proposed testing range in Junput will be the third major hub for DRDO after the Chandipur sites and the proposed testing centre in Andhra. India has one missile testing facility, known as the Integrated Test Range, which operates across two launch complexes in Odisha: Launch Complex-III at Chandipur-on-Sea and Launch Complex-IV, off Odisha coast.
While Launch Complex-III is used primarily for testing short-range tactical missiles, surface-to-air systems and multi-barrel rocket launchers like the Akash and Pinaka, Launch Complex-IV is designated for long-range strategic weapon trials, including Agni ballistic missile series and K-series submarine-launched missiles.The Chandipur testing facility provides a secure coastal location with a wide, unobstructed eastward trajectory over the Bay of Bengal. The proposed Junput range, located approximately 70km along the Bay of Bengal from Chandipur, will share the workload of the Odisha testing range.

Xinhua Headlines: Xi urges BRICS to stand on right side of history, play pioneering role
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:13:21 CST
07:13:21 KST

NEW DELHI, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Saturday urged BRICS countries to firmly stand on the right side of history and strive to be a pioneer of our times.
When addressing the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Xi noted that this year marks the 20th anniversary of BRICS cooperation, saying the mechanism has become the world's most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries.
Over the past two decades, BRICS has evolved into a broader platform for promoting shared growth, dialogue, and a greater representation of the Global South in international organizations, said analysts, noting that the group is expected to deliver more tangible results and foster a more balanced and inclusive world order in the future.
TWO DECADES OF BRICS COOPERATION
The BRICS cooperation mechanism was formally launched in 2006. The inaugural BRIC summit was convened in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. A year later, South Africa joined the grouping, turning BRIC into BRICS.
Since then, the mechanism has continued to expand in both membership and areas of cooperation. Today, BRICS countries account for nearly half of the world's population, around 30 percent of the global economy and one-fifth of global trade, serving as a force for fostering a more representative and multipolar world and enhancing the voice of the Global South.
Hailing the achievements over the past two decades, Xi said that the BRICS cooperation mechanism has continued to grow and expand, and has demonstrated remarkable vitality and dynamism.
Elaborating on the 20-year history of the mechanism, Xi said it has been 20 years of self-reliance and self-strengthening, adding that BRICS countries have actively explored development paths suited to their own national conditions, setting an example of self-strengthening through unity among emerging markets and developing countries.
The first decade of BRICS cooperation was primarily a period of institutional formation, and the second a period of expansion, said Rakhim Oshakbayev, director of the TALAP Center for Applied Research in Kazakhstan and former Kazakh vice minister for investment and development.
But the significance of BRICS goes beyond the growth of its membership.
Xi said that BRICS countries have established a comprehensive, multi-tiered framework for cooperation, and ushered in a new stage of high-quality development for greater BRICS cooperation.
Rather than replacing existing global institutions, BRICS seeks to strengthen dialogue, equality, mutual respect and cooperation among nations, said Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia.
BRICS, with its expanded membership, provides a platform for emerging economies across the globe to have a stronger voice in global issues such as trade, development, finance, climate change, peace and security, Demissie said.
PIONEERING ROLES
As to the future development of BRICS, Xi called on the grouping to pioneer in advancing innovation-driven development.
BRICS countries, he said, should strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence and push practical cooperation into new areas and to new heights.
China proposed an initiative to promote new industrialization through artificial intelligence among BRICS countries, and is willing to work with all parties to deliver more outcomes in research, development and application, and deepen cooperation in industrial and supply chains, he said.
Oshakbayev said emerging technologies such as AI risk creating new technological divides between countries that possess advanced models, computing power and standard-setting capabilities and those that remain mainly users of technology.
Joint research, research networks, education and training under BRICS could give developing countries greater opportunities to participate in technological innovation, he said.
Xi also called on BRICS to be a pioneer in upholding peace and stability.
Noting that the situation in the Middle East remains complex and fluid, Xi said this war has inflicted serious losses on the people of all countries in the region, and it is against the common interests of the international community.
China will work with fellow BRICS members to play a due role in bringing peace and tranquility to the Middle East, he said.
Diaa Helmy, founder and secretary-general of the Egyptian-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, said BRICS offers an important platform for cooperation rather than confrontation. "Within BRICS we do not compete; we complement one another," he said.
On exchanges among civilizations, Xi called on BRICS countries to champion the common values of humanity and advocate exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations as well as harmonious coexistence.
Such exchanges can help societies better understand one another while respecting differences, Oshakbayev said, adding that BRICS could contribute useful experience to dialogue among civilizations on an equal footing.
Xi further called on BRICS to be a pioneer in reforming and improving global governance.
He urged the group to keep pace with the trend toward greater democracy in international relations, promote a more just and equitable global governance system, and uphold the authority of the United Nations.
Demissie, the expert from Ethiopia, said BRICS is not seeking to replace existing global institutions, but to make global governance more representative and responsive to the interests and aspirations of the Global South.
BRICS RETURNS TO CHINA
In his address, Xi announced that China will assume the rotating chair of BRICS and host the 19th BRICS Summit next year.
During its previous chairmanships, China played a notable role in advancing the BRICS agendas. Over the past two decades, China has hosted three BRICS summits, each marking a new milestone in the group's evolution.
When China hosted its first BRICS summit in the tropical resort of Sanya in 2011, South Africa attended the gathering as a new member for the first time.
Six years later, in Xiamen, Xi proposed the "BRICS Plus" cooperation approach, inviting leaders from non-BRICS members to discuss international development cooperation and deepen South-South cooperation.
When China chaired BRICS again in 2022, the leaders met virtually. China called for a "more comprehensive, close, practical and inclusive high-quality partnership" and emphasized global development. That summit laid the groundwork for the group's major expansion the following year.
As BRICS cooperation enters its third "golden decade," a new chapter begins with China, with the Global South speaking with an even stronger voice.
China is expected to work with other BRICS members to promote a more just and equitable global governance system by advocating multilateralism, greater representation for the Global South in financial and political institutions, said Farhana Paruk, a Cape Town-based China-Africa specialist.
"I believe China's upcoming BRICS chairmanship could open a new phase that places greater emphasis on practical development and narrowing the gaps among the economies of member countries," said Salah El-Din Fahmy, professor of economics at Al-Azhar University in Egypt.
"BRICS is still evolving," Fahmy said, noting that China can help advance this process gradually during its upcoming chairmanship by focusing on areas of common interest among member countries and promoting cooperation that makes the group more cohesive and better able to confront global challenges. ■

Iran, Oman agree on details of Hormuz Strait's new entry, exit routes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:12:45 CST
07:12:45 KST

TEHRAN/DOHA, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Iran and Oman have agreed on the details of new entry and exit routes for the Strait of Hormuz and will brief Gulf countries on the outcome of their consultations at a regional meeting in Muscat on Monday, Iranian officials said on Saturday.
Citing a source close to Iran's negotiating team, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said that the understanding was reached after "intensive technical and diplomatic talks between Iran and Oman, which culminated in a final agreement in late August."
Under the understanding, the Gulf's entry route "lies entirely within Iran's territorial waters," and a portion of the exit route also falls "within Iranian territorial waters," the source said.
The source stressed that the route would operate under Iranian arrangements and the waterway's southern route will be closed once the new system becomes operational, noting that the United States had insisted that the southern route must be opened.
"The understanding in no way means that the Strait of Hormuz will be opened," the source said, adding that Iran has seven conditions for reopening the waterway and has conveyed them to the United States.
The source underlined that the waterway will remain closed unless those conditions are implemented, with reopening depending entirely on the U.S. behavior.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei announced on Friday that Gulf littoral states' foreign ministers are scheduled to meet in Oman on Monday to exchange views on regional issues, including the Iran-Oman talks on designating safe routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Baghaei said the gathering would "hopefully" be attended by foreign ministers from Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq.
"As part of the agenda, we are going to brief the delegations about the results of the Iran and Oman consultations regarding the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that the two countries had conducted the consultations as "the two coastal states of the Strait of Hormuz."
Late last month, Iran and Oman said in a joint statement that they had exchanged views on a proposed phased framework that includes establishing a temporary joint shipping corridor in the strait.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran restricted passage through the strategic waterway, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports.
The Strait of Hormuz, linking the Gulf with the Arabian Sea, is one of the world's most important routes for oil and gas shipments. Oman and Iran sit on opposite sides of the strait and have maintained consultations over maritime security and navigation in the strategic waterway. ■

KYIV-- Russia continued to pound the Ukrainian civilian population, killing at least nine people in attacks throughout the country, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated he'd be willing to meet Russia’s Vladimir Putin at the upcoming G20 summit -- something the Kremlin called “impossible.”
Russia has intensified air strikes throughout Ukraine over the past two months, with the Kremlin hitting power plants and other infrastructure as the potentially brutal winter months loom on the horizon.
Civilian deaths were reported in several cities and regions on September 12 as Ukraine struggles to secure its population amid a shortage of air defense weapons badly needed to intercept high-speed Russian missile.
In Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, the city of some 150,000 people -- which has been under Russian military pressure for months -- local authorities said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period.
"These are not military targets," the city council said in a statement. "They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business."
Vitaliy Bunechko, governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, said a Russian strike hit a grocery store, killing two people in the town of Zvyahel.
Ivan Fedorov, governor of Zaporizhzhia region, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other communities.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryviy Rih's military administration, said two people had been killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.
Russia’s military claimed its forces targeted Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro, and several plants in Kryviy Rih.
The claims could not independently be verified.
In response to Russian attacks, Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses, often deep inside Russia, causing acute energy shortages throughout the country, while both sides have targeted each others' shipping in and around the Black Sea.
Zelenskyy Willing To Meet In Miami
In a interview with German broadcaster Deutsche Welle released on September 12, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet with Putin for peace talks at the December 14-15 Group 0f 20 (G20) gathering in Miami.
"Yes, of course," he said when asked about a meeting.
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. Results matter."
The Kremlin immediately rejected Zelenskyy's offer.
"It is impossible," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told AFP, repeating Russia’s demand that such a face-to-face meeting could only take place in Moscow.
"There is a readiness to meet him in Moscow," said Peskov, who noted that it has not been decided yet whether Putin will attend the G20 gathering.
Zelenskyy has long rejected the possibility of meeting in Moscow at a time when his country is facing a full-scale invasion by Russian forces.
“He can come to Kyiv," Zelenskyy told ABC News in reference to Putin.
"I can't go to Moscow when my country's under missiles, under attack, each day. I can't go to the capital of this terrorist."
Washington is attempting to kick-start long-stalled talks on Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last week, while US President Donald Trump and Putin have conducted phone talks in recent days.
In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place on September 11 while he was in Canada, Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal" and that it was important the two had made a trip to Kyiv as well as Moscow.
Zelensky has said he he plans to meet Trump in late September, although details have not been confirmed.
Trilateral Talks
Meanwhile, a top Ukrainian official suggested US-Russia-Ukraine talks could resume as early as next month.
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office, said a new round of trilateral talks on ending the war may take place in October.
Speaking to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on the sidelines of the Yalta European Security forum in Kyiv, Budanov said Ukraine is preparing for a new meeting in the trilateral format, but he did not provide details.
Earlier, Budanov told The New York Times that the negotiation process would likely intensify after Russia's State Duma elections on September 18–20 and the US midterm elections on November 3.
The last direct talks between Russia and Ukraine came in February in Switzerland, with the US acting as mediator and with Budanov being a part of the Ukrainian delegation.

Both operators have been directed to recall products from market in accordance with Food Safety and Standards (Food Recall Procedure) Regulations, 2017. TNN

The singer wept as she opened her first full concert in six years, amid her battle with the incurable Stiff Person Syndrome

Autistic individuals might be somewhat better at reading emotions of other autistic people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:00:14 UTC
07:00:14 KST

A study comparing the abilities of autistic and non-autistic individuals to recognize other people’s emotions found no overall main differences between the two groups. However, autistic individuals were more accurate at reading the emotional valence of other autistic individuals. The paper was published in Molecular Autism.
Empathy is the ability to understand another person’s thoughts and feelings. It also includes the ability to respond emotionally in a way that reflects or fits what that person is experiencing. Researchers distinguish between cognitive empathy, which involves recognizing and understanding another person’s mental state, and affective empathy, which refers to emotionally responding to another person’s feelings.
Autism has traditionally been associated with difficulties in empathy, especially in understanding other people’s emotions, intentions, and social signals. More recent work, however, has challenged the idea that such difficulties can be explained solely by deficits within autistic individuals. One influential view is the double empathy problem hypothesis. This hypothesis proposes that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people are reciprocal rather than one-sided.
According to this view, autistic people find it difficult to understand non-autistic people, while non-autistic people likewise struggle to understand autistic people because the two groups tend to differ in how they experience and communicate about the world. Research has increasingly found that autistic people tend to report easier communication, stronger connection, and greater comfort when interacting with other autistic people. Likewise, non-autistic people can have more difficulty accurately interpreting the emotions and mental states of autistic individuals than those of other non-autistic people.
Study author Yonat Rum and colleagues conducted a study in which they tested the double empathy problem hypothesis. More specifically, they explored whether autistic and non-autistic individuals differ in their ability to empathize with autistic and non-autistic social targets. These authors hypothesized that non-autistic participants would better empathize with non-autistic social targets, while autistic participants would better empathize with autistic social targets. Empathizing, in this context, meant understanding another person’s feelings accurately.
Study participants were 235 individuals recruited through the Cambridge Autism Research Database (CARD) and word of mouth. 141 of them were autistic. 125 were female. 74% were from English-speaking countries, most often from the UK. Autistic participants’ average age was 48 years, while it was 51 for non-autistic participants.
Study authors prepared an empathic accuracy task that consisted of videos of 5 autistic and 5 non-autistic adults telling autobiographical stories. These individuals reported how they felt while telling the story using a slider on a scale ranging from negative to positive (affective valence). They were continuously adjusting this slider while telling the story. The slider’s position was recorded every 0.5 seconds. After completing the story, these 10 storytellers rated the degree to which they felt 12 emotions (embarrassment, anger, sadness, happiness, disgust, pride, fear, excitement, contentment, stress, calmness, and alertness) on a scale from 0 to 8.
In the course of the study, each participant watched 2 of these videos (randomly selected), one with an autistic storyteller and one with a non-autistic storyteller. They were not told the diagnosis of the storytellers. Participants provided the same ratings as the storytellers, and study authors assessed participants’ empathic accuracy by calculating how much participants’ ratings of a storyteller’s emotional state agreed with the storyteller’s own ratings. Aside from this, participants rated their own feeling of empathy and interest toward the storyteller.
Results showed that participants were somewhat accurate in determining whether a storyteller’s feelings were positive or negative. However, there were no main differences between autistic and non-autistic individuals in the overall accuracy of estimating the specific emotions of the storytellers in the videos. However, when tracking moment-to-moment emotional valence using the continuous slider, autistic individuals were significantly more accurate at tracking the emotions of autistic storytellers compared to non-autistic participants. This small-to-medium advantage suggests an own-group advantage for autistic individuals.
The two groups of participants were equally accurate when assessing non-autistic storytellers. Interestingly, non-autistic individuals rated their own empathy and interest in the storyteller as higher. Additionally, when providing free-text comments, autistic participants frequently described difficulties in identifying emotions and reflected on their own performance, whereas non-autistic participants mostly provided feedback on the task design. This led the researchers to suggest that autistic individuals may underestimate their own empathic abilities.
“Findings suggest partial support for the double empathy problem theory and potential underestimation of autistic participants of their own empathic abilities. Individual variability patterns caution against treating neurotypes as homogeneous categories that alone determine double empathy processes,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of autism. However, it should be noted that study participants rated pre-recorded videos, which is substantively different from assessing emotions during real-life social encounters. Authors also note that autistic participants in their study were volunteers i.e., self-selected, and may not adequately represent the full autism spectrum. The study sample likely did not include autistic individuals requiring greater support to engage in social interactions.
The paper, “Nuances of double empathy in autistic and non-autistic people: examination using the empathic accuracy paradigm,” was authored by Yonat Rum, Noa Feldman, Shir Genzer, Carrie Allison, Ofer Golan, Anat Perry, and Simon Baron-Cohen.

Yemen's government forces have struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea port city of Mocha, military officials announced, as renewed fighting drives tens of thousands of civilians from their homes.
State news agency Saba reported that government troops destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed several Houthi fighters near Mocha and on the city's outskirts.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed that Saudi aircraft carried out 129 air strikes against areas under their control over the past 48 hours.
The fighting follows a week-long Houthi offensive in which the group captured the remainder of Yemen's Red Sea coast and strategic islands, cementing its control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The waterway has become vital for Saudi oil shipments following disruptions to Gulf routes, while the Houthis have declared an active blockade against Saudi Red Sea ports.

Displacement surges
The clashes have triggered widespread displacement. The UN migration agency confirmed that 76,000 people have fled the fighting since July—a figure that has quadrupled over the past week alone—warning that humanitarian needs are severely outstripping available relief supplies.
The fall of Mocha forced thousands to flee toward Aden, the temporary base of the internationally recognised government.
Displaced residents reported being given half an hour by advancing forces to leave their homes, with many arriving in Aden without access to basic shelter.
Diplomatically, US news site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice with US President Donald Trump last week to request American air strikes against the Houthis, a request Washington rejected.
Trump acknowledged speaking with the Saudi crown prince, remarking that the Houthis "don't want to fight with us" and predicting that "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy."
More than 500 people have been killed since fighting flared in July, threatening to unravel years of relative calm.

Brics opposes unilateral trade steps like EU carbon border tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:35:56 UTC
06:35:56 KST

PM Modi in a family photo with other leaders at Brics Business Forum 2026. (ANI)
NEW DELHI: Brics nations Saturday opposed unilateral trade measures such as EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), saying such measures undermine efforts by developing countries aimed at addressing the adverse impacts of climate change.Though they recognised the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to meet climate goals, the grouping’s members sought to delink any unilateral punitive action from achieving a common goal and pitched for energy security for all based on a pragmatic approach where “fossil fuel”, they said, will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix”, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies, in addition to renewable sources and nuclear.
CBAM, which entered its operational regime on Jan 1, is a tool to put a price, through imposing a border tax, on carbon-intensive goods, like iron and steel, aluminium and cement, that are entering the 27 EU nations.Though BRICS nations opposed the proposal from the time it was conceived, arguing that the unilateral move placed an additional burden on businesses in developing economies due to embedded emissions in their products, they made their points a part of New Delhi Declaration calling it “punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures that are not in line with international law”.
Without any attempt to dilute their respective efforts to meet climate action goals under the Paris Agreement, the nations called for greater actions based on equity and the UN’s principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in light of different national circumstances.
They also highlighted the need to enhance energy security by ensuring energy market stability and maintaining undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources including fossil fuels. Incidentally, four of the BRICS group countries such as Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iran and UAE are among the major global exporters of fossil fuel.Sending a positive signal ahead of COP31, scheduled to take place in Turkey in Nov, they called on all countries to uphold their commitment to maintain and scale up efforts to combat climate change, and expressed their confidence in multilateralism to address the global challenge.

He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Citing the fuel price comparison portal clever-tanken.de, the newspaper added that a liter of diesel cost around 2.8 euros at one Berlin gas station on Saturday.
A day earlier, diesel had already reached a new monthly high, with the average daily price exceeding 2.38 euros, according to statistics from the consumer portal benzin.jetzt. There is no clear-cut answer to whether motorists should fill up despite such high prices, the newspaper said. The situation in Yemen escalated sharply in early September, when the Yemeni rebel movement launched an offensive in the southwest of the country. Israeli-directed film on Gaza killings wins Special Jury Prize at Venice Film Festival
"NAZA," a new documentary from two Israeli directors, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, the festival's third-most prestigious award for a screened film.
According to the film's official synopsis, "NAZA," directed by Oscar-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, reveals "in detail the systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza" during the war following Hamas' massacre on October 7, 2023. The film's title comes from the Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage.
Its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday earned a record 25-minute standing ovation. According to the festival's management, it was the longest recorded standing ovation for a filmmaker at any festival.

Revolut handed sensitive customer data to scammers – media

Unknown Publisher

06:32:31 KST

Revolut handed sensitive customer data to scammers – media
London-based fintech company Revolut disclosed sensitive customer information to scammers after receiving fraudulent requests sent from a “legitimate government agency email domain,” according to media reports on Saturday.
The exposed data included customers’ birth dates, phone numbers, postal and email addresses, as well as copies of passports and driver’s licenses, according to a notification Revolut sent to affected clients and cited by the online newspaper TechCrunch. The compromised data may also have included verification selfies, account statements, and transaction histories, according to the report.
Revolut confirmed the breach to both TechCrunch and Reuters, saying a “limited” number of customers had been affected by a “sophisticated external impersonation scam where an unauthorized third party utilized a legitimate government agency domain email to submit fraudulent requests for information.”
Co-founded by Russian-born entrepreneur Nik Storonsky in 2015, Revolut describes itself as the “world’s first truly global bank,” which provides digital banking services to more than 80 million customers worldwide.
The incident comes as Revolut has been rapidly expanding internationally. A little over a month ago, it was granted a banking license in France, while the company has also been expanding its presence in markets including India, Mexico, and the UAE. Last week, the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a conditional approval to Revolut, allowing it to set up a bank in the country.
Late last month, police on the British island of Jersey warned Revolut users of an uptick in fraud cases, where the victims had received a telephone call from scammers posing as Revolut support or security teams.
Several countries have also taken issue with the company’s practices in recent years. In April, Italian authorities slapped the online bank with fines totaling €11.5 million ($13.25 million) over alleged unfair commercial practices. Last year, the central bank of Lithuania fined Revolut €3.5 million, accusing it of failing to comply with money laundering prevention regulations.

Two pro-Russian 'media figures' from Mariupol charged with collaboration
The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"Under the procedural supervision of prosecutors from the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office, two residents of Mariupol and the Kalmiuske district were charged in absentia. They are accused of collaboration activities (Part 6 of Article 111-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), while one of them is additionally charged with justifying and denying Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine (Part 1 of Article 436-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)," the statement said.
In May 2022, a 30-year-old Mariupol resident, while in occupied Donetsk, met with representatives of a local "online publication." During the interview, he publicly accused Ukrainian defenders of shelling Mariupol. In particular, he voiced false Kremlin propaganda narratives alleging that the Ukrainian Armed Forces had deliberately targeted civilians at the beginning of Russia's invasion. According to the prosecutors, his account of the so-called liberators, accompanied by words of personal gratitude to the president of the aggressor state, was published on a pro-Russian social network.
According to the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office, in November 2023, the man became a correspondent for Komsomolskaya Pravda and RIA Novosti and continues to promote a negative attitude toward Ukraine among his audience.
The other suspect is a 42-year-old TV presenter for a "republican media holding," law enforcement officials said. In 2024, she hosted a program about a deceased participant in the so-called "special military operation." During a discussion with his relatives and other representatives of the Russian Armed Forces, the TV presenter deliberately manipulated public opinion, portraying the occupiers as "heroes." In 2026, during an interview with a "military cameraman" and a member of the "people's council" of the quasi-republic, she also approved of the actions of Russian forces on the front line and spoke positively about the activities of the occupation authorities.
The two "media figures," who have been placed on the wanted list, face up to 12 years in prison, with a ban on holding certain positions or engaging in certain activities for up to 15 years, as well as confiscation of property.

Free rail travel expanded to bereaved veteran families this Remembrance weekend
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

Free rail travel expanded to bereaved veteran families this Remembrance weekend
Bereaved military family members can travel for free on National Rail services to attend Remembrance events between 7 and 8 November 2026.
- hundreds of bereaved military family members will be able to travel by rail free of charge this Remembrance weekend across Britain
- offer will help families attend Remembrance services and commemorative events, including the Cenotaph, without the cost of travel being a barrier
- families have until 16 October 2026 to apply for free tickets, helping more bereaved relatives take part in the nation’s Remembrance
Hundreds of bereaved military family members will be able to travel by train free of charge this Remembrance weekend (7 to 8 November 2026), helping them attend memorial services and commemorative events to honour loved ones who died while serving in the Armed Forces.
For the first time, one next of kin of a service person who died while serving will be able to travel free of charge on National Rail services to attend Remembrance weekend events.
The move builds on the existing free travel offer for serving personnel and veterans, giving people breathing space and ensuring travel costs are not a barrier for families taking part in remembrance and reflection.
Eligible family members wishing to take up the offer have until 16 October to apply for a free ticket through the Defence Medical Welfare Service.
Rail Minister, Lord Hendy, said:
  Remembrance weekend is a time for the nation to come together to honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice whilst serving our country.
Bereaved families are at the heart of these commemorations and the cost of travel should not prevent them from being there to remember their loved ones.
Extending free rail travel to next of kin will help more families attend Remembrance events, standing alongside communities, veterans and serving members of our Armed Forces as we honour and remember those who served.
Minister for Veterans and People, Calvin Bailey, said:
  Remembrance is an opportunity for the nation to come together in recognition of the service and sacrifice of our Armed Forces. For bereaved families, this is a deeply personal time.
We must never forget that behind every name we remember is a family whose lives have been changed forever. Providing free rail travel will help bereaved relatives come together and honour their loved one without financial barriers.
Mikki Brett, the widow of the late Chief Petty Officer (CPO) Stuart Brett, who served in the Weapons Engineering branch of the Royal Navy and died in service in April 2023, spoke with Defence Minister Calvin Bailey this week.
Mikki Brett said:
  It’s fantastic news that the in-service bereaved have been recognised for the support given to their loved ones with free train fares to remembrance events this year.
Mikki is already registered to come to the Cenotaph on Remembrance Sunday and will benefit directly from the new travel offer for those bereaved in service.
Ola Ogun, Co-CEO of Rail Delivery Group, said:
  Railways have long been connected to remembrance commemorations, recognising the importance of their contribution during wartime. As an industry, we are proud to continue supporting this important national occasion by offering free travel to serving personnel and veterans.
This year, we are especially pleased to extend that support to one next of kin of those who died while serving in the Armed Forces, recognising not only the sacrifice of those who served, but also the families who continue to carry their legacy and honour their memory.
A spokesperson for SSAFA, the Armed Forces charity, said:
  SSAFA welcomes the Department for Transport’s decision to extend free travel to bereaved military families during the Remembrance weekend.
This change ensures that those who have lost loved ones in the service of their nation can travel to pay their respects without facing financial strain. It is a deeply meaningful gesture that properly honours the sacrifices of our Forces families, ensuring they can stand together with the nation in remembrance.
