Senegal eyes homemade satellites amid African space race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:07 UTC
01:36:07 KST

Senegalese engineers in hairnets and white gloves are carefully assembling a nanosatellite at a French lab — another step toward fostering their own space industry at home.
Preparations are already under way for the building of satellites at a new headquarters for Sensat, Senegal’s national space program, outside Dakar — part of a breakneck push by several African space agencies jostling for their own piece of the final frontier.
“We have mastered the manufacturing process,” Gayane Faye, chief of Sensat, told reporters in the sterile lab at the University of Montpellier in southern France.
Photo: AFP
The engineers from Sensat built their first satellite — Gaindesat-1A — in collaboration with the Montpellier scientists, launching it in 2024. Gainde means “lion” in the local Wolof language.
NO MORE COACHING
For the follow-up, Gaindesat-1B, which is designed to collect environmental and climate data, “we’ve removed the coaching component,” Faye said.
It is part of a drive for technological independence by Senegal, mirrored in many parts of Africa.
Representatives from the continent were a key presence at the International Space Summit in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.
Across Africa, national space budgets have grown to US$800 million, said Temidayo Oniosun, founder of Lagos-based consultancy Space in Africa, up from less than US$300 million in 2018.
That is a tiny fraction of the world total, which was US$132 billion in 2024, 60 percent of it from the US, but it is growing. The African Union has a new continental space agency in Cairo and the number of countries on the continent with a space program has jumped from eight to more than 20 since 2018, according to Oniosun.
Africa’s entry into space is not entirely new: Egypt launched its Nilesat 101 from French Guyana in 1998, a first for the continent.
Nigeria’s national space agency was founded the following year, sent its first device space-bound in 2003 and runs two satellites in orbit — one for communications and the other run by the military’s separate space agency, Oniosun said.
SOUTH AFRICA
South Africa, another historic player, is home to a ground station that has overseen communications for hundreds of launches and a second facility being developed with NASA is due to open within two years.
Italy built a satellite-launching station on the Kenyan coast in the 1960s that operated until 1988.
Kenya developed its own satellite, Taifa-1, that launched from a SpaceX rocket in 2023.
Even restive Somalia could have its own space port as part of a US$6 billion partnership with Turkey announced last year.
New players continue to join the rush: Ivory Coast named its first space agency director last month and is to host the African Space Expo later this month.
Better satellite data are seen as key for urban planning and environmental monitoring, which are major issues on a continent whose cities are growing at a rapid rate.
“For the first phase of Africa’s space development, success was often measured by whether a country could launch a satellite,” said Richard Folly of Togo-based African Geospace, whose company has worked on flood risk and disaster management. “The next phase has to ask a harder question: What economic, strategic or societal value is that satellite producing?”
There is also the question of independence in an industry still dominated by non-African space agencies and firms.
Despite the country’s long-running satellite program, Nigerian agencies “don’t build technology locally,” Oniosun said.
Senegal is determined to start generating its own satellite images, as “certain services cannot even be carried out because we lack the means to buy them,” Faye said.
For the next satellite, Sensat’s third, “we aim to move toward developing our own technology — specifically, our own payload to be flown on the satellite.” Then, if the infrastructure is ready, “the fourth satellite can be built entirely in Senegal.”

Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India yesterday called for calm in the Middle East, in a joint statement issued at a summit in New Delhi.
“We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation,” the statement said.
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with member states Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
Photo: Sputnik via Reuters
However, a statement was issued at the leaders’ meeting yesterday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India.
The statement also condemned attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities.
“We express serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law and relevant resolutions of the IAEA,” it said. “Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm.”
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), speaking yesterday at the opening of the two-day summit, said that the Middle East war “does not serve the common interests of the international community,” Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are all at the summit.

Live-fire test to be held near Pingtung this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:03 UTC
01:36:03 KST

The military is holding live-fire drills featuring missiles, rockets and drones, involving all service branches and the coast guard at Jioupeng Base (九鵬基地) in Pingtung County this week, a source said.
The exercise is expected to involve Patriot, Tian Kung (Sky Bow, 天弓), Hsiung Feng (Brave Wind, 雄風) and Land Sword II (陸射劍二) missiles to practice long-range precision strike capabilities, they said
Coast guard vessels would fire anti-ship missiles to drill the joint combat capabilities of the armed forces and the coast guard in wartime.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
With the exercise hosted annually on an rotating basis by the navy and air force, this year’s exercise is hosted by the navy, and a live-fire warning notice for sea and air targets was issued for the exercise area, which covers a large area off the east coast, the source said.
The navy’s announcement said three areas are designated for this exercise.
Zone 1 stretches from the sea east of Taimali (太麻里) in Taitung County, to Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻) in Pingtung County.
Zone 2 extends from the boundary between Taitung and Pingtung to the sea east of Green Island (綠島) and Orchid Island (蘭嶼).
Zone 3 is in the sea east of Taitung County’s Chenggong Township (成功) and Taimali.
The restricted sea and air zones are the same as those used in drills for the past three years.
Although the announcement only mentioned sea and air targets, without going into the specifics, the source said fighter jets, helicopters and drones would enter the area.
A military source said the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) rocket artillery, with its 300km range, and the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 missile, a major air defense system for western countries, are unlikely to be used for this exercise.
The military is expected to incorporate HIMARS batteries into future drills, they said.
The Patriot missile would not be featured in this live-fire exercise unless approved by the US, for two reasons, they said.
The first is to deny unfriendly observers a chance to see it in flight, as firing missiles could allow potential adversaries to gather performance data with reconnaissance or intelligence-gathering aircraft or vessels. The second is cost, as each missile fired costs more than NT$100 million (US$3.16 million), the source said.

Lawmaker urges review of risk to energy supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:03 UTC
01:36:03 KST

Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chen Kuan-ting (陳冠廷) yesterday urged the government to conduct an early energy risk assessment as Middle East tensions rise.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs, the Energy Administration, CPC Corp, Taiwan and Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) are among the authorities and companies Chen said should prepare.
Such preparations are necessary as the risks of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz increase, while Iran-backed Houthi militants are advancing into and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, potentially cutting off access to the Red Sea and Suez Canal, Chen said.
Photo: screen grab from the CPC Corp, Taiwan Web site
If the situation in the Middle East continues to worsen, air and sea freight costs would increase, as would costs for the petrochemical industry, driving up domestic commodity prices, he said.
CPC should compile a list of the dates, origins and routes of oil and natural gas tankers expected to deliver to Taiwan over the next few months, so it can determine which shipments are expected to cross the Strait of Hormuz or pass through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Chen said.
The company should also consult its contacts in the US, Australia and other non-Middle Eastern crude-producing countries to arrange possible alternative sources, he added.
Chen also suggested that the ministry conduct an energy-disruption stress test based on a scenario in which maritime shipments of crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait are disrupted.
The test should assess how long Taiwan’s reserves would last, priorities for supplying power to civilian and industrial users, and the time required to receive deliveries from alternative sources, he said.
Being prepared would reduce the costs Taiwan could face if countries around the world began competing for energy supplies and shipping capacity, Chen said.
Taiwan should also consider how the US is prioritizing its strategic and military resources, as security concerns in the Middle East, Europe and the Indo-Pacific region are simultaneously placing pressure on its production of air-defense missiles, munitions, ships and logistics, he said.
Taiwan’s preparations for energy, munitions, uncrewed vehicles, communications redundancy and critical goods would afford the nation more choices when responding to future changes in the regional situation, he said.
Chen cited a report by the US think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, which said that the US military has used large quantities of munitions in its military operations against Iran, with stocks of some air-defense and precision-strike missiles estimated to have fallen by more than half.
Taiwan should also diversify its sources of asymmetric-warfare equipment, Chen said, ensuring that production and replenishment capacity is available domestically and at overseas facilities.

US marks 25th anniversary of 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:01 UTC
01:36:01 KST

The US on Friday commemorated the 25th anniversary of the devastating Sept. 11, 2001, attacks with a poignant ceremony in New York marked by US President Donald Trump’s absence and searing criticism from victims’ relatives.
In an unusual move, Trump paid his respects at the Pentagon, not the event in New York, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and most of the 2,977 victims were killed, upending the global status quo.
The Republican billionaire sought to link the “war on terror” that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.
Photo: Reuters
“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today,” Trump said. “We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win.”
US Vice President J.D. Vance and Trump’s four living predecessors — Republican George W. Bush, who was in office during the attacks, and Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton — attended the event at Ground Zero in lower Manhattan. There, a huge crowd gathered for the somber annual ceremony, which retraced the events of 9/11 minute by minute, concluding shortly before 1pm.
As usual, the names of the victims were read out, and a bell was rung to mark major moments in the attack.
The event is generally apolitical with no speeches.
However, several bereaved family members who read out the names of those killed criticized Saudi Arabia and US leaders’ closeness to the kingdom.
Terry Strada, whose husband, Tom Strada, died in the Twin Towers, unleashed a stinging attack on Riyadh, accusing it of complicity in the attacks, and denouncing former presidents who were in attendance.
“You are missed more with each year that passes, but how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?” she asked.
The attacks were carried out by mostly Saudi hijackers and orchestrated by al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi.
“For 25 years, administration after administration — including leaders in front of us here today — chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with a 9/11 family,” Strada said, calling for action from the absent Trump.
In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim leader, attended the Ground Zero event despite a campaign urging him to stay away.
That effort was spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post newspaper and former New York mayor and Trump ally Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the crisis and was also present on Friday.
The petition gathered more than 100,000 signatures.
A small anti-Islam protest gathered at City Hall and marched towards Ground Zero, flanked by a heavy police presence and counter-protesters.
Mamdani won plaudits for revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.
After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.
The CIA also declassified and published dozens of 9/11-related presidential intelligence briefs to coincide with the 25th anniversary.
Nineteen al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four airliners on the nearly cloudless autumn day in 2001. Two of the jets slammed into the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, causing the iconic skyscrapers to collapse.
A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth — believed to have been aiming for Congress or the White House — crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.
About 100 million Americans have been born since or are too young to remember the traumatic day.
Sophia Rotunno, 58, said she remembered watching the first tower fall with colleagues back in 2001, and also remembered helping those affected in the aftermath.
“All we could do is support them, and be there for when they went to memorials, or be there for when they came home, and hug them, and pray for them,” she said. “It was a hard time for everybody afterward — and New York did recover.”

Taiwan in Time: When Keelung hosted Taiwan’s largest Korean community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:00 UTC
01:36:00 KST

Sept 14 to Sept 20
Hwang Tae-im’s in-laws were among the many Korean families that congregated in Keelung after World War II, hoping to board a ship home. Japanese colonial rule had ended in both Korea and Taiwan, and many Koreans were eager to return to their newly-liberated homeland.
Around 3,000 Koreans were recorded living in Taiwan in 1943, with Keelung hosting the largest population at 612.
Photo : CNA
However, only one ship arrived to repatriate civilians, leaving many, including Hwang’s in-laws, stranded in Keelung. When the Korean War broke out in 1950, they gave up going home and settled in Keelung’s Shengli Alley (勝利巷, now Lane 656, Zhongzheng Road), which became known as Korean Street. A 1947 register shows 197 Koreans in Keelung, accounting for more than half of the 358 recorded in Taiwan.
Hwang, who arrived in Taiwan in 1971 to marry her husband, is one of the last Korean residents of Shengli Alley. She operates a hair salon that also sells homemade kimchi.
An impromptu conversation with Hwang is the centerpiece of South Korean artist Ho Bin Kim’s latest three-channel video work. It is the 13th episode of his “Reality Sandwich” documentary series, which has evolved from free-form conversations with artists around the question “What is Reality Sandwich?” to exploring the global Korean diaspora in its past three episodes.
Photo courtesy of Ho Bin Kim
Kim spent the past four months as a resident artist at the Hsinchu City Art Site of Railway Warehouse (新竹市鐵道藝術村), where his solo exhibition opens Tuesday at 2pm.
“This part of Korean migration is a gap in history that’s not talked about a lot either in Korea or in Taiwan … A lot of people are surprised,” he says.
HARD LIFE ON THE DOCKS
Photo: Han Cheung, Taipei Times
Even after Japan annexed Korea in 1910, few Koreans moved to Taiwan. Government statistics show that there were only 20 Korean residents in 1918. Things started to change with the March First Movement against colonial rule in 1919, while the effects of colonial land policies contributed to increasing numbers of Koreans heading overseas in the 1920s.
Scholar An Seong-su’s study on the Korean Church in Keelung is one of the few academic resources on this migration.
By 1930, there were 898 Koreans in Taiwan. According to government data, most men either worked in the fishing industry or factories, or were traveling vendors and sailors. Women mostly worked in the service industry, with 160 listed as waitresses and 127 as sex workers. Aside from some business owners, most lived a hardscrabble life.
Photo: Photo courtesy of Ho Bin Kim
In 1935, Keelung’s Korean population reached 358, surpassing Taipei and Kaohsiung. This number continued to grow following the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937. The Japanese began sending Korean soldiers to Taiwan, while some Korean women were forced or deceived into coming here to work in the sex industry or as “comfort women” for the military.
The conscription of Japanese fishermen also created a labor shortage in Taiwan, as relatively few Taiwanese worked in the industry. This led to the recruitment of more Korean fishermen, especially to Keelung.
THOSE WHO STAYED
After Japanese surrender, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) announced in 1946 that a ship would arrive from China to repatriate Korean soldiers and residents. The soldiers were gathered in Taipei and underwent political reeducation classes for three months before being sent home.
Civilians across Taiwan sold their belongings and headed to Keelung to await repatriation. However, not everyone made it in time or got a space on the ship. Along with those who chose to stay, many left behind settled in Keelung’s Shengli Alley and found work in the fishing industry, where they initially received preferential treatment from the government because of the pressing need to keep the facilities vacated by the Japanese operating.
Researcher Yoshihisa Amae writes in “Becoming Korean: Decolonization, repatriation and the everyday lives of ethnic Koreans in postcolonial Taiwan” that 173 out of 197 Korean residents of Keelung were involved with the Taiwan Fishery Corporation, which offered stable jobs, free housing and opportunities to serve as captains and chief engineers.
Another group that stayed were sex workers who were struggling financially and unsure about their prospects in Korea. Others arrived afterward for different reasons, including those fleeing the Chinese Civil War.
A Korean elementary school opened in 1949 in a Taiwan Fishery Corporation warehouse. It got its own building in 1952. One of the better-known alumni is Jen Chiang-ta (任將達), founder of independent music pioneer Crystal Records. Born in 1956, he grew up in Shengli Alley at a time when about half the residents were Korean, he says in a Central News Agency article.
Taiwan’s first Korean Christian church was established in Keelung in 1950, serving as an key community institution. Hwang wanted to marry a Christian man, while her in-laws insisted that their children marry Koreans, so she agreed to move to Taiwan to join the family.
The advantage enjoyed by Korean fishery workers did not last long, however, and by the mid-1950s they were being replaced by trained Taiwanese, Amae writes. Many lost their jobs and suffered economically. This continued into the 1970s, improving only in the 1980s as their children graduated from university and landed better-paying jobs. Eventually, most Koreans of Shengli Alley either died or moved away.
REALITY SANDWICH?
Kim takes the title “Reality Sandwich” from Allen Ginsberg’s book, which he says he does not plan to ever read. Keeping the concept open-ended, he uses it as an abstract phrase in his documentaries, asking participants to offer their own interpretations or thoughts on what it might mean.
During his visit to Keelung, Kim stayed at the Aloha Hotel. Its old appearance allowed him to imagine what it might have been like for Koreans arriving in Taiwan decades ago, while its name also alludes to Korean migration to Hawaii and the US role in World War II, which helped shape the fate of Koreans in Taiwan. In one channel, he films himself discovering in his room six century-old articles about Korean immigrants that he found in the Taiwan Daily News.
Another channel shows a time-lapse overlooking the ocean and the area around Shengli Alley from Heping Island. The indoor and outdoor spaces converge in the center channel, which focuses on Hwang’s hair salon and its partially outdoor space.
The encounter with Hwang was unplanned. Kim had gone to Shengli Alley without knowing what he would find and happened upon her shop, the only one still open on Korean Street.
The conversation is casual, with Hwang talking about her experiences while also asking Kim questions about his personal life. At one point, a longtime customer arrives for a haircut.
“I tried not to ask a lot of questions,” he says. “All the information she gave me was because she wanted to give it to me.”
Hwang has retained her Korean citizenship, meaning she doesn’t receive social welfare or elderly benefits in Taiwan. She tells Kim that in South Korea, she is considered an overseas Korean and does not receive a pension there either.
“Even when I go back to Korea, I’m not Korean,” she says in the video. “I’m also not Taiwanese in Taiwan.”

Taiwan needs an economic shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:59 UTC
01:35:59 KST

Taiwan and its partners have devoted enormous attention to deterring a Chinese military attack. Taiwan is increasing defense spending, acquiring asymmetric capabilities, expanding civil defense and preparing critical infrastructure for a potential blockade or invasion. The US, Japan and Australia are simultaneously strengthening their military capabilities across the Indo-Pacific region.
These measures are necessary, but China does not rely exclusively on military power to pursue its political objectives, and the coalition seeking to preserve peace in the Taiwan Strait should not rely exclusively on military deterrence either.
Taiwan needs an economic shield.
China has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to use trade and access to its enormous domestic market as instruments of political pressure. Taiwan has experienced restrictions on agricultural products and the suspension of preferential tariffs. Australia faced restrictions affecting products including barley, wine and coal after relations with Beijing deteriorated. Lithuania encountered Chinese economic pressure after allowing Taiwan to establish a representative office in Vilnius using the name “Taiwanese.”
These cases demonstrate a fundamental advantage China possesses when exercising economic coercion: Beijing can concentrate economic pressure against one country while the target absorbs much of the disruption individually.
Taiwan and its partners could change that calculation by making economic coercion against one country a problem for many.
The US, Japan, Australia, the EU and Taiwan could establish a coordinated mechanism to support economies subjected to Chinese economic pressure. When Beijing restricts imports in response to a political disagreement, participants could increase purchases of affected products, accelerate investment, provide financing, facilitate access to alternative markets or temporarily reduce trade barriers.
The objective would not be to replace every dollar of trade lost with China. Nor should it be economic decoupling. China remains one of the world’s largest economies and an indispensable trading partner for many countries.
Instead, the objective should be to make it progressively harder for Beijing to individually isolate and punish countries.
Australia’s experience demonstrates why this could work. Chinese restrictions beginning in 2020 imposed significant costs on some Australian industries, but exporters redirected products toward other markets. Australia did not capitulate politically, and many restrictions were eventually removed as bilateral relations improved.
Lithuania provides another example. When it faced Chinese economic pressure over its relationship with Taiwan, the EU challenged China’s measures at the WTO and subsequently established its Anti-Coercion Instrument.
Economic coercion becomes less effective when its target has alternatives and external support. Rather than improvising that support after each confrontation begins, Taiwan and its partners could prepare it beforehand.
Beijing has spent decades reducing the number of countries formally recognizing the Republic of China. Countries switching recognition can subsequently develop commercial relationships, financing arrangements and political networks with China that increase the potential cost of reversing their decisions.
A government might eventually conclude that the economic benefits expected from relations with China have not materialized, that dependence on China has become excessive, or simply that restoring relations with Taiwan better serves its interests. Yet changing course could expose it to Chinese economic retaliation.
Beijing does not need to prove that retaliation would devastate a country considering returning to Taiwan. It only needs to make the potential costs sufficiently high and uncertain to discourage it.
A collective economic shield could weaken that deterrent.
If a former Taiwanese diplomatic partner independently decided to restore relations with Taipei, it would know that it would not necessarily confront the consequences alone. Taiwan could expand development cooperation and investment, while the US, Japan, Australia and European partners could help provide alternative markets and financing.
This should not become another form of checkbook diplomacy. Countries should remain free to maintain relations with Beijing if they believe doing so serves their interests. The purpose would be to ensure that recognition of China does not become economically irreversible simply because governments fear the consequences of reconsidering it.
The same architecture could become another component of deterrence across the Taiwan Strait.
A military coalition defending Taiwan would always face limitations. The US, Japan and potentially Australia possess military capabilities relevant to a Taiwan contingency, but many governments that would strongly oppose an attack would be unwilling or unable to send ships, aircraft or soldiers into a conflict with China.
Economic participation has a much lower threshold.
The EU could contribute through financial measures, technology restrictions, investment controls or alternative markets. Asian economies could help preserve supply chains. Pacific countries could provide diplomatic and economic cooperation. Latin American governments that would never contemplate military participation could contribute through trade and diplomatic coordination.
Taiwan’s deterrence coalition could therefore become much larger economically than it could ever become militarily.
That is important because deterrence depends on calculations made before aggression. Chinese leaders contemplating force against Taiwan must assess not only whether the People’s Liberation Army could achieve its military objectives, but also the economic and political consequences that would follow.
A prearranged economic coalition would make some of those consequences more predictable.
Participants would not need to promise identical sanctions. Instead, they could establish mechanisms for supporting countries subjected to retaliation, maintaining essential supply chains, providing emergency financing and coordinating responses to severe Chinese economic coercion.
This flexibility would allow countries to participate according to their capabilities. A government unwilling to promise military assistance might still commit economic assistance. Another might refuse sanctions but open its market to products excluded from China.
While military deterrence seeks to convince Beijing that conquering Taiwan would be extraordinarily difficult, economic deterrence could demonstrate that even military success would carry costs extending far beyond the battlefield.
China’s integration into the global economy is often described primarily as a source of Chinese influence. It is also a vulnerability. The more interconnected China becomes, the greater the potential consequences of a confrontation that causes other economies to coordinate against it.
Taiwan and its partners should not attempt to sever those connections. Instead, they should ensure that interdependence does not operate in only one direction.
China should continue benefiting from peaceful trade with the international community. However, Beijing should understand that using economic dependence to punish individual countries could cause those countries to support one another, and that attacking Taiwan could activate an economic coalition far broader than any conceivable military alliance.
Taiwan’s partners have spent years asking how many countries might help defend it if China attacks. They should also ask how many countries could help ensure Beijing never believes an attack is worth the price.
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduran journalist based in Taipei. His work on Taiwan-China-Latin America relations has been published in Nikkei Asia, The Diplomat and the Taipei Times.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:57 UTC
01:35:57 KST

Elon Musk’s lawyers put the makers of a new four-hour documentary about the multibillionaire on formal legal notice days before its premiere, warning that the film defames him.
The Sept. 3 letter from attorney Alex Spiro, addressed to a producer at Alex Gibney’s Jigsaw Productions, accuses the Oscar-winning documentarian of building Musk around a predetermined conclusion.
It also says Gibney refused to fact-check the film with the world’s richest man or the people close to him.
Photo: Reuters
“This project did not begin as an inquiry. It began with a conclusion,” Spiro wrote.
The film on Tuesday premiered at the Venice Film Festival to a lengthy standing ovation and strong reviews. Gibney traces the career and life of the South Africa-born Musk from dot-com entrepreneur in Silicon Valley in the early 2000s to becoming the world’s first trillionaire.
It also delves into his personal life, including his difficult childhood and the 14 known children he has fathered with a series of women.
Trade bible Variety called it a “lacerating portrait,” while Deadline said the “damning” film had “thrashed” Musk as “petty, narcissistic, megalomaniacal, cruel.”
The letter puts not only Gibney and Jigsaw on notice, but everyone involved in the film’s release, including HBO, Bleecker Street and Universal.
It focuses in particular on a sequence that Spiro said advances a conspiracy theory: that Musk knew early on election night 2024 that Trump had won, because his Starlink satellites had been used to influence the result.
Jigsaw hit back in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter, saying scrutiny of powerful public figures is protected by the first amendment of the US Constitution.
This was something all Americans should defend, “including the associates of Elon Musk, who has proclaimed himself to be a ‘free speech absolutist,’” the statement added.
Gibney’s documentaries have often delved into powerful groups, including the Church of Scientology, the Enron corporation and Israel-Iran spy wars in Zero Days. He won an Academy Award for best documentary for Taxi to the Dark Side, which tackles the US military’s interrogation practices in Afghanistan. On the grounds that litigation is “reasonably anticipated,” the letter from Musk’s lawyer orders the filmmakers to preserve every trace of the project, including footage, interview transcripts, research files and internal communications.
Musk has spent several days attacking Gibney on X, the platform he owns, calling the film a “hit piece that misses” and dismissing it as boring.

Leopard cat-safe measures linked to honey boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:56 UTC
01:35:56 KST

Leopard cat-friendly farming methods helped boost honey production by 10 percent over the past four years, a Miaoli County-based beekeeper said at an A-Hu Go (阿虎加油) brand event in Taipei yesterday.
The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Hsinchu branch yesterday launched the brand with a sales exhibition at the city’s Hope Plaza, which runs through today.
The brand was developed using the leopard cat-friendly farming label, which aims to raise the market visibility of products that support leopard cat conservation, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Web site
A-Hu Go products are packaged in paper boxes bearing a drawing of a leopard cat, it said, adding that the packaging can be tailored to the needs of products.
Chiang Kun-hsien (江坤憲), who runs the Chun Tsai Apiary in Miaoli’s Yuanli Township (苑裡) along with his sisters, said their bee yard’s annual honey production has risen at least 10 percent since they began applying leopard cat-friendly farming methods more than three years ago.
His sister, Chiang Chia-ching (江佳靜), said they struggled with mysterious bee deaths at the apiary until they attended a leopard cat-friendly farming workshop organized by the branch, at which they learned that pesticides can kill the insects.
“One of our customers was a leopard cat-friendly farming advocate and invited us to the workshop,” she said. “We used to mow to near ground level and use herbicides if the grass was too high, but the course taught us to keep it at 30cm or less for leopard cat conservation, and to conserve soil and water.”
Chiang Kun-hsien said maintaining the grass also helps nurture the bees.
“Our bees feed on the grass and wild flowers growing in the bee yard. They are rarely attracted to nearby pesticide-treated farmlands,” he said.
All agricultural products with a leopard cat-friendly farming label can apply to use the A-Hu Go brand, the branch said, adding that 16 agricultural products from Miaoli have been approved.
Guidelines for leopard cat-friendly farming requires adoption of grass cover cultivation, and not using herbicides, synthetic pesticides or fertilizers, and any supplies that might harm leopard cats or the environment, it said.
The guidelines also require operations to refrain from letting cats and dogs roam, or the feeding of strays near their fields, it added.
Miaoli County Agriculture Department Deputy Director Tsai Cheng-hsin (蔡政新) said that the county boasts the largest leopard cat population, as up to 88 percent of the region is slopeland.
Slopeland — defined by the Slopeland Conservation and Utilization Act (山坡地保育條例) as land with an elevation of more than 100m or a slope of at least 5 percent — provides lowland-hill habitats that leopard cats prefer, Tsai said.
The department aims to increase the county’s total leopard cat-friendly farming area to more than 2,400 hectares, he said.

MOHW urges public to help prevent suicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:55 UTC
01:35:55 KST

The public should listen to, understand and have empathy with others to build a resilient social safety net together, the Ministry of Health and Welfare (MOHW), healthcare workers and health groups said yesterday, echoing the message of World Suicide Prevention Day on Thursday.
World Suicide Prevention Day is observed on Sept. 10 annually. The theme for 2024 to this year is “Changing the Narrative on Suicide.”
Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Chuang Jen-hsiang (莊人祥) said “changing the narrative” is about shifting from a culture of silence, lack of understanding and even stigmatization, to one of openness, listening and empathy, allowing those who are struggling to feel accepted and supported.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
Taiwan Suicide Prevention Center director Huang Min-wei (黃敏偉) said the center’s surveys found that many people are aware that they should try to accompany those who are in need or encourage them to seek help, but up to 88 percent said they avoid talking about the issue directly with the person.
Only 18.4 percent said they know about the “Question, Persuade and Refer” (QPR) protocol — noticing warning signs and asking a direct question about suicide, listening closely to the person and convincing them to stay alive, and connecting the person to professional medical or mental health resources, he said.
People often have the misconception that those who commit suicide do not ask for help, but about 70 to 80 percent of people show signs of distress beforehand, Huang said, adding that sometimes, signals for help are mistaken for complaints.
Chuang said the ministry in August 2024 launched a mental health support program for young people and middle-aged adults, offering people aged between 15 and 45 up to three free psychological counseling sessions.
The program aimed to lower the barrier for those seeking mental health support, enable early detection of high-risk cases and provide timely intervention through professional assessments, Chuang added.
The ministry’s Department of Mental Health said that more than 57,000 people have used the service as of the end of last month, and more than 25 percent of them received referrals for further mental health services.
Chuang said the ministry plans to continue the program next year and has allocated about NT$430 million (US$13.59 million) in its budget proposal for it.
Other mental health resources include the 75 community mental health centers and 396 mental health counseling service locations across the country, the ministry’s free 24-hour suicide prevention hotline at 1925, the men’s care hotline at 0800-013-999, the online “Heart Healthier” Mental Health Learning Platform, he said.
Chuang urged the public to ask friends or relatives who are acting differently how they are doing, give them their full attention and listen without judging or offering solutions.
If the person seems to need further help, they should follow the QPR protocol and help the person receive timely professional support, he added.

Taiwan has right to make friends: VP

Taiwan has the same right as anyone else to make friends and work with like-minded partners despite Beijing’s efforts to restrict its international presence, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said on Friday.
“We believe strongly that like every citizen in the world, we have the right to make friends. We have the right to talk to our friends,” Hsiao said at the Second Ventotene European Conference for Freedom and Democracy on the Italian island of Ventotene.
Taiwan also has the right to work with like-minded partners on solutions to common challenges, she said, adding that it cherishes every opportunity to make its voice heard internationally.
Photo: CNA
Hsiao attended the conference on Friday as a guest of honor, accompanied by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). Her participation was not announced until after she arrived in Italy to prevent interference from Beijing.
The trip is Hsiao’s second to Europe since taking office in May 2024, following a visit to Brussels in November last year to address a meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China.
European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, the main organizer of the conference, said Hsiao’s presence had been kept confidential to ensure her participation.
Picierno said the European Parliament’s agenda would not be determined by Beijing.
“Free peoples speak the same language. Free peoples recognize one another,” she said in Italian.
Picierno also accepted Hsiao’s invitation to visit Taiwan, saying the trip would be arranged in the coming weeks and months.
Several Italian politicians also criticized Beijing’s formal protest over Hsiao’s visit.
Italian Senate Vice President Gian Marco Centinaio said hosting Taiwanese officials was an honor as he called China’s protest unacceptable.
Fabrizio Benzoni, deputy leader of the Action party’s group in the Italian Chamber of Deputies, said neither Italy nor the EU should tolerate vetoes or intimidation from Beijing.
Tiziana Nisini, a lawmaker from Italy’s League party, said democratically elected leaders had the right to travel and engage internationally.
Member of the European Parliament Engin Eroglu said Hsiao’s visit reflected Europe’s growing recognition of Taiwan as a partner, adding that increased high-level exchanges in the past few years had become institutionalized to some extent.
During the conference, Hsiao described Ukraine’s situation as a warning that Taiwan must do more to preserve peace by bolstering its defenses, securing its role in global technology supply chains and deepening international partnerships.
Taiwan would neither provoke China nor yield to coercion, and would not change its democratic way of life, she said.
Hsiao said China had long sought to constrain Taiwan’s international space and had targeted and sanctioned her, but that would not stop Taiwan from engaging with the world.
Hsiao recalled her nickname “cat warrior,” saying cats might appear small but can jump several times their height and survive difficult circumstances.
“We in Taiwan believe we are small, but we’re also mighty,” she said.

FEATURE:Chinese coast guard turns to the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:51 UTC
01:35:51 KST

For decades, China’s maritime pressure on Taiwan centered on the major shipping strait separating the two neighbors. Now, Beijing is piling unprecedented pressure on its Pacific coast — a vital lifeline with US allies.
China has deployed on average two Coast Guard cutters per month east of Taiwan since June, after Japan and the Philippines announced plans to define their overlapping maritime border in the region. The appearance of those vessels marks the first time such patrols have been reported in the area in data going back to January last year.
Patrols in these waters covered a vast area of 27,100 square nautical miles (92,950km2) — more than twice the size of Taiwan — based on Bloomberg calculations using ship-tracking data. Ships stayed 30 nautical miles (55km) from the nation’s eastern coast, remaining outside Taiwan-claimed waters.
Photo: CNA
Controlling the east would become essential to enforcing an effective blockade of Taiwan during a Chinese invasion of the island. Disrupting shipping off the Pacific coast would have global implications for commodities. Vessels ferrying oil, gas, iron ore and agricultural products made 527 transits through the east in June, exceeding the 420 through the generally busier Taiwan Strait, MarineTraffic data show.
“If the Taiwan Strait is the front door, the eastern waters have often been treated as the back door,” said Jing Ge, instructor at Florida International University’s politics and international relations department. “Beijing wants to demonstrate this back door is no longer uncontested.”
While the Taiwan Strait handles almost half the world’s container fleet, the nation’s eastern coast holds strategic importance by forming a maritime link with the Philippines and wider Pacific. Sea lanes in the area lead to key ports and military facilities, where the US and its regional allies could deliver supplies, while its deeper waters are ideal for submarines and undersea surveillance.
The Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) has described such deployments as “routine law-enforcement” patrols, and has pledged to strengthen patrols to safeguard Beijing’s maritime rights. China has in the past also conducted military drills, including in this area, to rehearse encircling Taiwan.
China’s activity is an attempt to “leverage ‘law enforcement patrols’ to establish a new normal for its maritime presence in the waters east of Taiwan,” the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration said. Vessels have been dispatched in a timely manner in response, it added.
The US has called China’s actions “deeply destabilizing.” Despite that opposition, the CCG announced last week it had deployed a new set of vessels east of Taiwan, sustaining its presence in the area.
The role of the CCG has moved beyond traditional law enforcement in the past few years. That was laid bare by the introduction of a Coast Guard Law in 2021, which expanded the agency’s reach by authorizing it to “take all necessary measures, including the use of weapons” to protect what Beijing defines as China’s sovereignty.
Its new operations around Taiwan started on June 1, when the CCG deployed two large patrol cutters — the Daishan and Baita — to waters east of the nation. Those vessels were previously used around the East China Sea, including the Japanese-controlled Senkaku islands, which China also claims.
Days earlier, Japan and the Philippines had announced plans to start negotiations to delimit their sea boundaries, as part of broader efforts from the two US allies to deepen their partnership. China opposed the talks, saying they had interfered with its own maritime claims in that region.
“Beijing is using the joint statement issued by Japan and the Philippines as a pretext for greatly expanding its presence in these waters,” said Ryan Martinson, assistant professor at the China Maritime Studies Institute of the US Naval War College.
Later in June, China sent larger law enforcement ships, the Haixun 09 and Haixun 06, to circle Taiwan. That rare multi-agency operation included China’s largest deep-sea survey ship and a rescue vessel.
During their five-day voyage, the vessels for the first time questioned foreign commercial ships passing along Taiwan’s Pacific coast. According to Chinese state media, the ships also “inspected” 198 passing vessels during the mission to reinforce traffic-control capabilities. It was unclear what the report meant by “inspected.”
“If those interactions become routine, the next question is whether Chinese authorities begin to request more information,” said Zack Liao, political risk analyst at UK-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute. “After that, whether they issue navigational instructions.”
US-based independent monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data has separately reported “a significant increase in research vessels operating at unusually slow speeds east of Taiwan” near undersea communications infrastructure.
China kept up the pressure by sending two more Coast Guard cutters to relieve the Daishan and Baita after a month in the area. That was described by a US congressional commission as Beijing’s way to establish a continuous presence.
“Using the CCG rather than the People’s Liberation Army Navy avoids military confrontations and allows Beijing to portray these activities as law enforcement while establishing the persistent presence necessary for a future blockade,” the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission said.
As activity ramped up, Taiwan held military exercises in mid-July on Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼) and Green Island (綠島), off its southeastern coast, for the first time in three decades. Weeks later, China staged passing exercises with Indonesia in the area, the first time Beijing has announced training with another country in the eastern waters.
China’s push to establish a presence east of Taiwan ultimately puts pressure on the US to respond, analysts say.
“What Beijing is testing east of Taiwan is whether it can gradually rewrite expectations about who governs navigation and maritime order in the Western Pacific,” said Liao. “That means the response should also be international,” he added.

The BRICS at 20
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:35:48 UTC
01:35:48 KST

Twenty years ago this month, the foreign ministers of Brazil, Russia, India and China held the first meeting of the BRICs. Since then, the grouping has been formalized — the first BRIC summit took place in June 2009 — and expanded, with South Africa joining in 2011 and several more countries later coming on board, either as full members or official partners. Today, the BRICS represents a highly consequential experiment in international cooperation, which epitomizes the gradual rebalancing of global power away from the West and the emergence of a multipolar order.
Few acronyms have undergone as dramatic an evolution as the BRICS. Coined by then-Goldman Sachs investment management division managing director Jim O’Neill in 2001 to encapsulate four fast-growing emerging markets, the “BRICs” grouping has developed into the BRICS, an 11-country political and economic coalition and an increasingly influential voice for the Global South.
Since adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates to its ranks in 2024 to last year, the BRICS accounts for nearly half of the world’s population and about 40 percent of global GDP (in purchasing-power-parity terms).
Illustration: Constance Chou
By contrast, the G7 accounts for less than 10 percent of the global population and less than 30 percent of world GDP. And whereas the BRICS’ share of the global economy continues to grow, the pace of productivity and economic growth in advanced economies has been declining steadily since the 1990s.
This economic reversal is increasingly matched in the geopolitical domain, with Western global dominance giving way to a more diffuse distribution of power and influence. Amid this transformation — the likes of which occur only once every 50 to 100 years — the BRICS has challenged the assumption that global governance should remain centered on the Western-led institutions established after World War II.
For non-Western countries, the BRICS represents a hedge against rising economic and geopolitical uncertainty—generated, not least, by a US seemingly bent on withdrawing from global leadership — and an institutional platform for advancing strategic autonomy and broadening economic cooperation. Small wonder there has been such enthusiasm for joining: more than three dozen countries have formally applied or expressed interest in becoming members, including Turkey, a NATO member, and Bahrain, the primary operational hub for US naval forces in the Middle East.
The BRICS also has 10 “partner countries” — Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam — which can participate in summits. This framework helps to expand the BRICS’ network for cooperation and bolster its ability to represent the Global South, without jeopardizing cohesion.
The BRICS is much more than a symbolic grouping — merely a message to the world that the era of Western dominance is coming to an end. The grouping has made tangible progress on institution-building. The New Development Bank (NDB) is the first multilateral development bank with global scope conceived and led solely by emerging economies, with the founding BRICS members holding equal shares and voting rights.
By contrast, the US is the largest shareholder at the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, where it holds effective veto power. Unlike these US-led institutions, the NDB does not attach political conditions to its infrastructure financing, allowing borrowers to retain greater policy autonomy.
The BRICS has also been working to reduce vulnerabilities within the international financial system. Contrary to speculation, a single BRICS currency akin to the euro is not on the agenda. Instead, the upcoming summit would focus on expanding trade settlement in national currencies, improving interoperability among members’ digital payment systems, linking central bank digital currencies and developing alternative cross-border payment infrastructure. The goal is not to upend the global financial system and supplant the US dollar, which still accounts for about 57 percent of foreign exchange reserves held by central banks worldwide, but rather to bolster resilience against external financial shocks.
However, as much progress as the BRICS has made over the past 20 years, the grouping also faces significant headwinds, rooted not least in its exceptional internal diversity. The BRICS includes liberal democracies and authoritarian states, leading energy exporters and major energy importers, manufacturing powers and commodity economies. The grouping also includes geopolitical rivals: China and India, Iran and Saudi Arabia, and Egypt and Ethiopia. Divisions exist even among its founding members, with Brazil and India generally advocating reform of existing international institutions, while China and Russia seek to challenge the US-led world order.
Diversity brings different ideas and advantages to the table, and ideological uniformity and close strategic alignment are not necessarily prerequisites to cooperation. However, a highly diverse grouping, with sharply divergent priorities and geopolitical concerns, would always struggle to forge consensus. Every round of enlargement compounds the challenge, even as it raises the BRICS’ profile as a broadly representative international coalition.
As the group convenes in New Delhi for its 18th summit, one might ask whether it has lived up to its original promise. If that promise was to establish a monetary union, a single market or a tightly integrated political alliance, the answer is plainly no. However, if it was to reshape international relations, broaden the space available to emerging economies on the world stage, deepen South-South cooperation and increase pressure for reform of existing international institutions, the BRICS has exceeded expectations.
More fundamentally, the BRICS has normalized an idea that once seemed impossible: that emerging economies can cooperate with one another, build their own institutions and change how the international order is organized. That is no small feat.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research and Fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin, is the author of Water, Peace, and War: Confronting the Global Water Crisis.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:30:46 UTC
01:30:46 KST

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russia President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian (PTI Image)
NEW DELHI: India hosted the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for discussions on global conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy, technology, climate change and reform of international institutions. India used its 2026 chairship to push a people-centric agenda centred on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.The summit was marked by high-level bilateral meetings, visible displays of bonhomie among leaders and efforts to bridge differences over the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM Modi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, while leaders also participated in the Brics Business Forum and other summit engagements.
From PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex to PM Modi and Xi sharing warm moments and the leaders participating in a gala dinner and cultural engagements, the summit combined diplomacy with symbols of Brics unity.Also read - 'Global South must be rule-shaper, India ready to take lead': PM Modi at Brics SummitThe summit adopted the New Delhi Declaration, a 45-page document containing 140 points that brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi bilateral: Boundary question and reset in ties
PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, with both sides stressing the importance of viewing India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.The two leaders committed to seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and highlighted the importance of mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The discussions also covered peace and tranquillity along the border, economic relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting came as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise bilateral ties while continuing to manage differences over the boundary.The Modi-Xi meeting was one of the summit's most closely watched engagements, given the strategic importance of India-China relations and their simultaneous participation in an expanded Brics framework.
PM Modi-Putin meeting: Ukraine, West Asia and $100 billion trade target
PM Modi held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting with Putin on the eve of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to contribute to peace efforts.Five Indian seafarers have died in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine hostilities, making maritime safety an important concern for New Delhi.The two sides also discussed defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia agreed to work towards taking bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.Putin also invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit. The dates will be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Car diplomacy: PM Modi and Putin travel together
After their bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The unusual visual quickly became one of the defining moments of the summit, highlighting the close nature of the India-Russia relationship amid continuing geopolitical pressure on Moscow and India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.PM Modi later highlighted the growing India-Russia economic relationship, including the participation of companies from both countries at the INNOPROM industrial exhibition held at Bharat Mandapam.
PM Modi presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.The gift was presented as a cultural bridge between India and Russia and reflected the emphasis placed by India on people-to-people links during its Brics chairship.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks: West Asia and regional peace
PM Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the summit, with the two leaders discussing India-Iran relations, Brics cooperation and the conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's position that disputes must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region.The discussions also covered freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers, issues that have acquired greater importance amid disruption to shipping routes in the region.The meeting followed the leaders' earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India also stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade channels and pursuing a long-term and mutually beneficial relationship with Iran.
PM Modi, Xi, Putin and leaders showcase Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals showing leaders of the expanded grouping interacting informally.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.Also read - Big reunion at Brics: PM Modi, Xi & Putin meet for 3rd time in 3 yrs; PM shares photoPM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The images were widely seen as a demonstration of the grouping's effort to project unity despite differences among members on major geopolitical issues.The presence of leaders from Russia, China, Iran, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, South Africa and other member states underscored the diversity of interests represented within the expanded grouping.
Gala dinner: Leaders gather for cultural evening
The Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner hosted during the summit, providing an informal setting for interactions between heads of government and state.Also read - Gucchi marmik, millet pulao, khumb galouti: What's on the Brics gala dinner menuThe cultural programme and dinner formed part of India's effort to showcase its heritage alongside the formal diplomatic agenda. The event brought together leaders who had spent the summit discussing contentious issues ranging from wars and terrorism to trade and global governance.The informal interactions added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by difficult geopolitical negotiations.
Banyan tree plantation: Symbol of Brics unity
A symbolic tree plantation ceremony was also organised during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the planting of a Banyan tree.The Banyan tree, known for its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".Also read - PM Modi, Brics leaders take part in joint tree plantation at Bharat Mandapam: WatchThe plantation also reflected India's attempt to connect the summit's diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum: Trade, investment and technology
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying:"Today, BRICS nations represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of its GDP, and over 25 per cent of global trade. Moreover, while global GDP has grown approximately two-and-a-half-fold over these years, the combined GDP of BRICS nations has expanded nearly four-and-a-half-fold. In other words, the economic strength of BRICS has grown at nearly twice the pace of the rest of the world.""The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date," the Prime Minister added.Also read - Brics New Delhi Declaration adopted: Terrorism, conflict resolution, tariff concerns addressed; key pointsPezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing."We believe that the true strength of BRICS is not confined merely to the size of its members' economies; rather, it becomes more apparent when these capacities are transformed into a network of trade, investment and joint financing – a transition from potential cooperation to operational one," he said.Putin stressed the importance of business-to-business relations and economic partnerships, arguing that they could help create more resilient international economic relations.
Putin attacks trade restrictions, backs new growth platform
At the Business Forum, Putin criticised what he described as attempts by Western competitors to regain their former economic leadership."We have always been told that competition is a sacred cow, something that must not be touched," Putin told a BRICS business forum event. "Yet, unfortunately, today your Western competitors are trying by any means necessary to regain their former leadership.""This competition is sometimes assuming unsightly forms," he said. "They even include direct physical attacks or the destruction of industrial and logistical facilities, pipelines, and so forth."Putin also criticised restrictions on international transport corridors, shipping and trade and called for Brics to contribute to building "a new, sustainable platform for global growth".
India-Russia economic partnership gets push
The summit also provided an opportunity for India and Russia to discuss expanding economic cooperation amid Western sanctions and geopolitical uncertainty.The two countries discussed the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030 and cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, critical minerals and civil nuclear energy.The sides also explored industrial cooperation in railways and tunnelling, the steel value chain and greater access to the Russian market for Indian exporters.India continues to maintain strong energy ties with Russia, while seeking to expand trade beyond traditional sectors.
Brics pushes practical cooperation across sectors
India's 2026 chairship focused heavily on converting Brics into a platform for practical cooperation rather than limiting it to political declarations.More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were organised across approximately 30 cities during India's chairship. These covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.PM Modi said: "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability have been our priorities.""Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."
Agriculture: Digital farming and climate resilience
Brics countries agreed on new mechanisms to strengthen agricultural cooperation.These include Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology for research and knowledge sharing on natural, organic and regenerative farming, a Brics Network on Digital Agriculture using artificial intelligence, geospatial intelligence, IoT-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics, and BRICS AGRIN, a voluntary framework covering agricultural inputs, seeds and genetic resources.The initiatives seek to promote climate-resilient farming and greater technology-driven cooperation among member countries.
Health: Lifestyle, traditional medicine and mental health
The Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle was launched along with a roadmap for joint cooperation for 2026-2029, focusing on preventive approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.Members also agreed to establish an Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine, covering research, evidence generation, academic exchange, quality standards and protection of traditional knowledge.Mental health cooperation was also strengthened through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating centre.
Energy: Smart grids and storage
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The initiative will provide a platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, policy and regulatory cooperation and pilot projects among member countries.The summit also placed emphasis on energy security, diversified energy sources and equitable energy transitions.
MSMEs and startups: New platforms for businesses
India pushed stronger cooperation for micro, small and medium enterprises and startups.The Brics MSME Cooperation Portal will connect MSMEs, technology centres, trade associations, financial institutions and policymakers across member countries.A Brics Incubator Network will connect startups with incubators in other member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.
Logistics and global supply chains
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.The initiatives are intended to reduce vulnerabilities caused by fragmented supply chains, improve connectivity and promote economic diversification.
Urban mobility and climate-resilient infrastructure
The summit also advanced cooperation on sustainable urban development.A Brics Urban Mobility Hub was established as a platform for technical cooperation and knowledge sharing. Members also adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure.An Urban Research and Knowledge Network was established to facilitate cross-border research, peer learning and institutional cooperation.
Skilling, youth and sports technology
India also advanced cooperation on skills and employment through BRICS CONNECT, a voluntary network covering capacity building, social security, women's workforce participation, employability and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation.Sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a working group focusing on technical information, research, institutional experience and best practices.
Science and research cooperation
The Brics Science and Research Repository was welcomed as a structured platform for sharing scientific knowledge among member countries.The initiative is intended to strengthen research collaboration and facilitate greater exchange of scientific information across the expanded grouping.
Brics 2026: A wider and more diverse grouping
Brics currently comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.The expansion has significantly widened the grouping's geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. It has also brought together countries with different political systems, economic priorities and positions on major international conflicts.India's chairship therefore focused not only on expanding cooperation but also on finding consensus among members with competing interests.
New Delhi Declaration: Key outcomes
The summit concluded with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration 2026, following intensive negotiations among members. The 45-page declaration contains 140 points and represents India's central diplomatic outcome from its 2026 chairship.The declaration addresses terrorism, conflicts, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.
Terrorism: Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemns terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and calls for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemns the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemns cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards the adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Ceasefire, diplomacy and two-state solution
The declaration expresses deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and calls on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stresses dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and calls for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for the upholding of a ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian aid and an end to forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral war condemned
The declaration condemns unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance because Brics includes members with differing positions on the major conflicts in West Asia and the wider international system.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to bridge differences between members and produce a common position.
UN reform and greater Global South representation
Brics reaffirmed its support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the Security Council.The grouping called for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
Trade: Opposition to tariffs and protectionism
The declaration expresses concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.Brics reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization.The grouping also called for the restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.
Brics voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter.The declaration calls for such measures to be eliminated and highlights their impact on international economic relations.The position reflects a longstanding Brics push for a more balanced international economic and political order.
Local currencies and cross-border payments
The declaration supports greater use of local currencies in cross-border payments and trade settlements among Brics countries.Members acknowledged ongoing work on interoperability between payment and messaging systems and efforts to facilitate trade settlements and investment in local currencies.The initiative forms part of the wider Brics effort to strengthen financial resilience and cooperation.
Energy security and transition
The declaration calls for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets.It also supports just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions while recognising the differing circumstances and priorities of member countries.Brics backed cooperation involving renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and other low-carbon technologies.
Women and inclusive development
The declaration recognises women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.It highlights women's participation in governance, entrepreneurship, employment and peacebuilding and calls for greater financial and digital inclusion.The grouping also emphasised skills development and access to productive and social services.
Tackling organised crime and illicit financial flows
Brics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug trafficking, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing, human trafficking and organised crime.The grouping called for stronger cooperation between member countries to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds and tackle transnational criminal networks.
The larger message from New Delhi
The New Delhi Declaration combines a strong political message on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia and global governance with a broad economic and development agenda.
For India, the outcome represents an effort to demonstrate that the expanded Brics can reach consensus despite major geopolitical differences. The declaration also places India's priorities of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability at the centre of a wider agenda covering trade, technology, energy, health, agriculture, finance and development.The summit therefore ended with two parallel messages: Brics wants a stronger collective voice in global affairs, while India wants that voice translated into practical cooperation that reaches businesses, communities and ordinary people.

His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life.
He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.
