Left with nothing, people in Gaza are forced to rent generators by the hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:43:28 UTC
20:43:28 KST

Left with nothing, people in Gaza are forced to rent generators by the hour
Israel’s destruction of homes and infrastructure in Gaza has left few working household items and expensive services for daily chores.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – For more than four hours, Hajj Rabhi al-Fairi, 79, has been standing outside his home in Gaza City with his children and neighbours waiting their turn to use a small generator.
The generator’s owner pours in the fuel, starts a timer and switches on the machine.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
- list 2 of 4Shift in British policy on Israel is palpable
- list 3 of 4Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
- list 4 of 4Israeli strikes devastate homes, displace families across Gaza
Each family gets a few minutes to operate a pump that pushes water up to a storage tank on the roof, before the generator moves on to the next house.
For al-Fairi and his neighbours, this is how they get water.
“We have an old water pump, but there is no electricity to run it. We have to rent a generator,” al-Fairi tells Al Jazeera.
Since the family returned to their home in October 2025, after fleeing a month earlier during Israel’s assault on their neighbourhood, the generator has become a familiar sight on the streets of Nassr.
When it arrives, residents gather around it, each carrying a jerrycan of diesel to operate the machine, which they have to pay for themselves.
“We came back and found the place a tragedy,” he says.
Their neighbourhood and home were badly damaged from years of Israeli bombing, with no municipal electricity or water supplies functioning. The family depends on an old pump – but without electricity, it cannot bring water up to the rooftop tank.
Each family needs only about seven or eight minutes to fill up their tanks, but with the number of flats in their building, the generator needs to be rented for about an hour.
The cost has also risen. Al-Rabhi says families used to pay about 80 to 90 shekels ($26-30) to rent a generator for an hour. At different times, the price has risen to about 100 or 120 shekels ($33-40) an hour, excluding the cost of diesel.
A generator on wheels
Khalil Abu Ouda, 39, takes a machine mounted on a horse-driven cart from one house to another. The generator’s metal body is covered in black soot and grease, and white smoke rises from the engine when it operates.
At each house, Abu Ouda connects long electrical cables to the water pump. The cables stretch across the street as neighbours gather around the machine to wait their turn.
“Go on, switch it on,” someone calls.
For Abu Ouda, this machine is both a service for the neighbourhood and an essential source of income for his family.
He says there are very few small, mobile generators, like his, left in working condition in Gaza. Many have broken down, while spare parts are difficult to find or too expensive to source due to Israel’s siege.
Mechanics are also expensive to hire, while fuel and engine oil are increasingly scarce and costly.
“If I could, I would lower the price as much as possible,” he says.
At the same time, demand has never been higher.
“People are under pressure and they need water. If I stayed working until morning, I would keep working,” Abu Ouda says.
To cope with the demand, he often works for 10 to 12 hours a day, putting pressure on himself and the machine.
“But this is our livelihood. There is no alternative,” he said.
When the home stops providing
With most Palestinians in Gaza having no home or losing their possessions due to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, they have to rent or hire items or services for the most basic household chores.
This includes washing clothes, something once done at home but now impossible to do with no power.
Earlier in the war, Abeer Ghorab, 52, used to wash everything herself. Now she gathers clothes from her tent and takes them to a nearby laundry, where they can be washed and dried in far less time and with less effort.
“When these laundries started opening, they gave us some relief,” Ghorab said.
The difference is particularly important in winter, when heavy clothes, blankets and bedding can take time to dry.
“In winter, the tracksuits are heavy. They need another day to dry,” she said. “When I bring them here, they wash and dry them for me, and I get them back clean and dry. That really helps.”
But due to a limited income, Ghorab cannot afford to use this laundry service every day.
Before the war, Ghorab had a washing machine, a refrigerator and regular electricity at home.
“Things we once took for granted have become dreams. Now we have to pay for every little thing we used to do at home.”
The loss of the household
Across Gaza, the infrastructure that once allowed families to carry out everyday tasks at home has been severely disrupted.
A recent United Nations assessment found that 91 percent of surveyed households experienced moderate-to-high water shortages in early August.
A separate damage assessment by the authority found that 107,941 of the 178,632 housing units inspected – about 60 percent – were severely damaged, destroyed or otherwise considered uninhabitable.
Water systems, electricity, sanitation and household appliances, which families relied on to manage daily life, have also been disrupted.
For families living in damaged homes, tents or makeshift shelters, everyday tasks must be paid for.
A laundry adapting to shortages
Fadi Abu Shawarb, 23, has worked at his family’s al-Hurriya laundry for six years.
Before the war, the business relied on large, 50kg (110lb) washing machines for carpets, blankets and other heavy loads. But due to the high cost of operation, these machines are far too expensive to run.
“We started replacing the 50kg machines with 25kg ones because there is not enough electricity,” Fadi says. “There are no solar panels, no reliable power, and the generators are always breaking down.”
Most of his customers are displaced families who lack electricity, water or washing machines at home.
The laundry now handles about 20 to 30 loads a day, with clothes-washing among the most in-demand services.
A load costs six shekels ($2) when the laundry can use solar power and 12 shekels ($4) when it relies on a generator.
But even that is hard for people to pay. “People’s situation is difficult,” he says.
For Ghorab, the laundry is only one of the many expenses she now has to budget for.
“I feel like I’m going through a difficult time,” she says. “I have to pay for every little thing in my day, and with how difficult things are, it’s hard to keep up with everything.”

Ukraine's Zelenskyy offers to meet Putin at G20 summit in December

2026-09-12
11:41:13 UTC
20:41:13 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a G20 summit in December, in an interview released on Saturday, as efforts intensify to end the conflict.
Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled negotiations to find a solution to the conflict, Europe's deadliest since World War II, with US negotiators recently visiting Kiev and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks on the conflict over the phone.
The United States holds this year's presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union, and culminates in a leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Russia's finance minister has already attended one G20 meeting, causing discomfort among some of Ukraine's allies, and a Russian diplomat said on Saturday that Moscow will also send some officials to a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week.
Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelenskyy told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: "Yes, of course.
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions.
"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter. Matters only result. Result matters. That's it."
Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Putin and Trump also discussed the war earlier in the week in what the Kremlin termed an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long phone call.
Diplomatic efforts intensify
In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place Friday in Canada, Zelenskyy said that Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal", and it was important the pair had visited Kiev as well as Moscow.
"It's respect to our people," he said.
Zelenskyy has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kiev.
Asked about Ukraine's position ahead of possible negotiations, Zelenskyy responded: "Ukraine now is much more stronger than last year on the battlefield."
Russia was sustaining heavy battlefield losses, paying a "big price" for "very slow moves on the battlefield," he said.
"That's why we think that we have now good position for negotiations."
Kiev has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kiev have shifted their positions.
Both Moscow and Kiev have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Zelenskyy also repeated his call for Ukraine's allies to provide more interceptor missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.
"Russia produces... today 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need 280... You will never have 280 missiles per month," he said.
It was a "huge challenge" to have 100 a month, he said.

Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:41:00 UTC
20:41:00 KST

Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
September 12, 2026
Uganda has concluded a nine-day period of mourning for King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.
A funeral was held for the Tooro Kingdom's late monarch in the western city of Fort Portal on Saturday.
Oyo, who once held the unofficial title of the world's youngest king, ascended the throne as a young child in 1995 and died last month of cancer aged just 34, with his death prompting a bitter succession dispute.
Thousands gathered as Oyo was laid to rest
The casket carrying the king's body, which was draped in the blue-and-yellow Tooro flag, was carried by hearse from the royal palace in Fort Portal in a procession accompanied by royal guards dressed in orange tunics and beating wooden sticks.
Thousands of people gathered for the procession.
The ceremony in St. John's Cathedral was attended by hundreds of mourners, including senior Ugandan government officials.
After the service in the cathedral, Oyo was buried at the site of the royal tombs.
At the burial ceremony, tradition dictates that the successor should throw nine coffee berries into the grave.
"He had a gift to make people laugh," his sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said at the burial ceremony.
"He always knew how to brighten my day."
Dispute over Oyo's successor
However, the question of that successor has aroused considerable controversy, and it was in doubt until late on Friday who would carry out that rite.
On Wednesday, a committee made up of members of the royal clan announced it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, as the new king.
Kijanangoma, 54, is a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC.
But the immediate family of the late king said that the latter's will had called for a son who was born out of wedlock and has yet to be identified to succeed him.
Additionally, there have been claims on social media that there are at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo's children.
Those supporting Kijanangoma say Oyo's family has so far failed to come up with concrete information on the alleged son, while traditionalists also favor the choice of an adult as new monarch.
A source with knowledge of crisis talks on the matter said authorities had managed to get Kijanangoma officially accepted as successor on Friday.
Beloved traditional monarchs
Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined the family's ability to mourn the king's death.
"I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: Please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."
Although Uganda is led by an elected head of state, it still possesses several kingdoms that were restored in 1993 after being banned for some three decades following the country's independence from British colonial rule.
The monarchs of such kingdoms are often beloved but hold no formal power. Instead they are seen as guardians of traditional identity and heritage.

Ukraine’s parliament changes how military budget is cleared, and freezes money behind one of war’s cleverest supply schemes, defense-industry council says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:40:49 UTC
20:40:49 KST

New changes to the legislation from Ukraine's parliament have jammed the money in one of the war's cleverest supply schemes: the system that lets frontline units turn confirmed kills into new weapons. Under the program, known as eBaly, a military unit can earn points for verified strikes on Russian targets and spend them on Ukrainian-made drones and other gear, which the makers deliver first and get paid for later. The makers have kept delivering. The payments have stopped, according to Ihor Fedirko, who runs the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry.
The freeze is real money to real firms. Fedirko says the companies are owed between $540,000 and several million dollars each for equipment already handed over and have gone roughly two months without payment. It matters because eBaly is not a fringe experiment: units have ordered and received more than 181,000 drones, robots, and electronic-warfare systems through it in 2026, choosing the gear that performs best in combat.
The Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry brings together more than 300 private manufacturers and key associations of Ukraine’s defense-industrial sector.
A budget change froze the money
The problem, Fedirko said, affects every delivery made through eBaly. Under the updated 2026 budget, the split of Ukraine's military income tax stayed the same: 60 percent to the Defense Ministry, 30 percent to the state communications service, and 10 percent straight to military units.
But the ministry's and the communications service's shares now have to be signed off by the Ukrainian National Security Committee.
"Now, the committee approves not individual payments or deliveries but the general directions of spending," Fedirko wrote.
It is unclear what is causing such delays in obtaining signatures on committee decisions and what is lacking to enable swift decision-making.
It is worth noting that the Ebaly system reduces the risk of ministries approving procurement through “their own” companies, since hundreds of companies participate in it and are selected by hundreds of commanders.
Small firms feel it first
For the largest defense companies, a delay of a million or two dollars is a manageable cash-flow gap, Fedirko said. For small ones, the same money was meant to cover wages, buy components, and fund the next production run.
"Some enterprises have already run into problems paying salaries," he wrote.
Producers have spent about two months appealing to the responsible institutions to clear the debt for gear already delivered, without result.

====================================================================================================

'Our Loves' is a film about people, not October 7, Israeli filmmaker Avi Nesher tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:40:29 UTC
20:40:29 KST

‘When something horrible happens to you, you can succumb to the tragedy and get swallowed by the abyss – to paraphrase Nietzsche – or you can say, ‘OK, what do we do now? What do we change?’” said Avi Nesher, whose latest movie, Our Loves, is a beautiful and moving film about ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances. It’s suspenseful, sad, and sometimes even funny, the kind of movie that can change the way you see the world – and yourself. It tells the stories of a group of people “who think they are having the worst day of their lives on October 6, 2023” and who go on to spend much of the movie fighting to survive the attack that begins a day later.
Our Loves will have its world premiere on September 13 at the Toronto International Film Festival, in the prestigious Centerpiece section. It will then open the Haifa International Film Festival on September 26 and will be released in theaters throughout Israel on October 15, prior to an international release.
It is Nesher’s 22nd feature film and probably the most anticipated movie he has ever made. He became one of Israel’s leading directors decades ago when he released the now-classic movies The Troupe (Ha-Lahaka) and Dizengoff 99, back-to-back in the late ’70s. After their success, Hollywood called, and he spent over a decade making genre films there. But he just couldn’t quit Israel and came back in 2001, releasing an extraordinary series of diverse and quintessentially Israeli movies over the last two decades, such as Turn Left at the End of the World (2004) and The Matchmaker (2010).
Now in his early 70s, he might be expected to be winding down his career, especially after his family suffered a tragedy in 2018, when his son Ari was killed in an accident at the age of 17. His daughter, director Tom Nesher, made Come Closer in 2024, a movie about a young woman who loses her brother that was clearly inspired by Ari’s death, but Nesher prefers to make movies that explore his emotions without delving too closely into his biography. Following his loss, he chose to keep working and made some of the best films in recent years, including Image of Victory, a drama about young people on a southern kibbutz during the Independence War.
A film about October 7?
After the Hamas massacre took place on October 7, 2023, it seemed obvious to many that Nesher would want to make sense of the tragedy by creating a film about it, although he didn’t quite see it that way at first.
“I was at home, horrified. Horrified,” he said, when I asked him about his experience on that day. “It was something that couldn’t possibly have happened. It seemed like, somehow, we were getting it all wrong, because this cannot happen. Yes, we can get some missiles shot at Tel Aviv. OK. We can have a few Hamas people penetrating the border. OK. But we cannot have Hamas people inside the kibbutzim. That’s not Israel. That’s not the Israel I grew up in, and it’s not part of my sense of safety living in this country. Hamas people in all those kibbutzim? Unbelievable. People on the roads, people in Ofakim. Oh God, this cannot be happening. And then you go: Where is the government?... No one knew anything.”
The shock brought back memories for him of an earlier war, in which the IDF and government were similarly blindsided. “I’m a veteran of the Yom Kippur War, so I know about impending doom,” he said.
Nesher, who spent much of his adolescence in New York, where his family moved because of his father’s career, and who attended Columbia University, came back to Israel to join the army. He initially served in the elite Sayeret Matkal unit until he sustained an injury and was an intelligence officer when the Yom Kippur War broke out.
“October 7 was even worse, because in 1973, I was a soldier. I had something to do,” he said.
In the weeks following October 7, as he reeled in shock along with the rest of the country, it didn’t cross his mind to make a movie about the attack.
“Early on... there’s just trying to survive, trying to bounce back, grieving. I know a thing or two about losing dear ones. My heart breaks every day,” he said.
The fact that he could empathize so deeply with those who had lost family on October 7 initially made him feel less, rather than more, inclined to make a movie about it. “People asked me if I wanted to make a movie about October 7, and I said, ‘No, no, no. You can’t make a movie about October 7. It has to be done by historians.’”
An unexpected and deeply moving experience soon led him to change his mind, which was connected to the release of his film The Monkey House, a literary mystery/comedy, a week before October 7. It received rave reviews and sold over 100,000 tickets – until the war broke out and the theaters closed.
“But I thought: Who cares about that? There’s so much horror around.” Then he got a call from a man from one of the kibbutzim that was decimated in the massacre, who told him he and his wife had bought advance tickets for the movie and had been looking forward to seeing it on the evening of October 7. Housed in a hotel at the Dead Sea following the massacre, he asked if Nesher could bring them the movie and show it there.
'My last memory of myself as a human being'
Nesher was a bit bewildered by the call. “But then this man said, ‘It’s my last memory of myself as a human being. The last time I remember myself just living my life, just buying tickets. So, please bring your movie.’ I said, ‘Of course I’ll get you the movie. No problem.’ And he says, ‘And I want you to come and talk about the movie.’
“But I said, ‘This I cannot do.’ Because when I had that awful time, with what happened to Ari, if somebody had talked to me about cinema, I would have slapped him. What the f***? And he said, ‘No, no, we’re not like that.’ I told him my own story, which he knew, and he said, ‘No, it’s different. Please come.’ Of course, you cannot say no. I came there, and I went up on stage and apologized. And he said, ‘Please, Mr. Nesher, let’s see the movie.’ They screened the movie, and they laughed. A lot. And they clapped at the end. A lot. I got up on stage, and it was the longest Q&A I’ve ever done in my life.”
It ended so late that he stayed over in the hotel and spent more time with them, learning their stories.
At breakfast, they told him, “‘You see these two young people sitting in a corner? They met on October 7. Because he was running, he had no place to go, and she took a chance and opened her mamad [safe room] and let him in. And now they’re a couple.’ They fell in love. Can you imagine? With all this horror and bloodiness, can you imagine? Suddenly you feel these people are trying somehow to regain sanity. They’re trying to grab hold of what’s left. They kept telling me more about the way they got into October 7, more about what they were doing before October 7, than about October 7. And then someone jokingly said there were some people who actually thought October 6 was the worst day of their lives.”
A movie about the human spirit
This was a lightbulb moment for Nesher. “I said, ‘Really? Like who?’ Mostly people with severe romantic problems or family problems, they said. And I said, ‘Hmm. That’s interesting.’ I thought maybe I could make a movie not ‘about October 7’ – of course, you go into October 7 – but you make a movie about the human spirit, and especially the Israeli spirit, which ultimately triumphs. Then you can make a movie that will give hope.
“Because it seemed to me: You think October 6 is the worst day of your life, then you go through the horrible ordeal. You make it out alive somehow. And then you have to rethink all of your life. If I survived this, how do I make it better? It’s a movie about change… It has to do with a personal, possibly with the national, redemption. Things have to change. I thought that was really interesting.”
He turned to Emilio Schenker, the CEO of the Israel-based, global entertainment company, SIPUR. “Emilio completely understood the vision, which is rare – and they hired three wonderful researchers who scouted and found people who survived October 7 who had personal, romantic, parental, religious, and whatever other kind of problems.”
People opened up to him and his researchers, and he began writing. “My thing was basically to use only what they told me. Not to make anything up. It’s so interesting, because you make a movie whose first third will play almost like a romantic comedy, and then the sky will fall. Then you have to survive somehow. And then, when you come out, you have to reconsider everything, and you have to appreciate life. You have to say, ‘Life is a great gift, and I’m here.’ Again, I know about this stuff because this is pretty much what I went through myself, with Ari.”
Our Loves is true cinema
Our Loves presents a stark contrast to previous movies and television series that have focused on the attack, which were basically reenactments of the experiences of real people with actors. Instead, Our Loves is a carefully shaped dramatic story, true cinema, that features three-dimensional characters and even some darkly funny moments. It opens at a concert on the night of October 5, 2023, where most of the main characters happen to be, for different reasons.
These include a religious young woman, Sapir (Daniel Gimpel), who has just been dumped by a guy she hoped she would marry and who has decided to rebel by attending the Nova music festival, and who ends up running and hiding with a drug dealer (Leib Levin) who keeps his stash in his underwear. There’s also a retired general, Shabi (Shalom Michaelswilli), who is suing his ex-wife to force her to sell their house, which deepens the rift between him and his children, especially his young adult daughter (Noa Cohen). The latter storyline will remind people of several real-life stories of retired generals who grabbed a weapon and headed south when the attack began, but it has a twist.
“This guy was really a son of a bitch. He was a terrible father,” Nesher said. He managed to use this story to insert some comic moments into the film. Many of them involve four hopeless recruits, who have only been in the army a week – “the leftovers of the leftovers of the leftovers” – whom the retired general picks up along the way to help him in his quest.
“Now, in a way, this guy has to become their parent because he has to somehow make them into fighters.” One of the most moving and surprising aspects of the story is how, in the course of schooling these bumbling soldiers, the retired general is schooled as well.
“It’s easier being a hero than being a human being,” said Nesher. “I don’t mean to downplay heroism. But some of these people were amazingly flawed as human beings. And they did a heroic deed because it was the right thing to do. But then the event changed them... The trick was to make a movie about people caught in a situation, not about the situation.”
Eventually, he gave the script to Schenker. “Emilio read it and said, ‘This is great writing. It’s not a war movie. It’s about people,’” said Nesher. At a later stage, two important international producers, Danny Cohen, president of Access Entertainment, and Fernando Szew, president and head of FOX Entertainment Studios, signed on as co-producers. Moshe Edery, Nesher’s longtime collaborator, also co-produced the movie for United King Films.
Nesher has made movies about true historical stories in the past, but never before had he done a movie where the majority of the cast and crew had lost friends in the event, and the filming was an emotional roller coaster.
“Interestingly, in the crew we had two girls who were at Nova. They came to work for us in order to deal with the fear of going back. It was amazing to see them dealing with trauma,” Nesher said.
While it is hard to discuss specifics of the plot without revealing spoilers, Our Loves ends with a character uttering the line, “I’m not leaving.”
When asked what the line refers to, Nesher mentioned a moment in this character’s storyline but agreed that it could have a deeper significance as well. I asked whether, on some level, it is he who is making this affirmation, especially since he could have stayed in Hollywood and been sitting by his pool today.
He acknowledged that was true. “Obviously, it’s appropriate for this character to be saying this, but this message is my message… Yeah, I could have stayed in Hollywood and made American movies. Easily.”
The movie has gotten great word-of-mouth reaction from previews in Israel, and Nesher spoke with anticipation about showing it abroad. It will be the sixth time one of his movies has premiered at Toronto, although a few things will undoubtedly be different this time around.
“The great thing about the Toronto Film Festival is that they’ve always stood for great cinematic values. As opposed to other festivals that are about ideology – if you say the right word, they’ll get you in – Toronto was always about cinema. They have great taste. They have great people selecting films. I guess they just saw the movie and thought it belonged. That’s why they put it in Centerpiece, which has great movies. I salute these people, and I salute this festival and all the values it stands for,” he said.
Israeli movies in the current film industry
He is aware, of course, that many in the film industry have called for all Israeli movies to be boycotted.
“In the ’60s we knew how to protest – all these great antiwar marches. But they were against the US government. Against Robert McNamara. LBJ, against the Vietnam War... Nobody thought for a second of boycotting Hollywood. Nobody thought for a second of boycotting American literature or American music or Andy Warhol.”
Nesher is no cheerleader for the Israeli government and spoke openly about his hope that the elections will bring a change in leadership. Noting that at the time of the October 7 attack, about half of all Israelis were fighting to preserve and strengthen democracy against government interference, he said, “As always, at the forefront of every fight for democracy are people from the arts. So, you want to stay away from movies and culture and handicap the people fighting for democracy?... Either you are really stupid, which I don’t think you are, or there is a tinge of antisemitism in this, because you did not boycott Iranian art. You did not boycott the art of any other country when you disagreed with their government.”
He knows that there may be protests in Toronto against Our Loves, and he is ready for them. “For me, this conflict is not about land. The conflict is about story. The conflict is about narrative,” and he is eager to present this narrative to audiences.
He is also well aware that he is likely to be asked why the story is not told, at least in part, from the perspective of the Hamas terrorists.
“Actually, I got an offer from an Italian producer: If I would do Our Loves like Image of Victory [which features a major character who is an Egyptian photojournalist embedded with Egyptian troops], he would come in with an investment of a million euros,” said Nesher.
“I told this producer, ‘Sadly, I cannot do it.’ In Image of Victory, I could write the Egyptian side because the Egyptian side was just like us, only in Arabic,” he said. “But Hamas is a whole different thing. It’s like ISIS... I would not know how to direct Charles Manson, how to tell his story. I just would not know.”
When it comes to Hamas, “I do not know how to direct people who did these horrible things... I do not understand the guy who gets pleasure out of killing a baby, out of burning families alive. So, I did not take the money. And we made the movie anyway.”
Toward the end of Our Loves, some characters make it to a hospital, and the doctor in charge is an Arab physician, played by Hisham Suliman.
“Twenty percent of the population is Arab, and they’re going to remain here, and there has to be a way of making it work,” he said. “The truth is, it simply wouldn’t be realistic if I showed a hospital in Israel without Arab employees. But beyond that, it makes a point: Let’s not get confused. Arabs are not our enemy. Hamas is our enemy. It’s a whole different thing.”
The more he talks, the more it becomes obvious that he is the perfect director to tell this story right now: An Israeli who is equally comfortable in America, but also an ardent Zionist who cares deeply about what happens in Israel. It’s clear from his personal story that he empathizes with grieving families and can identify with all those who suffered loss on October 7 and since. And he wants to fight back with the most potent weapon he knows – story.
“That’s the beauty of cinema. Cinema gets you to accept a different normal than the one you’ve been told before… And again, there’s this Israeli spirit, which I have admired since young childhood. I think that’s why we all live in this country even though it makes no sense at all. We’re not going anywhere. We’re not leaving,” he said, echoing his movie’s last line.

What does the joint declaration say?
On the first day of the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of a joint declaration.
The joint declaration adopted by the BRICS coalition calls for "maximum restraint" in the Middle East.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the statement read.

Since the bloc inlcuded Iran and US-ally UAE both, it was expected that reaching a concensus will be difficult.

What does a joint declaration against war mean for the bloc's influence?
"It’s all done," Indian prime minister Narendra Modi said. And what he meant was this: BRICS has an approved joint declaration for 2026. The leaders agreed on the text of the Delhi Declaration on day one of the summit after their plenary session.
It is important to keep in mind that, for the first six months of the Iran war, the grouping of Global South nations failed to issue a joint statement. The US-Israel-led attack on Iran has put enormous strain on the bloc.
The war directly involves three BRICS members: Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. But not as allies. Iran has attacked the UAE and Saudi Arabia, seeing them as proxies for the US.
The war has been devastating for the Global South, which BRICS represents. Think oil and fertilizers — and food security.
The compromise now found in Delhi appears to be a joint declaration condemning unilateral wars, without naming any country.
That is rather low-key — but perhaps better than nothing, especially for BRICS chair India, which can claim this as a diplomatic victory. As former UN diplomat and prominent Indian foreign policy voice Shashi Tharoor had told me before the summit:
"There is very little doubt that all the BRICS members have not necessarily upheld the UN Charter, the inviolability of borders, the sovereignty of member states of the UN, and the inadmissibility of the use of force to settle international disputes."
The BRICS countries now number 11 and represent about half of the world’s population. And when economies are measured by what people can actually buy, they account for around 40 percent of global economic output.
So BRICS leaders feel they have a strong case for criticizing western political hegemony and the dominance of the US dollar. They argue that global institutions such as the UN, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank no longer reflect the rising power of emerging economies and the Global South.
In his opening address, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that reform of the UN Security Council cannot wait any longer.

It "does not serve the common interests of the international community", Xi said, according to Xinhua.

In his closing remarks for the first session at the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a joint declaration on Saturday, the first day of their annual summit in New Delhi.
Reuters news agency, citing four anonymous sources, had earlier in the day reported that members of the BRICS coalition have agreed on a joint declaration which does not name any country but will condemn unilateral war by any country.
The members include Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.
Can BRICS Really Challenge the Dollar? Not Quite, Says BRICS Expert
As leaders gather in New Delhi for the 2026 BRICS Summit, talk of "de-dollarization" is everywhere. But Anuradha Mitra Chenoy, Professor and former dean at School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, argues the real story is more modest, and more interesting.
Every BRICS summit now comes with the same headline: is this the moment the bloc finally dethrones the US dollar? For Chenoy, the question itself is the problem.
"The debate is often overstated," she told DW. BRICS countries, in her reading, are not on a mission to replace the dollar. What they are doing is settling more of their bilateral trade in local currencies — a shift that has less to do with ideology than with practicality. It cuts transaction costs, speeds up payments, and makes trade more predictable for businesses that used to route everything through dollars by default.
A dollar that’s been "weaponized"
If there’s a political edge to this trend, Chenoy locates it elsewhere, in how the dollar itself has been used as a tool of coercion. US sanctions, tariffs, and the freezing or outright confiscation of foreign reserves have all pushed countries, particularly across the Global South, to think harder about their exposure to the American financial system.
That calculus matters most for heavily indebted developing economies. By trading directly in local currencies with partners like India, China, Russia, and South Africa, these countries can sidestep some of their need to hold dollars just to settle trade. The payoff, Chenoy says, is twofold. Firstly, lower transaction costs, and secondly, in some cases, less reliance on dollar-denominated debt.
India’s balancing act
New Delhi has backed greater use of local currencies and cross-border payment mechanisms within BRICS, even as it keeps its economic relationship with Washington firmly intact.
For Chenoy, It’s also not a new one. She points back to the Rupee-Ruble trading arrangement India ran with the Soviet Union decades ago — a reminder that local-currency trade has deep roots in Indian economic policy, long before "de-dollarization" became a buzzword.
Chenoy says what’s actually happening inside BRICS — not a coordinated campaign to topple the dollar, but a pragmatic hedge that countries are spreading their financial risk across more currencies and more systems, one bilateral deal at a time.

India faces balancing act between US and China: DW's Head of Geopolitics reports from Delhi
The BRICS summit is packed with bilaterals for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Yesterday, he walked hand in hand with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hugged Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Today, he has already met the prime ministers of Ethiopia, Malaysia and Vietnam, as well as the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. More meetings are to follow as the clock counts down to 5:45 pm local time. That is when Modi is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping. And that's a big thing — especially for Indian media, which are broadcasting live around the clock.
Modi and Xi have, of course, met several times in recent years on the sidelines of multilateral summits — at the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024, and at the SCO summits in Tianjin in 2025 and Bishkek just two weeks ago. But Xi has not been to India since 2019. This will be his first visit to the country in seven years.
Relations between the two Asian powers froze after a deadly clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border, known as the Line of Actual Control. Direct flights and visas were suspended, while political engagement and trade ties suffered a major setback.
Today’s meeting could mark another step in the cautious thaw between the two nuclear-armed Asian powers, which have spent years drifting apart. But beneath the expected smiles and handshakes, deep mistrust remains — especially over their disputed border and over who gets to shape the future of Asia.
India's huge trade deficit with China might surface in discussions. Bilateral trade has nearly doubled in five years, but so has India's dependence on Chinese imports. Trade between the two countries reached $151.1 billion (€130.22 billion) in the 2025–26 financial year, making China India's largest trading partner. But the imbalance is striking: India imported $131.6 billion worth of goods from China, while exporting just $20 billion.
And when it comes to BRICS,India has no appetite for turning the bloc into an anti-Western platform that could jeopardize its relationship with the United States. A trade agreement with Washington is still pending, and India remains dependent on US technology. At the same time, China has become the world’s second-largest economy.
The elephant in the room here at BRICS 2026 in New Delhi, of course, is the US president. While Trump continues to threaten India with sanctions and tariffs for doing business with Iran and Russia, he is taking a softer line with China as he tries to get closer to Xi.
For New Delhi, then, the challenge is to deepen ties with China without drifting too far from the US — and to use BRICS to strengthen India's room for manoeuvre without turning it into an anti-Western alliance.

A train derailment in France may have been sabotage; investigators consider this version the priority
Kyiv • UNN
A TER train derailed in Normandy, injuring 44 people. Investigators found a foreign piece of rail and are examining the possibility of sabotage.
French investigators are considering possible deliberate interference as the leading theory behind the derailment of a TER passenger train in Normandy, which injured 44 people. A piece of rail that should not have been there was found between the tracks at the crash site, BFMTV reports, writes UNN.
Details
The accident occurred on the evening of September 11 near the town of Cléon in the Seine-Maritime department. The train, which was traveling between Rouen and Caen, was carrying 186 passengers.
According to BFMTV, the theory of deliberate action became the leading one precisely after the discovery of the foreign piece of rail. Investigators have yet to determine whether the train collided with it and whether this caused the carriages to derail.
The prosecutor's office is investigating the origin of the piece of rail
Rouen Prosecutor Sébastien Gallois confirmed that the main hypothesis at present is that a piece of rail was lying on one of the tracks and may have caused the accident. It is not yet known how or why it ended up there.
Forty-four people were injured in the derailment. An 18-year-old female passenger was initially evacuated by helicopter in critical condition; however, the prosecutor's office later reported that her life was not in danger. Another 43 people sustained minor injuries.
The driver's alcohol and drug tests were negative. A total of 130 firefighters, 5 medical teams and around 80 vehicles were involved in dealing with the aftermath of the accident.

Listening for schizophrenia: how AI can help with early diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:37:56 UTC
20:37:56 KST

Schizophrenia is tough to diagnose. Patients may present with hallucinations (sometimes), social withdrawal (maybe) or delusions (not always). More generally, they just sound unlike themselves. Clinicians rely on their expertise and subtle cues to determine how different patients’ speech is, along with which symptoms appear over time, to justify leaning toward schizophrenia rather than another mental illness. This leads to delays in diagnosis. Americans with psychotic disorders — more than 3 million of whom have schizophrenia — receive a diagnosis a year and a half, on average, after their first symptoms appear.
Researchers are now investigating whether artificial intelligence could improve diagnosis and care by listening to and analyzing what clinicians can’t hear or quantify, even if the software is working off just a few minutes of conversation. AI won’t make its grand entrance into the clinic tomorrow. But it’s being hailed as the new frontier in psychiatric care, one that could enable early, accurate detection and personalized monitoring of illnesses based on indistinct symptoms.
“We have the tools to do that with the kind of precision that we have never had before,” says Thomas Insel, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist who led the US National Institute of Mental Health for 13 years.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Schizophrenia is a disorder that interferes with people’s perception of reality, their thinking and their emotional regulation. It affects about 23 million people worldwide and is usually diagnosed between the late teens and early 30s. No one knows what causes it, but research suggests it could be a combination of genetics, environment, brain chemistry and substance use.
Clinicians stress the importance of detecting the disorder as early as possible, because the longer it is left untreated, the poorer the response to treatment and the greater the risk of brain tissue loss, worsening symptoms and suicide. But psychiatrists often make errors.
Part of the problem is that diagnosis currently depends on subjective assessments. Based on what a patient says and how they say it, clinicians fill out one of several different rating scales to rank the severity of symptoms and arrive at a diagnosis. But the process is difficult to standardize, and clinicians’ scores for a given patient can differ by 30 to 50 percent.
Artificial intelligence could help to automate the process, making diagnosis both speedier and more accurate. “For the first time, we could have a way of saying objectively, how delusional is this? How loose are these associations? How incoherent is it?” says Insel.
Psychiatrists view speech as a solid marker to evaluate someone’s mental state since it can indicate disordered thinking, a hallmark of schizophrenia. People with disordered thought tend to move erratically from idea to idea — a chaotic path that AI could help to identify. Clinicians also know that schizophrenic patients sound different. Their tone can be more monotonous or robotic, they can take longer pauses. And the volume of their voice can lack contrast compared to that of healthy people who speak louder or quieter depending on the context and content of the conversation. But these differences are hard to use for diagnosis, especially in the early stages.
A team of researchers in the Netherlands wondered whether AI could help. They selected audio recordings of people who had previously been diagnosed with schizophrenia by psychiatrists, then used software to measure 88 features, such as loudness, length of pauses, vowel pronunciation and intonation. They then used these measures to train an AI program to distinguish people with and without schizophrenia.
When the team tested their AI using audio files from new patients it had not heard before, it differentiated schizophrenic patients from healthy controls with 86.2 percent accuracy and could even distinguish between different subtypes of the illness.
The approach isn’t especially useful for the clearest cases, says study coauthor Alban Voppel, a researcher now at McGill University in Montreal who studies the use of AI in psychiatry. But AI could help to detect patients in early stages or at high risk of becoming schizophrenic, and to predict relapse. “There are hopeful signs that we can pick up on very subtle things and things that psychiatrists find much harder to detect or harder to predict,” he says.
Sunny Tang, a psychiatrist and researcher at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research near New York City, took a different approach. Instead of studying the sounds of speech, her team looked at its content. They built a type of AI called a machine learning model to assign a mathematical address, similar to the address of a house, to each word in a transcript of a patient’s conversation. By looking at the constellation of addresses, Tang’s program can tell whether a sentence stays in the same general neighborhood or leaves town and returns again, indicating disorganized thinking. In this way, Tang says, she can measure “how the meaning flows in the course of what somebody says.”
When Tang provided transcripts of speech by people with and without schizophrenia, she found that the AI could distinguish the two groups with 87 percent accuracy. Clinical raters, who assessed patients without the AI, were only 68 percent accurate.
Beyond diagnosis, clinicians may eventually be able to use AI for routine monitoring of the severity and progression of a patient’s symptoms over time. Such tracking helps clinicians provide more precise and responsive care, by evaluating whether a treatment is producing the desired effects and detecting early signs of relapse.
Today, such monitoring requires clinicians to meet with patients regularly, at a huge cost of time and money. AI could potentially provide the same care for a fraction of the cost, and enable it to be done remotely. “You can have someone speak into an app or a device for a couple of minutes and give a fairly competent, confident rating on this person’s psychosis,” says Tang, who is hoping to have a tool ready for clinical trials in 2030.
Much work remains before AI diagnosis is ready for the clinic, however. For one thing, artificial intelligence is only as good as the data it’s trained on — and there are serious deficiencies in those data. Many studies use small groups of people who are not representative of the population as a whole, according to a survey of studies using AI to make psychiatric diagnoses. “We need bigger samples, more diverse samples,” says Jeffrey Girard, a psychologist at the University of Kansas who led the analysis, published in the 2026 Annual Review of Clinical Psychology.
Another problem is that people can speak more slowly not because they are mentally ill, but because they are older or speaking a second language. People may also sound different in stressful contexts such as an emergency room, or under the influence of medications or physical illness, notes Sandra Just, a clinical psychologist at UiT the Arctic University of Norway.
This creates a “research-to-practice gap” where voice markers can do well in studies but poorly in the real world, says John Torous, a psychiatrist and informaticist at Harvard’s Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
Ideally, doctors would know what a patient usually sounds like to see if their speech has changed. But collecting such baseline data would involve identifying people at high risk of schizophrenia, then recording their calls, asking them to engage with an app daily or keeping track of clinical interviews — even if they currently show no symptoms.
Doing that raises sticky ethical issues around privacy and security. “This is a really complicated problem,” says Brita Elvevåg, a cognitive neuroscientist at UiT the Arctic University of Norway who has studied speech patterns for nearly 30 years. “How can we preserve personal privacy now that we’re starting to use technology? It worries me that people don’t necessarily take that into consideration.”
Because of all these limitations, researchers don’t see AI becoming a schizophrenia diagnostician anytime soon. “It’s a tool, it’s not a panacea,” says Vijay Mittal, a researcher and clinical psychologist at Northwestern University in Illinois. “It’s early days and there’s a lot of excitement [but] there needs to be a lot of caution.”

On the night of September 12, Ukrainian drones attacked a number of targets in the Russian cities of Taganrog and Tolyatti.

In Taganrog, the Rostov region, NASA’s FIRMS satellites have detected several fire hotspots. Local residents have also confirmed this information.
One of the targets was likely the Beriev Aircraft Company. A fire was reported in the vicinity of the facility.
The aircraft plant specializes in the maintenance and modernization of A-50 long-range radar detection aircraft, Be series amphibious aircraft for the Russian Navy, and Tu-95MS/MSM strategic bombers, which Russia uses to launch X-101 cruise missiles at Ukraine.
The Taganrog-Yuzhny airfield, which serves as the main test base for the Beriev Aircraft Company, is located nearby.
In addition, satellites detected another fire near a local automobile plant, which is located not far from the aircraft plant.
In the city of Tolyatti, the Samara region, drones attacked the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant. A fire subsequently broke out on the plant’s grounds, which was captured on video and in photos by local residents.
The main products of the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant are caprolactam, polyamide-6, industrial yarn, ammonium nitrate, urea, ammonium sulfate, ammonia, and nitric acid.
The company is one of Russia’s leading manufacturers of chemical products.
The plant is one of the largest producers of caprolactam and nitrogen fertilizers, as well as a supplier of raw materials for the chemical and textile industries. Caprolactam, in particular, is used in the production of polyamide plastics and synthetic fibers.
Ukrainian defense forces had already attacked this facility in March 2026.

German police bodycam captures dramatic arrest of suspected power saboteur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:36:01 UTC
20:36:01 KST

Police in North Rhine-Westphalia have released bodycam footage showing the arrest of alleged power saboteur Daniel V., with officers drawing their weapons as new details emerge in the case.
Police in Cologne have released bodycam footage showing the arrest of suspected power saboteur Daniel V.
The footage, recorded by an officer's bodycam, shows Daniel V. lying face down on the ground as armed officers approach him with their weapons drawn. They then handcuff him and escort him to a patrol car.
The video also shows a tent where Daniel V. is believed to have been sleeping.
Meanwhile, further details about the investigation are emerging. North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul (CDU) told the state parliament's internal affairs committee that investigators have identified additional possible crime scenes. These are reportedly located not only in North Rhine-Westphalia but also in other German states and neighbouring countries.
According to Reul, investigators in North Rhine-Westphalia alone have so far discovered more than 40 devices capable of firing conductive material at power lines near substations. Investigators believe the devices may have been intended to cause short circuits and trigger power outages.
Investigators reportedly gained further leads from a vehicle seized from the suspect. According to Reul, officers found a notebook containing handwritten notes about more than 150 potential sabotage targets. The locations were subsequently checked. Following his arrest, Daniel V. is also said to have identified seven sites where he had allegedly established depots.
“We have not only caught the suspected perpetrator of the attacks, but may thereby have prevented a whole series of further attacks,” Reul said.
Police arrested the 48-year-old, who had been the subject of a days-long search, on Tuesday. According to the dpa news agency, he was apprehended near the Weisweiler power station outside Aachen. The newspaper Welt reported that the arrest took place during a traffic stop.
What is known so far
The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office has taken over the investigation, citing the case’s particular significance. According to a spokeswoman, investigators are examining, among other allegations, whether the suspect targeted the constitutional order through acts of sabotage.
Given the large number of devices discovered, investigators are also looking into whether Daniel V. could have carried out the alleged acts alone. Reul told the committee that authorities were also considering the possibility that the suspect may have been acting on behalf of a foreign power. However, the minister stressed that there is currently no evidence to support this theory.
“The investigation is continuing at full speed,” Reul said.
The minister also provided further details about documents found in the seized vehicle. According to the information provided by Reul, the notebook contains references to more than 160 known or potential additional sabotage targets. The locations listed in the notebook have since been checked by investigators.
An “extraordinary” case
In recent days, investigators have been dealing with several suspected acts of sabotage targeting power infrastructure in North Rhine-Westphalia and Brandenburg. Among other methods, improvised rockets were reportedly used to fire conductive material at high-voltage power lines. The incidents did not result in any major power outages.
In several letters claiming responsibility, an unknown author said they were behind incidents at various power plant sites in both states. However, Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster (CDU) urged caution against drawing premature conclusions, describing both the alleged method of attack and the confession letter as unusual.

Jiao Boqiao (R) of China vies with Mohamed Juma of Bahrain during the group C match between China and Bahrain at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- China secured its second consecutive victory in the men's basketball tournament at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, routing Group C rival Bahrain 105-59 on Saturday.
China took immediate control with a 9-0 opening run. Hu Jinqiu dominated in the paint, while Zhu Junlong and Li Hongquan hit shots from beyond the arc. Liao Sanning scored 10 points in the first quarter alone, helping China build a 46-29 lead by halftime.
Pang Zhenglin sparked another offensive surge in the final period to push the lead beyond 40 points and put the game well out of reach.
"Today we found our rhythm. Every game is different, so we approached this one seriously and prepared thoroughly," Li Hongquan said.
Liao led China with 23 points and six assists, followed by Li Yuezhou with 18 points. Pang, Wang Junjie and Hu added 11 points apiece. Jakarr Sampson scored a team-high 17 points for Bahrain.
China will play its final group-stage match on Monday against the Philippines, which knocked China out in the semifinals of the Hangzhou Asian Games.
"First, we need to rest well over the next two days because we have just finished back-to-back games. Some of our players also have minor injuries, so we hope they can recover during that time. Then we will review the good and bad parts of this game, study the individual characteristics of the Philippines players, and execute the coach's plan," Li added when asked about facing the Philippines. ■

Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
September 12, 2026
Germany's Welt am Sonntag (WaS) newspaper has cited intelligence reports tying the recent failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport directly to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.
In an article published on Saturday, Welt am Sonntag said that a man with known ties to the GRU was responsible for operational logistics in the attempted attack.
Further, it said those ties were known to German authorities when the man entered the country from Turkey, nevertheless, he was not surveilled after arrival.
Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the Russian national is now in his home country after departing to Serbia on a flight from Berlin-Brandenburg Airport.
A second man, a Belarus citizen, was also cited as an accomplice in the report.
Explosives thought to have entered Germany from Bulgaria and Serbia
German intelligence sources said that the explosives used in the incident were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia and then stored in underground depots once they arrived in Leipzig.
Berlin quickly made clear that forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms used in other Russian hybrid attacks — pointed to a Russian plot.
In early August, German tabloid BILD reported that authorities had found DNA traces on the drone's remote control antenna. Those samples were said to have matched DNA found at the scene of a July 20, 2024, arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility operated by German courier company DHL.
Leipzig attack averted but Russian escalation will continue
The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine — occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was found near a Ukrainian transport jet.
Authorities were able to disarm the drone and after public speculation that Moscow was behind the incident the German government officially blamed Russia in early September.
Saturday's article said Berlin made the attribution on the basis of the intelligence reports cited.
In response to its conclusion, Germany announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.
The Kremlin in turn reacted by closing Goethe Institutes — a German cultural exchange outfit — across Russia.
As in numerous similar hybrid attacks prior, Russia has denied any involvement in the incident.

Xinhua News | Xi says China will take over BRICS presidency next year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:57 CST
20:29:57 KST

Source: Xinhua
Editor: huaxia
2026-09-12 18:48:16
Xi says China will take over BRICS presidency next year #XinhuaNews
From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Commentary: China's vision and action promote BRICS cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:47 CST
20:29:47 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- BRICS is returning to China once again. At the ongoing BRICS summit in New Delhi, India, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced on Saturday that China will host the BRICS gathering next year.
The long journey of BRICS began with an idea. The term "BRIC" was coined in 2001 by former Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill to describe Brazil, Russia, India and China as emerging economies with significant growth potential.
Over the past two decades, China has hosted three BRICS summits, each marking a new milestone in the group's evolution, expanding the scope of cooperation and strengthening the representation of the Global South.
When China hosted its first BRICS summit in the tropical resort of Sanya in 2011, the grouping officially became BRICS with South Africa joining as a new member.
The Sanya Declaration adopted at that summit called for closer cooperation in areas including trade, finance and agriculture, while urging the members to play a greater role in global economic governance.
Six years later in south China's coastal city of Xiamen, Xi hosted BRICS leaders for the first time as Chinese president.
At the gathering, the Chinese leader proposed the "BRICS Plus" cooperation approach, and invited leaders from non-BRICS members including Egypt, Mexico, Thailand and Guinea to discuss international development cooperation and deepen South-South cooperation.
Xi also announced the creation of the BRICS Partnership on New Industrial Revolution innovation center in Xiamen. Since its birth, the center has facilitated more than 100 cooperation projects, with a total investment of over 9.24 billion U.S. dollars. It has also launched a scholarship for emerging industries, helping BRICS countries train talent across a range of fields, including industry and communications.
It was also at the Xiamen summit that the BRICS mechanism entered a new stage, with people-to-people exchanges added as a new pillar alongside economic and political cooperation.
When China chaired BRICS again in 2022, the leaders reconvened in virtual format as the COVID-19 pandemic was still spreading. At the summit, Xi called for a "more comprehensive, close, practical and inclusive high-quality partnership" and emphasized global development.
The summit also further promoted discussions among BRICS members on BRICS expansion process, laying the groundwork for a wave of expansion at the 2023 BRICS Summit in Johannesburg, South Africa.
Today, the BRICS has expanded to 11 member countries and 10 partner countries, becoming a force for advancing a multipolar world and greater democracy in international relations.
"China has consistently provided a clear vision and momentum for BRICS and the SCO, both conceptually and practically," said Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia.
It transformed BRICS into a broader platform for cooperation among developing countries and the wider Global South, he added.
As the BRICS cooperation mechanism is embarking on its third golden decade, its expanded membership and growing network of partners will bring new opportunities as well as new demands for cooperation.
With joint efforts, it is expected that the next summit in China will help BRICS build even stronger consensus, deepen practical cooperation and strive for a greater voice of the Global South. ■

Feature: Myanmar embraces Chinese traditions at ceremony marking Mid-Autumn Festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:38 CST
20:29:38 KST

People write Chinese calligraphy during an event to celebrate the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival at the China Cultural Center in Yangon, Myanmar, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Brushes dipped in black ink moved across paper as around 200 people gathered at the China Cultural Center in Yangon on Saturday to celebrate the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on September 25 this year.
The festive event offered participants an immersive experience of traditional Chinese customs, featuring hands-on calligraphy, DIY bookmark crafting, tea tastings, mooncakes and other festive foods. Lively dance performances, singing, and poetry recitations further heightened the festive atmosphere.
For Li Li Myint, president of the Myanmar-China Women's Association, the Mid-Autumn Festival represents far more than a seasonal holiday; it is a meaningful symbol of unity and family reunion.
Just as the full moon and traditional mooncakes are round, the holiday brings families together in a complete circle. For those living far from home, looking at the moon serves as a warm reminder of their parents, teachers, and friends, she said.
Beyond the traditions of sharing meals and appreciating the full moon, she noted that the true essence of the festival is fostering a unified spirit and sharing love.
Chaw Yu Mon Soe, 25, said she regularly attends cultural events at the center and believes such activities help people in Myanmar experience Chinese traditions.
"Some Chinese people born in Myanmar may be far from their culture, but they can come here, enjoy the event and experience the culture by taking part in these activities," she said, adding that practicing traditional ink-brush calligraphy was her favorite.
Su Zarchi Kaung, who participated in the event as a dancer and singer, said she was proud to perform at the event.
She also saw similarities between the Mid-Autumn Festival and Myanmar's Thadingyut Festival, one of the Southeast Asian nation's most significant religious festivals.
In Myanmar, during Thadingyut, family members who work in different places return home. Families reunite, eat together and pay respects to their elders, she said.
"Through this cultural exchange, every participant can experience and appreciate Chinese culture while deepening the 'Paukphaw' (fraternal) friendship," Xiang Jianbo, director of the China Cultural Center in Yangon, said. ■

Feature: Namibian students turn everyday problems into science fair projects
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:14 CST
20:29:14 KST

WINDHOEK, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- When Soini Shoonga noticed that many of his classmates were struggling with mathematics, the Grade 7 student began looking for a way to make the subject easier to learn.
His solution was a solar-powered electrical math game made with recycled materials, which he brought to Namibia's National Science Fair in Windhoek on Friday.
"A lot of learners in my class actually failed mathematics last time, so I came up with this idea," Shoonga told Xinhua.
An online search led him to an electrical game designed for biology learning. He wondered whether he could adapt the idea to help his classmates practice mathematics.
"I wondered what if I just convert it into an electrical math game," he said.
Shoonga was among students from across Namibia presenting projects inspired by problems they had encountered in their classrooms and communities, ranging from difficulties with schoolwork to inefficient use of water in farming.
For Maxnoah Lukas, a Grade 11 student from Kavango East Region, the starting point was the gap he saw between farming practices in his community and the possibilities offered by computers.
Farmers struggled with inefficient water use, he said, prompting him to develop an automated system designed to monitor growing conditions and irrigate crops when needed.
The project combines sensors with a program written in Python to monitor crops' water needs, including when farmers are away.
"I noticed that there's a gap between agriculture and computers," Lukas said.
He said he wanted to make technology more useful to farmers in his community, helping them produce food without wasting resources.
"My main motivation is that I like automation," added Lukas, who hopes to pursue engineering.
Organized by the National Commission on Research, Science and Technology (NCRST) in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sports, Arts and Culture, the annual fair allows students to conduct scientific investigations and present their findings.
Exhibits ranged from working prototypes to research projects, with participants exploring subjects including agriculture, energy, mathematics and health.
Mokgadi Tittus, a member of the fair's Quality Assurance Committee, said identifying projects that respond to practical problems was an important goal.
"This platform creates an opportunity for learners to be identified and for projects to be continued further," he told Xinhua.
Tittus said the NCRST aimed to identify promising projects and help develop them further for potential use in local markets.
For Shoonga, taking part in competitions had already helped him improve his design. Feedback from judges at an earlier round prompted him to add more questions and a selector to his math game.
"At first, it didn't have a selector and only had a few questions," he said. "The judges at the circuit told me it would be more fun and interactive if it had a lot of questions, so I expanded it."
The fair, which commenced on Wednesday and opened to the public on Friday, formed part of the broader 2026 Mathematics and Science Promotion Program, a national initiative that brought learners from regions across Namibia together to compete in the National Science Fair, the Namibia Mathematics Olympiad and the National Science Quiz. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: What to know about Sweden's parliamentary election
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:12 CST
20:29:12 KST

STOCKHOLM, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Swedish voters will head to the polls on Sunday in a closely contested parliamentary election that will determine whether Prime Minister (PM) Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc can retain its parliamentary majority.
Recent polls put the opposition ahead, but the race has tightened in the final weeks. The result could also reshape Sweden's political landscape, with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) potentially entering government for the first time, while divisions among opposition parties could complicate their path to power.
HOW DOES THE ELECTION WORK?
Voters will elect all 349 members of Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, for a four-year term. Regional and municipal elections will also take place on Sunday.
Sweden uses proportional representation. Of the 349 parliamentary seats, 310 are distributed across 29 constituencies, while the remaining 39 are adjustment seats used to make the nationwide result more proportional.
A party generally needs at least 4 percent of the national vote to enter parliament. Voters do not directly elect the PM. The speaker of the Riksdag nominates a candidate, who is approved unless at least 175 lawmakers vote against the proposal.
WHO IS COMPETING?
The election pits two broad political groupings against each other.
Kristersson heads a three-party minority government comprising the Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals, with parliamentary support from SD.
The arrangement took shape after the 2022 election, when the four parties won a narrow parliamentary majority with a combined 176 seats. SD won 20.54 percent of the vote and 73 seats in 2022, becoming Sweden's second-largest party, but remained outside government because of longstanding resistance from mainstream parties.
Under the Tido Agreement reached after the election, SD supported the government in parliament while gaining greater influence over policy. The four parties are often collectively referred to as the Tido parties.
This year, the Liberals dropped their previous opposition to SD joining the cabinet, opening the way for a four-party government if the bloc wins. SD leader Jimmie Akesson has made clear that his party wants formal government participation, saying it would be "either in government or in opposition" after the election.
On the other side, former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats are seeking to return to power with support from the Green Party, Left Party and Centre Party.
Andersson could face complicated negotiations among the four opposition parties, as they have yet to agree on a government formula. The Centre Party has ruled out a government including the Left Party, saying it would rather face an extraordinary election, while the latter has demanded cabinet representation. Swedish Television (SVT) has described the problem as an "impossible equation."
WHAT ARE THE KEY CAMPAIGN ISSUES?
SVT's final party leaders' debate on Friday focused on the economy, education, climate, crime, integration and healthcare.
Healthcare remains voters' top concern. An SVT/Verian survey published on Aug. 20 found that 64 percent of respondents regarded it as one of the most important political issues, up from 55 percent in May. The Moderates want to shorten the healthcare waiting-time guarantee from 90 days to 30, while the Social Democrats have pledged to increase healthcare funding in line with inflation.
Migration and integration remain a major dividing line. Sweden has tightened migration policy during the current parliamentary term. According to Sveriges Radio on Friday, SD is the only one of the eight parliamentary parties calling for further restrictions after the election, while several opposition parties favor easing some recent measures.
Climate policy is also contested, with parties divided over the pace and cost of the green transition. SD opposes setting Swedish climate targets more ambitious than those of the European Union, arguing that stricter targets could impose additional costs on industry, rural communities and motorists.
WHAT DO POLLS SHOW?
The opposition leads in most final polls, but surveys differ over the size of its advantage.
An Ekot/Indikator poll published on Friday put the four opposition parties at 50.8 percent and the four Tido parties at 47.6 percent, a gap of 3.2 percentage points. The final SVT/Verian poll showed a wider opposition lead of 5.6 points. SVT said the differing surveys meant Sunday's election could still become a "thriller."
The Liberals remain a key uncertainty. The party won 4.61 percent and 16 seats in 2022 but has spent much of the current term below the 4-percent threshold in opinion polls.
Its support has rebounded in the closing stages. The Ekot/Indikator poll put the Liberals at 5.4 percent, while SVT/Verian put them at 5.5 percent. Their survival in parliament could prove crucial to Kristersson's chances of retaining a majority.
WHY COULD THE RESULT MATTER BEYOND SWEDEN?
The election comes amid the growing influence of radical-right parties across Europe. Just a week before Sweden's vote, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a record 43.8 percent in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The rise of these parties has sharpened the question of how mainstream center-right forces should respond. Germany's established parties continue to reject cooperation with the AfD, while Sweden has moved from isolating SD to relying on its parliamentary support, with the possibility of bringing it into government.
The Nordic region offers another comparison. In neighboring Finland, the Finns Party already serves in the governing coalition, reflecting what the Finnish Institute of International Affairs has described as the growing influence of radical-right forces in Nordic politics. SD's entry into government would mark a further step in that shift. ■

He attended meetings in Dublin, before travelling to County Clare for the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament.
Trump said a united Ireland would happen eventually and that the Taoiseach was "the right man over here to get it moving".

- Trump's comments on a united Ireland may have targeted audience across the Atlantic
