During his meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House, in Phoenix Park, Trump said a united Ireland would be a "fantastic thing", and added: "now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"
A spokesperson for Number 10 referred to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's words on Wednesday in the House of Commons that he "will stick to it (the Good Friday Agreement) 100%".
On Wednesday, Burnham added that "the question of a border poll" was for the Northern Ireland secretary "when there is clear consensus in the country - when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered".
A spokesperson for Martin said Trump's comments should "come as a surprise to no one" and the US president has been "consistent in his view that he sees unity in Ireland as the optimal outcome".
The Good Friday Agreement says the secretary of state must hold a border poll if it appears likely that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish unification - and the circumstances of when that could happen is the subject of constant debate in Northern Ireland and the Republic.
Earlier this week, Martin said there needed to be more clarity on when a border poll can be called, while Burnham ruled out calling a referendum, describing a poll as "off the table".
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said she acknowledged Trumps comments on a united Ireland and said the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.

Former DUP MP Ian Paisley and close friend of the Trump family said: "everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it's wrong".
Welcoming his comments, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Claire Hanna said there was something "fairly extraordinary" about Trump standing in Dublin and talking openly about Irish unity.
"When even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted."
The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said while America is an "important ally," Northern Ireland's future will be decided by its people".
The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said Trump "is not the first US President to meddle in the affairs which don't concern him".

"It's something that that we have to work on and we have to work towards."
Later, while attending an event at the US Ambassador to Ireland's residence, Trump said there is "no good answer" to a question about a united Ireland.
Recalling the moment, he said: "Oh that's a nice question, I have a nice answer, I think, we'll read about it tomorrow."
Trump also said his country's relationship with Ireland is "stronger than ever".
During his meeting with the Taoiseach, Trump said: "We've a big relationship with Ireland."
"The two countries do very well together," he said, adding: "It's never been as good as it is right now."
He said they discussed various topics, including trade.

The two heads of state met earlier on Saturday morning.

"As a country which has suffered famine, colonisation and the violence of the Troubles, but also the importance of the long and challenging road to peace, I emphasised the unique insight which Irish people can bring to the resolution of conflict," she said in a statement issued after the meeting.
Irish authorities have been planning for Trump's visit for months in what is one of the biggest security operations in the history of the state.

Zelensky outlines Ukraine's need for Patriot missiles ahead of winter
He made these remarks in an interview with DW on Friday at the Canadian military base in North Bay, according to Ukrinform.
The Ukrainian leader noted that Russia is currently producing 140 ballistic missiles per month, whereas, according to NATO standards, a 1-to-2 ratio is required to destroy them—that is, 280 interceptor missiles. Zelensky emphasized that it is impossible to obtain such a number of missiles, adding that for Ukraine, receiving even 100 interceptor missiles per month is a “huge challenge.”
“I want to have 100–120 [interceptor missiles] for these difficult months, especially the cold months. We’ll see how many months this winter lasts—that is, these cold months: one, two, three. We don’t know. This is truly a major challenge,” Zelensky said.
The president noted that Ukraine could receive missiles from U.S. reserves or production, as well as as part of an aid package from Europe. He added that he is discussing supplies with countries in the Middle East.
Zelensky called on European countries to provide Ukraine with maximum support, also mentioning the pan-European anti-ballistic missile system FREYJA. He said that as part of this project, the goal is to receive the first such system for testing by the end of December, after which production will begin.
“This is a major experiment, but it is realistic,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney agreed on substantial support for Ukraine in various areas, including seven new aid packages, six joint initiatives, and three cooperation agreements.

Iranian civilians are struggling to pay for fuel and other essentials as the Rial plunged to 2.3 million per one US dollar and the economic impact of war takes hold, according to a Thursday Wall Street Journal report.
The economic fallout from the war and the US's naval blockade on Iranian ports along the Strait of Hormuz is driving up the price of goods for Iranians, many of whom earn roughly $250 a month, according to a study by Euronews.
On Monday, the Iranian regime doubled the price of gasoline for users surpassing 110 liters per month. The increases targeted passenger vehicles exceeding their allocated quotas following Tehran’s slashing of monthly subsidies. The shrinking gas supply has reportedly left some drivers stranded without fuel, prompting taxi and truck drivers to go on strike.
The regime is also attempting to repair damage sustained by its refineries during the war and faces difficulties importing fuel and other goods due to the US naval blockade.
In a conversation with a representative for the Union of Truckers and Drivers Organizations Across Iran, a trade union representing the transport sector, a driver in northeast Iran said he had been stranded at a gas station with his family, unable to refuel.
The fuel crisis leaves drivers without work for a third of the month
“They say the gasoline is finished until tomorrow,” the driver said in the video. Workers across Iran have reportedly been protesting deteriorating living standards and are now being joined by transportation industry workers, who are disproportionately affected by the fuel shortages.
Late last week, 120 taxi drivers in the eastern Iranian province of Kerman said the government's fuel cuts left them out of work for a third of every month, according to the WSJ.
“We are waiting 20 days for passengers, 10 days struggling with fuel shortages!” one driver said.
Workers for Snapp, the Iranian delivery and ride-share service, went on strike across the country. The company is one of the largest employers in Iran, with roughly 3 million drivers nationwide, according to the WSJ. Rising costs and shrinking fuel rations have led dozens of Snapp employees to state they can no longer make ends meet.
“We’ve all stopped; no one is working,” said one of the drivers at a protest in Semnan, a city east of Tehran, in a video verified by Storyful.
The fuel crisis has also sparked protests among other parts of the transportation sector. Truck drivers on the border with Iraq went on strike to protest fuel shortages, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency, a US NGO.
Last week, truckers in the port of Bandar Abbas along the Strait of Hormuz warned they might also go on strike, according to the WSJ.
“It is the driver and the driver’s family who have to pay for it from their pockets,” the port’s truckers said about fuel price hikes in a statement posted by Iran’s Union of Truckers and Drivers. “The issue is that we can no longer bear these pressures.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

As his presidency enters its final stretch, Isaac Herzog lays out his three priorities for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:23:27 UTC
20:23:27 KST

President Isaac Herzog has a little under two years left before he completes his seven-year term of office. His three key priorities in the months ahead will be diplomacy, strengthening the bonds of Jewish peoplehood, and healing divisions within Israeli society.
He intends to visit more of the communities that have consistently faced rising antisemitism since October 7.
Such visits, he says, are at the core of two of his initiatives. One is Voice of the People, which brings together a global council of Jews from Israel, North America, and the rest of the Diaspora to unite in building the future leadership of the Jewish people. Applications for the second cohort of Voice of the People are due to open shortly.
The selection process will be conducted by an algorithm. Herzog urges all those who care about the future of the Jewish people to lodge an application.
Time to Talk, the president’s second major initiative, is designed to heal rifts within Israeli society and to foster dialogue, understanding, and mutual respect.
Principles 'put to the test' this election season
Herzog believes that as Israel approaches the Knesset elections in October, the principles of negotiation and mutual respect will be put to the test.
Since taking office in July 2021, Herzog has visited some 35 countries – some on state visits and some for special occasions such as the coronation of Britain’s King Charles, the Paris Olympics, the 80th anniversary of the Babi Yar massacre in Ukraine, and the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. State visits have been to countries as distant as Azerbaijan in the north and Australia in the south.
All of the president’s trips abroad are marked by a strong diplomatic element. “Since October 7, Israel has faced an onslaught of lies, attacks, and delegitimization in the international arena,” explains Herzog. “I will continue to present the real truth in diplomatic forums and the media. I will also work to strengthen Israel’s diplomatic ties with our partners and friends both near and far. In the Middle East, we continue to see the great importance of strengthening the Abraham Accords and expanding this circle of peace in our region.”
On the subject of Jewish peoplehood, Herzog places great significance in assuring Jewish communities abroad that the president of Israel cares about them and what they are experiencing.
He meets with Jewish community leaders in Israel and in their home countries. He hosts Jewish community delegations and listens closely to all the participants. A feature of such meetings is that Herzog does not confine himself to listening only to the president, chairperson, and CEO of an organization, but asks each and every participant to introduce themselves and to impart whatever it is that they want to tell him.
Herzog’s rapport with Diaspora Jews comes naturally. He spent part of his youth as a student at the Ramaz School in New York and at New York University during the period in which his father headed the Israeli delegation to the United Nations. More recently, Herzog came to the presidency straight from the chairmanship of the Jewish Agency, whose multi-level relationship with Diaspora Jewish communities is ironclad.
With one possible exception, all of Israel’s presidents came from extensive political backgrounds. Yet the presidency in Israel is an apolitical role even though the president is elected by Knesset vote. The head of state treads a very fine line in an effort to keep the office aloof from politics, but in a country in which everything is tainted by politics, it is very difficult for Citizen No.1 to express approval or disapproval of any development without someone placing a political interpretation on that statement.
Violence in the West Bank
An example is Herzog’s reaction to the violence in the West Bank village of Kusra, where local and foreign media personnel have reported that masked Israelis are creating anarchy and are attacking innocent Palestinians and setting fire to their property. Political pundits insist that it is more than a criminal issue. It is also a political issue that serves the interests of the far Right, and to some extent the interests of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, even though Netanyahu has more than once castigated those Israelis who are targeting innocent Palestinians.
In condemning the Israeli vigilantes, Herzog declared, “The government, security agencies, judicial authorities, and law-enforcement bodies must act now, using every possible means to root out this unacceptable phenomenon and bring the perpetrators to justice.”
Several politicians on both sides of the political divide have voiced concerns about the harm that the anarchists are doing to Israel’s image. This is one of the reasons that Herzog has chosen to make diplomacy one of his priorities.
His gift for diplomacy may be hereditary. His father was a diplomat before he was a politician and a president, and his grandfather used diplomacy in his efforts to rescue child survivors of the Holocaust and bring them to Israel.
Given Herzog’s own diplomatic successes, some people might want to see him as a future ambassador or foreign minister. But Herzog has other plans. He wants to be a teacher and join with those who are shaping Israel’s next generation.

China's Xi urges BRICS to help advance peace in Middle East

Saadet Gokce
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Saturday urged BRICS countries to help advance peace in the Middle East, saying the ongoing war does not serve the common interests of the international community.
 
"The situation in the Middle East and the Gulf region continues to evolve, the war there has caused serious losses to people across the region and does not serve the common interests of the international community," Xi said during the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
 
The statement by the Chinese president comes amid the ongoing US war with Iran, which has damaged civil and military infrastructure across the Middle East as well as disrupted global energy supplies.
 
Xi called on BRICS countries to "firmly stand on the right side of history," saying Beijing would work with other members to play their "due role in achieving peace and tranquility in the Middle East and Gulf region."
 
He also urged BRICS members to take the lead in promoting mutual learning among civilizations and improving global governance.
 
Xi described the BRICS cooperation mechanism as the "world's most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries."
 
Stressing opposition to a "Cold War mentality and bloc confrontation," he called on the emerging economies bloc to "oppose violations of other countries' sovereignty, interference in their internal affairs."
 
Rejecting "all forms of protectionism," the Chinese leader urged the BRICS to "lead global governance in cyberspace, outer space, deep sea, and amplify the voice of the Global South."
 
Emphasizing that BRICS should "pioneer in improving global governance," Xi called on the bloc to uphold the UN authority and strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence.
 
The weekend summit in New Delhi is attended by the Chinese, Russian and Iranian presidents, among other leaders, and comes as the US-Iran war has dragged on for seven months and the Russia-Ukraine war has continued for more than four years.
 
China will take over the rotating BRICS presidency next year after India's term ends.
 
On Sunday, the BRICS leaders will attend an open session titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.”
 
The group now represents about 49.5% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to figures cited by BRICS.
 
The last summit was held in Rio de Janeiro in 2025 and next will be hosted by China.

Brics New Delhi Declaration adopted: Terrorism, conflict resolution, tariff concerns addressed; key points
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:18:45 UTC
20:18:45 KST

The adoption comes after reports of late-night negotiations that continued until 4 am, as India led efforts to bridge differences between the UAE and Iran.
NEW DELHI: The Brics countries on Saturday unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026 at the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi. The 45-page declaration, comprising 140 points, was discussed under the theme “Strengthening Cooperation to Promote Fair Competition, including in Renewable Energy Markets”, with the aim of supporting sustainable energy transitions.“No member has raised any objection. The New Delhi Declaration 2026 is adopted unanimously,” PM Modi said at the summit.The declaration focused on condemning terrorism, conflict prevention and peaceful resolution of disputes, stronger multilateralism and concerns over unilateral trade measures.
PM Modi, in his separate opening remarks, called for reforms in global governance and proposed 10 measures to be developed into a Brics reform roadmap. He also called for greater representation of the Global South in international decision-making, describing the existing system as a “pyramid of privilege” that should become a “platform of partnership”.The declaration was adopted on the first day of the two-day Summit being hosted by India in New Delhi. The joint declaration came after intensive negotiations that continued until 4 am on Saturday, with India leading efforts to bridge differences between the UAE and Iran over the Middle East conflict.
The talks followed an earlier Brics foreign ministers’ meeting under India’s presidency that ended without a consensus, prompting prolonged negotiations to ensure the summit resulted in a joint statement.India is chairing Brics in 2026 under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.
Key points of the declaration
The Declaration addressed various key issues and concerns affecting the global order, such as:TerrorismBrics strongly condemned terrorism in all forms, including cross-border terrorism, terrorism financing and safe havens, condemned the April 22, 2025, terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, and called for zero tolerance, accountability and early adoption of the UN Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. "We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens," it said."We reiterate that terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law," it continued, adding, ""We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism."Brics cooperationThe bloc reaffirmed its commitment to mutual respect, sovereign equality, solidarity, inclusiveness and consensus, and pledged to strengthen cooperation across its three pillars: political and security, economic and financial, and cultural and people-to-people cooperation. "We commend India for hosting the Outreach/BRICS Plus Dialogue segment of the 18thBRICS Summit, which injects new impetus to strengthen international cooperation andsolidarity," it further statedConflict preventionBrics countries stressed the importance of efforts to prevent conflicts, including by addressing their root causes. The declaration reaffirmed a commitment to resolving disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy. Brics further urged all parties to uphold the Gaza ceasefire and ensure unhindered humanitarian aid, opposed the forced displacement of Palestinians, and reaffirmed support for a two-state solution with an independent Palestinian state based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders."We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East...call for exercising maximum restraint...avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation."Drugs and arms traffickingBrics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug-related crimes, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing and organised crime, and called for stronger cross-border cooperation to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds. “We express our concerns about illicit financial flows including, financing of terrorism, trafficking of firearms, trafficking in persons, the laundering of drug related crimes proceeds,” the declaration said.Tariff concernsBrics voiced concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, warning they could hurt global trade and disrupt supply chains. “We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules,” the declaration said.It reaffirmed support for a WTO-centred multilateral trading system and called for the immediate restoration of a “fully functioning, two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism”, along with the appointment of new Appellate Body members. The bloc also condemned unilateral economic and secondary sanctions. “We condemn the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law,” the declaration said, calling for their elimination as they “undermine international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.”It also backed Ethiopia and Iran’s WTO membership bids and noted China’s move to extend zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties.Energy security and transitionThe declaration called for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets, while recognising that fossil fuels will continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies. “We acknowledge fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world's energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs),” it said. It also backed “just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions” and a technology-neutral approach covering renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and low-carbon technologies.Women’s empowermentBrics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation, stressing their participation in governance, economic life, peacebuilding and climate action."We affirm that women's participation in governance; their financial and digital inclusion; their capacity building, access to skill development and entrepreneurship opportunities, support to entrepreneurship, access to productive and social services and their crucial role in climate action, food security and nutrition, which are interconnected is key for sustainable development," the declaration said."We also recognise the importance of policies that support women's full participation in economic life, including through appropriate care policies, in accordance with national circumstances," the leaders further said.Local currencies' pushBrics backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using member countries’ local currencies, while respecting national priorities. “We acknowledge the work done to study the cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels, and the discussions on promoting trade settlements and investments using BRICS local currencies,” the declaration stated.Supporting India's role in UNSCBrics reaffirmed support for reform of the UN, including the Security Council, to make it more democratic and representative and give developing countries a greater role. China and Russia, as permanent members of the Security Council, reiterated their support for Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council. “China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterate their support to the aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council,” the declaration said.
Sports technologyBrics recognised the growing role of technology in improving sports performance, athlete welfare, governance and inclusion, and encouraged greater cooperation among member countries through exchanges of good practices, technical information and research. “We welcome the proposal for the BRICS Sports Goods Manufacturing Conclave to promote cooperation in sports goods manufacturing, research and innovation,” the declaration stated. It also encouraged discussions on forming a dedicated Working Group on Sports Technology.

Anthropic report exposes AI misuse across world, MENA region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:15:01 UTC
20:15:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Anthropic reveals attempted use of AI for Houthi ballistic missiles, UAE influence operations
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic released a report on Thursday detailing misuse of its Claude LLM by a variety of actors, both state and non-state, worldwide, from cyber and influence operations to biological misuse and weapons development.
Spanning eight months, Anthropic said the report includes cases that "aren't typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date".
The New Arab takes a look at the key misuses identified in the report relating to the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region.
Yemen
One of the most significant misuses identified by Anthropic is from "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen running three weapons development programs".
These programmes include a guided rocket using a flight computer with final-phase homing guidance, a multi-stage ballistic missile with a range of 2,000km, and a multivariant missile that also includes a variant with a hypersonic glide vehicle.
Though not explicitly mentioned, it is likely the company is referring to Yemen's Houthi rebels, which, through cooperation with Iran, have developed and fired ballistic missiles, most notably at Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Israel, and against Yemen's UN-recognised government in Yemen.
Claude was used by the group to develop guidance, navigation and control software that both steers and stabilises any flying vehicle, Anthropic said, using the LLM in several instances at once, including through writing code, research, and reviewing the code produced by the first instance.
AI models can be broken down into separate instances to perform multiple tasks at once.
"These actors carried out a sustained effort to develop guided weapons, including using Claude to design guidance software," Anthropic said, adding that it did not have evidence that the group succeeded.
However, Anthropic noted that not all efforts to block use requests were successful, and that there was evidence the group "had already built an offline simulation toolkit that does not rely on Claude or other engineering computing environments".
Iran
Alongside Yemen, Anthropic also caught several misuses of Claude relating to Iran.
This includes using Claude for state-aligned influence operations as part of a "'soft war' or 'cognitive warfare'", meaning "a non-military plan to shape public opinion at home and abroad".
State entities identified by Anthropic include the Islamic Culture Communications Organization, the Islamic Propaganda Office of Khorasan Razabi, and the Islamic Propaganda Organization’s Bina Cultural Observatory.
"In each case, the operation relied on Claude to build campaign plans, doctrine manuals, persona systems, target databases, and ministerial planning documentation," the report stated, adding that these were meant to produce pro-Iran propaganda during the war, attributing false claims to Western research institutions, and "deploying aggressive counter-narrative content targeting the Baha'I", as well as international officials and opposition figures.
In a separate case, Anthropic banned 16 Claude accounts that were linked to the Iranian paramilitary and domestic security agencies, "with high confidence," that were involved in building domestic surveillance capabilities.
This includes using Claude to build "a front end to what is likely a government-controlled surveillance case-management system, and running social-network analysis over 155,216 tweets," with a separate unit building an extension to the internet browser Firefox, to mass-harvest user identities from social network platforms.
As well as surveillance of domestic opposition, Claude was also used in another instance for the mass surveillance of the profiles of Israeli and Jewish individuals to enrich a pre-existing target list.
Another case saw Anthropic close Claude accounts that were being used to collect and analyse data to develop targeting recommendations against US naval forces in the region, using public military photographs, publically accessible ship and aircraft transponder identifiers, commercial satellite-imagery scripts, and inventories from public websites documenting US naval movements.
The same account was developing domestic mass-surveillance systems through Claude to "design software components of a domestic mass-surveillance platform that combined automatic license-plate recognition with mobile-device identifier interception".
As well as the Iranian government, Anthropic also disrupted an influence operation by the People’s Mojahedin Organisation of Iran and the National Council of Resistance of Iran attempting to target domestic and diaspora Iranians, including distributing their own talking points, alongside fabricated claims.
UAE
The UAE's government was identified as misusing Anthropic in the report, with a Claude account under the persona "Deadshot" being identified as running "a sustained influence operation against the Muslim Brotherhood".
As part of this effort, the operation built 300 influencer social media accounts, and created a front NGO based on the identity of a real Swiss organisation to publish state-authored human rights reports, ghostwrite testimonies delivered by two people at the 62nd Session of the UN Human Rights Council.
The account also "researched and profiled 18 members of the European Parliament and prominent journalists", building out their profiles, and compiled dossiers on UN special rapporteurs who criticised the UAE's conduct in Sudan.
Anthropic said that though the operation was built so it would not be traced to any actors, "our investigation linked it with high confidence to UAE government officials
Uyghurs in Syria and Turkey
Anthropic identified a Chinese-aligned operation to track, profile and recruit Uyghurs and Uyghur armed formations in Syria. The Uyghurs are a Muslim ethnic minority in Eastern China, which rights groups say are subjected to human rights abuses by Beijing.
"The armed targets were ethnic Uyghurs who had recently joined the newly formed Syrian Army, formations the PRC government designates as terrorists," the report said.
The actor attempted to communicate with people in Syria who had access to these formations and recruit them, offering payments for reporting.
The actor also used Claude to locate Uyghur businesses and points of interest in Syria, including journalists from the Uyghur diaspora in Syria.
"We assess with low confidence that the actor was a contractor working on behalf of PRC state security rather than a state security organ acting directly."
China-based actors were also banned from targeting dissidents in Uyghur advocacy organisations and Uyghur cultural event venues in Turkey.
The Gulf
Claude accounts were identified as being misused in the Gulf, with Anthropic banning an account that used Claude to "build a commercial surveillance platform to analyse, classify, and profile the social media activity of users in Iran and the Persian Gulf region".
According to Anthropic, the account was linked to S2T Unlokcing Cyberspace, which they say their research suggests is an Israeli-Singaporean commercial intelligence vendor.
The report says that the operation "mapped the locations of the social media users, sorted the population into coded demographic groups, and produced Arabic-language intelligence briefings written in the register of a government report".
The actor identified was found to be "building a portfolio of multi-branded systems" serving Arabic-language customers in the Gulf, capturing and storing the locations of diaspora social network users, categorising them in pro-government or opposition camps, as well as placing them into a demographic scheme comprising urban, clerical, military, youth, diaspora, and rural groupings.
A secondary workstream was also identified with more than 255 synthetic social media accounts, suggesting that the "actor was building a stock of fake accounts built to be deployed later".
Anthropic said that the activity was in a pilot stage, and that there was no evidence that later stages of the group's surveillance changes were used against real targets before the account was banned.

Tallinn has 50 kilometers of walkable underground pipes
Unknown

Tallinn has 50 kilometers of walkable underground pipes
Tallinna Vesi development manager Marti Vaksmann says that there are 3,000 kilometers of pipelines beneath Tallinn, including 50 kilometers of large pipes where a person can walk. He notes that being inside a wastewater collector is not the most pleasant experience, but it is part of the job.
Construction has been underway all summer at the Hipodroom intersection in Tallinn, and the reason for the repairs lies underground.
"We're going about four meters deep here, but in Tallinn some places reach depths of up to 30 meters," said Vaksmann, development manager for water and sewerage assets at Tallinna Vesi. "We've measured that Tallinn has 3,000 kilometers of pipelines, and about 50 kilometers of those are large enough for us to walk through."
The existing pipes were installed nearly a century ago, when Tallinn still used a combined sewer system, with stormwater and wastewater flowing through the same pipe. "Today we're building a separate stormwater pipeline right under the Hipodroom intersection. We're planning for the next 50 years, assuming rainfall may become more intense, so we won't need to rebuild this pipe again. If it seems to passersby that not much construction is happening at Hipodroom site, that's because most of it is underground," Vaksmann said.
Vaksmann said he likes pipes and doesn't feel afraid walking inside them. "Many people don't like tight spaces, but that's our job. Right now we're in a stormwater collector, but there are also wastewater collectors, and walking in those is not the most pleasant — but someone has to do it."
"In addition to the large pipelines, there's also a water pipe here, a sewer pipe, heating pipelines, and various cables under the sidewalks. Whenever possible, we shift pipelines under the sidewalk," Vaksmann explained. "There are no buildings directly above us."

Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:06:16 UTC
20:06:16 KST

Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding
TLAOLA, Mexico, Sept 12 - Nestled in the lush green mountains of Central Mexico, next to a sparsely traveled gravel road, few people had reason to wander close enough to hear the loud, mechanical whirring of a clandestine cryptocurrency farm.
What led police to the ramshackle building, suspected of mining virtual coins to launder illicit funds, was not only the noise but the vast amount of electricity needed to power and cool hundreds of specialized computing units, at levels far surpassing the needs of the small communities scattered around the Sierra Norte region of Puebla state.
Crypto mining — which uses powerful computers to generate virtual assets such as bitcoin — represents a new frontier in Mexico's fight against organized criminal groups, which have extended their reach beyond drug trafficking and extortion into the murkier realm of financial crime.
In Puebla, authorities discovered 300 graphics processing units (GPUs), 80 medium-voltage terminals and eight satellite antennae — all geared to compete against millions of other machines to solve puzzles and create valuable new crypto coins.
While a relatively modest operation by international commercial standards, it is the fourth such crypto farm uncovered in the area since early last year.
"Drug cartels appear to have reached a new level of sophistication," said David Saucedo, a Mexico-based security analyst, adding that setting up such an operation would have required technical expertise and backing from a well-financed group, such as one of Mexico's most powerful cartels.
Mexico's federal attorney's office declined to comment, citing an active investigation.
ELECTRICITY THEFT FUELS OPERATIONS
Globally, illicit cryptocurrency transactions more than doubled in 2025, with addresses linked to criminal activity receiving an estimated $154 billion, up from $59 billion a year earlier, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, which analyzed transaction volumes sent to illicit wallet addresses.
Chainalysis attributed much of the increase to a surge in transactions linked to sanctions evasion, including payments involving sanctioned governments.
As more people and institutions worldwide adopt virtual currency, most within the confines of the law, Latin American cartels are among those increasingly using crypto transfers and mining operations to launder money, said Caio Motta, the firm's Latin American specialist.
"These locations will have very cheap electricity, or be in an area under the influence of organized crime so they're able to steal electricity and establish a large infrastructure to mine cryptocurrency," Motta said.
Electricity is the biggest cost for mining crypto, as energy prices have increased and the process of minting a single unit of virtual currency has become more resource-intensive.
The University of Cambridge's Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index estimates the cost of minting one bitcoin — the most widely used cryptocurrency — at nearly $45,000. This would still bring a substantial profit when sold at current prices of around $78,000.
"If they were stealing the electricity, the main costs of the operation would be, well — nothing," said Samuel Leon, an expert in energy theft at Mexico's Iberoamericana University, referring to the Puebla operation.
Mexican authorities said they are investigating whether the crypto farm was stealing electricity from a nearby hydroelectric dam.
HIDDEN IN REMOTE MOUNTAIN TERRAIN
The bushy forests and scattered communities of the Sierra Norte, where the Puebla crypto farm was found, made for an ideal hiding spot.
Two people living in neighboring communities, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, told Reuters that the whirring noise could be heard one kilometer (0.6 mile) away. The crypto farm was located approximately twice that distance from the nearest village.
Three other similar crypto farms were found last year in the vicinity of the nearby hydroelectric dam in northern Puebla. Local authorities said they are collaborating with nearby states to investigate the possibility of more hidden operations.
Similar raids have taken place in Brazil, the U.S. and Southeast Asia, including a major bitcoin mining operation in Thailand that spanned five provinces.
According to Motta of Chainalysis, rising global cryptocurrency use will likely push crypto-related crime to new records in the years ahead, as virtual currencies become more accessible even as investigators improve their ability to trace online transactions.
"Law enforcement agencies are becoming far more equipped to fight organized crime using cryptocurrency," he said. REUTERS

NIA searches J&K locations to trace LeT handlers’ local support network (file photo)
NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Saturday conducted searches at 10 locations across Jammu and Kashmir in connection with a cross-border terror conspiracy involving Pakistan-based handlers of the proscribed Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and their alleged network of local Over Ground Workers (OGWs).The searches were carried out in Kupwara, Kulgam, Bandipora, Baramulla and Sopore to gather further evidence related to the conspiracy and ascertain the roles of individuals allegedly providing logistical and other support to infiltrated terrorists, the NIA said.During the searches, incriminating material relevant to the case was seized or secured, according to the agency. The material is being examined and corroborated with other evidence collected during the investigation.
Investigation began with OGW arrest
The case was initially registered at Police Station Zakoora in Srinagar and was subsequently re-registered by the NIA under Section 23 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, Sections 7 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959, and Section 4 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908.The investigation began after the arrest of an alleged LeT-linked OGW at a naka point during the night of March 31, 2026. A hand grenade and live ammunition were recovered from his possession, the NIA said.
Further investigation led to the arrest of Pakistani nationals allegedly linked to the conspiracy and helped investigators identify the suspected roles of members of the local support network.According to the NIA, the investigation so far has revealed links between Pakistan-based LeT handlers and their local associates. These associates were allegedly being used for communication, movement and concealment of infiltrated terrorists, as well as providing shelter, conducting reconnaissance and facilitating other logistical requirements.
NIA examines financial, communication trails
The agency is also examining the financial trail, communication channels and movement of the accused, along with the source and supply chain of arms and explosives.The objective, according to the NIA, is to establish the complete network and determine the extent of its activities.The latest searches are part of the agency's continuing investigation into the larger conspiracy and the support mechanism allegedly facilitating cross-border terrorism.The NIA said it would continue its investigation to identify all persons involved in the alleged conspiracy and establish their respective roles. Further legal action, including arrests and recoveries, may follow depending on the outcome of the investigation.
Hafiz Saeed warrant in related terror case
The searches come amid the NIA's wider investigations into LeT-linked terror networks in Jammu and Kashmir.A Special Court in Jammu on September 8 issued a non-bailable warrant against LeT founder Hafiz Saeed in a terror case related to the alleged supply of weapons, funds and directions to terror groups operating in the Union Territory.It was the second non-bailable warrant issued against Saeed by the Special NIA Court in Jammu in two months.The warrant was issued after the NIA described Saeed, a resident of Sargodha in Pakistan's Punjab province, as an “absconding accused” in a case concerning the arrest of Mohammad Naqeeb Bhat during a check at Pandach on the outskirts of Srinagar earlier this year.
A China-made grenade and 15 live rounds were recovered from Bhat, who was booked under the UAPA, Arms Act and Explosive Substances Act.The subsequent investigation led to the alleged busting of a terror network and the arrest of several more terrorists associated with LeT and its offshoot The Resistance Front (TRF), as well as two Pakistani nationals.The NIA told the court that Saeed was allegedly operating from Pakistan and providing weapons, money and directions to terrorists in the Kashmir Valley.The court observed that Saeed's involvement had surfaced during the investigation and that he was “allegedly involved in terrorism”.The latest warrant followed an earlier non-bailable warrant issued against him on July 8 in connection with the Pahalgam terror attack case.

The gathering of world leaders takes place on Dec 14-15 and there has been no confirmation yet as to whether Putin would attend.
Asked if the Kremlin was considering an alternative location for a meeting with Zelensky, Peskov replied: “There is a readiness to meet him in Moscow.”
Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelensky aimed at brokering an end to more than four years of war, which have killed thousands of people and crippled both countries’ economies.

The latest offer comes as Washington seeks to kick-start long-stalled talks on Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II, with US negotiators visiting Kyiv and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks over the phone.

The United States holds this year’s presidency of the G-20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union.
Russia’s finance minister has already attended one G-20 meeting.
Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelensky told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: “Yes, of course.”
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter.”
All that mattered were “results”, he added.
In June, Zelensky said he had proposed meeting Putin in the United States during a call with Trump, and was waiting to see what came of it.
The Ukrainian leader previously said that Putin ignored an invitation to meet him at a G-7 summit in France the same month.

Zelensky has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv.

Jamaican delegation defends legal route of petition to King Charles for slavery reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:00:34 UTC
20:00:34 KST

A palpable surge of emotion swept through Brixton’s New Park Road Baptist church as the packed congregation rose to sing Bob Marley’s Redemption Song.
The service on Sunday marked the anniversary of the 1781 Zong massacre, when more than 100 enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so the ship’s owners could claim insurance for “lost cargo”.
And the song – a lament for the horrors of transatlantic slavery and a tribute to the resilience of those who fought for freedom – set the tone for a landmark visit to the UK by Jamaican officials to petition King Charles over reparations for slavery.
The petition, backed by leaders of other Caribbean nations, asks the monarch to request legal advice from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
It asks Charles, who is still Jamaica’s head of state, to seek guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Led by the culture minister, Olivia Grange, the Jamaican delegation included lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparations.
The delegation met diaspora communities, UK politicians, church leaders and institutions – including the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts.
Grange also held talks with the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, though sources say these were not focused on reparations.
Jamaica’s petition has ignited a fierce debate about the legality of transatlantic slavery and political implications. The former privy council member Lord Sumption dismissed the legal strategy as “nonsense” and argued that the issue was “not a question of law at all” but one of morals and politics. Jamaican experts have defended the legality of the petition.
Speaking at a briefing for UK parliamentarians, Edward Fitzgerald KC insisted Jamaica was acting in accordance with a little‑used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833 which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts.
Harj Narulla, a member of the UK team of counsels, told the Guardian it was an “obvious jurisdictional route”.
“It was quite clear you can’t do a judicial review, for example, of some government decision … The issue is with the state itself, with the United Kingdom, which is the state responsible for slavery in Jamaica,” he said.
Ulele Burnham, another member of the UK legal team, added: “The petition argues that the atrocities, the forced uprooting, the violent subjugation for profit was of course immoral, everyone knows that. But the petition’s very focus is to show that it was also clearly inconsistent with the law of the time. Non-Europeans did not suddenly become human when slavery ended. They always were. And even in those days, humans had some rights in English and international law.”
In Jamaica, though the pursuit of reparations is supported by the two main parties, members of the opposition People’s National party raised concerns that the delegation had not managed to secure a meeting with the king. Grange said a meeting with Charles “was not part of the plan”.
“Before we came to London, we had consulted with both the Palace and the privy council to confirm the correct legal process for filing the petition. Both confirmed the correct process was to file it by post and email, which is what we did,” she said.
The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro‑Addy, the chair of the all‑party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said Jamaica was well within its rights to petition the monarch. “Due to colonialism, which obviously initially had its root in enslavement, there are certain responsibilities that [the UK] has. We don’t get the privilege of still having Jamaica as part of the realm … without them also in turn having the right to petition King Charles. They are enacting their rights under English law and they have the right to ask those questions,” she said.
In December 2024, Jamaica’s government tabled a bill in parliament to remove the king as the country’s head of state. The bill has not progressed to becoming a law.
Pointing to recent global momentum – including 123 nations voting for a UN resolution describing chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity – Ribeiro‑Addy said it was time for Britain to confront its past and the decisions that continue to shape the present.
She described headlines quoting huge reparation figures (which were not mentioned in the Jamaican petition) as a distraction. “What seems to happen a lot when we talk about reparations is people want to distract people with figures,” she said. “They divorce themselves from the reality of what we are talking about. No one is saying that reparative justice will never include any sort of payment. But that is never the starting point. And we have to remember that this country refuses to even apologise. This country refuses to do the things that it can do, which don’t cost any money at all.
“The enslavement of peoples of African descent … meant that anybody who was not white was considered less than … almost being classified as not quite human. And that is a serious issue. If we are ever going to challenge racism properly, we have to get down to its very root.”
As the delegation lodged the petition on Monday, a spokesperson for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.
Ribeiro‑Addy said it would be an insult to African and Caribbean countries if Britain refuses to discuss reparations at the upcoming Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua, which the king is scheduled to attend.
“We’re meant to no longer be a group of countries under an empire. We were meant to be a group of countries with a shared history and who are treated as equals,” she said. “The idea that all of the countries bar one want to have a discussion and so the discussion is stopped has to be wrong … if we do things like that, I think we will soon see the crumbling of the Commonwealth. And that would be a huge shame.”

‘I said, if you want to fire me, just fire me. And so he did’: my showdown with Donald Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:00:32 UTC
20:00:32 KST

Gene Folkes, 62, based in Manhattan, was a contestant on season 10 of The Apprentice, which aired in 2010. A former air force recruiter until 1991, he retrained as an investment banker, then launched his own business before appearing on the reality show. He was fired by Trump in episode 5. He now runs the technology consulting firm OshunX and hosts a podcast, Folkes Unfettered.
I didn’t audition to be on The Apprentice. I received the call out of the blue: “Would you be interested in doing this show?” I didn’t know a lot about it. However, like any young business person, you look for people who you consider titans. There’s this mythology around Trump. He was one of the people I wanted to emulate.
The first morning, wardrobe comes into your room at 3.30am. You meet the other contestants for the first time, then within an hour you’re on your first task. You learn really quickly that you’re playing a game and the rules can change at any moment.
The first time we met, Trump was outside his building on Wall Street. He is an imposing figure. When he walks into a place he owns the room and there’s not a lot of air for anyone else to breathe. I thought, “OK, he’s presenting as exactly who I believed him to be.” There was a sense of admiration and aspiration. It was only when you dug deeper that you realised the emperor had no clothes.
In the corporate world, there are certain things you just don’t do without consequences. And they were so natural for him. The first time we met him in the boardroom, Trump asked us if we thought the women were attractive. He would make these innuendoes – things that were sort of hard to pin down – but you felt kind of icky afterwards.
The first round was split men v women. I put myself forward to be the project manager for the men’s team. Task one was to design a modern office space. We won that task, and my prize was a one-on-one with Trump. His desk in Trump Tower was rather small and somewhat messy. Initially, I felt he knows how to connect with people. There was charisma, there was charm; he evokes a certain amount of confidence. You can really get drawn into all things Donald, but as I sat back and started really listening to him, I thought, “Oh, I don’t think this is the person that I have tried to model myself after.”
I didn’t feel empathy from him: I was more product than person. I think about it a lot now, because I believe that anyone who wants to lead a nation has to have a certain amount of empathy. If you don’t, then how can you relate to someone who’s a single mom or dad who’s struggling to put food on the table?
A producer told me the series was mine to lose. The week I got fired, I didn’t feel like it was coming. We had to put on a fashion show for Rockport. When you’re an air force recruiter, like I had been, all you do is publicly speak, so my project manager selected me to be master of ceremonies. I wear glasses. In that episode I decided to wear my contacts. They weren’t bifocals, and I remember saying, “I need to go back and get my glasses.” We never got to it. We got on to the test and I couldn’t read a freaking thing on the script.
When we went to the boardroom and we lost, they brought in three of us. Trump really took me off guard. The narrative shifted from, “Hey, I couldn’t see, and I wasn’t going to admit that I couldn’t see, because I didn’t want to start making excuses”, to one where I became illiterate: I couldn’t read; I couldn’t speak. It was very coded language that I was familiar with. It dawned on me: oh my God, he is framing me as a dumb person of colour. I’m sitting here with a degree in finance and he’s talking to me like I’m a moron. At that point I pushed back and said, “No one gets to talk about my speaking abilities. I don’t know what the bleep you’re talking about, but that’s not me.”
His face was red. He was visibly angry. One of the things he did when pushed back on was escalate. It was like he didn’t hear anything you said. He was animated but in a controlled way. He was playing to camera. He knew the audience was salivating for his line.
I finally said, “You know what? If you want to fire me, just fire me.” And so he did.
I did not feel anger. I felt relief. At that point you realise you’re playing in a system that’s rigged. And the person in power controls the narrative, controls the outcome. This was a game, but my real-life consequences were: what is my life going to look like after the programme, for my relationships, business dealings, opportunities?
When I watched the series, I got on the phone with NBC to say, “Holy crap, that’s where you guys want to go with that? That I was uneducated, ignorant?” There was no sense of empathy or compassion from the network or him.
Afterwards I did not want to leave the house. I could not get out of bed some mornings. I really became almost a recluse for three months. It took me years to get comfortable talking about it. I was depressed.
When I got a hold of myself, I began to do what I normally do: I started fighting. I wrote a blog where I gave my opinion on Trump considering running for the presidency. NBC asked me to take it down, which I refused to do.
I remember someone saying to me, “You’re hurting the Trump brand, you’re hurting the NBC brand and you’re hurting the Apprentice brand”, and I remember saying, “But you’re hurting the Gene Folkes brand, and I didn’t sign off for this crap.”
In the 15 years since I was on The Apprentice, media, entertainment, politics and news have started converging. Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology.
When I served in the military, there were certain leaders you would follow to death. You knew they loved and cared about you. They were able to manage their emotions. They realised that the goal of the team outweighed their individual personality. Trump is the opposite. He’s all personality; there is no team.
Good leaders want to be challenged. And what I learned from The Apprentice, and what I’m seeing now in politics, is consistent: don’t challenge him.
As told to Kate Lloyd
NBC declined to comment.
‘Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did was struggle to keep the train on the track’
John Bolton, 77, based in Washington DC, is an attorney and former ambassador to the United Nations who was national security adviser from 2018 until 2019, under Trump. His exit from government was announced by the president over Twitter on 10 September 2019: “I informed John Bolton last night that his services are no longer needed at the White House. I disagreed strongly with many of his suggestions, as did others in the administration, and therefore I asked John for his resignation, which was given to me this morning.” Bolton says things played out differently.
For me, there was no one straw that broke the camel’s back, and I think that’s true in many resignation situations. It was an accumulation of factors. I had had a resignation letter drafted, and kept one copy in my desk drawer in the office and one copy at home, knowing I could print it out whenever I needed to.
It was basically a one-sentence resignation, which was the way I wanted to do it. And it finally came to that in September 2019.
The last conversation really was on 9 September. He was complaining about this and complaining about that, having heard, obviously from people inside the administration, of something I had done that they didn’t like. And I said to him, “Well, look, if you feel that way, I’ll resign.” And he was leaving the Oval Office to go and give a speech. [Trump told Bolton they would talk about his resignation offer the following morning.]
I went back to my office and I just thought, I am going to resign; I’m not going to talk to him. So I did a few other things that evening and then I went home, and came in early the next morning. There were a couple of meetings I wanted to finish up, particularly the freeing up of the security assistance to Ukraine. I got that done and I gave the letter to my secretary and said, “I’m going home. I’ll call you when I’m there.” I wanted to get out of the blast zone. So I told her to hand it to Trump’s secretary and then be prepared that she would probably be leaving soon thereafter.
The only mistake I made was that I should have tweeted right then that I had resigned, because when Trump saw it he went through the roof. I did get one tweet out saying I had resigned, and then they closed my Twitter account. I had to fight later to get it back.
I believe in pre-emptive strikes, and I had failed to follow my own advice. I should have fired first, but I was pursuing old-fashioned norms.
I tell this story in my book: before the Singapore meeting with Kim Jong-un, the first in the series on the North Korean nuclear programme, there was a chance that Trump was going to cancel, which I thought was exactly the right thing to do. I thought the whole thing was going to be a terrible waste of time. He was going off to a dinner, I think, with state governors, and as he was leaving, I said, “We can send out something saying we’re not coming if you want to do that.” And he said, “Let me think about it.” He said, “When I was dating, I always liked to be the one to break up with the girl. I never wanted the girl to break up with me.”
I didn’t keep that much stuff in the White House office. A lot of things – pre-government files of clippings and things – I thought my secretary would be able to walk out with because they clearly weren’t government property. But we had to fight over that, too. There were several other of my staff who were also let go within 24, 48 hours. Some of their stuff was taken as well.
I don’t think I get called naive very often. I thought I knew what I was getting into, largely because I thought that the weight of the decisions Trump would have to make in the national security area, the gravity of the responsibility, would discipline him. It turned out I was completely wrong about that. Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did in my 17 months was struggle to keep the train on the track. Things like long-range planning? Forget it. By and large, there just wasn’t time to do it.
I firmly believed that Trump would be no different from his predecessors. And, to me, it just exemplifies that it really is an aberration in American politics – I’d say almost in world history – to have somebody who performs the way he does. People would just ignore the [national security council policymaking] process and go directly to Trump. It was the phenomenon of the last person in the room gets his attention.
There was this occasion when the Iranians shot down an American drone over the Persian Gulf, in what we believed was international airspace. We sized up what we were going to do, came up with retaliation, the president ordered it, then literally as planes were in the air, he changed his mind. So that leads people to say, why are we doing this? Why do we even bother?
Look, everybody’s got an ego. Politicians notoriously have bigger egos than most. But I’ve never seen a politician where the ego wasn’t subsumed to at least some extent by bigger considerations. With him, it’s not subsumed by anything. That was part of the mistake I made. I just had never seen a personality like that before.
As told to Julian Borger
‘I was at the school drama club when I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. “Message from the president.” I thought, well, that can’t be good’
Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, 45, lives in Maryland. A Democrat, she was appointed to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), an independent agency of the US government, by Donald Trump in 2018. The FTC’s work includes fighting illegal business practices, safeguarding online privacy and promoting competition to keep prices down for consumers. Slaughter was fired last year and fought a protracted legal battle, arguing that Trump did not have the right to remove an agency commissioner without cause. This culminated in the supreme court case Trump v Slaughter, which decided in favour of the president’s at-will removal power, overturning a 91-year-old precedent.
It was an incredible privilege and honour to work for the FTC. In the time I was there we blocked the largest grocery store merger in history, which would have raised grocery prices even further. We sued big tech platforms for violating children’s privacy, for subscription traps that charged people more money than they should have been paying. We investigated things like the price of insulin and the role of pharmacy benefit managers in keeping drug prices unnaturally high.
Right after the inauguration in January 2025, the president removed commissioners at a different independent board, the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board. But he didn’t fire me or my colleague, commissioner Alvaro Bedoya. We went through a period from mid-January through mid-March thinking, is he going to fire us today? He didn’t fire us today. Does that mean he’s not going to fire us? We don’t know.
We decided early on that we couldn’t and wouldn’t operate in a way that was inconsistent with our oaths of office or our principles in order to avoid getting fired. We were just going to do the jobs we had as well as we could, and we couldn’t control how the president was going to react.
On 18 March 2025, I worked a full day in the office then went to our local public elementary school, where I was volunteering in the evenings with the drama club production of Beauty and the Beast. I was the parent lead for this production. But, much more importantly, my second kid was playing Belle. She was in fifth grade. This was the culmination of all of her hopes and dreams in her 10-year-old life.
I was sitting outside the dusty elementary school gym, children were running around pretending to be plates and spoons, inviting my daughter to come be their guest, and I checked my work phone and I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. I can’t remember what it was titled – “Message from the president” or something like that.
I thought, well, that can’t be good. I opened it, and it was a very long email, purportedly on behalf of the president, clearly not written by the president – many legal citations, no words in caps – the culmination of which was, your continued service on the FTC is inconsistent with my priorities, therefore you are terminated effective immediately.
I took a deep breath and said some expletives in my head. I looked at the other parent volunteers sitting next to me and said, “I think I might have just gotten fired. Is it OK if I step outside to deal with this?” They said, “No, go home, go take care of what you need to do.” I said, “Oh no, I am not leaving Beauty and the Beast.”
The rest of that evening is a blur in my mind. I talked to my husband, who was in California. I talked to my staff. I talked to a million reporters. We hastily organised a press conference that I participated in from the parking lot, holding a phone in front of my face, under the floodlights with a brick background behind me.
I didn’t want my daughter to hear about this from other parents or other kids. I pulled her aside after they got through the run-through and said, “I have to tell you something. It’s going to sound scary but we are going to be OK and I don’t want you to be worried about it.” She said, “OK, what?” I said, “I got fired this evening.”
I could see her little face well up. She said, “Are you going to have to stop working on the show?” I said, “No, I’m not going to let that happen”, and she said, “OK.” That was the key information she needed. You can try to take my job but you cannot take drama club from me.
Alvaro [who was also fired] and I knew pretty quickly that we wanted to challenge our dismissals in court, because if we failed to do so it would be like acceding to this blatant violation of the law and destruction of these institutions, but the timing and structure of doing that were all questions we had to sort through.
I was doing that until about midnight when my doorbell rang, which I thought was odd. I went to the door and there was a pizza delivery guy there. I said, “I didn’t order any pizza.” He showed me an order form with my name, my personal email address, my cellphone number, my home address. I said, “Well, I didn’t order it and I’m not gonna pay for it, so, sorry.”
I called my husband and I was, like, this weird thing happened. Isn’t that funny? He goes, “No, it is not funny. That’s a thing that online trolls do to people, especially people who the president doesn’t like, in order to scare them.” I didn’t like that I was home with my four kids in the middle of the night when this happened. I talked to Alvaro, who also got a pizza. His take was, thank God, I’m starving, I haven’t eaten all evening!
I don’t feel angry on my own behalf. It is very much not about me. I don’t feel any personal animus. I do feel a lot of anger on behalf of institutions of government, of public servants throughout the government. I have a lot of anger for those reasons.
Donald Trump doesn’t think about me at all. I don’t think he knew that he fired me; I don’t have any evidence he actually knew and was involved in it. The president cares a lot about a ballroom and gold plating the White House and building monuments to himself. I don’t think he’s thinking about conservative legal theory. I also don’t think he is thinking about the American people.
Last summer, in my interregnum period, I knew that I needed a project, so I signed up for the New York City marathon and ran it for charity. I had never run a marathon and I always thought it was impossible, and it felt like a metaphor for the professional experience I was going through. It was hard. It didn’t go as well as I had hoped or trained for, but I finished anyway. And that was also the metaphor for me: we do the hard things because they’re the right things to do, and that is the reward – even if it doesn’t turn out exactly the way you envision.
‘He didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people’
Barbara Res, 76, based in New Jersey, met Donald Trump in 1978, when she was working as an assistant superintendent for the contractor HRH, building the Grand Hyatt hotel in New York. Two years later, he hired her to lead construction on Trump Tower. She eventually became senior vice-president and executive vice-president of the Trump Organization. She quit after a final stint as a consultant, when the redevelopment of the Ambassador hotel site in Los Angeles fell apart amid a prolonged condemnation battle with the Los Angeles school district and a collapsing real-estate market. Res says a last‑minute change in leadership, made by Trump against her advice, undermined negotiations that she believed could have allowed the project to finish with a small profit. She has written two books about her experiences over those years. She retrained as a lawyer and is now semi-retired.
I worked for Donald for close to 18 years. I left on friendly terms. If I saw him at a function, we’d nod to each other. But in 2016 I wrote an op-ed in the New York Daily News about my experiences with him. He came out blazing guns against me at rallies and on Twitter. He released emails I had written to him five years earlier when I was looking for a job. A tabloid newspaper wrote that he had “got rid” of me and that I had begged him for a job. Both lies. His supporters tweeted things about me like “glad Trump fired her”. I wasn’t fired.
I’d impressed him when I was working for HRH. In meetings the project managers and superintendents would talk about different problems on the job, and the architect would often blame the contractor or the subcontractors. I’d say, “That’s bullshit.” He loved that.
At a meeting at his apartment, Donald asked me to be in charge of the construction of Trump Tower. I remember it was in a nice building on Fifth Avenue. Everything inside was white: the carpet, the upholstery, the walls, the ceiling. Donald went through a spiel about what he was building. I was to be the last word on site, he said. “You’ll be like a Donna Trump.” He offered me almost twice the salary I was getting.
I liked being there. Trump Tower was a big deal and I had the best crew in the world. There were times when Donald was actually like a human being. We used to go into his office and sit and talk. He’d tell jokes. He was pretty funny. Now, I’m not saying he was a nice guy. Not at all. Any time anyone really disagreed with him, he would yell at them. He always needed someone to blame. If he screamed at me in front of the team it didn’t matter, because they were all getting screamed at. If he’d screamed at me in front of an architect or an investor, I would have walked out the door.
When he wanted to do something that we thought was wrong or illegal, you couldn’t just say that. He couldn’t handle it. So we found ways of working around it – making him think that a substitute idea we’d come up with was his. I used to put him in a good mood by saying, “Hey Donald, did you see Ivana this morning? What an incredible outfit she’s wearing. She’s so gorgeous.” We were able to keep him somewhat under control. Nobody does that now.
I was offered a partnership elsewhere and left. Donald threw a massive party for me. He got me a Cartier bracelet, signed, “Towers of thanks, love Donald.” A few years later, I got back in touch with him for some advice and he hired me again, this time to be in charge of all construction, then construction and development, for the Trump Organization.
When I went back in 1987, he was surrounded by yes‑sayers. His book Trump: The Art of the Deal absolutely changed him in terms of his picture of himself. Even though he always said he was the smartest, now he thought he was a real big-time player. Everybody knew everything about him: how great he was, how brilliant he was.
The second time I left was around 1990, when I was running Trump’s big West Side project on the riverfront. Neighbourhood groups and some big-name opponents – including Christopher Reeve – were fighting it hard. And a friend of Donald’s came to him and said, “You’ve got to meet with these people, and you’ve got to make a deal with them.” He wanted to build 14m sq ft. He made a deal to build just 7.5m. In that deal, the opposition group put their person in charge of the project. They wanted a semi‑famous lawyer who worked in development and didn’t have construction experience. I quit primarily because they brought in this other person.
I told Donald I had to leave. My son has to have surgery, I said. The surgery was a big deal, but I wouldn’t quit over that. I told him it to soften the blow.
I stayed on as a consultant on two other projects. One of those was the Ambassador hotel. One of our partners was going under. He wanted to be in charge of everything. My assistant and I told Donald this would blow up the project, which it eventually did. Donald allowed him to take over against our advice. Afterwards, at a big meeting with the realtor and the partners, Donald came down on me. I told him, “I told you not to let this guy get involved.”
He started screaming. His face was contorting. That was the only time he’d ever done that in front of external people. I was enraged. I looked at him and I said, “You know, Donald, there are medicines that can help you control that.”
He got crazy about that.
After the people left, I went back up to Donald’s office and said, “Look, I can’t do this, I’m leaving.” And he said, “Why?” I didn’t say, “Because you made a fool out of me in front of the partners.” I said, “I’m looking after my son, I’m still having problems” – which was not true. “They’re just going to start school now, and I think I really should find something that won’t take me to California every week.”
Donald talked about running for president when I was at the Trump Organization. I thought at the time that he was a very good manager, given the right people, and that he could be a decent president. I didn’t know then that he had zero knowledge of government.
The Apprentice thing I’ve always thought of as a big joke. In my experience, he didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people. He didn’t want to look bad. If someone was going to get fired, he wasn’t doing it.
In my case, we had a woman who was working on some lobbying efforts we were doing. She had gotten pregnant. He found out and said, “Fire her.” I said, “You can’t, that’s against the law.” He got angry at me. “Fire her now!” I did it. It was terrible. I told her I would support her if she wanted to go after him because I knew that it was illegal to fire her.
Here’s another story I remember: when we needed an apartment manager at Trump Tower, he found a guy and hired him to work under me. He was terrible. We didn’t like him; he had a bad attitude. I told Donald, “We’re going to fire him.” He said, “Go ahead.” We fired him, and he went across the street to where Donald’s office was at the time. Donald was convinced by him. He told us, “Give him another chance.” And that happened twice. It took three times to fire this guy.
I think all the firing he has done in government shows a big shift in his attitude. But he has to blame someone. And how do you prove someone is at fault better than firing them? Even if they didn’t do anything wrong.
As told to Kate Lloyd
Tower of Lies: What My Eighteen Years of Working With Donald Trump Reveals About Him by Barbara Res (Graymalkin Media, £14.99) is available now.
