Russian GRU Organized Drone Attack at Leipzig Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:24:25 UTC
19:24:25 KST

German investigators have determined that the preparation for the drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport was organized by an employee of Russian military intelligence—the GRU.
This was reported by WELT am Sonntag, citing investigation materials.
According to the publication, the suspect arrived in Germany via Turkey and later flew to Serbia. He is currently in Russia, WELT claims.
German intelligence agencies were aware of his probable connection to intelligence services when he entered the country, but did not place him under surveillance at that time.
Back in early September, ZDF reported on two identified suspects, one of whom played an organizational role.
Links between the attack itself and Russian military intelligence had been suggested earlier.
In August, a U.S. intelligence source reported that the explosives and the design of the drone found were characteristic of devices used by the GRU.
As a reminder, the drone carrying explosives was discovered on August 4 near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport.
The device did not explode; it was defused, and later two more drones were found.
It was previously reported that the An-124 was loaded with ammunition. Subsequently, the German Interior Ministry denied that there were any weapons on board the aircraft.
These events fit into a broader picture described in a report by the U.S. Congressional Research Service. Following the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia expanded its campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, and other covert operations in Europe.
Weakening European support for Ukraine is cited as one of the possible goals of this campaign.

Dragons collect NRLW wooden spoon after Sharks defeat and Eels down Cowboys in thriller
Parramatta has scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.
None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.
The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.
In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.
After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.
The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.
Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.
Cowboys hooker Alisha Foord snuck over two minutes into the second half, and another four-pointer followed quickly to Makenzie Weale to give North Queensland a 22-6 lead.
However, with veteran Kennedy Cherrington sin-binned, the 12-player Eels scored tries to Zali Fay and Jasmin Morrissey to get within six points.
Keilee Joseph then made it three tries in eight minutes to tie things up.
Cowboys interchange hooker Nadia Windleborn put her side back on top, before Joseph again tied the scores.
Experienced half Rachael Pearson stepped up to nail a one-pointer for Parramatta with four minutes remaining, before Owen sealed victory with a stunning 90m effort moments later.
In Saturday's second game, the Sharks came out firing in the second half to defeat the Dragons at Sydney Football Stadium, handing their local rivals the wooden spoon.
It marked Cronulla's first back-to-back wins in 2026 following their upset of the Warriors in Auckland last week.
It took 20 minutes for the first points to be registered, Dragons front-rower Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis powering over from 12 metres out for the only score of an opening half littered with 15 errors.
It didn't take as long for points in the second period, with Sharks half Chantay Kiria-Ratu delivering a beautiful short ball two minutes in for China Polata to run 50m to score.
Four minutes later Georgia Hannaway dived over from dummy half for Cronulla's second.
Ellie Johnston made it three tries within 13 minutes for the Sharks, and when Dragons centre Tyra Ekepati was sin-binned for a high shot it looked like Cronulla may run away with it, but the Dragons held strong in those 10 minutes.
Shenae Ciesiolka scored a consolation try for the Dragons in her 50th NRLW appearance, but it was too little, too late.

Brics Summit 2026: PM Modi pitches emergency support network for safety of seafarers

Unknown Publisher

PM Modi proposes seafarers' safety network on the opening day of Brics summit
The safety of Indian seafarers has emerged as a recurring focus of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Brics engagements. On Saturday, he proposed a seafarers emergency support network among BRICS members to provide distress alerts, medical aid, family communication and evacuation support.The proposal came on the opening day of the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi, where the safety and wellbeing of seafarers emerged as a recurring theme in PM Modi’s remarks amid heightened tensions in West Asia and disruptions to key shipping routes.
“Seafarers make a significant contribution to global trade, but they often find themselves without adequate support during difficult times. My proposal is: Can we create a Seafarers Emergency Support Network?”, PM Modi said during his opening remarks while addressing the summit.“Through this, the Maritime Authorities and Missions of the concerned countries can be connected. It can provide support for distress alerts, medical assistance, informing families and evacuation,” he added.
Modi’s proposal follows his remarks at the Brics Business Forum on Friday, when he highlighted the importance of safe sea lanes and the protection of seafarers, particularly amid the conflict in West Asia.
“Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes remain open, and seafarers are safe. That is why India is a staunch advocate of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers,” PM Modi said at the forum.The issue also featured in PM Modi’s meeting with Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday. According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), PM underscored the need to ensure “freedom of navigation and commerce, and the safety and well-being of seafarers” during discussions on the conflict in West Asia.The concern has a direct bearing on India, which has a large seafaring workforce and has faced casualties amid the wider regional conflict. In July, the government had said in Parliament that 16 Indian nationals, including 10 seafarers, have lost their lives in the region since the outbreak of the of the conflict, while 75 have been injured.The summit is taking place against the backdrop of continuing geopolitical and economic uncertainty, including the West Asia crisis, disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, the Russia-Ukraine war and US trade and tariff policies. India has repeatedly stressed the importance of keeping shipping and commercial routes open.On Saturday, PM Modi also linked the maritime proposal to a wider call for Brics to translate its consensus into practical outcomes as the grouping marked two decades since its formation.“I am delighted to welcome you all to India. India’s chairship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability have been our priority,” PM Modi said.
He said India had organised more than 350 meetings across nearly 30 cities during its chairship and thanked member countries for their participation.“This year's Brics summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Brics. In human life, the age of twenty heralds the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility,” PM said.
“This is the stage where responsibility aligns with aspirations, and potential finds a new direction. Today, Brics, too, is at a moment of coming of age,” he added.“Now is the time for us to translate the unity and consensus within Brics into tangible outcomes on the global stage.”The summit was attended by Chinese president Xi Jinping, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto, among other leaders and representatives.
Subhadra Srivastava is a journalist with The Times of India, covering geopolitics, international and national affairs. With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

US President Donald Trump said Saturday that the war with Iran could end “very soon,” claiming Tehran is seeking to prolong the conflict to influence elections.
Speaking after a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Ireland, Trump said he expected the war to end shortly, while reiterating that Iran must not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
“I think very soon,” Trump said when asked when the war would end. “I think it'll be probably right after election times.”
Trump alleged that Iran was trying to “hold out as long as they can to complicate the election,” but said the US would not allow Tehran to acquire nuclear weapons.
“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. It's very simple,” he said, adding that oil prices would fall sharply once the conflict ends.
He also addressed tensions in the Red Sea, saying Yemen's Houthis had contacted the US and indicated they did not want a confrontation with Washington.
“They don't want to fight with us,” Trump said, adding that the group was allowing most ships to pass through the waterway.
Trump claimed the US had established strong control over the area through an aggressive naval blockade and was intercepting about 25 boats a day, “most of them at night.”
The president said the US had anticipated that the conflict would drive up oil prices, but suggested prices would decline once the war with Iran comes to an end.
Trump also defended his administration's role in Gaza, rejecting criticism that Washington was facilitating genocide or Israel's occupation of the West Bank.
“When you say Gaza, you know we put out the fire and we get all the hostages,” he said, referring to efforts that he said had secured the release and recovery of hostages held in Gaza.

In St. Petersburg, 2-kilometer queues formed at gas stations due to a fuel shortage
Kyiv • UNN
Drivers wait for hours at gas stations, where fuel is dispensed with a limit of up to 60 liters. The shortage is linked to an attack on the Kirishinefteorgsintez oil refinery.
In St. Petersburg, amid a fuel shortage, drivers are standing in queues at gas stations for hours, with some lines stretching for 2 km. The latest escalation of the fuel crisis began after a Ukrainian attack on one of Russia's largest oil refineries, Kirishinefteorgsintez, ASTRA reports, writes UNN.
Details
Local residents began to complain en masse about the situation on September 9. One of ASTRA's sources said that the day before, he had spent 4.5 hours waiting in line at a gas station.
According to him, cars occupy an entire traffic lane, and the queue at one of the Gazprom gas stations began approximately 2 km from the station itself. Due to the large number of cars, public transportation is experiencing problems on some sections.
Gas stations are introducing limits
At the gas station mentioned by the St. Petersburg resident, there was a limit of no more than 60 liters of gasoline per vehicle. A liter of fuel cost about 73 rubles. At the same time, only 2 of the 6 pumps were operating; the reasons for this are unknown.
According to ASTRA's source, transport services are also recording violations by drivers who stop under prohibition signs because of the queues, after which they may be fined.
ASTRA links the new wave of fuel problems in St. Petersburg to an attack by Ukraine's Defense Forces on the Kirishinefteorgsintez refinery in the Leningrad region. The enterprise is one of Russia's largest oil refineries.

Revealed: the university courses students regret – and those they don’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:20:02 UTC
19:20:02 KST

Gloomy headlines might claim that a degree is less worthwhile than it once was, but one sliver of good news is that the most recent graduates don’t regret their time on campus.
When those who graduated in the summer of 2024 were surveyed 15 months later, more than eight out of 10 said they would still go to university ahead of any other option, despite a media drumbeat of pessimism about graduate jobs and increasing levels of student debt.
Matt Hiely-Rayner, an analyst who compiles the Guardian’s University Guide, says the new data supplied by the Higher Education Statistics Agency, was positive news. “Very few students say they would do something different than go to university – only about 20% of graduates say they would do something completely different.
“And the proportion who are happy with the provider they selected has stayed strong and has actually gone up slightly this year, suggesting that people were more satisfied with their choice.”
But fewer of the recent graduates appeared to be happy with their choice of subject, with just 70% saying they would stick with their original subject.
“Even that is relatively good, there hasn’t been a collapse, which is interesting because we’ve seen positive outcomes around graduate jobs continue to come down faster than in previous years,” says Hiely-Rayner. “So with hindsight, 15 months after graduation, students are more likely to regret their subject choice than they are going to university at all or which institution they went to.”
According to the latest data, the University of Bath’s graduates were happiest with their choice of institution, leaping above its rivals at Oxbridge and the Russell Group of research universities. The top five universities clustered around 90% of their graduates saying they remain happy with their choice, with just 0.8 of a percentage point separating Bath at the top from Oxford in fifth place.
But that happiness doesn’t extend to subject choices – with dissatisfaction visible even among most highly selective professional courses that offer well-paid graduate careers.
Fifteen months after graduation, fewer dentists, vets and paramedics than in the previous year said they would choose the same course, while architecture and computer science have fallen out of the top 10 in terms of course satisfaction.
The fall in computer science may be linked to the way AI has replaced entry-level jobs, as well as early career employment opportunities not being as abundant as they once were. Four years ago, 66% of computer science students went on to graduate-level employment but the latest figures show just 56% did so.
AI may also be harming the career prospects of graduates who studied animation and game design, who are now among the least enthusiastic about their career choices. Fewer than two out of three animation and game design graduates would choose the same course again, putting it in the same league as journalism, marketing and PR graduates for highest levels of regret.
The latest data also highlighted a surprising fall in satisfaction in economics, which regularly tops league tables for graduate pay and has seen a surge in interest among A-level students and university applicants.
This may reflect the fact that not all economics courses are created equal, says Hiely-Rayner. “Economics has always been quite a secure one [in terms of graduate jobs]. It seems like a safe bet, but the proportion who are getting a job varies by institution.”

Diesel in Portugal hits record high, Spain introduces new discount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:19:13 UTC
19:19:13 KST

Many Portuguese already cross the border to fill up; the trend is now even clearer, as Spain's government adds a 20-cent-per-litre discount, making Spanish diesel the second cheapest in the EU.
The price of diesel is expected to rise slightly in Portugal at the start of next week, according to forecasts from the National Association of Fuel Retailers (ANAREC), while the price of petrol is set to fall. However, the increase is being offset by changes to the discount on the Petroleum Products Tax (ISP) announced by the Portuguese government on Friday evening.
The new rates unveiled on Friday effectively raise the tax on petrol by about one cent per litre, meaning the price of a litre of 95 unleaded petrol should fall by around five cents on Monday, instead of the six cents previously forecast.
The price of diesel, meanwhile, is set to continue breaking historic records. The increase in the tax discount announced by the government is very small, at only around 0.10 cents, leaving virtually unchanged the forecast rise of four cents per litre. As a result, the indicative price of a litre of diesel is expected to reach about €2.15 from this Monday, a new all-time high.
ANAREC president João Durão accuses the government of "lying" to Portuguese people when it says it is not profiting from rising fuel prices.
Spanish government introduces €0.20 discount
Speaking to journalists at a petrol station in Caminha, in Alto Minho near the Spanish border, the head of the main industry association said the government would have to take action against what he described as "fuel smuggling from Spain", where fuel is 30 to 40 cents per litre cheaper, and warned of the loss of competitiveness this is creating. He insisted that, contrary to the government's claims, the state is profiting from the rise in fuel prices, since "out of one euro spent on diesel, 60 cents are taxes" and "in Spain that is not the case", in his words.
In fact, more and more Portuguese drivers are filling up on the other side of the border. Unlike in Portugal, fuel prices in Spain are among the lowest in Europe.
That gap has widened further with the introduction of a discount of 20 cents per litre, brought in last week by Pedro Sánchez's government to counter the impact of the price rises.
Previously, seven countries had cheaper diesel and petrol than Spain, but now only Malta manages to offer even lower prices. Spain now has the second-cheapest diesel in the European Union, at €1.795 per litre. Malta has the lowest prices, followed by Spain, Bulgaria and Hungary. In the case of the Mediterranean island nation, prices have been frozen by the government since 2020 at €1.34 per litre of petrol and €1.21 per litre of diesel.
At the other end of the scale, it is in Finland that motorists pay the most for a litre of diesel (€2.477), followed by the Netherlands (€2.442), Denmark (€2.434) and Germany (€2.328).
The Middle East crisis triggered by the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran in February, and the resulting blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has been pushing oil and fuel prices to record highs. The price of crude oil has recently risen above 100 dollars per barrel.

Nigel Farage’s Reform UK Party cashed two separate £36 million donations from crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, giving the populist leader a financial head start in his bid to win the UK’s next general election.
A statement issued by Reform UK on Saturday confirmed that Harborne matched a £36 million donation from Delo announced on Friday.
Each of the two donations are the largest ever given to a political party in the UK, dwarfing a £9 million gift to Reform UK in 2025 from Harborne.
Advertisement
Delo argued in an opinion piece for The Telegraph that Reform needed the injection to make the election “a fair fight.” Delo, who was already one of Reform’s largest donors, said he wanted to give Reform “a level playing field” at the next general election.
The paper on Saturday also published an opinion piece from Harborne, where he called his donation “a philantropic gift to our country.”
Farage thanked the two men for their contributions. “Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around,” he said in a statement.
Reform UK was leading the polls since April 2025, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. But the party has now slumped slightly behind Labour, with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the helm and after a bizarre by-election where Farage defeated satirical candidate Count Binface.
The right-wing force is currently rushing to get battle-ready amid speculation Burnham could trigger an early general election, though one is not due until 2029. Reform UK is on the hunt for potential candidates to run as MP, and has only about 100 star candidates considered ready to run at the moment.
Both Reform as a party and Nigel Farage have faced scrutiny over recent years about donations and how they reported them. The party is currently under investigation from the Metropolitan Police over allegations it broke foreign funding laws. The right-wing populist has also faced repeated questions over a separate £5 million cash gift from Harborne, which Farage said he accepted in early 2024 in “a purely personal capacity.”

‘New &amp; ambitious agenda’: PM Modi proposes Brics continuity mechanism with Troika system, digital repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:16:37 UTC
19:16:37 KST

PM Modi speaks during the 18th Brics Summit, at the Bharat Mandapam, in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday proposed a new implementation and continuity mechanism for Brics, anchored by a “Troika” system and a secure digital repository to track decisions, nodal points and timelines as the grouping’s annual presidencies rotate.Addressing the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi under India’s 2026 chairship, PM Modi said a seamless follow-up mechanism was essential to maintain institutional momentum as Brics entered its third decade and began shaping an ambitious agenda for the next 20 years.
“We need to work on a new and ambitious agenda for the next 20 years. We must begin this process with our own internal working systems. While the Brics presidency rotates annually, this should not disrupt our institutional momentum. I propose the establishment of a Brics continuity and implementation mechanism,” PM Modi said.He said the proposed mechanism would allow initiatives and outcomes to be followed up through the Troika arrangement.“This would enable the follow-up of all initiatives and outcomes through the 'Troika' arrangement. We could also create a secure digital repository to record the nodal point, timeframe, and implementation status associated with every decision,” PM Modi said.
The Troika mechanism provides for coordination among the previous, current and incoming Brics chairs to ensure continuity as the presidency changes annually.The proposed system draws a parallel with the G20 Troika, under which the previous, current and incoming presidencies work together to maintain continuity in the grouping’s agenda and priorities. PM Modi’s proposal seeks to apply a similar continuity framework to Brics, alongside a digital repository to track the implementation of decisions.
PM Modi calls for time-bound global governance reforms
Alongside reforms to Brics' internal working system, PM Modi called for time-bound changes to global multilateral institutions, saying reform of the United Nations Security Council could no longer be delayed.He proposed a three-pillar framework of Representation, Responsiveness and Rule-making to guide the future roadmap for global governance and the Global South.“In formulating this roadmap, we must focus on three key aspects: Representation, Responsiveness, and Rule-making. Regarding representation, I would like to state that reform of the UN Security Council can no longer be postponed. Negotiations on this matter must be linked to a definite timeframe and clear outcomes,” PM Modi said.He also called for voting power, leadership positions and policy priorities within international financial institutions to reflect current economic realities.“Countries that drive global economic growth should also play an appropriate role in shaping global economic governance,” he said.PM Modi said developing countries continued to face an imbalance in global decision-making and proposed that Brics members jointly formulate 10 proposals for global governance reform, with the aim of finalising them as a Brics reform roadmap by the next summit.“Today, the Global South stands in the front row of global crises but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this 'pyramid of privilege' into a 'platform of partnership'—one where every nation has a voice, every member has a stake, and the development of humanity lies at the heart of every endeavour,” he said.The Prime Minister said the existing global governance structure resembled a pyramid, with power and decision-making concentrated at the top while countries affected by those decisions remained unable to shape them.“While strengthening Brics, we must also chart a course for global reform. The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid: power and decision-making are concentrated at the top, while the lower tiers consist of nations that are affected by these decisions yet unable to shape them,” PM Modi said.The Prime Minister said the Global South must become a “rule shaper” to deal with the challenges facing the world. He also proposed a seafarers’ network among Brics countries to ensure their safety.
Brics marks 20 years as India hosts summit
PM Modi thanked participating countries for their contribution and support during India’s Brics chairship, describing the grouping’s 20th anniversary as a historic milestone.“I express my heartfelt gratitude to all of you for your active contribution and support in making India’s Brics chairmanship a success. This year’s Brics summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Brics. In human life, the age of 20 marks the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility,” he said.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit under its 2026 chairship, with the grouping entering its third decade.The summit is expected to deliberate on protecting developing economies from the global impact of wars in Ukraine and West Asia.PM Modi also said Brics had established a distinct identity on the global stage and was “not against anyone”.The summit is being attended by leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.Other leaders attending include Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung.
Joint statement after intensive negotiations
A joint statement is also set to be issued by Brics nations during the summit after intensive negotiations.The negotiations continued until 4 am on Saturday, with differences reported on several contentious issues. India led consultations to bridge competing positions and build consensus among members.
The statement comes against the backdrop of differing positions among Brics members, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, on regional and geopolitical issues.India assumed the Brics chairship for 2026 under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”The theme focuses on strengthening existing achievements and institutional effectiveness while placing development, sustainability and innovation at the centre of the grouping’s agenda.PM Modi welcomed Brics delegates, including Xi and Putin, to Bharat Mandapam, the venue for the summit in New Delhi.Brics has emerged as a platform for cooperation among major emerging economies, with its agenda covering development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges.

The parties agreed on what leaders and government officials should do at their level, and what manufacturers and developers should do at theirs.
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European anti-ballistic system, the first track of the Anti-Ballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point General and Technical Director Iryna Terek said that development had reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, the launcher, the data transmission channel, and the command center—and that tests are being conducted up to twice a week.

19:09:32 KST

Ahmad Adil
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday called for equal participation in global rule-making as well as reform of the UN Security Council.
Delivering an opening statement at the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Modi said the bloc was at its "coming-of-age" moment.
“Today, the Global South is at the forefront of global crises. But it is in the back row of decision-making. We have to turn this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership,” he said, while addressing the two-day BRICS Leaders’ Summit in the Indian capital.
Proposing global governance reform, Modi said BRICS has to "focus on three main aspects of this roadmap (which include) representation, responsiveness, and rule-making."
"First, I would like to say that the UN Security Council reform cannot be delayed any longer," he stressed.
It is “important to ensure equal participation in deciding the global rules of the future," said the Indian prime minister.
Noting that the BRICS bloc members “respect each other's views and move forward with consensus,” Modi said, “We do not oppose anyone, but try to move forward with the thought of taking everyone along. Now is the time to turn our unity and co-operation on the global stage into strong results.”
Turning to economics, Modi said voting power, leadership positions, and policy priorities in financial institutions should be "based on today's economic realities."
"Countries that accelerate global economic growth should also play a role in guiding global economic governance," he added.
The weekend summit in New Delhi is attended by the Chinese, Russian and Iranian presidents, among others, and comes at a time when the US-Iran war has dragged on for seven months, while the Russia-Ukraine war has continued for more than four years.

Zelensky says he is ready to meet Putin at G20 summit in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:06:55 UTC
19:06:55 KST

Editor's Note: Read Russia's response to Zelensky's statement here.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he is prepared to travel to the G20 summit and meet Vladimir Putin there if the Russian leader attends, he told Deutsche Welle in an interview published on Sept. 12.
The G20 leaders' summit is scheduled to take place in Miami in December.
"Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," Zelensky told DW.
"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter," Zelensky added. "Results matter. That's it."
Zelensky and Putin have not met in person since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow had not yet discussed whether Putin would attend the G20 summit, he told the pro-Kremlin outlet Izvestia on Sept. 12.
"As for the possibility of Putin's trip, this issue has not even been discussed yet," Ushakov said, adding that preparations for the summit were continuing at the expert level.
Putin has not personally attended a G20 leaders' summit since 2019, according to DW.
Later on Sept. 12, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters that Zelensky should come to Moscow if he wishes to meet directly with Putin.
Zelensky's comments come amid renewed U.S.-led efforts to bring Kyiv and Moscow back to negotiations. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier in September after talks in Moscow.
Zelensky told DW that Ukraine was now in a "good position for negotiations," arguing that Russia continues to suffer heavy battlefield losses for relatively limited territorial gains.
He also said Kyiv had discussed a possible energy and grain ceasefire with the U.S. envoys as a potential first step toward broader negotiations.
"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Zelensky said.
The latest U.S. diplomatic push has so far failed to produce a breakthrough. People familiar with the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow remained unwilling to make meaningful concessions, despite revised U.S. proposals aimed at reviving talks. Zelensky said after the Kyiv meeting that he expected the war to continue into the winter.
The Kremlin has said it does not rule out renewed trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S., though no date or venue has been agreed.

US House Prepares Vote on Russia Sanctions Bill Giving Trump 100% Tariff Powers

US House Prepares Vote on Russia Sanctions Bill Giving Trump 100% Tariff Powers
The US House of Representatives plans to hold a vote next week on a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that recently passed the Senate with strong bipartisan support, according to Bloomberg on September 11.
The legislation would grant US President Donald Trump the authority to impose 100% tariffs on the five largest foreign buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as the five top nations helping bypass energy restrictions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Countries like China, India, and Turkey currently lead as the largest importers of Russian energy products.
Floor action will proceed under a standard voting procedure requiring a simple majority for passage. The measure has generated pushback among some House lawmakers who express concern over broadening executive tariff powers and triggering higher oil prices.
Despite those concerns, House leadership resolved to move forward with the bill—which maintains support from both parties and the White House—following their return from a Republican retreat.
At the same time, retail associations and the US Chamber of Commerce have voiced worry that the bill provides the White House with fresh legal grounds for expansive tariffs. In response, business coalitions drafted a letter urging congressional leaders to alter the text.
“We urge Congress to remove the tariff authority from the bill and instead focus on targeted sanctions, stepped-up enforcement against sanctions evasion, and coordinated diplomacy with nations purchasing Russian energy,” the groups stated.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act passed the Senate with an overwhelming 86-11 majority after more than two years of development.
However, the bill was omitted from the House’s immediate voting schedule as lawmakers returned from their summer recess, which placed the high-profile legislation at serious risk of languishing indefinitely ahead of the congressional elections.
House Republican leadership showed little momentum toward bringing the measure to the floor, while Speaker Mike Johnson remained noncommittal on whether the bill would receive a vote.

Russia Expands Ready-to-Launch Nuclear Arsenal to Highest Level in Nine Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:05:51 UTC
19:05:51 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Expands Ready-to-Launch Nuclear Arsenal to Highest Level in Nine Years
Russia has expanded the number of nuclear warheads ready for deployment to 1,796, reaching its highest level in nine years, according to The Moscow Times on September 11.
Data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) shows that Moscow has increased the quantity of nuclear warheads mounted on delivery systems for four consecutive years.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In 2026, Russia’s total nuclear arsenal stood at 5,420 warheads.
This total includes 2,604 warheads stored in reserve, 1,020 categorized as retired and awaiting dismantlement, and 1,796 active charges mounted directly on operational missiles and heavy bombers. Moscow expanded its deployed warhead stockpile by 78 units over the past year.
In contrast, the United States maintained an unchanged inventory of 1,770 deployed warheads out of a comparable overall nuclear capacity. Other major nuclear powers kept their deployed counts stationary, with France holding 280 and the United Kingdom maintaining 170.
China increased its deployed warheads to 34, up from 24 in 2025, out of a total stockpile of 620. India placed 12 warheads into deployed status for the first time, out of an estimated total arsenal of 190.The volume of operational Russian nuclear warheads has risen every year during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Records show 1,588 deployed charges in 2022, 1,674 in 2023, 1,710 in 2024, and 1,718 in 2025. Compared to 2020 figures, the Kremlin has expanded its active delivery-ready nuclear strength by 14 percent, adding 226 warheads to achieve its highest deployment count since 2017, when the total reached 1,950.
Russian land-based nuclear forces, consisting of silo launchers and mobile missile systems, have the physical capacity to hold 1,092 warheads. Current operational deployments occupy 892 of these slots, with the remaining allocation kept in storage facilities.
Across the naval branch, 13 strategic submarines operating in the Northern and Pacific Fleets are built to carry 208 missiles and 928 warheads. However, because two submarines are currently undergoing full overhauls, the total number of naval warheads available for immediate deployment drops to 704.
An additional 586 warheads are assigned to strategic bombers. This figure remains below the maximum potential load of 650 warheads that Russian heavy aviation can carry.
Analysts noted that only a portion of the bomber fleet is in fully operational condition, pointing out that Russian Aerospace Forces sustained operational aircraft losses following military strikes during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) dismantled Russia’s RM-48U ballistic missile and revealed that the weapon was assembled from repurposed S-300 and S-400 missile components.
Intelligence analysts discovered that the missile relied heavily on foreign electronics, including dozens of parts manufactured by companies based in the United States.
Following their technical assessment, HUR published a detailed breakdown of the missile on its War&Sanctions portal, showcasing its internal systems, electronic components, and an interactive 3D model.

====================================================================================================

Kfar Aza’s slow return after October 7: ‘We’re rebuilding trust’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:05:47 UTC
19:05:47 KST

Nearly three years after the October 7 massacre, residents of Kfar Aza are beginning to return home. The key word in that sentence is "beginning."
This is not a single moment, not a day when the gates open and the entire community returns together, but a slow, cautious and sometimes painful process in which one family after another packs up its life again and tries to imagine rebuilding it in a place where everything has changed.
Many are still debating whether to return and many will not. On Sept. 1, the sound of children could once again be heard in the kibbutz. Kindergartens opened, the clinic is on the way, the resilience center is being rebuilt, a pre-military academy is already operating there and amid the returning signs of life, tractors are everywhere.
After a prolonged evacuation, spent mainly at Kibbutz Shefayim and Kibbutz Ruhama, the official return began last month. About 50 families out of roughly 300 households that lived in Kfar Aza before the war have already returned, with another one or two families arriving each week. The community hopes the pace will accelerate after the holidays.
But there is still a long way to go. About 30% to 40% of families remain undecided about whether to return at all, while 10% to 15% have said they will not return and are looking for alternatives.
The shadow of October 7 alongside every sign of life
The kibbutz estimates that about 70% of residents will return by the end of 2027. "That's a realistic target that depends on the security situation," said Sigal Moran, chairwoman of the kibbutz.
"The return process is complex. It is shaped by fears, trauma and a lack of trust. We are rebuilding the kibbutz and rebuilding trust."
Tzion Regev, the community manager, said: "We're celebrating and not celebrating. It's moving to see the kindergartens open on Sept. 1. You start seeing people walking around, there are students from the new pre-military academy, new residents are arriving, new families. Life is starting to return."
But he, too, knows there is no room yet for a full celebration. "Everything is incredibly sensitive. We're cautious about our celebrations. Many people still aren't coming back. There's uncertainty. People are still deciding."
That may be the most striking thing about Kfar Aza these days: Alongside every sign of life, the shadow of October 7 remains.
According to an IDF investigation, about 250 terrorists invaded the kibbutz that morning. For the first two hours, 14 members of the local security team fought them alone. Half were killed.
The terrorists breached the fence, and among the first to enter the kibbutz were attackers who arrived on paragliders.
ynet photographer and kibbutz member Roy Idan, who documented the invasion in those first minutes, was murdered along with his wife, Smadar, and their daughter Abigail was kidnapped.
Now, nearly three years later, people are returning to the place where it all happened. The most powerful symbol in the kibbutz of that catastrophic failure is the devastated "Young Generation" neighborhood, where 11 residents were murdered and seven were abducted, including captivity survivors Gali and Ziv Berman and Emily Damari, who strongly opposed demolishing the homes.
In a vote among kibbutz members, residents decided to clear the neighborhood and move several buildings to a memorial site outside the kibbutz.
Several bereaved families who oppose the evacuation petitioned the Supreme Court sitting as the High Court of Justice. Until the court rules, the kibbutz decided to reroute the entrance to the neighborhood outside the community and erect a fence that will separate and conceal it from the rest of the kibbutz.
'We wanted to stop feeling like our lives were temporary'
Viki and Nadav Nasi Tzantzifer arrived in Kfar Aza only in September 2022. They wanted to leave Ashkelon and move somewhere more rural, and with the help of Nadav's cousin, a kibbutz member, they found an apartment.
Within a year, they already felt at home and described it as nothing short of a dream year.
On October 7, Viki was six months pregnant with Guy, who is now almost 3.
On the morning of the massacre, they were at home. The sirens caught them, like everyone else. They entered the safe room and remained there for hours.
Gunfire, shouting and exchanges of fire could be heard outside. The safe room's exterior wall carried the sounds of shooting directly to them, and at one point Nadav saw a cell of terrorists outside the house.
They sat on the floor in darkness and silence, without food or water, and a laundry basket became a makeshift toilet.
Then came the moment that frightened Viki most: She stopped feeling the baby move.
"It was very frightening," she said. "Every so often I felt short of breath and had some anxiety. It came and went. At one point I stopped feeling the baby's movements, and then I started to panic."
Nadav also remembers the fear. "There was a very real fear that she would give birth right then. It's an extreme situation. You don't know how you'll react or how the body will react. The terrorists reached the entrance to the house."
They were evacuated from the kibbutz close to midnight.
Then began a journey that seemed endless: a month in Shefayim, nearly a year in Tel Aviv, a month at Viki's parents' home in Ashkelon, then Ruhama.
Including their move back to Kfar Aza three weeks ago, they lived in five different places in less than three years.
"The dream was to walk with the stroller along the kibbutz paths, not through the streets of Tel Aviv or Yarkon Park."
They even expanded their family while living in Ruhama. Viki became pregnant with their second child, but their desire to return to Kfar Aza only grew stronger.
"It was clear to us that we wanted to return," she said. "There were important things we needed in place to make that possible, like an education system. The rest mattered less."
For Nadav, returning was also an attempt to escape the sense of limbo that had been imposed on them.
"It was a complicated period. It's a new place, we're carrying everything that happened in the kibbutz and trying to understand what is happening to us, and suddenly a new member joins the family.
"Today we understand how important it is to have a community surrounding you. We had a very strong desire to return to the kibbutz and get out of that feeling of 'temporariness' in Ruhama. They were wonderful hosts, but we wanted to go home."
Their original house, however, was no longer an option. After several attempts to enter it, they realized they would never be able to live there again.
"We went into the safe room and I told Nadav there was no chance, that I couldn't do it," Viki said.
They found another apartment to rent and decided to start over somewhere else within the same place.
On Aug. 21, they returned to Kfar Aza. The kibbutz they found was completely different from the one they had left.
"The kibbutz looks like a construction site today. Everything is torn up, and some of that keeps that day present," Nadav said.
Still, amid the ruins and construction work, he feels he has come home. "With all the difficulty — and there is difficulty — it's good for us here. We want to raise our children here."
The war beyond the fence can still be heard. Sometimes it brings the memories back with it. But now there is also a community around them.
"We see friends who have also returned walking along the kibbutz paths, because now there's one area where people can move around. It's complicated, but we're dealing with it. I'm glad to be among the first to return to the kibbutz, and it gives me a sense of pride," Nadav said.
Viki feels the return is also a kind of repair. "There's an element here of deciding for yourself what you do with yourself and your family. There's also a feeling of rebuilding and of being able to help shape the place."
For Guy, meanwhile, the rehabilitation effort is mainly one enormous show of tractors and excavators. "He's thrilled," she said.
Both know the Kfar Aza they will live in will be different from the one they knew. But for them, that is not necessarily bad news.
"It will be good here, and we hope it will be even better," they said. "It will be different, that's for sure, but different in a good way."
The couple are expecting another child in October.
'People are moved to tears seeing the kindergarten operating'
And then there are the children. If there is one sign that Kfar Aza is truly beginning to come back to life, it can be found along the kibbutz paths leading to kindergarten.
Einat Hemias Bons, 54, a kibbutz member, has been a special education teacher for 20 years.
When she realized the kindergartens were about to reopen in Kfar Aza, she took unpaid leave from the Education Ministry and decided not only to return home, but also to run the kindergarten.
"I felt this was what I needed to do right now," she said. "I told myself, I'm doing it. Mainly to give those returning a sense of security, so there would be someone from the kibbutz with experience and they could at least feel calm about that."
She moved from Ruhama, where the community had been evacuated, back to Kfar Aza at the end of August.
Alongside boxes in her new home, she also prepared the kindergarten.
On Sept. 1, 10 children entered it, with several more expected to join after the holidays. One of them is Guy, Viki and Nadav's son.
On October 7, Einat was at home in the kibbutz with her eldest son, Ofek. "Luckily, he had been playing on the computer until late and decided to sleep here instead of going back to his apartment in the 'Young Generation' neighborhood," she said. "His neighbors were murdered."
Her former partner, Yaron, tried to reach Kfar Aza. On the way, he evacuated wounded people and the bodies of partygoers who had fled the Nova festival. He later entered the kibbutz and fought terrorists in the "Young Generation" neighborhood. He was shot twice in the chest and critically wounded.
During those hours, Einat and her son were in the safe room. Terrorists took positions on the roof of her home and a gunbattle later erupted. The terrorists were killed, but Einat and her son were not evacuated until nighttime.
"I remember walking toward the entrance to the kibbutz. We called it the 'death march.' We walked on foot and crouched down because we were afraid of gunfire. There were bodies of terrorists along the way. From there, they took us to the gas station at the entrance."
In Shefayim, the family gradually began to understand the scale of the disaster — who had been killed, who had been abducted and who had survived.
Einat stayed there for a year, then moved to Ruhama. But for her, the question of whether she would return to Kfar Aza was never really open. The only question was when.
When she decided to take over the kindergarten, she realized she could not do it from Ruhama. "I told myself I wasn't going to live in Ruhama and run the kindergarten here. I need to live here and set an example."
But returning has not been easy. Her neighbors have not returned, and many of them lost loved ones. "I still don't walk around the kibbutz. I drive from home to the kindergarten and back. It's still hard for me to walk around," she said.
"When a few more people return, it will be easier. For now, the children and the work fill me up. It's simply happiness. I'm tired from the work, but they fill me up. That's what occupies me and helps me, because I'm busy with good, positive things."
When she sees children heading to kindergarten and walking along the kibbutz paths, she sees something larger than the start of another school year.
"People are moved to tears seeing the kindergarten operating, seeing children on the paths after three years. To me, the children coming to kindergarten are the revival. They are the foundation of the kibbutz."
Moran, the kibbutz chairwoman, said of the reopening of the kindergarten and daycare center: "It's not a rational step because most of the community is still in Ruhama, but it creates movement in the kibbutz and it's symbolic."
'The dream is on hold — but home is home'
Sharona Kessler, 60, and her husband Alon arrived in Kfar Aza in 2020. During the massacre, they were in Haifa, but their daughter and two grandchildren were in the kibbutz, in the heart of an area where heavy fighting took place.
From afar, she tried to understand what was happening and help her family while Alon, an IDF colonel, was called up for reserve duty.
"It was an insane feeling of helplessness." The family moved from place to place. First they evacuated themselves to Shoham, then to Shefayim, Tzukey Arsuf and Rishpon.
Four different apartments, with a family of 10 trying each time to turn a temporary place into a home. "We moved around as a tribe. Good people opened their hearts to us," she said.
But at some point even the best hospitality could not replace the feeling of home. "We were tired of another temporary house. We wanted to take responsibility for our lives and decided we were going back to Kfar Aza."
In October 2024, while most of the community moved to Ruhama, Sharona and Alon returned to Kfar Aza. They knew they would be almost alone, that they were pioneers. They knew the place was still far from ready.
Even so, they chose to return. "We fully accepted that we'd be pretty much alone here. We understood that this was what the moment required," Kessler said. "We told our daughters, 'We're part of the community' — active, involved grandparents."
Sharona, an interior designer by profession, did not only return to live in Kfar Aza. She is also working on its rehabilitation.
The kibbutz workshop she operated during the evacuation moved with her from Shefayim to Ruhama. Later, she began helping with renovation and planning projects, and today she works on the rehabilitation and infrastructure team.
Among other things, she is involved in renovating the building for veteran members, known as "the Vatican," and developing a building that will become a welfare and treatment center for the community.
"For me, it meant getting under the stretcher and working for the community. Nothing feels normal, but because both Alon and I are part of the rehabilitation and the team working here to bring the kibbutz back to what it was and make it even better, it's actually very rewarding to live here too.
"Every little patch of grass that's planted, every path that's poured — I see it and I'm part of it. We're walking through powdery dirt and dust, but we can see the progress."
She knows some people prefer to return only when everything is ready. To her, that is also a legitimate choice. "It's important to me that people take a deep breath and feel: Here I am, I'm home."
Her and Alon's dream was to live in Kfar Aza as an extended family, with their children and grandchildren around them. For now, that dream remains distant.
One daughter will return, but another, whose children experienced October 7 in the kibbutz, still cannot bring herself to come back.
"Right now that dream is on hold, or maybe it won't happen at all. We'll continue to be involved grandparents even if they don't live nearby."
'We just need quiet in Gaza — everything depends on that'
As noted, the return to Kfar Aza is unfolding alongside a debate over what the kibbutz should look like after the disaster. For now, the kibbutz has decided not to take any irreversible steps regarding the "Young Generation" neighborhood.
"Until the High Court ruling, we're not touching anything and we're not doing anything irreversible. We didn't receive an injunction or anything like that, but we decided to respect the process. We're planning, but for now we're waiting patiently for final decisions," community manager Regev said.
Outside the kibbutz, construction of a visitors center is moving ahead, while tours for the general public inside the kibbutz have already been canceled. The sense of security is still far from taken for granted.
Kites that recently crossed in from the Gaza Strip and were found in the border communities caused anxiety among residents.
The community is working with an expert to rebuild its emergency system and operational procedures for the local emergency response team.
Soldiers stationed in the area give some residents a sense of security, but the larger question remains unresolved: Will it be possible to live here again without the constant fear that history could repeat itself?
"We have no control over the security situation," Moran said. "A return to the border conditions that existed before October 7, Hamas rebuilding its strength — these are things that influence people's decisions about whether to return."
Regev, the community manager, is optimistic. "I see the future kibbutz as a large community. We were 950 people, but obviously we're not starting again from the same point. There are people who were murdered, there are people who won't return, but the young people's neighborhood will be full and the kindergartens will be full. "We just need quiet in Gaza. Everything depends on that."
Moran wants to highlight the community's demand that the state provide solutions for those who are unable to return to the kibbutz. "We are working to ensure that the state fulfills its duty to those who still don't know how to return, and we need to help those who have to rebuild their lives."
With elections approaching, Kfar Aza residents say they hope for change. Nadav said he "hopes things will be better." Viki said change is essential.
Sharona wants leadership that will see the residents of the Gaza border communities and restore their trust.
Einat, who prefers not to discuss politics, put it simply: "Anyone who was here on October 7 needs to hand over the keys and go home. That's how we'll regain our trust."
Kfar Aza is still far from what it once was. There are homes that will no longer stand, families that will not return, memories that will not disappear and questions with no answers.
But after nearly three years in which home existed mainly as a memory, the sounds of life are beginning to be heard there again.

Kinmen uses spray drones to control fire ant population

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Kinmen's Animal and Plant Disease Control Center said Friday that spray drones are reducing fire ants in the region.
Fire ants are said to have migrated to Taiwan in freight containers. They have been sighted feeding on crops in regions like Taoyuan and Chiayi, causing huge economic losses for decades.
The center sprays bait over fire ant mounds two to four times a year. It has accelerated the effort by flying more drones this year.
The center conducted drone sprays at Lieyu Township in May and has since expanded to Jinning in June and Jinsha in September. Spraying is typically scheduled after dawn, at temperatures between 21 and 38 C on sunny days, as ants dislike wet bait.
The center said spraying does have its limits. It said that patrolling populated areas is what's leading to fewer fire ants. It said that the county still needs to coordinate district offices for frequent patrols at busy venues like Otter Park.
Director Fan Te-cheng (樊德正) said the initiative began in 2024, when the Ministry of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Agency and National Fire Ant Prevention Center met with Kinmen officials to discuss drone deployment.
Fan said that with agency support, trial runs saw immediate effect, as drones can reach areas inaccessible to field agents, with precise and controlled spraying at predetermined locations. He said the entire county has adopted the tactical measure ever since.
Fan said Kinmen also encourages residents to actively participate. He noted the center has invited experts such as Prevention Center Chief Lai Hung-kuan (賴鴻寬) for seminars and hands-on training.
Regarding wildlife conservation, Kinmen’s two artificial wetlands were invaded by fire ants, which drove away the sea otters there. The county said outdoor cameras spotted otters returning after six months of spraying in cooperation with conservation groups.
Fan said the plan was proven effective as the otters gradually returned in droves. He said the measure extended to the county itself, prioritizing more populous settlements.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Coast Guard vessels will fire Hsiung Feng-series anti-ship missiles during a joint precision munitions exercise next week to test their ability to rapidly convert from peacetime law enforcement ships into wartime combat platforms.
The exercise will test a capability already demonstrated during the Han Kuang military exercises in August, when an Anping-class patrol ship underwent the conversion after arriving at a naval port, per Liberty Times. The process, from installing missile launchers to having a Navy weapons team board and deploy from port, can be completed within several hours, according to military sources.
Vessels from this class can be configured to carry up to 16 subsonic Hsiung Feng II or supersonic Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missiles, giving Taiwan an additional mobile coastal strike capability. The capability is intended to strengthen the military's deterrence and flexibility in littoral operations.
The vessels were built with space reserved on the aft deck for missile launchers, Liberty Times reported. Removable protective panels cover the area during peacetime, allowing the vessels to operate without missiles.
When a wartime conversion order is issued, a Coast Guard vessel can sail to a designated naval port, where personnel remove the protective panels and use heavy-duty cranes to install preassembled missile launcher modules. The launchers are secured to reserved mounts, and their signal cables are connected to interfaces built into the vessel.
Instead of replacing crews, the conversion lets the Coast Guard keep operating the ship while the Navy handles the missiles, according to Liberty Times. The Navy sends a weapons team of about four to six personnel, including a fire-control officer, operators, and communications specialists, to operate the missile-control system and receive target coordinates from military command networks.

What runs out on 15 September
The deadline falls on 15 September. ====================================================================================================

3D-printed food: from niche technology to a potential future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:02:21 UTC
19:02:21 KST

3D printers can now transform more than two dozen types of food into edible shapes. While the technology remains costly and impractical for everyday use, experts see significant potential in clinics, care homes and personalised nutrition.
3D printers have long since moved beyond producing plastic parts. Increasingly, they are also being used to print food: instead of plastic filament, the machines extrude soft ingredients such as chocolate, cheese or plant-based meat alternatives through a nozzle, building them up layer by layer. The desired shape must first be designed on a computer.
Several manufacturers are already established in the market, including the Ukrainian-Bulgarian company Chocola3D, the Spanish provider Natural Machines and the German firm Print2Taste. So far, the technology has mainly been used in niche applications, from patisseries to hospitals, while a breakthrough into everyday life has yet to materialise.
Printer can process more than 26 materials
According to the manufacturer, Chocola3D has been in development since 2014, with the company itself founded a few years later. The company says customers are now using the device in Ukraine, Bulgaria, Germany and Estonia. Users fill refillable syringes with pastes such as chocolate, cheese, meat, vegetables or pea protein. In total, the system is said to work with more than 26 different materials.
Unlike devices that use closed capsule systems, the Chocola3D does not tie users to specific refills. However, users have to determine the appropriate printing settings themselves. Depending on the manufacturer, food printers can cost anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand euros.
The shape of the food is designed digitally
Food technologist Mario Jekle from the University of Hohenheim is researching the technology independently of individual manufacturers. The individual steps are familiar from any kitchen, he explains in an interview with Euronews: “We first produce a fine paste, for example. This paste is then shaped, which is exactly what you do at home with a piping bag when making fine pastries. Then everything is heated, just as it would be at home in an oven or a pan.”
What is new above all, he says, is the digital preparation: “Bringing everything together, and above all the digital design.” The shape of the final product must first be created digitally.
Confectioners are already using the technology to make marzipan figures for wedding cakes. According to Jekle, its potential lies above all in customised products or small production runs of up to around 200 items. The bigger challenge comes after printing: the material has to be deposited in liquid form but must then become firm enough to be eaten with a knife and fork. This can be achieved by heating it in an oven or in a heated printing chamber.
Printing a plant-based steak at home could take just 15 minutes
Jekle also describes what using a food printer in everyday life could look like. Someone wanting to print a plant-based steak alternative would simply send the design to the printer, with the process taking between five and 15 minutes. The digital templates could come “either from databases, from an app, or from the specifications of the cartridge.”
For Jekle, the key advantage lies in the precise control of ingredients through a kind of modular building-block system. A printed meat alternative could, for example, have a significantly higher fibre content “than conventional meat, which contains no dietary fibre in the first place”.
He estimates that widespread household use is still at least five to ten years away, and there is currently no supply chain for refill packs. Jekle also believes it is important to use raw materials that require as little processing as possible. His team works, for example, with by-products from the food and agricultural industries – residual streams that are generated as part of conventional production – and uses 3D printing to turn them into new foods.
The less a raw material needs to be processed beforehand, the less energy is required – a benefit, Jekle says, for both the environment and consumers’ budgets.
Applications in medicine and care
The technology is most advanced in areas where small quantities need to be dosed precisely. As reported by the German newspaper Tagesspiegel, a team at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf is testing raspberry-flavoured chewable tablets in the shape of hearts and stars, designed to make it easier for children with cancer to take their medication during chemotherapy. Many children struggle with the taste or size of conventional tablets, says senior physician Beate Winkler. The hospital is also conducting trials of individually dosed medication for patients with Parkinson’s disease.
3D-printed food could also help older people who have difficulty chewing or swallowing. Nutrition scientist Dorothee Volkert from Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg investigated whether 3D printing could restore familiar shapes to puréed food – for example, creating a sausage-shaped dish that retains the appearance of the original despite its puréed consistency. The response was positive, and participants also consumed more energy and protein than before, as additional protein and fat can be incorporated into the food.
Meat from the 3D printer: many consumers remain sceptical
A representative Bitkom survey (source in German) of 1,004 people aged 16 and over, conducted in 2025, shows how open people in Germany are to the idea of printed food.
At present, 24 percent of people in Germany can imagine eating cultivated meat produced using a 3D printer, up from 13 percent six years ago. Cultivated meat is grown from animal cells in a bioreactor and given a meat-like structure using the printer.
Openness is greatest among younger people: around one third of those aged 16 to 49 would consider eating it, compared with 18 percent of 50- to 64-year-olds and 14 percent of those aged 65 and over.
Margareta Maier from Bitkom explains: “The process makes it possible to give products an appearance and texture similar to conventional meat, while having a significantly smaller ecological footprint.”
Price remains an obstacle: only 7 percent would be willing to pay more for 3D-printed meat than for conventional meat, and 17 percent regard it generally as a luxury product. Maier attributes this to the high purchase costs and the specialised ingredients: “That is why these products are not yet suitable for the mass market and are currently used mainly in catering and the food industry.”
How advanced is the technology?
Researcher Mario Jekle stresses that 3D-printed food is not intended to replace conventional food production: “We have no vision of replacing half of food production with this in the future. That is a utopia – and a misguided one at that.”
He sees the technology as particularly useful for people who do not have time to cook and for groups with specific nutritional needs, such as patients in hospitals or residents of care homes: “In effect, it gives us a way of producing food specifically for these smaller, clearly defined groups, containing exactly what they need.”
Another advantage, according to Jekle, is the potential to reduce food waste, as portions could be tailored more precisely to individual needs. A plant-based salmon alternative made using a 3D printer is already available in a major supermarket chain.
However, it will still be some time before food printers become common household appliances. As with 3D-printed houses, the technology is already viable for specific applications, but there is still a long way to go before it becomes part of everyday life.
